## Abhidhammapiṭake
## Atthasālinī nāma
## Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā
## Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
## Ganthārambhakathā
Just as the Great Compassion of the Great Sage, who seeks the noble aggregate of virtue and so forth, occurred towards all beings according to His wish, so too did His Wisdom occur towards all knowable things (ñeyyadhamma) according to His wish.

With a heart well-urged by that Great Compassion for beings, dwelling in the abode of the Thirty-three (Tidasa) at the end of the Twin Miracle.

Seated gracefully on the stone seat named Paṇḍukambala at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree, like the sun on Mount Yugandhara.

Surrounded by the host of gods who had come together from the ten thousand world-systems from all directions, placing His mother at the head, He set in motion the course of the Abhidhamma discourse for the gods by the power of His wisdom that is capable of knowing such knowable things.

Having paid homage to the feet of that glorious Buddha, having honored His Sublime Dhamma, and having made a gesture of salutation (añjali) to the Saṅgha.

By the power of this act of humility and homage performed towards the Triple Gem, having completely cleared away all obstacles.

Requested respectfully by the monk named Cūḷabuddhaghosa, who possesses pure conduct and virtue, and subtle, stainless wisdom, (I) ... Brahma, human

9. The Buddha, the God of gods, the Guide of those to be tamed, having taught that Abhidhamma in detail to the gods, then taught it in brief to the Elder Sāriputta by way of method.

10. That Elder Sāriputta, having performed his duties to the Great Sage at Lake Anotatta and having heard that Abhidhamma Dhamma, brought it to the surface of the earth, Jambudīpa.

11. That Elder taught it to the monks. Thus, the monks preserved the Abhidhamma in the order taught by Sāriputta. That same Abhidhamma was again recited at the time of the First Council by Vedehamuni (Venerable Ānanda).

12. I shall explain the meaning of that Abhidhamma, which is entered into repeatedly by those of profound wisdom and is variegated with various methods, from the beginning.

13. In the past, the Arahats who possessed the five masteries (vasī), such as Venerable Mahākassapa and others, recited the commentary. Later, Arahats such as Venerable Yasa and Venerable Moggaliputtatissa recited that same commentary again.

14. That most excellent commentary, which was recited in three councils, was brought to the island of Sīhaḷa by the Elder Mahinda. For the sake of the island dwellers, it was composed in the Sīhaḷa language.

15. Having removed that Sīhaḷa language, I shall present it in the stainless Magadhi language which follows the method of the Pāḷi texts.

16. Without mixing it with the views of other sects and without confusion, illustrating the decisions of the Great Elders dwelling in the Mahāvihāra.

17. Taking what should be taken from the Sutta commentaries and pleasing the wise, I shall explain the meaning.

18. Since all meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) along with temperaments (cariya), direct knowledge (abhiññā), and insight (vipassanā) have been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga,

19. Therefore, without taking those things here again, I shall perform the explanation of the meaning according to the sequence of words in the Pāḷi text itself.

20. While I am speaking this Abhidhamma discourse, listen with undistracted minds. For this discourse is difficult to hear.
3:
## Nidānakathā

In that context, for what reason is it called "Abhidhamma"? It is called "Abhidhamma" because of its sense of being a Dhamma that is extraordinary (atireka) and distinguished (visesa). Here, the word "Abhi" indicates the meaning of being extraordinary and distinguished. As in the sentences: "My painful feelings greatly increase (abhikkamanti), they do not decrease," and "A deity of surpassing (abhikkanta) beauty." Therefore, just as among many well-planted umbrellas and banners, that umbrella which is extraordinary in size and distinguished in color and shape is called an "Atichatta" (extraordinary umbrella); and that banner which is extraordinary in size and endowed with a distinguished color dyed with various hues is called an "Atidhaja" (extraordinary banner); and just as among many princes and gods assembled together, that prince who is most extraordinary and most distinguished by such accomplishments as birth, wealth, retinue, fame, and power is called an "Atirājakumāra" (extraordinary prince); and that god who is most extraordinary and most distinguished by such accomplishments as lifespan, beauty, power, retinue, and fame is called an "Atideva" (extraordinary god); and a Brahma of such nature is also called an "Atibrahma" (extraordinary Brahma); in the same way, this Dhamma is called "Abhidhamma" because of its sense of being a Dhamma that is extraordinary and distinguished beyond the Sutta teachings.

In the Suttas, the five aggregates are analyzed only partially (ekadesena), not exhaustively (nippadesena). But in the Abhidhamma, they are analyzed exhaustively by way of the Suttanta-bhājanīya, Abhidhamma-bhājanīya, and Pañhapucchaka methods. Similarly, the twelve bases, eighteen elements, four truths, twenty-two faculties, and the twelve-linked dependent origination are analyzed. However, in the Indriya-vibhaṅga, there is no Suttanta-bhājanīya; and in the Paccayākāra (Dependent Origination) vibhaṅga, there is no Pañhapucchaka. In the Suttas, the four foundations of mindfulness are analyzed only partially, not exhaustively. But in the Abhidhamma, they are analyzed exhaustively by way of all three methods. Similarly, the four right efforts, four bases of power, seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, four jhānas, four immeasurables, five precepts, and four analytical insights are analyzed. However, among these, in the Sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga, there is no Suttanta-bhājanīya. In the Suttas, knowledge is analyzed only partially, not exhaustively. Similarly, the defilements are analyzed. But in the Abhidhamma, having set down the matrix (mātikā) by the method of "The ground of knowledge in one way" and so forth...
4:
It is analyzed only in an exhaustive manner (without remainder). Likewise, the defilements are analyzed through many methods starting from the 'dyads' (ekaka). Upon reaching the Suttanta, the distinction of the planes of existence is analyzed only partially, not exhaustively. However, upon reaching the Abhidhamma, the distinction of the planes of existence is analyzed exhaustively through the power of the three methods. Thus, it should be known as 'Abhidhamma' because of its meaning as a special Dhamma that excels and surpasses the [other] Dhammas.

In terms of the division of books, this Abhidhamma consists of seven books: Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Vibhaṅga, Dhātukathā, Puggalapaññatti, Kathāvatthu, Yamaka, and Paṭṭhāna. This is the common view of the teachers regarding the division of books. However, a Vitandavādī (sophist) says: 'Why is the Kathāvatthu included? Was it not established by the Elder Moggaliputtatissa more than two hundred and eighteen (218) years after the Great Parinibbāna of the Buddha? Therefore, since it is a book spoken by a disciple, you should discard it.' When asked, 'Then is the Abhidhamma only six books?', he replies, 'I do not say so.' When asked, 'Then what do you say?', he replies, 'It is indeed seven books.' When asked, 'Which book do you take to make it seven?', he replies, 'There is a book named Mahādammahadaya; including that book, there are seven.' When it is said, 'In the Mahādammahadaya, there is no new discourse, only a few question-sections (pucchāvāra) remain; it is seven only with the Kathāvatthu,' he then says, 'Not with the Kathāvatthu, but there is a book named Mahādhātukathā; including that book, there are seven.' It is then replied, 'In the Mahādhātukathā as well, there is no new discourse, only a small amount of Pali remains. It is seven only with the Kathāvatthu.'

In truth, while the Buddha was teaching the seven books, upon reaching the Kathāvatthu, he established the Matrix (Mātikā) in the Discourse on the Person (Puggalavāra). He began with the logic of the views (vādayuttī) consisting of eight positions through the power of two pentads in the first four questions, and set the Matrix in Pali with the extent of an incomplete recitation-section (bhāṇavāra) throughout all the paths of discourse. That Matrix is as follows: 'Is the person perceived in the sense of a real and ultimate fact?' 'Yes.' 'Is that person perceived in the sense of a real and ultimate fact from that which is a real and ultimate fact?' 'One should not say so.' 'Acknowledge the refutation (niggaha)... [pe]... Is the person not perceived in the sense of a real and ultimate fact?' 'Yes, he is not perceived.' 'Is that person not perceived in the sense of a real and ultimate fact from that which is a real and ultimate fact?' 'One should not say so.' 'Acknowledge the refutation... [pe]... Is the person perceived in all places, is the person not perceived in all places, is the person perceived at all times, is the person not perceived at all times, is the person perceived in all [aggregates, bases, and elements], is the person not perceived in all [aggregates, bases, and elements], in the sense of a real and ultimate fact?' Thus, the first discourse...
5: The Teacher laid down the Mātikā, intending to show the first refutation based on the first discourse, the second refutation based on the second discourse... etc... and the eighth refutation based on the eighth discourse. In this manner, the laying down of the Mātikā in all sections should be understood. The Blessed One, while laying down that Mātikā, did so having foreseen this: 'Two hundred and eighteen years after my Parinibbāna, a monk named Moggaliputtatissa Thera, sitting in the midst of a thousand monks, will analyze and teach the Kathāvatthu, which is the size of the Dīgha Nikāya, by combining a thousand suttas—five hundred suttas in the Sakavāda (own-view) and five hundred in the Paravāda (other-view).' Elder Moggaliputtatissa also, when teaching this book, did not teach it by inventing it through his own wisdom, but taught it only by the Mātikā established according to the method given by the Blessed One. Thus, because it was taught by the Mātikā established according to the method given by the Blessed One, this entire book is truly the Word of the Buddha (Buddhabhāsita). How is this so? It is like the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta and others. In the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta, the Blessed One laid down the Mātikā: 'Bhikkhus, owing to whatever cause the perceptions and notions of mental proliferation (papañca-saññā-saṅkhā) beset a man; if there is nothing there to delight in, to welcome, or to remain fastened to, then this is the end of the underlying tendencies (anusaya) of lust, etc.,' and then he rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. The monks who received the teaching approached the Elder Mahākaccāna and asked for the meaning of the Mātikā laid down by the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala). The Elder did not explain it immediately upon being asked, but to show respect to the One of Ten Powers, he brought forth the simile of the heartwood tree, saying: 'Friends, just as a man in need of heartwood, seeking heartwood...' and said, 'The Blessed One is like a great heartwood tree, and the disciples are like the branches and leaves.' He praised the Teacher, saying: 'Friends, that Blessed One knows what is to be known, sees what is to be seen; he has become the Eye, become Knowledge, become the Dhamma, become the Brahma; he is the speaker, the proclaimer, the bringer of meaning, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of the Dhamma; such is the Tathāgata, endowed with such qualities.' Then, being entreated by the monks repeatedly, he analyzed and taught the meaning of the Mātikā laid down by the Teacher, and then dismissed them, saying: 'Venerable sirs, if you wish, approach the Blessed One himself and ask this meaning again. If it agrees and coincides with his Omniscient Wisdom, then accept it; if not, do not accept it,' with the intention: 'Whatever the Blessed One explains to you, so should you remember it.'
6:
Those monks approached the Teacher and asked him. The Teacher, without saying "Kaccāna has spoken poorly," raised his neck as if setting up a small golden drum, and filling his noble mouth which possessed the splendor of a well-blossomed lotus, he emitted a Brahma-voice endowed with the eight qualities, giving the Elder his approval by saying, "Sādhu, Sādhu!" He then said, "Monks, Mahākaccāna is wise. Monks, Mahākaccāna is of great wisdom. Monks, if you were to ask me the meaning of this matter again, I would explain it in the same way as it was explained by Mahākaccāna" (M. Ni. 1.205).

From the time the Teacher gave this approval, that entire sutta became known as the Word of the Buddha (Buddhabhāsita). The same principle applies to the suttas expanded upon by the Elder Ānanda and others. In the same manner, while the Fully Enlightened Buddha was teaching the seven books of Abhidhamma, when he reached the Kathāvatthu, he laid down the Mātikā (Matrix) according to the method already mentioned. While laying it down, he foresaw this: "Two hundred and eighteen years after my Parinibbāna, a monk named Moggaliputtatissa Thera, sitting in the midst of a thousand monks, will combine five hundred suttas from his own doctrine and five hundred suttas from other doctrines, and will divide the Kathāvatthu treatise, which is equal in size to the Dīgha Nikāya."

When Moggaliputtatissa Thera taught this treatise, he did not teach it by his own wisdom alone; he taught it using the Mātikā laid down by the method given by the Teacher. Because it was taught using the Mātikā laid down by the method given by the Teacher, this entire treatise also became the Word of the Buddha (Buddhabhāsita). Thus, the seven treatises together with the Kathāvatthu are called the Abhidhamma.

Among those seven treatises of Abhidhamma, in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī treatise, there are four divisions: Cittavibhatti, Rūpavibhatti, Nikkheparāsi, and Atthuddhāra. Among these four, the division that analyzes the eighty-nine (89) types of consciousness—8 from sense-sphere wholesome, 12 from unwholesome, 16 from wholesome resultant, 7 from unwholesome resultant, 11 from functional; 5 from fine-material sphere wholesome, 5 from resultant, 5 from functional; 4 from immaterial sphere wholesome, 4 from resultant, 4 from functional; 4 from supramundane wholesome, and 4 from resultant—is called Cittavibhatti. The name Cittuppādakaṇḍa is also a name for that same Cittavibhatti. In terms of the sequence of recitation, it consists of more than six bhāṇavāras; however, if taught in detail, it is endless and immeasurable.
7:
Immediately following that Cittuppādakaṇḍa is the Rūpavibhatti, which is shown by laying down the Mātikā through methods such as singlefold, twofold, and so on, and analyzing it in detail. The name Rūpakaṇḍa is also a name for that same Rūpavibhatti. In terms of the sequence of recitation, it consists of more than two bhāṇavāras. However, the word taught in detail is endless and immeasurable.

Immediately following that Rūpakaṇḍa is the collection of Dhamma taught by laying them down through categories such as roots, aggregates, doors, planes, meanings (consequences), dhammas (texts/nature), names, and genders; this is called Nikkheparāsi. Regarding that Nikkheparāsi—

Because it is taught by laying down [the Dhamma]
By way of roots, and also by way of aggregates,
By way of doors, and also by way of planes,
By way of meanings, by way of dhammas,
By way of names, and also by way of genders,
It is specifically called Nikkheparāsi.

The name Nikkhepakaṇḍa is also a name for that same Nikkheparāsi. In terms of the sequence of recitation, it has the extent of three bhāṇavāras. However, the word taught in detail is endless and immeasurable.

Immediately following that Nikkhepakaṇḍa is the division called Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa, which extracts the meaning of the Word of the Buddha known as the Tipitaka, and is laid down as far as the Sarana-duka. It is from this Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa that monks who study the Great Treatise (Paṭṭhāna), when unable to keep track of the enumerations in the Great Treatise, harmonize the enumerations (or carry them well). In terms of the sequence of recitation, that Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa has the extent of two bhāṇavāras. However, the word taught in detail is endless and immeasurable.

Thus, the entire Dhammasaṅgaṇī treatise consists of more than thirteen bhāṇavāras in terms of the sequence of recitation. However, the word taught in detail is endless and immeasurable. Thus—

Cittavibhatti, Rūpavibhatti, Nikkheparāsi,
And the Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa which illuminates the meaning—
This profound and subtle subject was also taught by the Buddha.

Immediately following the teaching of the Dhammasaṅgaṇī treatise is the treatise called Vibhaṅgapppakaraṇa (Vibhaṅga). That Vibhaṅga is divided into eighteen parts: Khandha-vibhaṅga, Āyatana-vibhaṅga, Dhātu-vibhaṅga, Sacca-vibhaṅga, Indriya-vibhaṅga, Paccayākāra-vibhaṅga, Satipaṭṭhāna-vibhaṅga, Sammappadhāna-vibhaṅga, Iddhipāda-vibhaṅga, Bojjhaṅga-vibhaṅga, Maggaṅga-vibhaṅga, Jhāna-vibhaṅga, Appamaññā-vibhaṅga, Sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga, Paṭisambhidā-vibhaṅga, Ñāṇa-vibhaṅga, Khuddakavatthu-vibhaṅga, and Dhammahadaya-vibhaṅga.
8:
Among those eighteen Vibhaṅgas, the Khandhavibhaṅga is divided into three parts: Suttantabhājanīya, Abhidhammabhājanīya, and Pañhapucchaka. In terms of recitation (vācanāmagga), this Khandhavibhaṅga consists of about five bhāṇavāras; however, when expanded in detail, it is endless and immeasurable. After that, the Āyatanavibhaṅga and others are also divided by these same three methods. Among those Vibhaṅgas, the Āyatanavibhaṅga exceeds one bhāṇavāra in recitation; the Dhātuvibhaṅga consists of about two bhāṇavāras. The Saccavibhaṅga is the same. In the Indriyavibhaṅga, there is no Suttantabhājanīya; in terms of recitation, this Indriyavibhaṅga just slightly exceeds one bhāṇavāra. The Paccayākāravibhaṅga consists of about six bhāṇavāras; in this Vibhaṅga, there is no Pañhapucchaka. The Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga just slightly exceeds one bhāṇavāra; likewise, the Sammappadhāna, Iddhipāda, Bojjhaṅga, and Maggaṅga Vibhaṅgas (also just slightly exceed one bhāṇavāra). The Jhānavibhaṅga consists of about two bhāṇavāras, and the Appamaññāvibhaṅga just slightly exceeds one bhāṇavāra. In the Sikkhāpadavibhaṅga, there is no Suttantabhājanīya; in terms of recitation, this Sikkhāpadavibhaṅga just slightly exceeds one bhāṇavāra, and the Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅga is the same. The Ñāṇavibhaṅga is divided into ten parts; in terms of recitation, this Ñāṇavibhaṅga consists of about three bhāṇavāras. The Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga is also divided into ten parts; in terms of recitation, this Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga consists of about three bhāṇavāras. The Dhammahadayavibhaṅga is divided into three parts; in terms of recitation, this Dhammahadayavibhaṅga just slightly exceeds two bhāṇavāras. When all these Vibhaṅgas are expanded in detail, they are endless and immeasurable. Thus, this Vibhaṅgapakaraṇa consists of about thirty-five bhāṇavāras in recitation, but in detail, it is endless and immeasurable.

Immediately following that Vibhaṅga is the treatise named Dhātukathāpakaraṇa. That treatise is divided into fourteen parts: Saṅgaha, Asaṅgaha, Saṅgahitena Asaṅgahita, Asaṅgahitena Saṅgahita, Saṅgahitena Saṅgahita, Asaṅgahitena Asaṅgahita, Sampayoga, Vippayoga, Sampayuttena Vippayutta, Vippayuttena Sampayutta, Sampayuttena Sampayutta, Vippayuttena Vippayutta, Saṅgahitena Sampayutta Vippayutta, Sampayuttena Saṅgahita Asaṅgahita, Asaṅgahitena Sampayutta Vippayutta, and Vippayuttena Saṅgahita Asaṅgahita. In terms of recitation, it just slightly exceeds six bhāṇavāras, but when expanded in detail, it is endless and immeasurable.

Immediately following that Dhātukathā is the treatise named Puggalapaññatti. That treatise is divided into six parts: Khandhapaññatti, Āyatanapaññatti, Dhātupaññatti, Saccapaññatti, Indriyapaññatti, and Puggalapaññatti. In terms of recitation, it exceeds five bhāṇavāras, but when expanded in detail, it is indeed endless and immeasurable.
9:
Immediately following that (Puggalapaññatti) is the treatise named Kathāvatthu. That treatise is analyzed by combining one thousand suttas: five hundred suttas of one's own doctrine and five hundred suttas of others' doctrines. In terms of the order of recitation, not taking the text currently written on palm leaves but according to the method established at the Councils, it is equal in volume to the Dīgha Nikāya; however, in detail, it is endless and immeasurable.

Immediately following that (Kathāvatthu) is the treatise named Yamaka. That treatise is analyzed into ten parts: Mūlayamaka, Khandhayamaka, Āyatanayamaka, Dhātuyamaka, Saccayamaka, Saṅkhārayamaka, Anusayayamaka, Cittayamaka, Dhammayamaka, and Indriyayamaka. In terms of the order of recitation, it consists of one hundred and twenty bhāṇavāras; however, in detail, it is endless and immeasurable.

Immediately following that (Yamaka) is the treatise named Mahāpakaraṇa. The name Paṭṭhāna is also the name of that same Mahāpakaraṇa. That treatise is first analyzed into twenty-four parts by way of conditions: Hetu-paccaya, Ārammaṇa-paccaya, Adhipati-paccaya, Anantara-paccaya, Samanantara-paccaya, Sahajāta-paccaya, Aññamañña-paccaya, Nissaya-paccaya, Upanissaya-paccaya, Purejāta-paccaya, Pacchājāta-paccaya, Āsevana-paccaya, Kamma-paccaya, Vipāka-paccaya, Āhāra-paccaya, Indriya-paccaya, Jhāna-paccaya, Magga-paccaya, Sampayutta-paccaya, Vippayutta-paccaya, Atthi-paccaya, Natthi-paccaya, Vigata-paccaya, and Avigata-paccaya.

In this context, the Paṭṭhāna should be properly maintained. The twenty-two triplets beginning with the Kusala-tika are called 'Tikas'. These couplets such as 'HETŪ DHAMMĀ NAHETŪ DHAMMĀ ... SARAṆĀ DHAMMĀ ARAṆĀ DHAMMĀ' are called the one hundred 'Dukas'. Other couplets such as 'VIJJĀBHĀGĪ DHAMMĀ AVIJJĀBHĀGĪ DHAMMĀ ... KHAYE ÑĀṆAṀ ANUPPĀDE ÑĀṆAṀ' are the forty-two 'Suttantika-dukas'. Among these Tikas and Dukas, this Mātikā consisting of the twenty-two Tikas and one hundred Dukas is called the Mātikā of the seven treatises, which was taught by the Omniscient Buddha, being the words of the Buddha, spoken by the Exalted One by touching the vocal organs.

If that is so, from where did the other forty-two Suttantika-dukas originate? Who established them? Who taught them? They originated from the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta; they were established by him; they were taught by him. However, in establishing these couplets, the Elder did not establish them through his own knowledge produced independently. Rather, he established them by collecting them from the Ekakanipāta, Dukanipāta, Saṅgīti Sutta, and Dasuttara Sutta of the Ekuttara Nikāya, so that the monks studying Abhidhamma would not be exhausted. Those (Tikas and Dukas) are only in one Nikkhepakaṇḍa...
10:
These triads (tikas) and dyads (dukas) are analyzed and brought to completion in the Nikkhepa-kaṇḍa (Summary Section) alone. In the remaining parts of the Abhidhamma discourse apart from the Nikkhepa-kaṇḍa, the Abhidhamma is analyzed only up to the Saraṇa-duka.

Indeed, in the Anuloma-paṭṭhāna (Positive Patthana), the Blessed One taught the Tika-paṭṭhāna based on the twenty-two triads. He taught the Duka-paṭṭhāna based on the one hundred dyads. After that Duka-paṭṭhāna, He showed the Duka-tika-paṭṭhāna by taking the twenty-two triads and inserting them into the one hundred dyads. After that, He showed the Tika-duka-paṭṭhāna by taking the one hundred dyads and inserting them into the twenty-two triads. He showed the Tika-tika-paṭṭhāna by inserting triads into triads alone. He also showed the Duka-duka-paṭṭhāna by inserting dyads into dyads alone. Thus:

The noble Tika-paṭṭhāna and the eminent Duka-paṭṭhāna,
The Duka-tika-paṭṭhāna and the Tika-duka-paṭṭhāna,
The Tika-tika-paṭṭhāna and the Duka-duka-paṭṭhāna—
These six methods in the Anuloma are extremely profound.

In the Paccaṇīya-paṭṭhāna (Negative Patthana) as well, the Tika-paṭṭhāna is shown based on the twenty-two triads. The Duka-paṭṭhāna is shown based on the one hundred dyads. The Duka-tika-paṭṭhāna is shown by inserting the twenty-two triads into the one hundred dyads. The Tika-duka-paṭṭhāna is shown by inserting the one hundred dyads into the twenty-two triads. The Tika-tika-paṭṭhāna is shown by inserting triads into triads alone. The Duka-duka-paṭṭhāna is shown by inserting dyads into dyads alone. Thus, in the Paccaṇīya as well, the Paṭṭhāna is shown by way of six methods. Therefore:

The noble Tika-paṭṭhāna and the eminent Duka-paṭṭhāna,
The Duka-tika-paṭṭhāna and the Tika-duka-paṭṭhāna,
The Tika-tika-paṭṭhāna and the Duka-duka-paṭṭhāna—
These six methods in the Paccaṇīya are extremely profound.

After that, in the Anuloma-paccaṇīya (Positive-Negative) as well, He showed the six methods by this very same means. Therefore:

The noble Tika-paṭṭhāna and the eminent Duka-paṭṭhāna,
The Duka-tika-paṭṭhāna and the Tika-duka-paṭṭhāna,
The Tika-tika-paṭṭhāna and the Duka-duka-paṭṭhāna—
These six methods in the Anuloma-paccaṇīya are extremely profound.
11:
Furthermore, in the Paccaṇīya-anuloma (Negative-Positive) as well, it is explained by these very same six methods. Therefore, the Commentator said:

"The noble Tika-paṭṭhāna and the supreme Duka-paṭṭhāna,
The Duka-tika-paṭṭhāna and the Tika-duka-paṭṭhāna,
The Tika-tika-paṭṭhāna and the Duka-duka-paṭṭhāna—
In the Paccaṇīya-anuloma, there are six extremely profound methods."

Thus, there are 6 types of Paṭṭhāna in the Anuloma, 6 in the Paṭiloma (Paccaṇīya), 6 in the Anuloma-paccaṇīya, and 6 in the Paccaṇīya-anuloma. This collection of twenty-four Samanta-paṭṭhāna texts is called the Mahāpakaraṇa (The Great Book).

Now, in order to make known the profundity of this Abhidhamma Dhamma, the four oceans should be understood: Saṃsāra-sāgara (the ocean of saṃsāra), Jala-sāgara (the ocean of water), Naya-sāgara (the ocean of methods), and Ñāṇa-sāgara (the ocean of knowledge). Among these four, the Saṃsāra-sāgara is as follows:

"The uninterruptedly occurring succession
Of the aggregates, elements, and bases
Is called Saṃsāra."

This refers to the round of saṃsāra (saṃsāra-vaṭṭa). This round of saṃsāra is such that the prior limit (the beginning) of the arising of these beings cannot be known. There is no such delimitation as: "Beings arose above this many hundreds, thousands, or hundreds of thousands of years, or above hundreds, thousands, or hundreds of thousands of aeons (kappas), and they did not exist before that"; or "They arose in the time of such-and-such a king, or they arose in the time of such-and-such a Buddha, and they did not exist before that." By this method of teaching—"Bhikkhus, the prior limit of ignorance (avijjā) is not evident; before this time ignorance did not exist, it only arose later"—the ocean of saṃsāra is indeed without discoverable beginning (anamatagga).

The great ocean, however, should be known as the Jala-sāgara (the ocean of water). That ocean is eighty-four thousand yojanas deep. In that ocean, the name for comparing the quantity of water by hundreds of āḷhakas, thousands of āḷhakas, or hundreds of thousands of āḷhakas...
12:
There is no such thing as a comparison for the quantity of water. Indeed, it is reckoned only as an incalculable and immeasurable great mass of water. This is called the Jalasāgara (the ocean of water). What is the Nayasāgara (the ocean of methods)? It is the Word of the Buddha, the Tipitaka. For sons of good family who are endowed with faith, full of devotion, and possessed of superior wisdom, an infinite joy and gladness arise when they reflect upon the two traditions of the Pali Canon. What are the two? They are the Vinaya and the Abhidhamma. 

When monks versed in the Vinaya reflect on the Vinaya Pali, they consider the laying down of training rules according to the offense—that when this fault or this transgression occurs, it becomes such-and-such an offense—and they realize: "This laying down of training rules is not the domain of others; it is the domain of the Buddhas alone." Infinite joy and gladness also arise in those who reflect on the Uttari-manussadhamma-peyyāla, the Nīla-peyyāla, and the Sañcaritta-peyyāla. 

Likewise, for monks versed in the Abhidhamma, as they reflect on the various aggregates, the various bases, the various elements, the various faculties, the various powers, the factors of enlightenment, the results of kamma, and the subtle and profound Dhamma that is the discernment of mind and matter, infinite joy and gladness arise as they reflect on the Abhidhamma Pali, thinking: "Our Teacher has indeed shown the analysis of mental and material phenomena by dividing them into parts and portions, like one grasping the stars in the sky."

In this regard, the following story should be understood concerning the arising of such joy: It is said that the Elder Mahāgatigamiya Tissadatta, while traveling to the other shore by ship to worship the Great Bodhi Tree, sat on the upper deck and looked out at the great ocean. At that time, neither the other shore nor this shore was visible; only the great ocean appeared, pervaded by the spray of water rising from the force of the waves, resembling a spread of jasmine flowers on a silver plate. The Elder thought: "Is the force of the waves of the great ocean more powerful, or is the method of the Samantapaṭṭhāna (the Book of Relations) with its twenty-four divisions more powerful?" Then, the limitation of the great ocean became apparent to him: "This ocean is bounded below by the great earth, above by the sky, on one side by the Cakkavāḷa mountains, and on the other side by the shore." But as he reflected on the subtle and profound Dhamma, the limitation of the Samantapaṭṭhāna did not appear to him, and powerful joy arose. Suppressing that joy and developing insight, he exhausted all defilements while sitting in that very position and, established in the highest fruit of Arahatship, he uttered this inspired utterance:

"That disciple of the Buddha who, through penetrative knowledge, sees the Samantapaṭṭhāna—consisting of twenty-four treatises, deep in nature, extremely difficult to understand, which the Great Sage taught in its entirety and in due order, having realized it himself with his own higher knowledge along with its causes—just as one sees a physical object in one's hand, such a disciple indeed exists in this Dispensation."
13:
"That disciple of the Buddha who, through penetrative knowledge, sees the Samantapaṭṭhāna—deep in nature, extremely difficult to understand, which the Great Sage taught in its entirety and in due order, having realized it himself with his own higher knowledge along with its causes—just as one sees a physical object in one's hand, such a disciple indeed exists in this Dispensation."

This is called the Nayasāgara (the ocean of methods). What is the Ñāṇasāgara (the ocean of knowledge)? Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) is called the Ñāṇasāgara. Because it is impossible to know by any other knowledge that "this is the Saṃsārasāgara (the ocean of saṃsāra), this is the Jalasāgara (the ocean of water), and this is the Nayasāgara," but it is possible to know only through Omniscient Knowledge, therefore Omniscient Knowledge is called the Ñāṇasāgara. Among these four oceans, the Nayasāgara is intended in this context. Indeed, only the Omniscient Buddhas first penetrate this Nayasāgara.

Our Blessed One, while dwelling at the foot of the Bodhi tree, reflected on the Dhamma he had penetrated, thinking: "Having penetrated this Nayasāgara—while I was searching and seeking for this Dhamma, four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons passed; now, as I sit upon this throne, having exhausted the one thousand five hundred defilements, this Dhamma has been penetrated by me." Thus, reflecting on the Dhamma he had penetrated, he sat for seven days in a single cross-legged posture. Thereafter, rising from that throne, he stood for seven days gazing at the throne with unblinking eyes, thinking: "Upon this throne, Omniscient Knowledge was penetrated by me."

Then, a thought arose in the minds of the deities: "Even today, it seems there is still something to be done by Prince Siddhattha; for he does not yet give up his attachment to the throne." The Teacher, knowing the thoughts of the deities, immediately ascended into the air to calm their thoughts and displayed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya). The miracle performed at the throne of the Great Bodhi, the miracle performed at the assembly of his kinsmen, and the miracle performed at the assembly of the Pāṭiyaputta ascetics—all were just like the Twin Miracle performed at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba mango tree. Having thus performed the Twin Miracle, he descended from the sky and walked in meditation for seven days between the throne and the place where he had stood. During these twenty-one days, not a single ray of light yet issued from the Teacher's body.

In the fourth week, however, he sat in the Ratanaghara (the House of Gems) in the northwest direction. The Ratanaghara does not refer only to a house made of the seven precious gems, but rather to the seven treatises of the Abhidhamma...
14:
The place of contemplation should be known as the Ratanaghara (Jewel House). Even while contemplating the Dhammasaṅgaṇī in that Ratanaghara, the rays did not yet emit from the Buddha's body. Even while contemplating the Vibhaṅga, Dhātukathā, Puggalapaññatti, Kathāvatthu, and Yamaka, the rays did not yet emit from His body. However, when He descended into the Mahāpakaraṇa (the Paṭṭhāna) and began the contemplation: "Hetupaccayo, ārammaṇapaccayo ... avigatapaccayo," the Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññutañāṇa) of the Buddha, who was contemplating the Paṭṭhāna endowed with the twenty-four conditions, truly found its scope only in the Mahāpakaraṇa.

Just as the great fish named Timira and Tipingala find their scope only in the great ocean, which is eighty-four thousand yojanas deep, so too did the Omniscient Knowledge truly find its scope only in the Mahāpakaraṇa.

From the body of the Blessed One, who was contemplating the subtle and profound Dhamma as He pleased with the Omniscient Knowledge that had thus found its scope, the six-colored rays—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and brilliant—emerged. Blue rays emitted from His hair and beard, as well as from the blue portions of His eyes. By the power of those blue rays, the sky became as if strewn with collyrium powder, as if covered with blue pea flowers and blue lotus petals, like ruby fans being waved, and like a spread-out blue cloth.

Yellow rays emitted from His skin and from the yellow portions of His eyes. By the power of those yellow rays, the quarters of the world shone as if being sprinkled with streams of liquid gold, as if a golden canopy were spread out, and as if pervaded with kunkuma powder and kaṇikāra flowers.

Red rays emitted from His flesh and blood, as well as from the red portions of His eyes. By the power of those red rays, the quarters of the world shone as if dyed with vermilion powder, as if being sprinkled with well-boiled lac, as if wrapped in red blankets, and as if pervaded with jayasumana, pāribhaddaka, and bandhujīvaka flowers.

White rays emitted from His bones and teeth, as well as from the white portions of His eyes. By the power of those white rays, the quarters of the world shone as if pervaded with streams of milk poured from silver pots, like spread-out silver canopies, like silver fans being waved, and as if covered with flowers such as jasmine, white water lilies, sinduvāra, sumana, and mallikā.
15:
Crimson and brilliant rays also emerged from various parts of His body. Thus, these six-colored rays emerged and pervaded the massive earth.

The great earth, two hundred and forty thousand yojanas thick, became like a mass of pure gold free from impurities. Then, piercing through the earth, they pervaded the body of water below. The body of water supporting the earth, four hundred and eighty thousand yojanas thick, became like molten gold poured from golden pots. Piercing through the water, they pervaded the body of air. The body of air, nine hundred and sixty thousand yojanas thick, became like a great golden pillar set upright. Piercing through the air, they rushed into the unobstructed open space below.

Ascending upwards, they also pervaded the Cātumahārājikā deva realms. Piercing through those realms, they reached Tāvatiṃsa, then Yāma, then Tusita, then Nimmānarati, then Paranimmitavasavatti, then the nine Brahma worlds, then the Vehapphala realm, and piercing through the five Suddhāvāsa realms, they pervaded the four Āruppa realms. Piercing through the four Āruppa realms, they rushed into the unobstructed open space.

In the transverse directions, they rushed into infinite world systems. In all these places, there was no moonlight in the moon, no sunlight in the sun, and no starlight in the stars. In the gardens, mansions, and wish-fulfilling trees of the devas, as well as in their bodies and ornaments—in all places, there was no radiance. Even a Mahābrahmā, who is capable of pervading a hundred thousand crores of world systems with his light, became like a firefly when the sun rises. Only the outlines of the moon, sun, stars, deva gardens, mansions, and wish-fulfilling trees remained visible. All these regions were pervaded only by the Buddha's rays.

This power was neither the psychic power of determination (adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi) of the Buddhas, nor was it psychic power born of meditation (bhāvanāmaya-iddhi). Rather, as the Lord of the World (Lokanātha) contemplated the subtle and delicate Dhamma, His heart-blood became clear, His heart-base matter (hadayavatthu-rūpa) became clear, and His skin-complexion became clear. The color-element (vaṇṇadhātu) produced by the mind remained steady in the surrounding area of about eighty cubits. In this manner, He contemplated for seven days.

How vast was the Dhamma contemplated for seven days and nights? It was infinite and immeasurable. This is known as the 'teaching by mind' (manasā-desanā). When the Teacher, having thus reflected on the Dhamma with His mind for seven days, began to teach it by breaking into speech...
16:
It should not be said that it is impossible to finish preaching even in a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand years. Indeed, at a later time, the Tathāgata, seated on the Paṇḍukambala stone at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, amidst the deities of the ten thousand world-systems, making his mother (who had become a deva) the primary witness, preached the Dhamma: 'Wholesome states (kusala dhammā), unwholesome states (akusala dhammā), and indeterminate states (abyākata dhammā).' Moving from one point of Dhamma to another by hundredths, thousandths, and hundred-thousandths, he preached. That teaching, which proceeded continuously for three months, was like a waterfall flowing with great speed, or like a stream of water pouring from an overturned water-pot, becoming infinite and immeasurable.

Even when the Buddhas give a brief blessing (anumodanā) after a meal, if they expand it slightly, that teaching is equivalent in volume to the Dīgha Nikāya or Majjhima Nikāya. When preaching to an assembly that has gathered after a meal, the teaching is equivalent to the two great collections, the Saṃyutta Nikāya and Aṅguttara Nikāya. Why? Because for the Buddhas, the transition of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is swift, the lips are well-aligned, the opening of the mouth is precise, the tongue is soft, the voice is sweet, and the speech turns quickly. Therefore, even the Dhamma preached in that brief moment is of such magnitude. But the Dhamma preached for three months is truly infinite and immeasurable.

The Elder Ānanda, who was of great learning and a bearer of the Tipiṭaka, could learn, recite, or teach fifteen thousand verses and sixty thousand words while standing, as if pulling a flowering creeper. This amount was just one of the Elder's methods of recitation. No one other than the Fully Enlightened One could keep up with or match the Elder in providing the word-for-word recitation. Only the Fully Enlightened One could match him. Even a disciple endowed with such supreme mindfulness, intelligence, and energy, though learning for a hundred or a thousand years, would not be able to reach the end of the teaching preached by the Teacher in this manner for three months.

How did the physical body (upādinnaka-sarīra) of the Tathāgata, which is dependent on nutriment (kabaḷīkārāhāra), endure while he was preaching continuously for three months? It endured through care and maintenance. For the Buddhas, each specific time is well-determined, well-defined, and clearly perceived. Therefore, while preaching the Dhamma, the Blessed One looked at the time in the human world. At that time...
17:
Noting the time for the alms-round, the Buddha created a 'Created Buddha' (Nimmitabuddha) and resolved: 'Let the manner of holding the robe, the manner of holding the bowl, the tone of voice, and the deportment of this Created Buddha be like this; let him preach this much Dhamma.' Then, taking his bowl and robe, he went to Lake Anotatta. Deities offered him tooth-sticks made of nāgalatā. Having used the tooth-stick and cleansed his body at Lake Anotatta, he stood on the Manosilā plateau, donned his well-dyed double-layered undergarment, wrapped himself in his upper robe, and taking the dark stone bowl offered by the Four Great Kings, he went to Uttarakuru. Having brought alms-food from there, he sat on the shore of Lake Anotatta and partook of the meal. Then, he went to the Sandalwood Forest (Candanavana) for the day-abiding.

The Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, also went there, performed the duties for the Fully Enlightened One, and sat to one side. Then the Teacher gave him the 'method' (naya). He said, 'Sāriputta, this much Dhamma has been preached by me.' When the Fully Enlightened One gave the method in this way to the Chief Disciple who had attained the Analytical Knowledges (paṭisambhidā), it was like pointing out the ocean by standing on the shore and stretching out a hand. To the Elder, the Dhamma preached by the Blessed One became clear through hundreds, thousands, and hundreds of thousands of methods.

At what time does the Teacher, after sitting for the day-abiding, go to preach the Dhamma? There is a time for preaching to the sons of good family residing in Sāvatthī who have arrived; he goes at that time. Who knows and who does not know when he is going to preach or returning? The great deities (mahesakkha) know, but the lesser deities (appesakkha) do not know. Why do they not know? Because there is no difference in the radiance and so on between the Fully Enlightened One and the Created Buddha. Indeed, there is no difference in the radiance, the voice, or the speech of both.

The Elder Sāriputta also brought the Dhamma as it was preached by the Teacher and taught it to his five hundred resident pupils. This was their previous connection: It is said that in the time of the Buddha Kassapa, they were born as small bats. While hanging in a mountain cave, they heard two monks who were experts in Abhidhamma reciting the Abhidhamma. Although they did not know the dark side or the light side (wholesome or unwholesome), by merely taking the sound as an object, they passed away and were reborn in the celestial world. After living in the celestial world for the interval between two Buddhas, they were reborn in the human world at this time. Having gained faith in the Twin Miracle (yamaka-pāṭihāriya), they went forth as monks in the presence of the Elder. The Elder brought the Dhamma as it was preached by the Teacher and taught it to those monks. Of the Fully Enlightened One...
18:
The conclusion of the Blessed One's Abhidhamma teaching and the completion of the learning of the seven books of the Abhidhamma by those monks occurred simultaneously.

In the Abhidhamma, the lineage of oral instruction (vācanāmagga) originated from the Elder Sāriputta. In the Great Treatise (Mahāpakaraṇa), the method of enumeration (gaṇanacāra) was also established by the Elder. This is because the Elder established the method of enumeration so that one could easily learn, bear in mind, study, and teach the different categories of Dhamma without confusion by this method. If so, was the Elder the first expert in Abhidhamma (Ābhidhammika)? No, he was not. The Fully Enlightened One alone was the first expert in Abhidhamma. That Blessed One, while sitting upon the seat of the Great Enlightenment (Mahābodhi), penetrated and realized that Abhidhamma. After attaining Buddhahood, while sitting for seven days in a single cross-legged posture, he uttered this inspired utterance (Udāna):

“When indeed phenomena become manifest
To the ardent, meditating brahmin,
Then all his doubts vanish,
Since he understands a phenomenon together with its cause.

“When indeed phenomena become manifest
To the ardent, meditating brahmin,
Then all his doubts vanish,
Since he has understood the destruction of conditions (Nibbāna).

“When indeed phenomena become manifest
To the ardent, meditating brahmin,
He stands routing the army of Māra,
As the sun stands illuminating the sky.”

This is known as the First Words of the Buddha. However, the reciters of the Dhammapada say:

“Through many a birth in saṃsāra have I wandered, seeking but not finding the builder of this house; painful is birth again and again.

“O house-builder, you are seen! You shall not build the house again. All your rafters are broken, the ridge-pole is shattered. My mind has attained the unconditioned (Nibbāna); it has reached the end of craving.”

Saying thus, they consider this to be the First Words of the Buddha.
19:
The words spoken while reclining between the twin Sāla trees at the time of his Parinibbāna: “Behold now, bhikkhus, I exhort you: All conditioned things are subject to decay; strive on with diligence” are known as the Last Words of the Buddha (Pacchimabuddhavacana).

The Sublime Dhamma that reveals the Deathless, taught during the forty-five years between these two (the first and the last), like stringing a garland of flowers or threading a string of jewels, is known as the Middle Words of the Buddha (Majjhimabuddhavacana).

When all these words of the Buddha are collected together, by way of Piṭaka, there are three Piṭakas; by way of Nikāya, five Nikāyas; by way of Anga, nine Angas; and by way of Dhamma-units (dhammakkhandha), eighty-four thousand Dhamma-units. How? All these words of the Buddha, by way of Piṭaka, have a threefold division: Vinaya Piṭaka, Suttanta Piṭaka, and Abhidhamma Piṭaka. Among them, the two Pātimokkhas (of Bhikkhus and Bhikkhunīs), the two Vibhaṅgas, the twenty-two Khandhakas, and the sixteen Parivāras—this is called the Vinaya Piṭaka. The Dīgha Nikāya, which is a collection of thirty-four suttas beginning with the Brahmajāla Sutta; the Majjhima Nikāya, which is a collection of one hundred and fifty-two suttas beginning with the Mūlapariyāya Sutta; the Saṃyutta Nikāya, which is a collection of seven thousand seven hundred and sixty-two suttas beginning with the Oghataraṇa Sutta; the Aṅguttara Nikāya, which is a collection of nine thousand five hundred and fifty-seven suttas beginning with the Cittapariyādāna Sutta; and the Khuddaka Nikāya, which has fifteen divisions by way of Khuddakapāṭha, Dhammapada, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Suttanipāta, Vimānavatthu, Petavatthu, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, Jātaka, Niddesa, Paṭisambhidā, Apadāna, Buddhavaṃsa, and Cariyāpiṭaka—this is called the Suttanta Piṭaka. The seven treatises beginning with the Dhammasaṅgaṇī are called the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. Therein:

Because it contains various and special methods, and because it disciplines body and speech,
This [teaching] is called 'Vinaya' by those who know the meaning of Vinaya.

In this Vinaya, there are various methods such as the fivefold recitation of the Pātimokkha, the seven groups of offenses beginning with Pārājika, the Mātikā, and the Vibhaṅga; these methods are special supplementary regulations (anupaññatti) that serve the purpose of strengthening or relaxing [the original rules]. This Vinaya disciplines the body and speech by prohibiting transgressions of body and speech. Therefore, because of its various methods, special methods, and its disciplining of body and speech, it is called 'Vinaya'. Thus, it is said as follows to provide skill in the meaning of the word 'Vinaya':
20:
“Because it contains various methods and special methods, and because it disciplines body and speech, those who know the meaning of Vinaya call this Vinaya 'Vinaya'."

As for the Sutta, other than the Vinaya, it is called 'Sutta' because it indicates meanings, is well-spoken, produces benefits, yields benefits, protects well, and is like a carpenter's thread.

Indeed, that Sutta indicates meanings divided into one's own benefit, the benefit of others, and so forth. The meanings in this Sutta are said to be well-spoken because they are taught in accordance with the inclinations of those to be guided (veneyya). Just as a crop produces fruit, so this Sutta produces benefits. Just as a cow yields milk, so this Sutta yields benefits. It also protects those benefits well. Furthermore, this Sutta is like a carpenter's thread. Just as a thread is a standard for carpenters, so this Sutta is a standard for the wise. Just as flowers strung together with a thread are not scattered or destroyed, so the meanings gathered by this Sutta are not scattered or destroyed. Therefore, for the sake of skill in the word-meaning of 'Sutta':
“Because it indicates meanings, is well-spoken, produces benefits, yields benefits, protects well, and is like a carpenter's thread, it is called Sutta.”

The word-meaning of Abhidhamma has already been stated. Alternatively:
Because in this Abhidhamma, dhammas that are increasing, possessed of their own characteristics, revered, distinguished, and excellent are taught, it is called 'Abhidhamma'.

This prefix 'abhi' is found in the senses of increase, characteristic, reverence, distinction, and excellence. Indeed, in such passages as "My painful feelings increase (abhikkamanti), they do not decrease," it occurs in the sense of increase. In passages such as "Those nights which are well-known (abhiññātā) and marked (abhilakkhitā)," it occurs in the sense of characteristic. In passages such as "The king of kings (rājābhirājā), the lord of men," it occurs in the sense of reverence. In passages such as "He is able to guide in Abhidhamma and Abhivinaya," it occurs in the sense of dhammas and vinaya that are distinguished and free from mutual confusion. In passages such as "With surpassing (abhikkantena) beauty," it occurs in the sense of excellence.
21:
In this Abhidhamma, dhammas that are increasing (vuḍḍhimanta) are taught in such ways as: "He develops the path for rebirth in the fine-material sphere, and dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness." Dhammas possessed of their own characteristics (salakkhaṇa) are taught in such ways as: "Whether it is a visible-form object or a sound object," because they are characterized by their objects and so forth. Revered dhammas (pūjita), meaning those worthy of reverence, are taught in such ways as: "Dhammas of those in training (sekkhā), dhammas of those beyond training (asekkhā), and supramundane (lokuttara) dhammas." Distinguished dhammas (paricchinna) are taught in such ways as: "Contact (phassa) occurs, feeling (vedanā) occurs," because they are distinguished by their own natures. Excellent dhammas (adhika) are taught in such ways as: "Great dhammas (mahaggatā), immeasurable dhammas (appamāṇā), and unsurpassed (anuttarā) dhammas." Therefore, for the sake of skill in the word-meaning of 'Abhidhamma', it is said:

"Because in this Abhidhamma, dhammas that are increasing, possessed of their own characteristics, revered, distinguished, and excellent are taught, it is called Abhidhamma."

As for the word 'Piṭaka', which is common to this (and the Vinaya and Sutta):

Those who know the meaning of Piṭaka say it is 'Piṭaka' because of the meanings of learning (pariyatti) and vessel (bhājana);
By combining it with that word, the three—Vinaya and so forth—should be understood.

Indeed, learning (pariyatti) is called 'Piṭaka' in such Pali passages as "Do not go by the authority of the Piṭaka (mā piṭakasampadānena)." Any kind of vessel is also called 'Piṭaka' in such Pali passages as "Then a man might come taking a hoe and a basket (kudālapiṭaka)." Therefore, those who know the meaning of Piṭaka say it is 'Piṭaka' because of the meanings of learning and vessel.

Now, how the three Piṭakas—Vinaya and so forth—should be understood in combination with the word 'Piṭaka': By forming a compound with the word 'Piṭaka' which has these two meanings, it is 'Vinaya Piṭaka' because it is both Vinaya and Piṭaka in the sense of learning and being a vessel for various meanings. In the same manner, it is 'Suttanta Piṭaka' because it is both Sutta and Piṭaka. It is 'Abhidhamma Piṭaka' because it is both Abhidhamma and Piṭaka. Thus, the three Piṭakas—Vinaya and so forth—should be understood.

Having understood this, for the sake of further skill in the various aspects of these Piṭakas:

One should clearly explain the distinctions of teaching (desanā), instruction (sāsanā), and discourse (kathā) in those Piṭakas,
As well as the training (sikkhā), abandonment (pahāna), and profundity (gambhīra) as appropriate.

One should also explain all the ways in which a monk attains the distinctions of learning (pariyatti), success (sampatti), and failure (vipatti) in whichever Piṭaka.
22:
In these three Piṭakas, there are such clarifications and expositions. These three Piṭakas are called, in order, the Teaching of Authority (āṇādesanā), the Teaching of Conventional Language (vohāradesanā), and the Teaching of Ultimate Reality (paramatthadesanā); the Instruction according to Offenses (yathāparādhasāsana), the Instruction according to Disposition (yathānulomasāsana), and the Instruction according to the Dhamma (yathādhammasāsana); and the Discourse on Restraint and Non-restraint (saṃvarāsaṃvarakathā), the Discourse on the Unravelling of Views (diṭṭhiviniveṭhanakathā), and the Discourse on the Delimitation of Mind and Matter (nāmarūpaparicchedakathā).

Among these three Piṭakas, the Vinaya Piṭaka is called the "Teaching of Authority" (āṇādesanā) because it was taught primarily through authority by the Blessed One, who is worthy of exercising authority. The Suttanta Piṭaka is called the "Teaching of Conventional Language" (vohāradesanā) because it was taught primarily through conventional language by the Blessed One, who is skilled in conventional language. The Abhidhamma Piṭaka is called the "Teaching of Ultimate Reality" (paramatthadesanā) because it was taught primarily through ultimate reality by the Blessed One, who is skilled in ultimate reality.

Likewise, the first, the Vinaya Piṭaka, is called the "Instruction according to Offenses" (yathāparādhasāsana) because in it, beings who have many offenses are disciplined according to their offenses. The second, the Suttanta Piṭaka, is called the "Instruction according to Disposition" (yathānulomasāsana) because in it, beings with various inclinations, latent tendencies, temperaments, and intentions are disciplined according to their disposition. The third, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, is called the "Instruction according to the Dhamma" (yathādhammasāsana) because in it, beings who perceive "I" and "mine" in what is merely a collection of ultimate phenomena are disciplined according to the nature of things (dhamma).

Likewise, the first, the Vinaya Piṭaka, is called the "Discourse on Restraint and Non-restraint" (saṃvarāsaṃvarakathā) because in it, restraint and non-restraint, both minor and major, which are the opposites of bodily and verbal transgression, are taught. "Restraint and non-restraint" refers to both minor and major restraint, just as there are minor and major actions (kammākamma) or minor and major fruits (phalāphala). The second, the Suttanta Piṭaka, is called the "Discourse on the Unravelling of Views" (diṭṭhiviniveṭhanakathā) because in it, the unravelling of the knot of wrong views, which is the opposite of the sixty-two types of wrong views, is taught. The third, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, is called the "Discourse on the Delimitation of Mind and Matter" (nāmarūpaparicchedakathā) because in it, the delimitation of mind and matter, which is the opposite of lust and so forth, is taught.

In these three Piṭakas, the three trainings (sikkhā), the three kinds of abandoning (pahāna), and the fourfold depth (gambhīrabhāva) should be understood. Specifically, in the Vinaya Piṭaka, the training in higher virtue (adhisīlasikkhā) is taught; in the Suttanta Piṭaka, the training in higher mind (adhicittasikkhā) is taught; and in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññāsikkhā) is taught.

In the Vinaya Piṭaka, the abandoning of transgression (vītikkamappahāna) is taught because virtue (sīla) is the opposite of the transgression (vītikkama) of defilements. In the Suttanta Piṭaka, the abandoning of obsession (pariyuṭṭhānappahāna) is taught because concentration (samādhi) is the opposite of the obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna) of defilements. In the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, the abandoning of latent tendencies (anusayappahāna) is taught because wisdom (paññā) is the opposite of the latent tendencies (anusaya) of defilements.
23:
In the first, the Vinaya Piṭaka, the abandoning of defilements by substitution of opposites (tadaṅgappahāna) is taught. In the other two, the Suttanta and Abhidhamma Piṭakas, abandoning by suppression (vikkhambhanappahāna) and abandoning by eradication (samucchedappahāna) are taught. Furthermore, in the first Piṭaka, the abandoning of the defilement of misconduct (duccarita-saṃkilesa) is taught, while in the other Piṭakas, the abandoning of the defilements of craving (taṇhā) and views (diṭṭhi) is taught.

In each of these three Piṭakas, the fourfold depth (gambhīrabhāva) consisting of dhamma, attha, desanā, and paṭivedha should be understood. Therein, 'dhamma' refers to the Pali text (tanti). 'Attha' refers to the meaning of that very text. 'Desanā' refers to the oral teaching of that text as determined by the mind. 'Paṭivedha' refers to the penetration and understanding of the text and its meaning as they really are. These four—dhamma, attha, desanā, and paṭivedha—are profound because they are difficult to enter and offer no footing for those of dull wisdom, just as the great ocean is difficult to enter and offers no footing for small animals like hares. Thus, in each of these Piṭakas, the fourfold depth should be understood.

Alternatively: 'Dhamma' refers to the cause (hetu). For it has been said: "Knowledge of the cause is the discrimination of the Dhamma (dhammapaṭisambhidā)." 'Attha' refers to the result of the cause (hetuphala). For it has been said: "Knowledge of the result of the cause is the discrimination of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā)." 'Desanā' refers to designation (paññatti); it means teaching in accordance with the Dhamma, or teaching by way of direct and reverse order, brevity and detail, and so forth. 'Paṭivedha' refers to realization (abhisamaya). That realization is both mundane and supramundane. It is the understanding of causes in accordance with their results, of results in accordance with their causes, and of designations in accordance with the path of designation, both by way of object and by way of non-delusion. Or, it is the non-perverted nature, known as the individual characteristic (salakkhaṇa), of the various dhammas taught in those Piṭakas, which is to be penetrated.

Now, in these three Piṭakas, there is the cause (dhammajāta) or the result (atthajāta) that is to be made known. There is the teaching (desanā) that illuminates that meaning so that it becomes clear to the knowledge of the listeners. There is also the penetration (paṭivedha) known as non-perverted understanding, which is the non-perverted nature known as the individual characteristic of those various dhammas to be penetrated. All these four things combined are profound because they are difficult to enter and offer no footing for those of little wisdom who have not accumulated the requisites of merit, just as the great ocean is for hares. In this way too, the fourfold depth in each of these Piṭakas should be understood. By this much, the meaning of the verse:

"One should explain the distinctions of teaching (desanā), instruction (sāsana), and discourse (kathā) in them as appropriate, as well as the training (sikkhā), abandoning (pahāna), and depth (gambhīrabhāva),"

has been explained.
24:
The monk reaches which division of learning (pariyatti), which success (sampatti), and which failure (vipatti) in which place; all that I shall explain. In this regard, the threefold division of learning in the three Piṭakas should be understood. Indeed, there are three types of learning: the simile of the snake (alagaddūpamā), for the sake of deliverance (nissaraṇattha), and the treasurer-like (bhaṇḍāgārika).

Among these three, that learning which is wrongly grasped and studied for the sake of criticizing others and so forth is called the simile of the snake. With reference to such wrong learning, it was said: 'Monks, for example, a man wanting a snake, seeking a snake, wandering in search of a snake, might see a large snake. He might seize that snake by its coils or by its tail. That snake, having turned back, might bite that man on his hand, his arm, or any other limb or part of his body. On account of that, that man would meet death or deadly suffering. For what reason? Because, monks, the snake was wrongly grasped. In the same way, monks, here some worthless men (mogha-purisa) learn the Dhamma—the Sutta... (pe)... the Vedalla. Having learned that Dhamma, they do not examine the meaning of those teachings with wisdom. Because they do not examine the meaning with wisdom, those teachings do not withstand their reflection. They learn the Dhamma for the sake of the advantage of criticizing others and for the sake of the advantage of releasing themselves from accusations. They do not experience the benefit for the sake of which they learn the Dhamma. Those teachings, being wrongly grasped, lead to their harm and suffering for a long time. For what reason? Because, monks, the teachings were wrongly grasped.' (M. Ni. 1.238).

However, that learning which is rightly grasped and studied by one who desires only the fulfillment of the groups of virtue (sīla) and so forth, and not for the sake of criticizing others and so forth, is called 'for the sake of deliverance'. With reference to such right learning, it was said: 'Those teachings, being rightly grasped, lead to their benefit and happiness for a long time. For what reason? Because, monks, the teachings were rightly grasped.' (M. Ni. 1.239).

Furthermore, that learning which an Arahant—one who has fully understood the aggregates (khandha), abandoned the defilements (kilesa), developed the path (magga), penetrated the Dhamma, realized cessation (nirodha), and is free from taints (khīṇāsava)—studies solely for the sake of preserving the tradition of the Dispensation and for the sake of protecting the lineage, is called 'treasurer-like learning'.

A monk who practices well in the Vinaya, depending on the perfection of virtue, attains the three knowledges (tisso vijjā), because the divisions of those three knowledges are taught in that Vinaya Piṭaka. A monk who practices well in the Sutta, depending on the perfection of concentration (samādhi), attains the six higher knowledges (chaḷabhiññā), because the divisions of those six higher knowledges are taught in that Sutta Piṭaka. A monk who practices well in the Abhidhamma, depending on the perfection of wisdom (paññā), attains the four...
25:
...analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), because the divisions of those analytical knowledges are taught in that very Abhidhamma Piṭaka. Thus, one who practices well in these three Piṭakas attains this success (sampatti) consisting of the divisions of the three knowledges, the six higher knowledges, and the four analytical knowledges in due order.

However, one who practices wrongly in the Vinaya Piṭaka, because of the similarity of touch with the permitted comfortable rugs and robes, etc., perceives no fault in the forbidden touch of women and so forth. Thus it was said: 'I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in such a way that those things called obstacles by the Blessed One are not actually obstacles for one who indulges in them' (said by the monk Ariṭṭha). Because of such perception of faultlessness, he reaches the state of immorality (dussīlabhāva).

One who practices wrongly in the Sutta Piṭaka, not knowing the intention of the Blessed One in such passages as 'Monks, there are these four persons existing in the world', etc., grasps a wrong view. With reference to such grasping of wrong view, it was said: 'By his own wrong grasp, he misrepresents us, digs himself up, and produces much demerit.' Because of such grasping of wrong view, he reaches the state of wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi).

One who practices wrongly in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, by over-reaching in the contemplation of the nature of things (dhamma), thinks about even the unthinkable (acinteyya). Because of such thinking, he reaches mental distraction (cittakkhepa). Thus it was said: 'Monks, there are these four unthinkables; they should not be thought about. One who thinks about them would experience madness and frustration.' Thus, one who practices wrongly in these three Piṭakas reaches this failure (vipatti) consisting of the divisions of immorality, wrong view, and mental distraction in due order.

By this sequence of words—
The divisions of learning (pariyatti),
And the success and failure which a monk reaches in which place,
All that has been clearly explained.

This verse also has the meaning already stated. Thus, having known the Piṭakas through their various divisions, when all these words of the Buddha are collected by means of those Piṭakas, they constitute the three Piṭakas.

How are there five Nikāyas by way of collection? All these words of the Buddha are indeed of five divisions: Dīgha Nikāya, Majjhima Nikāya, Saṃyutta Nikāya, Aṅguttara Nikāya, and Khuddaka Nikāya. Among those five, what is the Dīgha Nikāya? It consists of the thirty-four suttas, such as the Brahmajāla Sutta, collected into three groups (vagga).

There are exactly thirty-four suttas,
Collected into three groups (vagga),
That collection, which has a name consistent with its meaning,
Should be known as the first, the Dīgha Nikāya.
26:
Why is this collection called the Dīgha Nikāya? It is called the Dīgha Nikāya because it is a collection and a dwelling place of suttas of long length. Indeed, a collection and a dwelling place are called a 'Nikāya'. 'Monks, I do not see any other single collection so diverse as these animals; the collection of the Poṇika, the collection of the Cikkhallika'—such words from the Dispensation (Sāsana) and worldly usage are evidence for this term 'Nikāya' meaning a collection or dwelling place. Just as the meaning of the word 'Nikāya' is understood for the Dīgha Nikāya, so should it be understood for the remaining Nikāyas.

What is the Majjhima Nikāya? The one hundred and fifty-two suttas, such as the Mūlapariyāya Sutta, which are of medium length and are comprised of fifteen vaggas (chapters), are called the Majjhima Nikāya.

That collection in which there are
One hundred and fifty suttas
And two additional suttas,
Comprised of fifteen vaggas,
Is known as the Majjhima Nikāya.

What is the Saṃyutta Nikāya? The seven thousand seven hundred and sixty-two suttas, such as the Oghataraṇa Sutta, which are arranged by way of the Devatā Saṃyutta and so forth, are called the Saṃyutta Nikāya.

There are seven thousand suttas,
And seven hundred suttas,
And sixty-two suttas;
This is the collection of the Saṃyutta.

What is the Aṅguttara Nikāya? The nine thousand five hundred and fifty-seven suttas, such as the Cittapariyādāna Sutta, which are arranged by way of increasing one factor at a time, are called the Aṅguttara Nikāya.

There are nine thousand suttas,
And five hundred suttas,
And fifty-seven suttas;
This is the count in the Aṅguttara.

What is the Khuddaka Nikāya? The entire Vinaya Piṭaka, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, and the fifteen divisions of texts mentioned previously such as the Khuddakapāṭha and Dhammapada, and all the remaining Buddha-word excluding the four great Nikāyas, are called the Khuddaka Nikāya.

Excluding these four Nikāyas
Beginning with the Dīgha,
The rest of the Buddha-word
Is known as the Khuddaka Nikāya.

Thus, by way of Nikāya, there are five Nikāyas.
27:
How are there nine limbs (aṅgas) by way of limbs? All this Buddha-word is of nine divisions: Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla.

Among these nine, the Ubhatovibhaṅga, Niddesa, Khandhaka, and Parivāra; the Maṅgala Sutta, Ratana Sutta, Nālaka Sutta, and Tuvaṭṭaka Sutta in the Suttanipāta; and any other words of the Tathāgata bearing the name 'Sutta' should be known as Sutta. All suttas containing verses should be known as Geyya. Specifically, the entire Sagāthāvagga in the Saṃyutta Nikāya is Geyya. The entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka, suttas without verses, and any other Buddha-word not included in the other eight limbs should be known as Veyyākaraṇa. The Dhammapada, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, and those pure verses in the Suttanipāta not bearing the name 'Sutta' should be known as Gāthā. The eighty-two suttas connected with verses born of knowledge accompanied by joy (somanassa) should be known as Udāna. The one hundred and twelve suttas occurring by way of the method beginning with 'Vuttañhetaṃ Bhagavatā' (For this was said by the Blessed One) should be known as Itivuttaka. The five hundred and fifty birth stories beginning with the Apaṇṇaka Jātaka should be known as Jātaka. All suttas connected with wonderful and marvelous things, occurring by way of the method beginning with 'Monks, these four wonderful and marvelous things are found in Ānanda,' should be known as Abbhutadhamma.

All suttas asked and answered after repeatedly gaining wisdom and joy, such as the Cūḷavedalla, Mahāavedalla, Sammādiṭṭhi, Sakkapañha, Saṅkhārabhājanīya, and Mahāpuṇṇama Suttas, should be known as Vedalla. Thus, by way of limbs, there are nine limbs.

How are there eighty-four thousand Dhamma-groups (dhammakkhandhas) by way of Dhamma-groups? All this Buddha-word is:
'I received eighty-two thousand from the Buddha,
And two thousand from the monks;
These eighty-four thousand teachings
Are those I have in use.'
Thus, by way of the Dhamma-groups illustrated by this verse, there are eighty-four thousand divisions. Among those eighty-four thousand, a sutta with a single connection (anusandhi) is one Dhamma-group. In a sutta with multiple connections, the count of Dhamma-groups is by way of the connections. In verse compositions, a question asked is one Dhamma-group, and the answer is one. In the Abhidhamma, each division of a triad (tika) or dyad (duka), and each division of a mental cycle (cittavāra), is one Dhamma-group. In the Vinaya, there is the basis (vatthu), the summary (mātikā), the word-analysis (padabhājanīya), the offense (āpatti), the non-offense (anāpatti)...
28:
In the Vinaya teaching, there are intermediate offenses (antarāpatti) and sections on the cutting of the triads (tikaccheda). Among these seven groups (namely: vatthu, mātikā, padabhājanīya, āpatti, anāpatti, antarāpatti, and tikaccheda), each individual group should be understood as one Dhamma aggregate (dhammakkhandha). Thus, in terms of Dhamma aggregates, there are eighty-four thousand Dhamma aggregates.

In this way, during the First Council of the five hundred [Arahants], the assembly of masters led by the Venerable Mahākassapa, while chanting all these words of the Buddha, established this classification: "This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya; this is the first word of the Buddha, this is the middle word of the Buddha, this is the last word of the Buddha; this is the Vinaya Piṭaka, this is the Suttanta Piṭaka, this is the Abhidhamma Piṭaka; this is the Dīgha Nikāya ... this is the Khuddaka Nikāya; these, such as the Suttas, are the nine factors (navanga); these are the eighty-four thousand Dhamma aggregates." Not only did they establish this classification, but they also established various other classifications found in the three Piṭakas, such as the Udāna collection, Vagga collection, Peyyāla collection, Nipāta collections like the Ekanipāta and Dukanipāta, Saṃyutta collection, and Paṇṇāsa collection, and completed the chanting in seven months.

At the conclusion of the council, the great earth, as if giving a cry of "Sādhu" in joy, thinking, "The Venerable Mahākassapa has succeeded in making this Dispensation of the Ten-Powered One (the Buddha) endure for a period of five thousand years," shook, trembled, and quaked in many ways as far as the water's edge. Many wonders also appeared.

In this chanted word of the Buddha, this Abhidhamma is the Abhidhamma Piṭaka by way of Piṭaka, the Khuddaka Nikāya by way of Nikāya, Veyyākaraṇa (Exposition) by way of factor (anga), and consists of several thousand (twelve thousand) Dhamma aggregates by way of Dhamma aggregate.

Among the monks who preserved that Abhidhamma, in former times, a certain monk, sitting in the midst of a general assembly, wishing to preach the Dhamma by citing a text from the Abhidhamma, said: "The materiality aggregate is indeterminate (abyākata). The four [mental] aggregates may be wholesome (kusala), may be unwholesome (akusala), or may be indeterminate. Ten sense bases (āyatana) are indeterminate; two sense bases may be wholesome, may be unwholesome, or may be indeterminate. Sixteen elements (dhātu) are indeterminate; two elements may be wholesome, may be unwholesome, or may be indeterminate. The truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca) is unwholesome; the truth of the path (magga-sacca) is wholesome; the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca) is indeterminate; the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca) may be wholesome, may be unwholesome, or may be indeterminate. Ten faculties (indriya) are indeterminate; the faculty of grief (domanassindriya) is unwholesome; the faculty of 'I shall know the unknown' (anaññātaññassāmītindriya) is wholesome; four faculties may be wholesome or may be indeterminate..."
29:
"...the remaining six faculties may be wholesome, may be unwholesome, or may be indeterminate." Thus he preached the Dhamma discourse. A monk sitting in that place said, "Dhammakathika (Dhamma-preacher), you are bringing forth a long text as if encircling Mount Sineru. What is the name of this text?" "Friend, it is called the Abhidhamma text," he replied. "Why do you bring forth the Abhidhamma text? Is it not proper to bring forth other Suttas spoken by the Buddha?" "Who spoke the Abhidhamma?" "This is not spoken by the Buddha." "Friend, have you learned the Vinaya Piṭaka?" "Friend, I have not learned it." "I think you say this out of ignorance because you have not mastered the Vinaya." "Friend, I have learned only a little of the Vinaya." "Even that little you have learned poorly; it must have been learned while sitting at the edge of the assembly and nodding off. For a person like you, whether ordaining someone as a novice or as a monk, it is an offense." "For what reason?" "Because even the little Vinaya was learned poorly. For it has been said: 'In that Vinaya, there is no offense if, not wishing to disparage the Vinaya, one says: "Friend, first learn the Suttanta, or the verses, or the Abhidhamma, and later you will learn the Vinaya."' [Also:] 'Having asked for permission regarding the Suttanta, one asks about the Abhidhamma or the Vinaya; having asked for permission regarding the Abhidhamma, one asks about the Suttanta or the Vinaya; having asked for permission regarding the Vinaya, one asks about the Suttanta or the Abhidhamma.'" "But you do not know even this much." Thus, with just this much, the proponent of the other view was refuted.

The Mahāgosinga Sutta, however, is even more powerful than this Vinaya [evidence] in proving that the Abhidhamma is the word of the Buddha. In that Mahāgosinga Sutta, when the General of the Dhamma, the Venerable Sāriputta, approached the Blessed One to report the questions asked and answers given among themselves, and reported the answer of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, he said: "Here, friend Sāriputta, two monks engage in a discussion on the Abhidhamma. They ask each other questions and answer the questions asked of each other without faltering, and their Dhamma talk proceeds in accordance with the Dhamma. Friend Sāriputta, a monk of such a nature would grace the Gosinga Sāla wood." The Teacher did not say, "Those who are proficient in Abhidhamma are outside my Dispensation," but instead, raising his neck which was like a golden drum, and opening his great mouth which possessed the splendor of the full moon, he uttered his Brahma-voice, saying, "Sādhu..." (Well done).
30:
“Sāriputta, well said, well said!” Having given this approval to the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, the Buddha said, “Sāriputta, just as Moggallāna has answered correctly, so should one answer that question. Sāriputta, Moggallāna is indeed a preacher of Dhamma (dhammakathika).” It is said that only those monks who are proficient in Abhidhamma are true preachers of Dhamma; others, even when they preach the Dhamma, are not true preachers of Dhamma. Why? Because when they preach the Dhamma, they do so by mixing up and confusing various actions (kamma), various results (vipāka), the distinction between materiality and mentality (rūpa-arūpa), and various phenomena (dhamma). However, those proficient in Abhidhamma do not confuse these various phenomena. Therefore, whether a monk proficient in Abhidhamma preaches the Dhamma or not, he will be able to answer a question when asked. Such a person alone is a true preacher of Dhamma. With this in mind, the Teacher gave his approval and said, “Moggallāna has spoken well.”

One who rejects the Abhidhamma strikes a blow at this Dispensation (Jina-cakka) of the Conqueror. He rejects omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), obstructs the Teacher’s knowledge of self-confidence (vesārajja-ñāṇa), deceives the audience who wishes to hear the Dhamma, creates an obstacle to the Noble Path (ariya-magga), and is seen to be involved in one of the eighteen grounds for causing a schism in the Saṅgha. He is worthy of the act of rebuke (tajjannīya-kamma) and the act of suspension (ukkhepanīya-kamma). After performing those respective acts, he should be expelled with the words, “Go, live as a scavenger (vighāsāda).”

If it is argued, “If the Abhidhamma were the word of the Buddha, its prologue (nidāna) would have been composed in the same way as in many thousands of Suttas, such as ‘At one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha,’ etc.” That person should be refuted thus: “Just as the Jātaka, Suttanipāta, Dhammapada, and so on do not have such a prologue, yet they are not considered not to be the word of the Buddha, so it is here.” Furthermore, it should be said: “O wise one, this Abhidhamma is the domain (visaya) of the All-Knowing Buddhas only, not the domain of others.
