For the descent into the womb (okkanti) of the Buddhas is well-known, their birth (abhijāti) is well-known, their enlightenment (abhisambodhi) is well-known, the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma is well-known, the performance of the Twin Miracle is well-known, the ascent to the third heaven (tidivakkama) is well-known, the fact of preaching in the deva world is well-known, and the descent from the deva world (devorohana) is well-known. For example, it is impossible and groundless to steal a Universal Monarch’s elephant-treasure or horse-treasure and harness it to a small cart for travel; or to steal the wheel-treasure and hang it on a straw-cart for travel; or to put a gem-treasure capable of illuminating a whole league (yojana) into a cotton basket...”
31:
...to use it in such a way is impossible and groundless. Why? Because it is an object fit only for a king. In the same way, the Abhidhamma is not the domain of others; it is the domain of the All-Knowing Buddhas only. It is a teaching that can be taught only by the power of those All-Knowing Buddhas. For the descent into the womb of the Buddhas is well-known... (pe)... the descent from the deva world is well-known. “O wise ones, there is no such thing as a prologue-task (nidāna-kicca) for the Abhidhamma.” When this is said, an opponent is unable to provide a reasoned example.

However, the Elder Tissabhūti, who lived at Maṇḍalārāma, in order to show that this Abhidhamma has its origin (nidāna) at the Mahābodhi, cited and preached this Padesavihāra Sutta: “Monks, I have dwelt in a portion of that dwelling (vihāra) by which I first dwelt as one who had attained supreme enlightenment.” There are ten kinds of portions (padesa): the portion of aggregates (khandha), the portion of bases (āyatana), the portion of elements (dhātu), the portion of truths (sacca), the portion of faculties (indriya), the portion of the mode of conditions (paccayākāra), the portion of foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), the portion of jhānas, the portion of mentality (nāma), and the portion of phenomena (dhamma). Among these ten, the Teacher fully penetrated the five aggregates at the foot of the Mahābodhi tree and dwelt for these three months solely by the power of the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-kkhandha). He fully penetrated the 12 bases and 18 elements, and dwelt for these three months by the power of feeling in the base of phenomena (dhammāyatana) and by the power of feeling in the element of phenomena (dhammadhātu). He fully penetrated the 4 truths and dwelt for these three months solely by the power of feeling in the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca). He fully penetrated the 22 faculties and dwelt for these three months by the power of the five faculties of feeling. He fully penetrated the twelve-linked wheel of dependent origination (paccayākāra) and dwelt for these three months solely by the power of feeling conditioned by contact (phassa-paccayā vedanā). He fully penetrated the 4 foundations of mindfulness and dwelt for these three months solely by the power of the foundation of mindfulness on feeling (vedanā-satipaṭṭhāna). He fully penetrated the 4 jhānas and dwelt for these three months solely by the power of feeling within the factors of jhāna. He fully penetrated mentality (nāma) and dwelt for these three months solely by the power of feeling therein. He fully penetrated all phenomena (dhamma) and dwelt for these three months solely by the power of the triad of feeling (vedanā-ttika). Thus, the Elder preached the prologue of the Abhidhamma by the power of the Padesavihāra Sutta.

However, the Elder Sumanadeva, a village-dweller, while reciting the Dhamma on the lower floor of the Lohapāsāda, said: “This opponent, despite having protectors like us who know the prologue, is like one without a protector, raising his arms and wailing in the forest, or like one who judges a case without witnesses despite having them; he does not even know that there is a prologue in the Abhidhamma.” Wishing to preach the prologue, he said: “At one time the Blessed One was staying among the gods in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, on the Paṇḍukambala stone at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree. There, the Blessed One...”
32:
He preached the Abhidhamma to the devas of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, saying: "Wholesome states (kusalā dhammā), unwholesome states (akusalā dhammā), and indeterminate states (abyākatā dhammā)."

While other Suttas have only one origin (nidāna), the Abhidhamma has two: the Origin of Attainment (adhigamanidāna) and the Origin of Teaching (desanānidāna). Among these, the Origin of Attainment should be understood as starting from the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara up to the throne of the Great Enlightenment (Mahābodhi). The Origin of Teaching should be understood as extending up to the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakkappavattana). To gain proficiency in the origin of this Abhidhamma, which is endowed with these two origins, this set of questions should first be understood: By what was this Abhidhamma produced? Where was it matured? Where was it attained? When was it attained? By whom was it attained? Where was it reflected upon? When was it reflected upon? By whom was it reflected upon? Where was it taught? For whose benefit was it taught? For what purpose was it taught? By whom was it received? Who learn it? Who have completed their learning? Who bear it? Whose word is it? By whom was it brought?

The answer to these questions is as follows: To the question 'By what was it produced?', it was produced by faith in the aspiration for Enlightenment (bodhi-abhinīhāra-saddhā). It was matured in the five hundred and fifty Jātakas. It was attained at the foot of the Bodhi tree. It was attained on the full moon day of Visākha. It was attained by the Omniscient Buddha. It was reflected upon at the Bodhimaṇḍa. It was reflected upon during the seven days in the Jewel House (Ratanaghara). It was reflected upon by the Omniscient Buddha. It was taught in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. It was taught for the benefit of the devas. It was taught for the purpose of deliverance from the four floods (oghas). It was received by the devas. Trainees (sekhas) and virtuous worldlings (kalyāṇa-puthujjanas) learn it. The Arahants whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsavas) are those who have completed their learning. It is borne by those in whose hearts it remains. It is the word of the Blessed One, the Worthy, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. It was brought by the lineage of teachers (ācariya-paramparā).

This Abhidhamma was brought by the great elders such as the Elder Sāriputta, the Elder Bhaddaji, the Elder Sobhita, the Elder Piyajālī, the Elder Piyapāla, the Elder Piyadassī, the Elder Kosiyaputta, the Elder Siggava, the Elder Sandeha, the Elder Moggaliputta, the Elder Sudatta, the Elder Dhammiya, the Elder Dāsaka, the Elder Soṇaka, and the Elder Revata, up to the time of the Third Council. After that, it was brought by the succession of their disciples. Thus, it was first brought by the lineage of teachers on the surface of Jambudīpa. As for this island of Sīhala—
33:
Furthermore, the Elder Mahinda, the Elder Ittiya, the Elder Uttiya, likewise the Elder Sambala, and the wise Elder Bhaddasāla were great Arahants of great wisdom.

## They came here from Jambudīpa (Pari. 3, 8).

These five great Arahants brought the Abhidhamma. Furthermore, the lineage of teachers, known as the succession of disciples of those elders, has brought it down to the present day.

## Sumedhakathā (The Story of Sumedha)

Regarding this Abhidhamma thus brought, the Origin of Attainment from the Buddha Dīpaṅkara up to the throne of the Great Enlightenment, and the Origin of Teaching up to the preaching of the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, have been mentioned. To clarify these two origins, this sequential narrative should be understood:

It is said that four incalculables (asaṅkheyya) and a hundred thousand aeons (kappa) ago, there was a city named Amaravatī. In that city lived a Brahmin named Sumedha. He was well-born on both his mother's and father's side, of pure descent for seven generations, and was irreproachable and beyond reproach in terms of birth. He was handsome, pleasant to behold, inspiring, and endowed with the highest beauty of complexion. He did no other work but learned only the arts of the Brahmins. While he was still young, his parents passed away. Then, the minister in charge of the wealth brought the ledger of assets, opened the storehouses filled with gold, silver, gems, pearls, and the like, and said: "Young master, this much is your mother's property, this much is your father's, and this much belongs to your grandfathers and great-grandfathers," declaring the wealth down to the seventh generation, and said, "Take possession of this wealth."

The wise Sumedha thought: "My grandfathers, great-grandfathers, and parents, having accumulated this wealth, did not take even a single coin with them when they went to the next world. I, however, should act in such a way that I can take it with me."

He informed the king, had the drum beaten throughout the city, gave away his wealth in charity to the great multitude, and went forth as an ascetic.

At this point, the story of Sumedha should be told. This is stated in the Buddhavaṃsa as follows:

A hundred thousand aeons and four incalculables ago,
There was a city named Amara, beautiful and delightful to the mind.
34:
The city was never silent from the ten sounds, and was well-provided with food and drink; with the sounds of elephants, horses, drums, conchs, and chariots; and with the constant cries of the people regarding food and drink, "Eat! Drink!"

The city was complete in all aspects, endowed with all sensual pleasures, possessed of the seven treasures, and crowded with various kinds of people. It was prosperous like the city of the gods, the abode of those of meritorious deeds—such was the city of Amaravatī.

In the city of Amaravatī, there was a Brahmin named Sumedha, who had accumulated many crores of wealth and was rich in grain and assets. He was a reciter of the Vedas, a master of the mantras, and had reached the further shore of the three Vedas. He had attained perfection in the science of signs (lakkhaṇa), history (itihāsa), and his own Vedic duties.

On that occasion, having gone into seclusion and sitting down, I thought thus: "Rebirth is indeed suffering, and the breaking up of the body is suffering."

I am subject to birth, subject to aging, and subject to sickness. Therefore, I shall seek Nibbāna, which is free from aging, free from death, secure, and peaceful.

What if I were to discard this foul body, filled with various kinds of corpses, and go away without longing or need for it? There must surely be that path; it cannot be that it does not exist. I shall seek that path for liberation from becoming (bhava).

Just as when suffering exists, that which is called happiness also exists; even so, when becoming exists, non-becoming (vibhava) should also be desired. Just as when heat exists, there also exists another which is cold; even so, when the threefold fire exists, Nibbāna should also be desired. Just as when evil exists, good also exists; even so, when birth exists, non-birth should also be desired.
35:
Just as a man who has fallen into or is smeared with filth, seeing a pond full of water, does not seek that pond, the fault is not that of the pond but of the man himself; even so, while there exists the pond of the Deathless (Nibbāna) which washes away the stains of defilements, if one does not seek that pond, the fault is not that of the pond of the Deathless.

Just as a man surrounded on all sides by enemies, while there is a path of escape, does not flee, the fault is not that of the path but of the man himself; even so, when one is surrounded by the enemies of defilements, while there exists the path to peace (Nibbāna) where all dangers cease, if one does not seek that path, the fault is not that of the path to peace.

Just as a man suffering from a disease, while there is a physician to treat him, does not have that disease treated, the fault is not that of the physician but of the man himself; even so, when one is oppressed by the diseases of defilements and has reached suffering, if one does not seek that Teacher who can treat them, the fault is not that of the Buddha, the Guide.

Just as a man might untie and discard a repulsive carcass bound to his neck and go happily, freely, and at his own will; in the same way, I shall discard this foul body, a collection of various impurities, without attachment or desire, and go.

Just as men and women, having discarded excrement at a place for easing themselves, go away without attachment or desire; even so, I shall discard this body, filled with various foul odors, regarding it like a latrine, and go.

Just as boat owners, without attachment or desire, discard a decaying and broken boat that is taking on water and go away; even so, I shall discard this body, which has nine openings and is constantly leaking, just as owners discard an old boat, and go.

Just as a man carrying valuable goods, traveling with thieves, sees the danger of his property being plundered and discards those goods and goes away (so it is).
36:
This body is like a great thief. Therefore, fearing the danger of having my wholesome states (kusala) plundered and destroyed, I shall discard this body and go. Having thought thus, I gave away my wealth of many hundreds of millions to those with and without protectors, and then I approached the Himālaya mountains. Not far from the Himālayas, there is a mountain named Dhammika. On that mountain, my hermitage was well-prepared, and a leaf-roofed hut was well-created. There, I created a walkway free from the five faults, and living in that hermitage endowed with the eight qualities of a recluse's happiness, I attained the power of the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and insight (vipassanā). There, I discarded the cloth garment which possessed nine faults and donned the bark-garment endowed with twelve qualities. I abandoned the leaf-roofed hut, which was beset with eight faults, and approached the foot of a tree endowed with ten qualities. I completely abandoned sown and planted grains and consumed only naturally fallen fruits, which are endowed with many benefits. In that hermitage, I exerted effort in the postures of sitting, standing, and walking, and within seven days, I attained the power of the higher knowledges.

In the verses from the Buddhavaṃsa, 'My hermitage was well-prepared, and a leaf-roofed hut was well-created,' it is spoken as if the wise Sumedha created the hermitage, leaf-hut, and walkway with his own hands. However, the meaning here is this: Sakka, the king of devas, seeing the Great Being (Mahāsatta) setting out with the thought, 'Having entered the Himālayas, I shall today enter Mount Dhammika,' called the young deva Vissakamma and said, 'Go, dear one, this wise Sumedha has set out to ordain; create a dwelling place for him.' Vissakamma, accepting the command of Sakka, created a delightful hermitage, a well-protected leaf-hut, and a pleasant walkway. The Blessed One, referring to that hermitage which arose at that time through the power of his own merit, preached: 'Sāriputta, on that Mount Dhammika, my hermitage was well-prepared, the leaf-hut was well-created, and I created a walkway free from the five faults.' In the phrase 'my hermitage was well-prepared,' the meaning should be understood as 'it was well-made for me.' In the phrase 'and the leaf-roofed hut,' [it means] also the leaf-roofed hut...
37:
“My hermitage was well-made; the leaf-roofed hut was also well-fashioned. There, I created a walkway (caṅkama) free from the five defects,” he said. In this context, “My hermitage was well-made” means it was well-constructed by me. “The leaf-roofed hut was well-fashioned” means the hut covered with leaves was also well-constructed for me.

“Free from the five defects” refers to the five defects of a walkway: having hard and uneven ground, having trees within, being overgrown with thickets, being too narrow, and being too wide. Indeed, for one walking on a walkway with hard and uneven ground, the feet ache, blisters arise, the mind does not attain one-pointedness, and the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) fails. However, on a walkway with a soft and even surface, the meditation subject succeeds due to dwelling in comfort. Therefore, having hard and uneven ground should be known as the first defect. If there is a tree at the end, in the middle, or on the edge of the walkway, one who walks mindfully might strike their forehead or head; thus, having trees within is the second defect. One walking on a walkway overgrown with thickets such as grass and creepers might step on and kill creatures like snakes in the dark, or might suffer pain from being bitten by them; thus, being overgrown with thickets is the third defect. On an extremely narrow walkway, only one cubit or half a cubit in width, one walking might slip at the edge and break their nails or toes; thus, being extremely narrow is the fourth defect. On an extremely wide walkway, the mind of the one walking wanders to various objects and cannot attain one-pointedness; thus, being extremely wide is the fifth defect. A suitable walkway should be one and a half cubits in width, with a sub-walkway (anucaṅkama) of about one cubit on both sides, sixty cubits in length, with a soft surface and sand spread evenly. That walkway was like the walkway of the Elder Mahā Mahinda, who brought faith to the island of Sri Lanka, at Cetiyagiri. Therefore, he said, “There, I created a walkway free from the five defects.”

“Endowed with the eight qualities” means being endowed with the eight comforts of a recluse (samaṇa-sukha). These eight comforts of a recluse are: the absence of possessing wealth and grain; the state of seeking blameless alms; the state of eating alms in peace; the absence of the distress of national oppression caused by royal families who seize wealth or gold coins by oppressing the country; the state of being free from desire and lust for requisites; the state of being free from fear of robbery; the state of not associating with kings and great ministers; and the state of being unobstructed in the four directions. This is what is meant.
38:
The meaning is: “Just as one living in that hermitage is able to experience these eight comforts of a recluse, so I created that hermitage endowed with the eight qualities.”

“I brought the power of super-knowledge” (abhiññā-balamāhariṃ) means that later, while living in that hermitage, I performed the preparatory work for kasiṇa meditation and, in order to produce the super-knowledges (abhiññā) and attainments (samāpatti), I began insight meditation (vipassanā) on impermanence and suffering, thereby bringing forth the power of insight that had reached its peak. The meaning is that just as I was able to bring forth that power while living there, so I created that hermitage to be suitable for that power of insight and for the sake of those super-knowledges.

“There, I abandoned the cloth which possessed the nine defects”: the sequential account here is as follows. At that time, after creating a delightful hermitage suitable for seclusion—adorned with huts, caves, and walkways; covered with trees full of flowers and fruits; having a pond of sweet water; and free from dangerous wild beasts and frightening bird sounds—he prepared a support plank at both ends of the decorated walkway and created a flat, mung-bean-colored stone slab in the middle of the walkway for sitting. Inside the leaf-roofed hut, he created all the requisites of an ascetic, such as matted hair, bark garments, a triple staff, and a water pot; in the pavilion, water jars, conch shells for drinking, and drinking bowls; and in the fire hall, embers, fire-drills, firewood, and so on—everything that serves as a benefit for those who have gone forth. Then, after carving the letters on the wall of the hut, “Whoever wishes to go forth, let them take these requisites and go forth,” the celestial son Vissakamma returned to the deva realm. While the wise Sumedha was searching for a comfortable place suitable for his residence along the mountain gorges at the foot of the Himalayas, he saw the delightful hermitage at a river bend, which had been created by Vissakamma and given by Sakka. Going to the end of the walkway and seeing no footprints, he thought, “Surely, the resident monks must have gone to the nearby village to seek alms and, having returned exhausted, are now sitting inside the hut.” After waiting for a short while, he thought, “They are taking a very long time; I will find out,” and opened the door of the hut. Entering and looking here and there, he read the letters on the great wall. Thinking, “These are the allowable requisites for me; I will take these and go forth,” he abandoned the pair of cloths he was wearing. Therefore, the Blessed One said, “There, I abandoned the cloth.” O Sāriputta, in this way, I entered that hermitage and abandoned the lay cloth.
39:
Opening the door of the leaf-roofed hut and entering, he looked here and there and read the letters on the large wall. Thinking, "These requisites are suitable for me; I shall take these and go forth," he abandoned the pair of cloths he was wearing. Regarding this abandonment, the Blessed One said, "He abandoned the cloths there." "O Sāriputta, intending to make this known, when I entered the leaf-roofed hut, I abandoned the lay cloths in that hut."

## Navadosamupāgatan’ti
With this phrase, it is shown that when he abandoned the lay cloths, he did so seeing nine defects. To those who go forth as ascetics, nine defects appear in lay clothing. These nine are: (1) being of great value, (2) being dependent on others for its origin, (3) becoming soiled quickly through use (soiled cloth must be washed and dyed), (4) wearing out quickly through use (when worn out, it must be sewn or patched), (5) being difficult to find a replacement, (6) being unsuitable for the state of an ascetic, (7) being common to enemies (one must guard it so enemies do not take it), (8) serving as an ornament for the wearer, and (9) being a heavy burden on the shoulders or involving great desire when carrying it.

## Vākacīraṃ Nivāsesin’ti
"O Sāriputta, then seeing these nine defects, I abandoned the lay cloths and donned the bark garment." This means he took the bark garment, made by knotting together strips of muñja grass, for the purpose of wearing and covering.

## Dvādasaguṇamupāgatan’ti
He donned the bark garment which is endowed with twelve benefits. There are twelve benefits in a bark garment: (1) being of little value, excellent, and suitable for ascetics, (2) being able to be made with one's own hands, (3) becoming soiled slowly through use, and there is no delay even when washing, (4) no need for sewing even when worn out through use, (5) being easy to make when seeking a replacement, (6) being suitable for the state of an ascetic, (7) being of no use to enemies, (8) not serving as an ornament for the wearer, (9) being very light to carry, (10) having fewness of wishes regarding the requisite of robes, (11) its origin from bark being righteous and blameless, and (12) having no attachment even if the bark garment is lost.

## Aṭṭhadosasamākiṇṇaṃ, Pajahiṃ Paṇṇasālakan’ti
How did he abandon it? It is said that the ascetic Sumedha, removing the pair of noble cloths, took the red bark garment which was hanging on the robe-rack and resembled a garland of anoja flowers, and put it on. Over that, he donned another bark garment of golden hue. He placed a black antelope skin, which had claws and resembled a bed of punnāga flowers, over one shoulder.
40: Putting on the circle of matted hair, he inserted a wooden pin (or ivory pin) to keep it firm along with the topknot. He placed the coral-colored water pot into a net bag that resembled a pearl net. Taking a carrying pole curved in three places, he hung the water pot on one end of the pole, and on the other end, he hung the hook, basket, wooden tripod, and so on. Placing the loaded carrying pole on his shoulder and holding a staff in his right hand, he emerged from the hut. Walking back and forth on the sixty-cubit great cloister, he looked at his own appearance and thought: "My heart's desire has reached its fulfillment. How beautiful is my monkhood! I have attained this state of a monk which is praised and lauded by all wise men such as Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas. I have abandoned the bonds of the laity. I have gone forth into homelessness. I have obtained the supreme monkhood. I shall strive in the Dhamma of a recluse; I shall attain the bliss of the highest fruit." Filled with enthusiasm, he lowered the carrying pole and sat like a golden statue on a stone slab the color of mung bean soup in the middle of the cloister, passing the daylight hours. In the evening, he entered the hut and lay down on a wooden plank beside a bedstead made of cane, letting his body adjust to the temperature. Waking up at dawn, he reflected on the reason for his coming: "Seeing the danger in household life, I abandoned immeasurable wealth and endless fame, entered the forest, and became a monk seeking renunciation. From now on, it is not proper for me to live heedlessly. The mosquitoes of wrong thoughts bite one who wanders having abandoned seclusion. Now, I ought to cultivate seclusion. I came out seeing the bond and defect of household life. Yet this leaf-roofed hut is also pleasant. The ground is the color of a ripe wood-apple, the walls are white like silver, the leaf-roof is the color of a pigeon's foot, and the cane bedstead is like a colorful carpet. This dwelling place is so comfortable to live in that it seems no less than the excellence of my former house." Thus, while searching for the defects of the hut, he saw eight defects. There are eight disadvantages in using a leaf-roofed hut: (1) the disadvantage of having to seek and collect materials like timber with great effort, (2) the need to repeatedly repair it when grass, leaves, or lumps of earth fall...
41:
The constant need for cleaning and maintenance is the second disadvantage. A dwelling belongs to the elderly; for a junior monk who is made to get up at an improper time by an elder, there can be no one-pointedness of mind—thus, being made to get up is the third disadvantage. By warding off cold and heat, it makes the body delicate and tender; this is the fourth disadvantage. One who enters a dwelling can commit some evil; thus, the concealment of blameworthy acts is the fifth disadvantage. Taking possession of it as 'mine' is the sixth disadvantage. Having a dwelling is like living with a companion; this is the seventh disadvantage. Because it is shared with lice, bedbugs, house lizards, geckos, and so on, being shared with many creatures is the eighth disadvantage. Seeing these eight disadvantages, the Great Being abandoned the leaf-roofed hut. Therefore, he said, 'I have abandoned the leaf hut, which is crowded with eight defects.'

'I have approached the foot of a tree endowed with ten qualities,' he said, rejecting shelter and stating that he had reached the foot of a tree possessed of ten qualities.

In that regard, these are the ten qualities: Having little effort is the first quality (as it involves merely going there). Requiring no maintenance is the second quality (for it is pleasant to use whether it is swept or not). Not being made to get up by others is the third quality. Not concealing blameworthy acts is the fourth quality (for one who does evil there feels shame). Not pampering the body, as if living in the open air, is the fifth quality. Having no sense of possession is the sixth quality. Rejecting the attachment to a home is the seventh quality. Not having to evict others, as in a house shared with many where one says, 'I will clean this, get out,' is the eighth quality. Bringing joy to the dweller is the ninth quality. Having no anxiety or attachment because the dwelling at the foot of a tree is easily available wherever one goes is the tenth quality. Seeing these ten qualities, he said that he approached the foot of a tree.

Having reflected on and noted these reasons, the Great Being entered the village for alms on the following day. Then, in the village he reached, the people gave alms with great effort. After finishing his meal, he returned to the hermitage, sat down, and reflected: 'I did not become a monk because I could not get food. This refined food increases pride and intoxication. There is no end to the suffering rooted in food. It would be good if I were to give up food derived from cultivated and sown grain and become one who eats only naturally fallen fruit.' From that time on...
42:
Acting accordingly and striving with effort, within just seven days, he attained the eight meditative attainments and the five supernormal powers. Because of that attainment, he said:

'I completely abandoned cultivated and sown grain,
And partook of naturally fallen fruit endowed with many qualities.

In that practice of recluses, I exerted effort through sitting and walking,
And within seven days, I reached the power of the superknowledges.'

When I had thus achieved success and become proficient in the Dispensation, the Conqueror named Dīpaṅkara, the Leader of the World, arose.

While he was being conceived, being born, attaining enlightenment, and preaching the Dhamma, I did not see the four omens because I was absorbed in the bliss of jhāna.

People living in the border regions invited the Tathāgata and, with joyful hearts, were clearing the path for his arrival.

At that time, I had come out of my hermitage and, shaking my bark garments, was then traveling through the sky.

Seeing the people filled with awe, joy, and delight, I descended from the sky and immediately questioned the people:

'O people who are filled with awe, joy, and delight, for whom is this road, this path, being cleared?'

When I questioned them, they replied: 'The peerless Buddha in the world, the Conqueror named Dīpaṅkara, the Leader of the World, has arisen. It is for him that this road, this path, is being cleared.'

As soon as I heard the word 'Buddha,' rapture arose, and uttering 'Buddha, Buddha,' I expressed my joyful happiness.

Standing there, I thought with a joyful and stirred mind: 'I shall sow seeds of merit in this [fertile field of the Buddha]; let not the rare and auspicious moment of a Buddha's arising pass me by.'

'If you are clearing the path for the Buddha, give me a section as well; I too shall clear the path for the Buddha's arrival.'
43:
Then, those people gave me a spot to clear (the path). At that time, I cleared the path while contemplating, "Buddha, Buddha."

Before the spot I was clearing was finished, the Great Sage Buddha Dīpaṅkara, the Conqueror who had overcome the five Maras, arrived on that path, surrounded by four hundred thousand Arahants who possessed the six higher spiritual powers (abhiññā), who were unshakable in the face of the eight worldly conditions (tādi), and who were free from the impurities of mental defilements.

Welcoming ceremonies took place, and many drums were beaten. Both humans and devas were exceedingly joyful and raised shouts of "Sādhu!"

The devas saw the humans, and the humans saw the devas. Both, with palms joined in reverence, followed behind the Tathāgata. The devas followed the Tathāgata playing celestial instruments, and the humans followed playing human instruments.

The devas dwelling in the sky scattered celestial Mandārava flowers, Paduma lotuses, and Pāricchattaka flowers in every direction. The devas dwelling in the sky scattered celestial sandalwood powder and various excellent perfumes in every direction. The humans dwelling on the ground threw Champaka, Salala, Nīpa, Nāga, Punnāga, and Ketaka flowers in every direction.

Then, I loosened my matted hair and spread it out; and having spread my bark-garment and deerskin over that muddy place, I lay down prostrate. (I thought:) "Let the Buddha, together with His disciples, proceed by stepping upon me. Let Him not step on the mud. Such stepping upon me will be for my benefit and happiness for a long time."

As I lay prostrate on the ground, this thought occurred to me: "If I so desired, I could burn away my defilements this very day. What use is there for me to realize the Dhamma here in an unknown form (as a mere disciple)? Having reached Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), I shall become a Buddha in the world including the devas."
44:
"What use is there for me, being a man who sees his own strength, to cross over (the ocean of Saṃsāra) alone? Having reached Omniscience, I shall rescue the world including the devas.

By this extraordinary merit I have performed towards Buddha Dīpaṅkara, the Supreme Man, may I reach Omniscience and rescue the great multitude of people.

Having cut the stream of Saṃsāra and destroyed the three realms of existence, I shall board the ship of Dhamma and rescue the world including the devas."

Buddha Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the Worlds, the Recipient of Offerings, stood near my head and spoke these words:

"Behold this ascetic with matted hair, a practitioner of fierce austerities. In incalculable aeons from now (after four asankheyya and a hundred thousand aeons), he will become a Buddha in the world.

Departing from the pleasant city named Kapilavatthu, that Tathāgata, having exerted himself in the practice of meditation and having performed the difficult austerities (dukkaracariya),

That Tathāgata will sit at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree, and having received milk-rice there, He will go to the Nerañjarā River.

That Conqueror, having consumed the milk-rice on the banks of the Nerañjarā River, will proceed to the foot of the Bodhi tree by the prepared excellent path.

Thereafter, having circumambulated the enclosure of the Bodhi tree, that peerless and highly renowned Buddha will awaken at the foot of the Assattha tree (Ficus religiosa).

The mother who gives birth to this Buddha will be named Māyā, the father will be named Suddhodana, and this Buddha will be named Gotama.

Kolita and Upatissa, who are free from taints (āsavas), free from lust, with peaceful minds and concentrated, will be the chief disciples. An attendant named Ānanda will serve this Conqueror.

Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā will also be the chief female disciples, being free from taints, free from lust, with peaceful minds and concentrated."
45:
The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called the Assattha (Ficus religiosa). Citta the householder and Hatthāḷavaka will be the foremost male lay attendants. Uttarā and Nandamātā will be the foremost female lay attendants.

Upon hearing this prophecy of Buddha Dīpaṅkara, the Great Sage who seeks the collection of virtues such as peerless morality, the multitude of devas and humans were joyful, thinking, "This person is indeed a Buddha-seed."

Those living in the ten thousand world-systems, including the devas, raised shouts of applause, clapped their hands, laughed, and worshipped with palms joined.

(They thought:) "If we should miss the dispensation of this Buddha, the Lord of the World (without attaining the Paths and Fruits), may we meet this Noble One (Sumedha) face to face in the future (when he becomes a Buddha). Just as people crossing a river, if they miss the landing place directly opposite, they cross the great river by taking hold of a landing place further downstream; even so, if all of us miss this Buddha Dīpaṅkara, the Conqueror, may we meet this Noble One face to face in the future."

Buddha Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the Worlds, the Recipient of Offerings, having praised my meritorious deed (of laying down as a bridge at the risk of my life), lifted His right foot. All the sons of the Buddha (monks) who were there circumambulated me. Humans, Nāgas, and Gandhabbas worshipped me and then departed.

When Buddha Dīpaṅkara, the Leader of the World, together with the Saṅgha, had passed out of my sight, I then rose from my prostrate position with a heart full of joy and delight. I attained happiness through that happiness (born of the prophecy), I rejoiced with joy, and my entire body was suffused with rapture (pīti). At that time, I sat down cross-legged.

While sitting cross-legged, I then reflected thus: "I have become one who has mastery (vasībhāva) over jhāna, and I have reached the pinnacle of the higher spiritual powers (abhiññā)."
46:
“In the ten thousand worlds, there are no ascetics equal to me; I am peerless in the qualities of psychic power, and I have attained such happiness (born of the prophecy that I shall become a Buddha).”

While I was sitting cross-legged, the inhabitants of the ten thousand universes [the Brahmas] raised a great shout: “O Sumedha, surely you will become a Buddha!”

“The omens that appeared in the past when the Bodhisattas sat cross-legged on the noble seat, those very omens appear today. Therefore, surely you will become a Buddha.”

“Cold disappears and heat is subsided. Those omens appear today; surely you will become a Buddha.”

“The ten thousand world-elements are silent and undisturbed. Those omens appear today; surely you will become a Buddha.”

“Great winds do not blow, and the rivers do not flow but stand still. Those omens appear today; surely you will become a Buddha.”

“At that time, all flowers that grow on land and in water bloom. All those flowers have bloomed today; surely you will become a Buddha.”

“Whether they be vines or trees, at that time they become heavy with fruit. All those trees have borne fruit today; surely you will become a Buddha.”

“Gems situated in the sky and gems situated on the earth shine at that time. Those gems shine today; surely you will become a Buddha.”

“Human and divine musical instruments sound of their own accord at that time. Both kinds of instruments sound melodiously today; surely you will become a Buddha.”

“At that time, variegated showers of flowers fall from the sky. Those flowers fall today; surely you will become a Buddha.”

“The great ocean swirls, and the ten thousand world-elements tremble. Both of these resound of their own accord today; surely you will become a Buddha.”
47:
“In the hells of the ten thousand worlds, the fires are extinguished at that moment. Today those fires are extinguished; you will surely and certainly become a Buddha.”

“The sun is stainless and clear, and all the stars are fully visible. Today those stars are visible; you will surely and certainly become a Buddha.”

“Even without rain, water springs forth from the earth. Today that water has sprung from the earth; you will surely and certainly become a Buddha.”

“The multitude of stars and constellations shine beautifully in the firmament; the Visākhā constellation is joined with the moon. You will surely and certainly become a Buddha.”

“Beings that live in holes and caves come out from their dwellings. Today those beings have come out from their dwellings; you will surely and certainly become a Buddha.”

“There is no discontent among beings; at that moment they are filled with contentment. Today all beings are contented; you will surely and certainly become a Buddha.”

“At that time, diseases are calmed and hunger vanishes. Today those conditions are apparent; you will surely and certainly become a Buddha.”

“At that time, lust is thin, and hatred and delusion are destroyed. Today all those defilements have disappeared; you will surely and certainly become a Buddha.”

“At that time, fear does not exist; today that absence of fear is apparent. By that sign we know: you will surely and certainly become a Buddha.”

“Dust does not fly upwards; today that condition is apparent. By that sign we know: you will surely and certainly become a Buddha.”

“Unpleasant odors depart, and divine scents waft about. Today those divine scents are wafting; you will surely and certainly become a Buddha.”

“Except for the formless Brahmas, all devas and Brahmas become visible. Today all those devas and Brahmas are visible; you will surely and certainly become a Buddha.”

“All the hells that exist become fully visible at that moment. Today all those hells are visible; you will surely and certainly become a Buddha.”
48:
“At that time, walls, doors, and rocks are no longer obstructions. Today those things have become like open space; therefore, you will surely and certainly become a Buddha.”

“At that moment, the passing away and rebirth of beings do not occur. Those omens are apparent today; therefore, you will surely and certainly become a Buddha.”

“Exert your energy firmly; do not turn back, but go forward. We also know this omen; therefore, you will surely and certainly become a Buddha.”

Having heard the words of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara and the words of the devas in the ten thousand universes, I was then filled with joy and delight, and I thought thus:

“The Buddhas do not have double speech; the Victors (Jinas) do not have empty words. There is no falsehood in the Buddhas; therefore, I shall surely and certainly become a Buddha.”

“Just as a clod thrown into the sky surely falls to the ground, even so the word of the most excellent Buddhas is sure and eternal.”

“Just as the death of all beings is sure and eternal, even so the word of the most excellent Buddhas is sure and eternal.”

“Just as the rising of the sun is sure when the night has ended, even so the word of the most excellent Buddhas is sure and eternal.”

“Just as the roar of a lion that has left its den is sure, even so the word of the most excellent Buddhas is sure and eternal.”

“Just as the laying down of the burden (childbirth) by pregnant women is sure, even so the word of the most excellent Buddhas is sure and eternal.”

“Now I shall search here and there for the qualities that make one a Buddha. I shall search in the ten directions—above, below, and all around—throughout the entire Dhamma-realm (dhammadhātu).”

Searching then, I saw the first Perfection of Generosity (dāna-pāramī), the great path followed and practiced by the Great Sages of old.

“If you wish to reach Omniscience, first firmly undertake this Perfection of Generosity and fulfill it in due order.”
49:
Just as a pot filled with water, when overturned by anyone, pours out the water completely and does not keep any water remaining within it.

In the same way, when you see supplicants—whether they be lowly, excellent, or middling—give a gift completely, like the overturned pot.

These qualities of the Perfection of Generosity alone will not be the only ones to achieve Buddhahood; I shall search for other qualities that mature Enlightenment (Bodhi).

While searching then, I saw the second, the Perfection of Virtue (Sīla-pāramī), which was practiced and followed by the Great Sages (Mahesī) of old.

If you wish to attain Enlightenment, first undertake and fulfill this second Perfection of Virtue firmly.

Just as a yak (camarī), if its tail is caught in anything, would rather face death in that very place than allow its tail to be damaged, and thus protects it.

In the same way, fulfill the virtues pertaining to the four planes; always guard your virtue just as the yak guards its tail.

These qualities alone will not be the only ones to achieve Buddhahood; I shall search for other qualities that mature Enlightenment.

While searching then, I saw the third, the Perfection of Renunciation (Nekkhamma-pāramī), which was practiced and followed by the Great Sages of old.

If you wish to attain Enlightenment, first undertake and fulfill this third Perfection of Renunciation firmly.

Just as a man who has lived long in a dungeon and is oppressed by suffering, feels no attachment to that dungeon but seeks only liberation.

In the same way, you should look upon all existences (bhava) as a dungeon; be one who is inclined toward renunciation for the sake of liberation from existence.

These qualities alone will not be the only ones to achieve Buddhahood; I shall search for other qualities that mature Enlightenment.
50:
While searching, I then saw the fourth, the Perfection of Wisdom (Paññā-pāramī), which was practiced and followed by the Great Sages of old. If you wish to reach Supreme Enlightenment (Sambodhi), undertake and fulfill this fourth Perfection of Wisdom very firmly.

Just as a monk on alms-round obtains sufficient sustenance only by not avoiding any families—whether they be lowly, excellent, or middling—and visiting them in order; in the same way, by always questioning and discussing with wise people and fulfilling the Perfection of Wisdom, you will reach Supreme Enlightenment.

These qualities alone are not yet the qualities for becoming a Buddha; I shall further search for other qualities that mature Enlightenment.

While searching, I then saw the fifth, the Perfection of Energy (Viriya-pāramī), which was practiced and followed by the Great Sages of old. If you wish to reach Supreme Enlightenment, undertake and fulfill this fifth Perfection of Energy very firmly.

Just as the lion, the king of beasts, always possesses undaunted energy and a determined mind in sitting, standing, and walking; in the same way, by exerting firm energy in all existences and fulfilling the Perfection of Energy, you will reach Supreme Enlightenment.

These qualities alone are not yet the qualities for becoming a Buddha; I shall further search for other qualities that mature Enlightenment.

While searching, I then saw the sixth, the Perfection of Patience (Khanti-pāramī), which was practiced and followed by the Great Sages of old. By undertaking this sixth Perfection of Patience very firmly and having an undivided mind in that Perfection of Patience, you will reach Supreme Enlightenment.

Just as the earth endures everything thrown upon it, whether it be a clean object or an unclean object, and that earth does not feel anger toward you...
51:
In the same way, you too should be one who can endure the honor and dishonor of all beings equally, and by reaching the Perfection of Patience, you will attain Supreme Enlightenment.

These qualities alone are not yet the qualities for becoming a Buddha; I shall search for other qualities that mature Enlightenment. While searching, I saw the seventh, the Perfection of Truthfulness (Sacca-pāramī), which was practiced and followed by the Great Sages of old. Undertake this seventh perfection firmly first; by being one without double-speech (speaking only truth) in that Perfection of Truthfulness, you will reach Supreme Enlightenment.

Just as the Osadhī star (the morning star), which is like a balance for the world including the devas, does not deviate from its fixed path during the seasons of winter, summer, or rain; in the same way, do not deviate from your path in the matters of truth; by reaching the Perfection of Truthfulness, you will attain Supreme Enlightenment.

These qualities alone are not yet the qualities for becoming a Buddha; I shall search for other qualities that mature Enlightenment. While searching, I saw the eighth, the Perfection of Determination (Adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī), which was practiced and followed by the Great Sages of old. Undertake this eighth perfection firmly first; by being one who is immovable in that Perfection of Determination, you will reach Supreme Enlightenment.

Just as a great rocky mountain stands well-established and immovable, not shaking because of fierce storms but remaining only in its place; in the same way, be one who is always immovable and firm in determination; by reaching the Perfection of Determination, you will attain Supreme Enlightenment.

These qualities alone are not yet the qualities for becoming a Buddha; I shall search for other qualities that mature Enlightenment. While searching, I saw the ninth, the Perfection of Loving-kindness (Mettā-pāramī), which was practiced and followed by the Great Sages of old.
52:
Wise Sumedha, if you desire to reach Omniscience, undertake this ninth Perfection of Loving-kindness (Mettā) very firmly; be peerless in the cultivation of loving-kindness.

Just as water spreads its coolness equally over both good and evil people, and washes away the sweat and dust-grime from their bodies.

In the same way, you too should cultivate loving-kindness equally toward those who benefit you and those who harm you; by fulfilling the Perfection of Loving-kindness to the end, you will reach Omniscience.

The qualities that make one a Buddha are not only these; I shall search for other qualities that ripen toward Omniscience.

While searching, I then saw the tenth Perfection of Equanimity (Upekkhā), which was practiced and cultivated by the Great Sages of the past.

Undertake this tenth Perfection of Equanimity firmly and continuously; by being firm and steady like the needle of a scale in both pleasure and pain, you will reach Omniscience.

Just as the earth remains indifferent toward both impure and pure things thrown upon it, being free from both anger and attachment.

In the same way, you too should always remain steady like the needle of a scale in both pleasure and pain; by fulfilling the Perfection of Equanimity to the end, you will reach Omniscience.

In this world, these ten alone are the qualities that ripen toward Omniscience; there are no other causes beyond these ten; therefore, stand firm in these ten Perfections.

As the wise Sumedha was thus contemplating the ten Perfections that make one a Buddha, by their nature, function, and characteristics, the earth in the ten-thousandfold world-system shook violently through the power of those qualities.

Because of the shaking, the great earth roared; like a sugarcane press being squeezed, or like the wheel attached to an oil mill turning and vibrating, so did the earth tremble.

All the people present at the place where the Buddha Dīpaṅkara was being offered a meal, being terrified and trembling, were unable to stand and lay on the ground in a state of confusion and fainting.
53:
In that place, thousands of pots and hundreds of large jars were smashed to pieces as they struck one another.
The multitude of people, being terrified, trembling, and fearful, with agitated hearts, came together and approached the Blessed Buddha Dīpaṅkara.

"Will there be good or evil for the world? The entire world is being oppressed by calamities; O Lord endowed with the five eyes, please dispel this danger," they pleaded.

Then the Great Sage Dīpaṅkara Buddha informed those people:
"Be at ease; do not be afraid because of this earthquake.

This person to whom I have given the prophecy today will become a Buddha in the world; he is contemplating the Perfections practiced by the Buddhas of the past.

Because he is contemplating without remainder the Perfections that are the cause of becoming a Buddha, this earth of the ten-thousandfold world-system, including the devas, has trembled."

Upon hearing the words of the Buddha, their minds became calm at that very moment; all of them approached me and paid homage once again.

I, too, having undertaken the qualities of a Buddha and made my mind firm, paid homage to the Buddha Dīpaṅkara and then rose from my seat.

When I rose from my seat, both devas and humans showered me with celestial and human flowers.

Both devas and humans also expressed their wishes for my safety and well-being:
"May you obtain that great and desired knowledge which you have aspired for today.

May all calamities be avoided; may sorrow and disease be destroyed; may there be no obstacles for you; may you quickly reach the supreme Omniscience.

Just as trees that are meant to bloom do so when the season arrives, O Great Hero (Mahāvīra), in the same way, may you blossom with the knowledge of a Buddha."
54:
Just as all the Buddhas fulfilled the ten Perfections, in the same way, O Great Hero (Ascetic Sumedha), may you also fulfill the ten Perfections.

Just as all the Buddhas realized Omniscience at the terrace of enlightenment (Bodhi-maṇḍa), in the same way, O Great Hero, may you also realize Omniscience at the foot of the victorious Bodhi tree.

Just as all the Buddhas turned the Wheel of Dhamma, in the same way, O Great Hero, may you also turn the Wheel of Dhamma.

Just as the pure moon shines beautifully on the full moon day, in the same way, may you, with a fulfilled heart, shine beautifully in the ten-thousandfold world-system.

Just as the sun, released from the mouth of Rāhu the Asura, shines brilliantly with its heat, in the same way, may you, released from the world of defilements, shine with the glory of a Buddha.

Just as all rivers flow into and gather in the great ocean, in the same way, may the world of humans and devas approach and gather near you.

That ascetic Sumedha, who was thus greatly praised and admired by those devas and humans, having well-undertaken the ten Perfections and desiring to fulfill them, then entered the great Himavanta forest.

## The Story of Sumedha is Finished.

At that time, the people of the city of Rammavatī offered a meal to the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, the leader of the world, along with the Saṅgha, and they took refuge in the Teacher Dīpaṅkara, thinking, "This Buddha is our refuge."

The Buddha Dīpaṅkara established some people in the Three Refuges; some he established in the five precepts, and others in the ten precepts.

To some, he gave the Noble Path and the four supreme Fruits; to some, he gave the peerless qualities of the fourfold Analytical Knowledge (Paṭisambhidā).

That Lord of Men, the Buddha, gave to some the eight noble Attainments (Samāpatti); to some, he gave the three types of Knowledge (Vijjā), and to others, the six higher Psychic Powers (Abhiññā).
55:
With such means, the Mahāmuni Buddha admonished the multitude of people. Because of that admonition, the Dispensation (Sāsana) of the Buddha, the Lord of the World, became widespread and extensive.

The Buddha named Dīpaṅkara, who possessed a noble jaw and shoulders as full as those of a bull king, ferried many beings across the ocean of saṃsāra and liberated them from the woeful states (duggati).

The Mahāmuni Buddha, even if a person worthy of realizing the Four Noble Truths was a hundred thousand yojanas away, would perceive them and, arriving in an instant, would enable them to realize the Truth.

At the first realization of the Truth, the Buddha enabled one hundred crores of devas and humans to realize it. At the second realization of the Truth, the Lord enabled ninety crores of devas and humans to realize it.

When the Buddha preached the Dhamma in the celestial realm, the third realization of the Truth occurred for ninety thousand crore devas.

There were three assemblies of disciples for the Teacher Dīpaṅkara. The first assembly consisted of one hundred thousand crore monks.

Again, at the Narada peak, one hundred crore Arahants, who were free from taints and whose cankers (āsavas) were exhausted, gathered to attend upon the Victorious One (Jina) who was dwelling in seclusion.

At that time, the Mahāvīra Mahāmuni Buddha observed the Vassa and performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony at Mount Sudassana together with ninety thousand crore monks.

At that time, I was an ascetic of fierce austerities, capable of traveling through the air, and a master who had reached the further shore of the five supernormal powers (abhiññā).

The realization of the Truth occurred for ten thousand and twenty thousand people. As for the realization of the Truth by one or two individuals, they were so numerous as to be beyond counting.

At that time, the Dispensation of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara was well-purified, beneficial to the masses, prosperous, flourishing, and widespread.

Four hundred thousand Arahants, possessed of the six supernormal powers and great psychic potency, constantly surrounded the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the Worlds (Lokavidū).
56:
At that time, those who abandoned human life, the trainees (sekhas) who had not yet attained Arahantship, were those to be reproached (by the Arahants).

The Dispensation, well-blossomed with such Arahants who were possessed of the quality of being firm (tādi), whose cankers were exhausted, and who were free from the taints of defilements, was beautiful in the world together with the devas.

The birth city of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara was named Rammavatī; his father was King Sudeva, and his mother was named Sumedhā.

Sumangala and Tissa were the chief disciples (aggasāvaka); the monk named Sāgata was the attendant (upaṭṭhāka) of the Teacher Dīpaṅkara.

Nandā and Sunandā were the chief female disciples (aggasāvikā); the Bodhi tree under which that Blessed One attained enlightenment is called the Pipphalī tree.

The Mahāmuni Buddha Dīpaṅkara, eighty cubits in height, was as beautiful as a shining lamp-post or like a Sal king tree in full bloom.

The bodily radiance of that Buddha spread and traveled for twelve yojanas all around.

The lifespan of that Great Sage (Mahesi) was one hundred thousand years; remaining for that long a duration, he saved a great multitude of beings.

Having illumined the True Dhamma and saved the great multitude, he, like a great mass of fire that had blazed, attained Parinibbāna together with his disciples.

That psychic power, that fame, and those marks of the wheel on his feet—all have disappeared. Are not all conditioned things (saṅkhāra) indeed empty?

After the time of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, having passed one asankheyya, the Teacher named Koṇḍañña appeared. For that Buddha also, there were three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were one hundred thousand crores; in the second, one thousand crores; and in the third, ninety crores.

At that time, the Bodhisatta was a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) named Vijitāvī and offered a great gift (mahādāna) to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, numbering one hundred thousand crores. The Teacher, having given the prophecy to the Bodhisatta, "You will become a Buddha," preached the Dhamma. That (Bodhisatta)...
57:
(The Bodhisatta), having heard the Dhamma discourse of the Teacher, renounced the kingship and ordained. That Bodhisatta, having learned the three Pitakas and developed the eight attainments (samāpatti) and five supernormal powers (abhiññā), was reborn in the Brahma realm with undiminished jhāna. As for the Buddha Koṇḍañña, his royal city was named Rammavatī; his father was the king named Sunanda; his mother was the queen named Sujātā; Bhadda and Subhadda were the two chief disciples; the one named Anuruddha was the attendant; Tissā and Upatissā were the two chief female disciples; the Bodhi tree of enlightenment was the Sālakalyāṇī tree; his body was eighty-eight cubits high; and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.

After the time of that Buddha Koṇḍañña, having passed one asankheyya, four Buddhas named Maṅgala, Sumana, Revata, and Sobhita appeared in a single aeon (kappa). Among the three assemblies of disciples of the Blessed One Maṅgala, there were one hundred thousand crore monks in the first assembly. In the second assembly, there were one thousand crore monks. In the third assembly, there were ninety crore monks. Prince Ānanda, the half-brother of that Blessed One Maṅgala, went to the presence of the Teacher together with a retinue of ninety crores for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma. The Teacher preached the gradual discourse (anupubbīkathā) to that prince. He, together with his retinue, attained Arahantship along with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). The Teacher, looking into the past practice of those clansmen and seeing the supporting condition (upanissaya) for miraculous bowls and robes, stretched out his right hand and said, "Come, monks (Ehi bhikkhavo)." At that very moment, all of them, wearing miraculous bowls and robes, became endowed with the appearance of elders of sixty years' standing, and having paid homage to the Teacher, they surrounded him. This was the third assembly of disciples of that Buddha.

While the bodily radiance of other Buddhas generally extends only eighty cubits all around, it was not so for the Buddha Maṅgala. The bodily radiance of that Blessed One remained constantly pervading ten thousand world systems (lokadhātu). Trees, earth, mountains, oceans, and so forth, down to even rice pots and the like, appeared as if covered with gold plates. His lifespan was ninety thousand years. For this duration of time, the moon, sun, and stars were unable to shine with their own light; the distinction between night and day was not apparent. Beings lived constantly by the light of the Buddha, just as people move about by the light of the sun during the day. The people of the world (could know) the distinction between night and day only by the blooming of flowers in the evening and the singing of birds in the morning.
58:
(It should be understood.) If it is asked whether other Buddhas do not have such power and majesty, it is not that they do not; they indeed have it. For those Buddhas, if they so desire, can also pervade the ten thousand world systems or even more with their radiance. However, due to the power of a past aspiration, the bodily radiance of the Blessed One Maṅgala constantly pervaded the ten thousand world systems, just like the fathom-wide radiance of other Buddhas.

While that Blessed One Maṅgala was a Bodhisatta practicing the perfections, he existed in a state similar to King Vessantara and lived with his wife and children on a mountain like Mount Vaṅka. While he was living there, a yakkha named Kharadāṭhika, hearing of the Great Being's inclination toward generosity, approached in the guise of a brahmin and asked the Great Being for his two children. The Great Being, with an exceedingly joyful heart, thinking, "I shall give my little sons to the brahmin," gave both children, causing the earth to shake as far as the ocean's edge. While the Great Being was watching, the yakkha, leaning against a support board at the end of the walkway, ate the two children like a bunch of lotus stalks. Even when the Great Being looked at the yakkha and saw his mouth vomiting a stream of blood like a flame as soon as he opened it, not even a hair's breadth of displeasure arose in him. As he thought, "My gift was indeed well-given," great joy and happiness (pīti-somanassa) arose in the body of that Great Being. He made an aspiration: "By the result of this deed of mine, in the future, let rays of light emerge from my body in this very manner." Based on that aspiration, when he became a Buddha, rays emerged from his body and pervaded such an extent of space.

There is also another past deed of that Blessed One Maṅgala. While a Bodhisatta, seeing the cetiya of a certain Buddha, he thought, "It is fitting for me to sacrifice my life for this cetiya." He had his entire body wrapped in the manner of a torch, filled a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand [pieces] with ghee, which had a bud-like center for a thousand wicks, lit the thousand wicks in that bowl, placed it on his head, set his whole body on fire, and spent the entire night circumambulating the cetiya clockwise. Even though he strove in this way until dawn, not even a single pore of his skin felt heat; it was as if he had entered the interior of a lotus. For indeed, the Dhamma protects the one who protects himself [by practicing it]. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"The Dhamma indeed protects the practitioner of Dhamma,
Well-practiced Dhamma brings happiness.
This is the benefit of well-practiced Dhamma:
The practitioner of Dhamma does not go to a state of woe."

Due to the result of such a deed, the radiance of that Blessed One's body pervaded and remained in the ten thousand world systems. In the time of that Blessed One Maṅgala, our Bodhisatta was a brahmin named Suruci. Thinking, "I shall invite the Blessed One," he approached, heard the sweet Dhamma discourse, and said, "Venerable Sir, please accept my alms tomorrow." The Blessed One asked, "Brahmin, with how many monks do you wish [to give alms]?"
59:
"The Dhamma indeed protects the practitioner of Dhamma,
Well-practiced Dhamma brings happiness.
This is the benefit of well-practiced Dhamma:
The practitioner of Dhamma does not go to a state of woe."

Due to the result of this deed as well, the bodily radiance of that Blessed One pervaded and remained in the ten thousand world systems. At that time, our Bodhisatta, having become a brahmin named Suruci, approached thinking, "I shall invite the Teacher," and after hearing the sweet Dhamma discourse, said, "Venerable Sir, please accept my alms tomorrow." When asked, "Brahmin, with how many monks do you wish [to give alms]?", he replied, "Venerable Sir, how many monks are in your retinue?" At that time, it was the first assembly of the Teacher's disciples. Therefore, he said, "One hundred thousand crores (koṭi)." He said, "Venerable Sir, please accept my alms together with all of them." The Teacher consented.

After inviting them for the next day, the brahmin Suruci, while going home, thought: "I am not unable to give gruel, rice, robes, and so on to this many monks; I am able. However, how will the seating place be?" That thought of his caused the Sakka's Paṇḍukambala-silāsana (yellow stone throne), situated eighty-four thousand yojanas above, to become hot. Sakka, reflecting, "Who indeed wishes to displace me from this seat?", looked with his divine eye and saw the Great Being. He thought, "This Suruci Brahmin has invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha and is worrying about the seating place. It is fitting for me to go there and take a share of the merit." He manifested himself in the form of a carpenter, holding an adze and an axe in his hands, and appeared before the Great Being.

He asked, "Is there any work to be done for hire for anyone?" The Great Being saw him and asked, "What work can you do?" He said, "There is no craft unknown to me. Whether it be a house or a pavilion, I know how to build whatever anyone wants built." Then [the Great Being] said, "In that case, I have work." "What is it, master?" he asked. "I have invited one hundred thousand crore monks for tomorrow. Can you build a seating pavilion for those monks?" He said, "I can build it, if you are able to pay my wages." "My dear, I am able," he replied. "Very well, I shall build it," he promised, and went to look at a certain site.
60:
That area, measuring twelve or thirteen yojanas, became a level ground like a kasina disk. Sakka, the king of devas, thought, "Let a pavilion made of the seven kinds of jewels arise in this place," and he looked upon it. At that very moment, the pavilion emerged, breaking through the earth. On its golden pillars, there were pot-shaped finials made of silver. On the silver pillars, there were golden finials. On the gem-studded pillars, there were coral finials. On the coral pillars, there were gem-studded finials. On the pillars made of the seven kinds of jewels, the finials were also made of the seven kinds of jewels.

Then he thought, "Let a network of tinkling bells hang from the edges of the pavilion," and he looked. As soon as he looked, the network of bells hung down, and when stirred by a gentle breeze, it produced a sweet sound like that of five-fold musical instruments. It was like the time of a divine musical performance. He thought, "Let garlands of incense and flowers hang at intervals." At that very moment, the garlands hung down. He thought, "Let seats and bowl-rests for a hundred thousand crores of monks emerge, breaking through the earth." At that very moment, they emerged. He thought, "Let a large water jar emerge in every corner." At that very moment, the large water jars emerged. Having created such structures, he went to the Brahmin and said, "Come, sir, look at your pavilion and give me my wage."

The Great Being went and looked at the pavilion. Even as he looked, his entire body was suffused with five-fold joy. Then, looking at the pavilion, he thought: "This pavilion was not made by a human being. Surely, because of my intention and my merit, Sakka's Paṇḍukambala stone throne must have become warm. Therefore, this pavilion must have been caused to be built by Sakka, the king of devas." He then thought, "It is not proper for me to give alms for only one day in such a pavilion; I shall give alms for seven days."

Indeed, even if an external gift is that great, it cannot satisfy the Bodhisattas. Only when they give by cutting off their decorated heads, or plucking out their eyes anointed with collyrium, or extracting the flesh of their hearts, does satisfaction arise for the Bodhisattas based on their renunciation. Even our Bodhisatta, in the Sivi Jātaka, although he gave alms daily by spending five hundred thousand coins at the four city gates and in the center of the city, that gift could not produce satisfaction. But when Sakka, the king of devas, came in the guise of a Brahmin and asked for his eyes, then those eyes...
61:
...while he was plucking them out and giving them, joy arose; there was not even a hair's breadth of alteration in his mind. Thus, there is no such thing as being satiated for Bodhisattas when it comes to giving alms. Therefore, that Great Being also thought, "It is proper for me to give alms to a hundred thousand crores of monks for seven days." He invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha to sit in that pavilion and for seven days gave the alms known as gavapāna. Gavapāna refers to a food prepared by filling large pots with milk, placing them on hearths, and into the milk cooked until thick, adding a little rice, and seasoning it with honey, granulated sugar, and ghee. Humans alone were unable to serve, so the devas also joined in to serve at every other interval. Even an area twelve or thirteen yojanas wide was not enough to accommodate the monks. However, those monks sat by their own psychic power. On the final day, he had all the monks' bowls washed and, for the sake of medicine, filled them with ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses, and offered them together with sets of triple robes. Even the cloth for the triple robes received by the most junior monk in the Saṅgha was worth a hundred thousand.

While the Teacher was performing the appreciation (anumodanā), he reflected, "This man gives such a great gift; who will he become?" Seeing that "At the end of two asankheyyas and a hundred thousand aeons in the future, he will become a Buddha named Gotama," he addressed the Great Being and prophesied: "After passing such an amount of time, you will become a Buddha named Gotama."

Upon hearing the prophecy, the Great Being thought, "It is said that I shall become a Buddha; what use is the household life to me? I shall go forth." He abandoned such wealth like a glob of spit and went forth as a monk in the presence of the Teacher. After ordaining, he learned the word of the Buddha, attained the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and meditative attainments (samāpatti), and at the end of his life, was reborn in the Brahma realm.

As for the Blessed Maṅgala, his city was named Uttara. His father was a kshatriya named Uttara, and his mother was also named Uttarā. Sudeva and Dhammasena were the two chief disciples. There was an attendant named Pālita. Sīvalī and Asokā were the two chief female disciples. The Nāga (Ironwood) tree was his Bodhi tree. His body was eighty-eight cubits high. He remained for ninety thousand years, and when that Blessed One attained Parinibbāna...
62:
Simultaneously, the ten thousand world-systems became a mass of absolute darkness. In all the world-systems, there was great weeping and wailing among humans. After the passing of that Blessed One, who had left the ten thousand world-elements in darkness, the Teacher named Sumana arose. For him, too, there were three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were one hundred thousand crores of monks. In the second, on the Golden Mountain, there were ninety thousand crores, and in the third, eighty thousand crores of monks. At that time, our Bodhisatta was a Naga king named Atula, possessed of great power and majesty. Hearing that 'a Buddha has arisen,' he emerged from the Naga realm accompanied by his kinsmen. He offered worship with celestial musical instruments to that Blessed One, who was surrounded by an assembly of one hundred thousand crores of monks. After providing a great alms-giving and offering a pair of robes to each monk, he established himself in the three refuges. That Teacher also prophesied to the Naga king, 'In the future, you will become a Buddha.' The capital city of that Blessed One was named Mekhala. King Sudatta was his father, and Sirimā was his mother. Saraṇa and Bhāvitatta were his two chief disciples. He had an attendant named Udena. Soṇā and Upasoṇā were his two female chief disciples. The Nāga tree (Ironwood) was his Bodhi tree. His body was ninety cubits in height, and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.

After the time of that Blessed One, the Teacher named Revata arose. For him, too, there were three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, the number was beyond counting. In the second assembly, there were one hundred thousand crores of monks, and likewise in the third. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a Brahmin named Atideva. Having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma teaching, he established himself in the refuges. Placing his hands in anjali on his head, he praised the Teacher’s virtue in abandoning the defilements and offered his upper robe in worship. That Buddha also prophesied to him, 'You will become a Buddha.' The capital city of that Blessed One was named Sudhaññavatī. His father was a khattiya named Vipula, and his mother was also named Vipulā. Varuṇa and Brahmadeva were his two chief disciples. He had an attendant named Sambhava. Bhaddā and Subhaddā were his two female chief disciples. The Nāga tree was his Bodhi tree. His body was eighty cubits in height, and his lifespan was sixty thousand years.
63:
After the time of that Revata Buddha, the Teacher named Sobhita arose. For him, too, there were three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were one hundred thousand crores of monks; in the second, ninety crores; and in the third, eighty crores. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a Brahmin named Ajita. Having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma teaching, he established himself in the refuges and offered a great alms-giving to the Sangha of monks headed by the Buddha. That Blessed One also prophesied to the Bodhisatta, 'You will become a Buddha.'

The capital city of that Blessed One was named Sudhamma. His father was a king named Sudhamma, and his mother was also named Sudhammā. Asama and Sunetta were his two chief disciples. He had an attendant named Anoma. Nakulā and Sujātā were his two female chief disciples. The Nāga tree was his Bodhi tree. His body was fifty-eight cubits in height, and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.

After the time of that Sobhita Buddha, after the passing of one incalculable period (asaṅkheyya), three Buddhas—Anomadassī, Paduma, and Nārada—arose in a single aeon (kappa). For the Blessed One Anomadassī, there were three assemblies of disciples. In the first, there were eight hundred thousand monks; in the second, seven hundred thousand; and in the third, six hundred thousand. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a Yakkha general of great power and majesty, the leader of many hundreds of thousands of crores of Yakkhas. Hearing that 'a Buddha has arisen,' he came and offered a great alms-giving to the Sangha of monks headed by the Buddha. The Teacher also prophesied to that Yakkha, 'In the future, you will become a Buddha.'

The capital city of the Blessed One Anomadassī was named Candavatī. King Yasavā was his father, and Queen Yasodharā was his mother. Nisabha and Anoma were his two chief disciples. He had an attendant named Varuṇa. Sundarī and Sumanā were his two female chief disciples. The Ajjuna tree was his Bodhi tree. His body was fifty-eight cubits in height, and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.

After the time of that Anomadassī Buddha, the Teacher named Paduma arose. For him, too, there were three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were one hundred thousand crores of monks; in the second, three hundred thousand; and in the third, two hundred thousand monks who resided in a great forest grove far from any village. At that time, while the Tathāgata was residing in that very forest grove, the Bodhisatta was a lion king. Seeing the Teacher who had entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), he was filled with a devout heart, paid homage, and circumambulated him to the right...
64:
Filled with joy and happiness, he roared the lion's roar three times. For seven days, without letting go of the joy centered on the Buddha, and sustained only by that blissful joy, he did not go away to search for food. Instead, he remained there, sacrificing his life in devoted service. After seven days, the Teacher emerged from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). Looking at the lion, he thought, "I will inspire faith in him towards the Saṅgha of monks as well, so that he may pay homage to the Saṅgha." He then reflected, "Let the Saṅgha of monks come." At that very moment, the monks arrived. The lion felt faith in the Saṅgha. The Teacher, seeing the lion's mind, prophesied, "In the future, you will become a Buddha."

The royal city of the Blessed One Paduma was named Campaka. King Asama was his father, and Queen Asamā was his mother. Sāla and Upasāla were the two chief disciples. The monk named Varuṇa was his attendant. Rāmā and Surāmā were the two chief female disciples. The Soṇa tree (Trumpet flower tree) was his Bodhi tree. His body was fifty-eight cubits in height, and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.

After the time of the Blessed One Paduma, the Teacher named Nārada appeared. For that Blessed One also, there were three assemblies of disciples: in the first assembly, there were one hundred thousand crores of monks; in the second, ninety thousand crores; and in the third, eighty thousand crores. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having gone forth as an ascetic and having mastered the five higher powers (abhiññā) and the eight attainments (samāpatti), gave a great gift to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha and made an offering of red sandalwood. That Blessed One Nārada also prophesied to that ascetic, "In the future, you will become a Buddha."

The royal city of that Blessed One was named Dhanyavatī. King Sudeva was his father, and Queen Anomā was his mother. Bhaddasāla and Jitamitta were the two chief disciples. The monk named Vāsiṭṭha was his attendant. Uttarā and Phagguṇī were the two chief female disciples. The great Soṇa tree was his Bodhi tree. His body was eighty-eight cubits in height, and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.

After the time of the Buddha Nārada, after one incalculable period (asaṅkheyya) had passed, one hundred thousand kappas ago from this present age, a single Buddha named Padumuttara appeared in one kappa. For that Blessed One also, there were three assemblies of disciples: in the first assembly, there were one hundred thousand crores of monks; in the second, at Mount Vebhāra, ninety thousand crores; and in the third, eighty thousand crores. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a great governor named Jatila, and to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, [he gave a gift] along with robes...
65:
(The Bodhisatta, the wealthy man Jatila) gave the gift. That Blessed One Padumuttara also prophesied to that wealthy man, "In the future, you will become a Buddha." During the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, there were no heretics (titthiyas); all devas and humans took refuge only in the Buddha.
