Because those states like lust that cause lamentation do not exist in them by way of the aforementioned association or being abandoned together, they are called araṇa.

## Explanation of the Suttantika Dyad Matrix Terms

101-108. In the Suttantika dyads, because they resort to knowledge (vijjā) by way of association, they are called vijjābhāgī (partaking of knowledge). Because they exist in the portion or category of knowledge, they are also called vijjābhāgī. In this term vijjābhāgī, there are eight kinds of knowledge: insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa), mind-made power (manomayiddhi), and the six supernormal powers (abhiññā). By the first-mentioned sense, the states associated with those eight kinds of knowledge are also called vijjābhāgī. By the second-mentioned sense, any one unspecified knowledge among those eight is called vijjā, while the remaining ones are called vijjābhāgī. Thus, both the knowledges themselves and the states associated with knowledge should be understood as vijjābhāgī. However, in this dyad, only the associated states are intended. Because they resort to ignorance (avijjā) only by way of association, they are called avijjābhāgī (partaking of ignorance). Because they exist in the portion or category of ignorance, they are also called avijjābhāgī. In this term avijjābhāgī, there are four kinds of ignorance: the delusion that conceals the truth of suffering, and the delusions that conceal the truth of the origin, etc. Just as in the previous method, the states associated with those four kinds of ignorance are also called avijjābhāgī. Among those four kinds of ignorance, any one unspecified ignorance is called avijjā, while the remaining ones are called avijjābhāgī. Thus, both the ignorances themselves and the states associated with ignorance should be understood as avijjābhāgī. However, in this dyad, only the associated states are intended.

Furthermore, because they are unable to overwhelm the darkness of defilements and thus cannot destroy them, the three lower paths are called vijjūpama, having an illustration like lightning. Because it is capable of destroying the darkness of defilements without remainder, the path of Arahatship is called vajirūpama, having an illustration like a diamond weapon (thunderbolt). Unwholesome states are called bāla (foolish) because they reside in fools, or because they take the name of the fool. Wholesome states are called paṇḍita (wise) because they reside in the wise, or because they take the name of the wise. Alternatively, they are called bāla because they make one a fool, and paṇḍita because they make one wise. Because they make the mind lack radiance, they are called kaṇha (dark states). As for sukka (bright states)...
94:
Bright states make the mind radiant and brilliant. They are called kaṇha (dark) because they are the cause of a dark birth (rebirth in the woeful planes), or because they are the cause of the life of a poor person who is destitute of clothing. They are called sukka (bright) because they are the cause of a bright birth (rebirth in a happy destination). Because they cause burning in this life and in the life to come, they are called tapanīya. States that do not cause burning are called atapanīya.

The three dyads starting with the Designation Dyad (adhivacana-duka) do not differ in meaning; only the phrasing and syllables differ here. Terms like Sirivaḍḍhaka and Dhanavaḍḍhaka (applied to slaves, etc.) are called adhivacana (designation) because they arise based on mere words without having a true corresponding meaning. The grounds (meanings) of designations are called adhivacana-patha. 'Bhikkhus, they are called saṅkhāra because they process [conditioned things]'; such expressions (abhilāpa) that are stated with their reasons and derivations are called nirutti (language/expression). The grounds (meanings) of expressions are called nirutti-patha. Because they make things known in various ways such as takka (reasoning), vitakka (thought), and saṅkappa (intention), they are called paññatti (concept/description). The grounds (meanings) of concepts are called paññatti-patha. In this context, although only one dyad is taught, the purpose of teaching the remaining dyads should be understood in the same way as stated in the Root Cluster (hetu-gocchaka).

109-118. In the Name and Form dyad, it is called 'Name' (nāma) because of the sense of making a name, the sense of bending towards an object, or the sense of making the object bend towards itself. It is called 'Form' (rūpa) because of the sense of being deformed. This is a brief explanation here. The detailed explanation will become clear in the Nikkhepa-kaṇḍa (Summary Section). Ignorance (avijjā) is non-knowledge (aññāṇa) regarding the truth of suffering and so on. Craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā) is the longing for existence. Eternalist view (bhava-diṭṭhi) is the view that arises with the belief in eternity regarding existence, which is called bhava (becoming/existence). Annihilationist view (vibhava-diṭṭhi) is the view that arises with the belief in annihilation regarding non-existence, which is called vibhava. The view that occurs as 'the self and the world are eternal' is the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi). The view that occurs as 'it will be annihilated' is the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi). The view that occurs as 'it has an end' is the finite view (antavā-diṭṭhi). The view that occurs as 'it has no end' is the infinite view (anantavā-diṭṭhi). The view that follows after the beginning (the past) is the view following the past (pubbantānudiṭṭhi). The view that follows after the end (the future) is the view following the future (aparantānudiṭṭhi). Shamelessness (ahirika) is the state of being without shame, explained in detail as not being ashamed of what one should be ashamed of. Fearlessness of wrongdoing (anottappa) is the state of not being afraid, explained in detail as not being afraid of what one should be afraid of. Being ashamed is hiri; being afraid is ottappa. In the dyads starting with unruliness (dovacassatā), a person is 'difficult to speak to' (dubbaca) when they are difficult to talk to because they take a contrary position, delight in opposition, or show no respect. The action of such a difficult person is dovacassa. The state of that is dovacassatā. Because base persons such as those without faith (assaddha) are the friends of this person, he is called 'one with evil friends' (pāpamitta). The state of that is pāpamittatā. Unruliness (sovacassatā) and good friendship (kalyāṇamittatā) should be understood by way of the opposite of the method already mentioned.
95:
119-123. "The five groups of offenses are also called offenses; the seven groups of offenses are also called offenses." Skillfulness in these offenses as stated is called skillfulness in offenses (āpattikusala). Skillfulness in rehabilitation from those offenses is called skillfulness in rehabilitation from offenses (āpattivutthānakusala). Skillfulness in attainments is called skillfulness in attainments (samāpattikusala). This is a name for the wisdom that knows the delimitation of the absorption (appanā) of attainments. Skillfulness in emerging from attainments is called skillfulness in emerging from attainments (samāpattivutthānakusala). Skillfulness in the eighteen elements is called skillfulness in elements (dhātukusala). Skillfulness in attending to the characteristics, functions, manifestations, proximate causes, and so forth of those elements is called skillfulness in attention (manasikārakusala). Skillfulness in the eye-base and so forth is called skillfulness in bases (āyatanakusala). Skillfulness in the twelve-linked dependent origination is called skillfulness in dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppādakusala). Skillfulness in various causes is called skillfulness in causes (ṭhānakusala). A cause is called ṭhāna. In that cause, the result is said to 'stand' because it occurs depending on that cause; therefore, it is called ṭhāna (standing/place). Skillfulness in what is not a cause is called skillfulness in non-causes (aṭṭhānakusala).

124-134. The state of being upright is uprightness (ajjava). The state of being gentle is gentleness (maddava). The state of being patient, known as forbearance, is patience (khanti). The state of one who delights in the three beautiful conducts is composure (soracca). The state of being gentle and pleasant, which causes harmonious joy, is amenability (sākhalya). Conciliation through Dhamma or material things so that one's own faults do not exist along with others is hospitality (paṭisanthāra). The state of having unguarded doors in the six sense faculties, including the mind, which is called the destruction of sense restraint, is unguardedness of the sense doors (indriyesu aguttadvāratā). The state of not knowing the measure in receiving and consuming food is immoderation in eating (bhojane amattaññutā). The subsequent dyad should be understood by the opposite method of what has been stated. The state of being forgetful, called the loss of mindfulness, is forgetfulness (muṭṭhassacca). The state of not knowing thoroughly is lack of clear comprehension (asampajañña). It is called mindfulness (sati) because it remembers. It is called clear comprehension (sampajañña) because it knows thoroughly. The power called reflection, in the sense of being unshakable in non-reflection, is the power of reflection (paṭisaṅkhānabala). The power that arises in one who develops the seven factors of enlightenment, making energy the leader, is the power of development (bhāvanābala). It is called tranquility (samatha) because it calms opposing states. It is called insight (vipassanā) because it sees in various ways through aspects such as impermanence. The sign of tranquility (samathanimitta) is so called because the previous tranquility itself is the cause for the subsequent tranquility. The same method applies to the sign of exertion (paggāhanimitta). It is called exertion (paggāha) because it upholds associated states. It is called non-distraction (avikkhepa) because it does not allow the mind to wander.

135-142. The failure of virtue, called non-restraint, which destroys virtue, is failure in virtue (sīlavipatti). The failure of view, called wrong view, which destroys right view, is failure in view (diṭṭhivipatti).
96:
Accomplishment in virtue (sīlasampadā) is composure (soracca) itself, because it fulfills and completes virtue. The wisdom that is the cause for the fulfillment of view is accomplishment in view (diṭṭhisampadā). The purity of virtue, called virtue that has reached the state of purity, is purity of virtue (sīlavisuddhi). The purity of view, called vision (wisdom) capable of leading to the purity called Nibbāna, is purity of view (diṭṭhivisuddhi).

"Purity of view and the effort of one who strives according to that view" (diṭṭhivisuddhi kho pana yathādiṭṭhissa ca padhānaṃ) means both the purity of view, called the knowledge of ownership of kamma and so forth, and the effort (padhāna) associated with that wisdom of one who strives in accordance with the view that has arisen.

"Spiritual urgency" (saṃvega) is the agitation called fear arising based on birth and so forth. "Grounds for urgency" (saṃvejanīyaṭṭhāna) are the causes such as birth and so forth that produce spiritual urgency. "The wise effort of one who has felt urgency" (saṃviggassa ca yoniso padhānaṃ) is the striving through the right means by one in whom such urgency has arisen.

"Dissatisfaction with wholesome states" (asantuṭṭhitā ca kusalesu dhammesu) is the state of not being content while fulfilling wholesome deeds. "Unfaltering effort" (appaṭivānitā ca padhānasmiṃ) is the state of not turning back from striving until reaching the fruit of Arahantship.

It is called knowledge (vijjā) because it knows. It is called liberation (vimutti) because it is liberated.

"Knowledge of destruction" (khaye ñāṇaṃ) is the knowledge in the Noble Path that destroys defilements. "Knowledge of non-arising" (anuppāde ñāṇaṃ) is the knowledge in the Noble Fruit that arises at the conclusion of the non-arising of those respective defilements abandoned by the paths, which have reached the state of non-arising in terms of rebirth.

This is the sequential explanation of the terms of the Matika.

## The Explanation of the Terms of the Dyad Matika is finished.
97:
## Analysis of Wholesome States of the Sense Sphere

Now, in order to show the states summarized in the established Mātikā by way of their divisions, the Blessed One began this Word-by-word Analysis (Padabhājanīya) starting with "Which states are wholesome?" (Katamē dhammā kusalā?). In that analysis, sense-sphere wholesome states are shown first with the words "At a time when a wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere has arisen" (Yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti). In the exposition (niddesa) of those sense-sphere wholesome states, there are three great sections: the Section on the Determination of States (Dhamma-vavatthāna-vāra), the Section on Summary (Saṅgaha-vāra), and the Section on Emptiness (Suññata-vāra). Among these, the Section on the Determination of States is divided into two parts: the Brief Statement (Uddesa) and the Exposition (Niddesa). In the Brief Statement (Uddesa-vāra), there are four divisions: the Question (Pucchā), the Exposition of the Occasion (Samaya-niddesa), the Brief Statement of States (Dhamma-uddesa), and the Conclusion (Appanā). Among these four, the words "Which states are wholesome?" (Katamē dhammā kusalā?) are called the Question. The sequence of words "At a time when... at that time" (Yasmiṃ samaye... tasmiṃ samaye) is called the Exposition of the Occasion. The sequence of words "There is contact... there is non-distraction" (Phasso hoti... avikkhepo hoti) is called the Brief Statement of States. The words "Or whatever other incorporeal states are dependently arisen at that time—these states are wholesome" (Ye vā pana tasmiṃ samaye... ime dhammā kusalā) are called the Conclusion.

In the Brief Statement (Uddesa-vāra) which is established by these four divisions, the first division, the Question "Which states are wholesome?", is called the Question from a Desire to Explain (Kathetukamyatā-pucchā), as it arises from the wish to speak. There are five types of questions: the Question to Illuminate what is Not Seen (Adiṭṭha-jotana-pucchā), the Question to Compare what is Seen (Diṭṭha-saṃsandana-pucchā), the Question to Cut off Doubt (Vimati-cchedana-pucchā), the Question to Gain Consent (Anumati-pucchā), and the Question from a Desire to Explain (Kathetukamyatā-pucchā). Their distinctions are as follows:

What is the Question to Illuminate what is Not Seen? By nature, the characteristic [of a thing] is not yet known, not yet seen (by wisdom), not yet weighed, not yet scrutinized, not yet manifest to knowledge, and not yet made clear by knowledge. One asks a question for the purpose of knowing, seeing, weighing, scrutinizing, making manifest to knowledge, and making clear by knowledge that characteristic. This is called the Question to Illuminate what is Not Seen.

What is the Question to Compare what is Seen? By nature, the characteristic is already known, seen, weighed, scrutinized, manifest to knowledge, and made clear by knowledge. That person asks a question for the purpose of comparing and cross-checking with other wise people. This is called the Question to Compare what is Seen.
98:
What is the Question to Cut off Doubt (Vimati-cchedana-pucchā)? By nature, one who has fallen into doubt and uncertainty, being of two minds: "Is it thus? Is it not thus? What is it? How is it?" asks a question for the purpose of cutting off that doubt. This is called the Question to Cut off Doubt.

What is the Question to Gain Consent (Anumati-pucchā)? The Blessed One asks a question to gain the consent of the monks: "What do you think, monks, is form permanent or impermanent?" "Impermanent, Bhante." "Is that which is impermanent painful or pleasant?" "Painful, Bhante." "Is it fitting to regard that which is impermanent, painful, and subject to change as 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'?" "No, Bhante." This is called the Question to Gain Consent.

What is the Question from a Desire to Explain (Kathetukamyatā-pucchā)? The Blessed One asks a question from a desire to explain to the monks: "Monks, there are these four foundations of mindfulness. Which four?" This is called the Question from a Desire to Explain.

Among those questions, the first three types (Adiṭṭha-jotana, Diṭṭha-saṃsandana, and Vimati-cchedana) do not exist for the Buddhas. Why? Because for the Buddhas, there is nothing—whether a conditioned state (saṅkhata) within the three periods of time or an unconditioned state (asaṅkhata) liberated from time—that is unknown, unseen, unilluminated, unweighed, unscrutinized, unmanifest, or not made clear by knowledge. Therefore, the Question to Illuminate what is Not Seen does not exist for them. Since there is no need for the Blessed One to compare or cross-check the states he has penetrated with his own knowledge with other recluses, brahmins, devas, Māras, or Brahmās, the Question to Compare what is Seen does not exist for him. Since he is one who is free from perplexity, has crossed over doubt, and has removed doubt in all states, the Question to Cut off Doubt does not exist for him. Only the remaining two types of questions exist for the Blessed One. Among those two, this question ("Which states are wholesome?") should be understood as the Question from a Desire to Explain.

In those [words "Which states are wholesome?"], the states to be explained in detail are asked by the word "Which" (Katamē). By the mere words "states are wholesome" (dhammā kusalā), it is not possible to know "What kind of states are made?" or "What do they do?". Only when "Which" (Katamē) is said, is the fact that those states are being questioned understood. Therefore, it is said, "The states to be explained in detail are asked by the word 'Katamē'." By the two words "states are wholesome" (dhammā kusalā), the states asked in the question are shown. The meaning of those words has already been explained below (in the commentary on the Wholesome Triad).

Why, in this Exposition Section (Niddesa-vāra), is the word order "dhammā kusalā" used instead of "kusalā dhammā" as in the Mātikā? It is because [the teacher] wishes to show the states through their divisions, such as wholesome, and to show the states that possess those divisions. In this Abhidhamma, only ultimate realities (paramattha-dhamma) are to be taught. And those states have many divisions such as wholesome and so on. Therefore, in this Abhidhamma, only the states...
99:
They should be taught. This exposition is not a conventional teaching (vohāra-desanā). These states are also taught by way of many classifications, and not merely as phenomena. Because teaching by way of classification brings about the analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa) that dissects compactness, the Buddha showed the teaching of states by way of classification as 'Wholesome states' (kusalā dhammā). Now, in order to show those states that should be taught by that classification, it should be understood that this sequence of words, 'Which states are wholesome?' (katame dhammā kusalā), was made. For only when the states that possess classifications are shown, does the classification being shown become appropriate and easy to understand.

Now, in this phrase, 'At which time a wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere...' (yasmiṃ samaye kāမာvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ):
The Sage, having defined the occasion (samaya) by means of the consciousness, showed the consciousness in that occasion, in order to show the states therein by way of classification.

In showing 'At which time a wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere...', the Blessed One showed the consciousness in the occasion. For what reason? Having defined the occasion at the end of that consciousness which was defined by that occasion as 'at that time' (tasmiṃ samaye), even though there are various occasions, He intended to make known the states such as contact (phassa) and feeling (vedanā) which have classifications that are difficult to understand due to the compactness of continuity, group, function, and object, in that occasion defined by consciousness, in this manner: 'at whichever occasion consciousness arises, at that very occasion contact arises, feeling arises.'

Now, in these words 'At which time' (yasmiṃ samaye) etc., this is the sequential explanation of words. 'Yasmiṃ' is an indefinite locative designation. 'Samaye' is the clarification of the occasion designated indefinitely. By this much, the occasion is designated indefinitely. Therein, the word 'samaya' is seen in the senses of:
Confluence (samavāya), occasion (khaṇa), time (kāla), group (samūha), cause (hetu), view (diṭṭhi), acquisition (paṭilābha), abandonment (pahāna), and penetration (paṭivedha).

Indeed, in such passages as, 'Perhaps even tomorrow we might approach, depending on the time and the confluence of conditions' (D. Ni. 1.447), it has the meaning of confluence (samavāya). In such passages as, 'Monks, there is only one occasion and time for living the holy life' (A. Ni. 8.29), it means occasion (khaṇa). In such passages as, 'The hot time, the feverish time' (Pāci. 358), it means time (kāla). In such passages as, 'The great assembly (mahāsamaya) in the forest', it means group (samūha). In such passages as, 'Bhaddāli, that cause was also not penetrated by you'...
100:
"...Bhaddāli, the Blessed One is staying in Sāvatthī; the Blessed One will also know me as 'the bhikkhu named Bhaddāli is one who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher's Dispensation.' Bhaddāli, this cause (hetu) was also not penetrated by you" etc. (M. Ni. 2.135), it refers to the sense of cause (hetu). In such passages as, "At that time, the wanderer Uggāhamāna, the son of the shaven-headed female ascetic, who was a proponent of [various] views (samayappavādaka), was residing in the Mallikā park which had a fence of Tinduka trees and a single hall" etc. (M. Ni. 2.260), it refers to the sense of view (diṭṭhi).

"The benefit that is in the present life, and the benefit that is in the future life; because of the acquisition (abhisamaya) of these two benefits, the steadfast one is called wise" (S. Ni. 1.129) etc., it refers to the sense of acquisition (paṭilābha). "By the complete penetration (abhisamaya) of conceit, he has made an end of suffering" (M. Ni. 1.28) etc., it refers to the sense of abandonment (pahāna). "The sense of oppression of suffering, the sense of being conditioned, the sense of burning, the sense of change, the sense of penetration (abhisamaya)" (Paṭi. M. 2.8) etc., it refers to the sense of penetration (paṭivedha). Among these many [meanings of] samaya—

Confluence (samavāya), occasion (khaṇa), time (kāla), group (samūha), and cause (hetu)—these five [meanings of] samaya should be understood by the wise in this Dispensation.

In this context of wholesome states, "At which time a wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere arises," among those nine meanings of samaya, these five meanings starting with confluence (samavāya) should be understood by the wise.

Among those five, the harmony of conditions is called confluence (samavāya). As for occasion (khaṇa), it should be understood either as the single ninth occasion (the occasion of a Buddha's arising) or as the four wheels (the wheels of blessing).

That harmony of conditions which exists by way of producing a common result is to be understood here as confluence (samavāya). That ninth occasion alone, which was spoken of as, "Monks, there is only one occasion (khaṇa) and time (samaya) for living the holy life" (A. Ni. 8.29), should be understood as the single occasion. Otherwise, it refers to the four wheels spoken of as, "Monks, there are these four wheels; for the devas and humans who are endowed with them, the four wheels revolve," namely: "residing in a suitable locality, associating with good people, right self-direction, and having performed merit in the past" (A. Ni. 4.31).
101:
Alternatively, these four [wheels of prosperity] taken together are to be understood as 'moment' (khaṇa) in the sense of opportunity. For these wheels serve as the opportunity (locus) for the arising of wholesome states.

Having thus understood conjunction (samavāya) and moment (khaṇa), among the remaining [time, assemblage, and cause]:

That which is designated depending on various causes and is a mere conventional expression is called 'time' (kāla); the assemblage of states such as contact (phassa) and so forth is clearly shown as 'assemblage' (samūha).

In detail—time is designated depending on various causes such as: depending on states as in 'time of mind, time of matter'; depending on the occurrence of states as in 'past, future'; depending on the succession of states as in 'time of seed, time of sprout'; depending on the characteristics of states as in 'time of arising, time of decay'; depending on the functions of states as in 'time of feeling, time of perceiving'; depending on the activities of beings as in 'time of bathing, time of drinking'; depending on postures as in 'time of going, time of standing'; depending on the rotation of the moon and sun as in 'morning, evening, day, night'; and depending on the accumulation of time consisting of days and nights as in 'half-month, month'. Such is called 'time' (kāla). It should be understood that this time is a mere designation (paññatti), as it does not exist by way of ultimate reality (sabhāva). The assemblage of states such as contact (phassa) and feeling (vedanā) is clearly shown here as 'assemblage' (samūha). Having thus understood time (kāla) and assemblage (samūha), as for the remaining 'cause' (hetu):

In this context, 'cause' (hetu) is simply condition (paccaya);
Its multiplicity should be understood by way of doors or by way of conditions.

In this context, condition alone is called 'cause' (hetu). Its multiplicity should be understood by way of doors or by way of conditions. How is it to be understood? For eye-consciousness and so forth arising in the eye-door and so forth, there are conditions such as the eye-sensitivity, visible object, light, and attention. In the Great Treatise (Mahāpakaraṇa [Paṭṭhāna]), twenty-four conditions are taught, starting with 'root-condition' (hetu-paccaya) and 'object-condition' (ārammaṇa-paccaya). Among those twenty-four conditions, excluding the resultant condition (vipāka-paccaya) and the post-nascent condition (pacchājāta-paccaya), the remaining [twenty-two] are indeed conditions for wholesome states. All these are intended here as 'cause' (hetu). Thus, its multiplicity by way of doors or by way of conditions...
102:
...should be understood. Thus, it should be understood that these five meanings, starting with conjunction (samavāya), are encompassed here by the word 'samaya'.

Question: "Why, among these five meanings, are all of them encompassed instead of taking any single one?" Answer: "Because each specific meaning of samaya illustrates a particular distinction of meaning. Among these five, samaya in the sense of conjunction (samavāya) illustrates the occurrence [of states] due to multiple causes. By illustrating occurrence due to multiple causes, the doctrine of a single cause (ekakāraṇavāda) is refuted. Furthermore, what is called conjunction (samavāya) involves mutual dependence in producing a common result. Therefore, it also illustrates the meaning that 'there is no such thing as a single creator (such as Brahmā or Viṣṇu).' For when causes exist by their own nature, it is improper to ignore the dependence on other causes. By thus illustrating the absence of any single cause, false views such as 'happiness and suffering are self-created' are refuted."

In that regard, there might be an objection: "The statement that it illustrates occurrence due to multiple causes is incorrect." "For what reason?" "Because things that are not causes when not in harmony remain non-causes even when in harmony." "Indeed, if one blind man cannot see, a hundred blind men together still cannot see." This [objection] is not correct. The state that exists as a cause capable of producing a common result is what is called harmony (sāmaggī); it is not merely the meeting of many things. And the seeing of blind men is not a common result. "Why?" "Because even when there are a hundred blind men, that seeing does not exist. However, seeing is the common result of the eye and so forth, because it exists when they are present. The fact that the eye and so forth, which are not causes when not in harmony, become causes when in harmony is well-established (as in the case of carrying a palanquin). That state of being a cause should be understood by the absence of the result when not in harmony, and by its presence when in harmony. The absence of eye-consciousness etc. when the eye etc. are deficient, and their presence when not deficient, is evident to the world through direct perception." This is the meaning illustrated by samaya in the sense of conjunction (samavāya).

As for the ninth moment (khaṇa) which excludes the eight inopportune moments (akkhaṇa), and the moment spoken of in the sense of opportunity known as the four wheels (catucakka) such as living in a suitable locality—that moment cannot exist without the harmony of moments (khaṇasāmaggī) such as human birth, the arising of a Buddha, and the endurance of the True Dhamma. The rarity of human birth and so forth is taught through similes such as the blind turtle. Thus, because the moment is difficult to obtain, the wholesome state connected with the moment, which is a support for supramundane states...
103:
Wholesome states are indeed difficult to obtain. Thus, among these (five types of) occasions (samaya) such as concordance (samavāya), the occasion known as the 'moment' (khaṇa) illustrates the rarity of the arising of the wholesome. By illustrating this, it serves to prohibit the negligent living of those who, despite having attained the moment, fail to exert effort in that wholesome practice which is dependent on the moment, thereby making the moment in vain. This is the explanation shown by the occasion known as the 'moment'.

The period of occurrence of that wholesome consciousness is extremely brief. This extreme brevity should be understood by the power of the commentary on this Sutta: "Monks, just as the speed of that (swift) man, just as the speed of the moon and sun, just as the speed of the deities who run ahead of the moon and sun—life-formations (āyusaṅkhāra) perish even swifter than that" (Saṃ. Ni. 2.228). In that commentary, the duration of the material life faculty (rūpajīvitindriya) is said to be very brief. Within the duration that a present material form lasts, sixteen consciousnesses arise and perish. Thus, because the duration of those consciousnesses is so brief, there is not even a simile for it. Therefore, it was said: "Monks, it is not easy to give a simile for how quickly changing (lahuparivatta) the mind is" (A. Ni. 1.48). Thus, among these occasions, the occasion known as 'time' (kāla) illustrates the extreme brevity of the period of occurrence of the wholesome consciousness. By illustrating this, because it is such an extremely brief time, like threading a pearl by the light of a flash of lightning, this mind is difficult to penetrate; therefore, it serves as an instruction that great effort and care must be applied in the penetration of that mind. This is the explanation shown by the occasion known as 'time'.

The occasion known as 'collection' (samūha) illustrates the co-arising of many states. A heap of states such as contact (phassa) and so on is called a 'collection' (samūha). Since the consciousness arising in that collection arises together with those states, the co-arising of many states is illustrated. By illustrating this, the arising of a single state alone is prohibited. This is the explanation shown by the occasion known as 'collection'.

The occasion known as 'cause' (hetu) illustrates the state of being dependent on others (causes). For the meaning of the phrase 'yasmiṃ samaye' (at which time) is 'when there is a certain cause,' it illustrates the state of being dependent on others because it occurs only when a cause exists.
104:
By illustrating this (cause), this word 'samaya' serves to prohibit the false pride of thinking that states occur according to one's own will. This is the explanation shown by the occasion known as 'cause'. In that phrase 'yasmiṃ samaye', by the power of the occasion known as 'time', it means 'at which time'. By the power of the occasion known as 'collection' (samūha), it means 'in which collection'. By the power of the occasions known as 'moment', 'concordance' (samavāya), and 'cause' (hetu), the meaning should be understood as: 'When there is a certain moment, when there is a certain concordance of causes, when there is a certain cause (such as wise attention), sense-sphere wholesome consciousness arises; when it thus arises, contact and other states also arise.' Indeed, the occasions known as 'time' and 'collection' are the basis (adhikaraṇa) (of states). Therefore, the locative case (bhumma) is used here in the sense of the basis for the states mentioned in that occasion. Because the arising of those states is marked by the presence of the occasions known as 'moment', 'concordance', and 'cause', the locative case is used here in the sense of 'a state by which another state is marked' (bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇa).

'Sense-sphere' (kāmāvacara) refers to states included among the sense-sphere states mentioned in the following manner: 'Which states are sense-sphere? Making a limit from the Avīci hell below up to the Paranimmita-vasavatti heaven above' (Dha. Sa. 1287), and so forth. The definition of that word is: briefly, sensuality (kāma) is of two kinds: objective sensuality (vatthukāma) and the defilement of sensuality (kilesakāma). Between those two, the defilement of sensuality is essentially desire-and-lust (chandarāga), while objective sensuality is the round of existence (vaṭṭa) in the three planes. Here, the defilement of sensuality is called 'kāma' because it desires (kāmetīti kāmo); the other, objective sensuality, is called 'kāma' because it is desired (kāmiyatīti kāmo). The place where these two kinds of sensuality frequent by way of occurrence is the elevenfold place consisting of the four woeful planes, the human realm, and the six deva realms. Because sensuality frequents this place, it is called 'sense-sphere' (kāmāvacara), just like 'sassatthāvacara' (a place frequented by those bearing weapons). For example, just as a place where men bearing weapons frequent is called 'sassatthāvacara' even though other two-footed and four-footed creatures are present, because it is characterized by those men; so too, even though other fine-material sphere states and so on are present in these eleven sense-realms, this place is called 'kāmāvacara' because it is characterized by sense-states. In this word 'kāmāvacara', just as 'rūpabhava' is called 'rūpa' by dropping the latter word, it is also called 'kāma' by dropping the latter word 'avacara'. Thus, this consciousness is called 'kāmāvacara' because it frequents this sensuality known as the elevenfold place.

Although this consciousness also frequents the fine-material and immaterial planes of existence, just as a noble elephant that has received the name 'battle-frequenting' (saṅgāmāvacara) because it frequents the battlefield is still called 'battle-frequenting' even when moving in the city, and just as creatures that frequent land and water...
105:
Just as beings are called 'land-dwellers' or 'water-dwellers' even when they are in places that are neither land nor water, so too this consciousness should be understood as 'sense-sphere' (kāmāvacara) even when it wanders elsewhere (in the fine-material or immaterial planes). Alternatively, it is called 'sense-sphere' because desire (kāma) wanders within it by way of making it an object. Although desire wanders in the fine-material and immaterial spheres as well, just as not every creature that lows is called a 'calf' (vaccha) and not every creature that sleeps on the ground is called a 'buffalo' (mahiṃsa), so should this be understood. Furthermore, it is called 'sense-sphere' because it causes rebirth in the sense-existence known as the sense-sphere.

'Wholesome' (kusala) is so called because of meanings such as shaking or destroying contemptible (unwholesome) states. Alternatively, it is wholesome because of the sense of health (ārogya), the sense of faultlessness (anavajja), and the sense of being produced by skill (kosalla-sambhūta). Just as in the passage, 'Is the venerable one healthy (kusala)?', the word 'wholesome' is used in the sense of health, meaning the absence of illness or disease in the physical body, so too in mental states, it should be understood as wholesome in the sense of health due to the absence of the illness of defilements and the disease of defilements. It is wholesome in the sense of faultlessness because of the absence of the fault of defilements and the distress of defilements. Wisdom is called 'skill' (kosalla); because it is produced from that skill, it is wholesome in the sense of being produced by skill.

Granted that consciousness associated with knowledge (ñāṇa-sampayutta) is wholesome in the sense of being produced by skill, how is consciousness dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇa-vippayutta) wholesome? That too is wholesome by way of conventional usage (ruḷhī). For example, even if a fan is made of mats and not palm leaves, it is still called a 'palm-leaf fan' (tālavaṇṭa) because of its resemblance; similarly, consciousness dissociated from knowledge should be understood as wholesome. Strictly speaking, consciousness associated with knowledge receives the name 'wholesome' through all three senses—health, faultlessness, and being produced by skill—whereas consciousness dissociated from knowledge does so through only two senses (health and faultlessness). Thus, whatever is described as wholesome according to the Jātaka method, the Bāhitika Sutta method, and the Abhidhamma method, all of it possesses these three meanings in this consciousness.

By way of characteristics and so on, this wholesome state has the characteristic of being faultless and having a happy result, the function (rasa) of destroying the unwholesome, the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) of purity, and the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of wise attention (yoniso manasikāra). Alternatively, it has the characteristic of faultlessness because it is the opposite of fault, the function of being pure, the manifestation of having a desired result, and the same proximate cause as mentioned. Among characteristics and so on, the individual essence (sabhāva) or the general nature (sāmañña) of states is called 'characteristic' (lakkhaṇa). The task (kicca) or achievement (sampatti) is called 'function' (rasa). The mode of appearance or the fruit is called 'manifestation' (paccupaṭṭhāna). The immediate cause is called 'proximate cause' (padaṭṭhāna). Thus, wherever characteristics and so on are mentioned hereafter, the distinction of those states should be understood in this very manner.
106:
'Consciousness' (citta) is so called because it thinks of (cognizes) an object. The meaning of 'it cognizes' (vijānāti) is the same as 'it thinks' (cinteti). Alternatively, since the word 'citta' is common to all consciousness, among these, mundane wholesome, unwholesome, and great functional consciousness are called 'citta' because they accumulate (cinoti) their own continuity by way of the javana process through conditions such as repetition (āsevana). Resultant consciousness is called 'citta' because it is accumulated (cita) by kamma and defilements. Furthermore, all consciousness is called 'citta' because of its variegated nature (cittatā) according to its own circumstances. It is also called 'citta' because it performs variegated actions such as painting, or because it produces variegated results such as the realms of rebirth; thus should the meaning be understood in this term 'citta'. Among those types of consciousness, consciousness accompanied by lust is of one kind, consciousness accompanied by hatred is another, and consciousness accompanied by delusion is another. They also differ as sense-sphere consciousness, fine-material sphere consciousness, and so on; or as consciousness having a visible form as object, consciousness having a sound as object, and so on. Among those having a visible form as object, they differ as having a blue object, a yellow object, and so on. The same method applies to objects such as sound. Among all these, some are inferior, some are medium, and some are superior. Among the inferior and so on, some have desire as the predominant factor (adhipati), some have energy, some have consciousness, and some have investigation. Therefore, the variegated nature of this consciousness should be understood by way of associated states, planes, objects, and the qualities of being inferior, medium, superior, and predominant. Even if a single consciousness here is not variegated in this way, because it is included within the category of variegated consciousness, any one of them may be called 'citta' due to its variegated nature. Thus it is 'citta' because of its variegated nature.

How is it 'citta' because it performs variegated actions? In the world, there is no variegated work more extraordinary than the art of painting. Among such paintings, the one known as the 'Caraṇa' (wandering) painting is exceedingly variegated. For the painters who create that Caraṇa painting, a variegated perception (saññā) arises: 'Such and such figures must be made here.' Due to that variegated perception, variegated mental activities arise which accomplish the sketching, coloring, polishing, and detailing. Then, a certain variegated figure is completed in the painting called Caraṇa. After that figure is finished, they think, 'Let this figure be above this one, this one below, and this one on both sides,' and in the order as thought, they complete the remaining variegated figures. Thus, whatever variegated arts exist in the world, all are performed by the mind alone. Because the action performed is thus variegated, the mind that produces those variegated paintings and so on is likewise variegated. Alternatively, because it is impossible to complete everything exactly as thought without remainder, the mind is even more variegated than the painting. Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'Bhikkhus, have you seen the painting named Caraṇa?' 'Yes, Venerable Sir.' 'Bhikkhus, even that painting named Caraṇa was thought out by the mind alone. Bhikkhus, the mind is even more variegated than that Caraṇa painting.'
107: Likewise, the internal mind, which is diverse in terms of kamma, gender, perception, designation, and so forth, in the various destinations such as devas, humans, hell, and animals, is also created by the mind itself. In truth, because the mind accomplishes wholesome and unwholesome kamma—which manifests as bodily action and so forth through methods such as giving, virtue, harming, and deceit—there arises the diversity of kamma. Due to this diversity of kamma, there arises in those various destinations the diversity of gender, distinguished by the shapes of hands, feet, ears, bellies, necks, faces, and so forth. Due to the diversity of gender, there arises the diversity of perception, occurring through the power of the perceived shape as "this is a woman" or "this is a man". Due to the diversity of perception, there arises the diversity of designation among those who call out "woman" or "man" in accordance with that perception. By the power of the diversity of designation, one performs kamma that produces a particular individual existence, thinking, "I shall become a woman," "I shall become a man," "I shall become a khattiya," or "I shall become a brāhmaṇa." Therefore, from the diversity of designation, the diversity of kamma arises again. When that diversity of kamma brings about the desired existence, it does so by the power of the destination; therefore, from the diversity of kamma, the diversity of destination arises. It is through the diversity of kamma that for various beings in various destinations, there is the state of being footless, two-footed, and so forth; in various rebirths, there is the state of being high or low; in various individual existences, there is the state of being beautiful or ugly; and in worldly conditions, there is the state of having gain or loss, and so forth. Therefore, it should be understood that all this internal mind, which is diverse in kamma, gender, perception, designation, and so forth in the destinations of devas, humans, hell, and animals, is created by the mind alone. This meaning should be understood by the power of this sutta not included in the Sangīti. It is said thus: "Through the power of defining the diversity, multiplicity, and variety of kamma, there is the defining of the diversity, multiplicity, and variety of gender. Through the power of defining the diversity, multiplicity, and variety of gender, there is the defining of the diversity, multiplicity, and variety of perception. Through the power of defining the diversity, multiplicity, and variety of perception, there is the defining of the diversity, multiplicity, and variety of designation. Through the power of defining the diversity, multiplicity, and variety of designation, there is the defining of the diversity, multiplicity, and variety of kamma. Depending on the differentiation of kamma, the differentiation in the destination of beings is manifest—footless, two-footed, four-footed, many-footed; with form, without form; with perception, without perception, with neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Depending on the differentiation of kamma, the differentiation in the rebirth of beings is manifest—high and low, inferior and superior, happy destination and unhappy destination."
108: Depending on the differentiation of kamma, the differentiation in the individual existence of beings is manifest—beauty and ugliness, perfection and imperfection of existence, good proportions and bad proportions. Depending on the differentiation of kamma, the differentiation in the worldly conditions of beings is manifest—gain and loss, fame and obscurity, blame and praise, happiness and pain. Another sutta is also spoken thus: "Due to kamma and due to gender, the perceptions of gender occur. Due to that perception, they reach differentiation as 'this is a woman' or 'this is a man'." "The world revolves through kamma; the generation of beings revolves through kamma. Beings are bound by kamma, like the linchpin of a moving chariot." "Through kamma, one obtains fame and praise. Through kamma, one obtains loss, death, and bondage. Knowing such differentiation caused by kamma, why would one say there is no kamma in the world?" "Young man, beings are owners of kamma, heirs of kamma, born of kamma, related to kamma, have kamma as their refuge. Kamma alone distinguishes beings into the inferior and the superior." Thus, the variegation of the mind should also be understood through this state of the mind as the creator. For all these variegated effects are created by the mind alone. However, because a mind that has not obtained an opportunity or is deficient in the remaining conditions cannot perform certain variegated actions, the mind itself is even more variegated than the internal mind created by the mind. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, I do not see any other single group so variegated as this, monks, the animals... Monks, even more variegated than those animals is the mind itself." In the phrase "uppannaṃ hoti" (it has arisen), "arisen" (uppanna) has many divisions by way of the presently arisen (vattamanuppanna), the arisen having been and gone (bhūtāpagatuppanna), the arisen by way of opportunity (okāsakatuppanna), and the arisen by way of having obtained the plane (bhūmiladdhuppanna). Among these four, all conditioned phenomena endowed with arising, aging, and breaking up are called "presently arisen" (vattamanuppanna). That which has ceased after experiencing the taste of the object, called "experienced and gone" (anubhūtāpagata)...
109:
Wholesome, unwholesome, and the remaining conditioned phenomena, having reached the three sub-moments beginning with arising (uppāda) in succession and then ceasing, or having reached the three sub-moments and then disappearing and ceasing, are called bhūtāpagatuppanna (arisen by having been and passed away). Kamma, as taught in the passage 'This being has kammas performed in the past' and so on, even though it is past, is called okāsakatūppanna (arisen by opportunity made) because it stands by preventing other results (vipāka) and making an opportunity for its own result; and the result, which has been given an opportunity by that kamma, even though it has not yet arisen, is also called okāsakatūppanna because it will definitely arise once the opportunity is made. Unwholesome states that have not been eradicated in various planes are called bhūmiladdhuppanna (arisen by obtaining a plane). Here, the difference between 'plane' (bhūmi) and 'obtained by the plane' (bhūmiladdha) should be understood. 'Plane' refers to the five aggregates of clinging (pañcupādānakkhandhā) belonging to the three planes, which are the objects of insight (vipassanā). 'Obtained by the plane' refers to the collection of defilements (kilesa) that are liable to arise in those five aggregates. Because this plane is obtained through those defilements, it is called bhūmiladdha. Among these four types of 'arisen' (uppanna), only vattamānuppanna (presently arisen) is intended here.

The meaning of the word 'uppanna' is: it is called 'uppanna' because it has transcended the preceding past states and is directed towards arising (uppāda) and so on. This word 'uppanna' is seen in many senses: the past, the obtained, the risen up, the not suppressed, the not eradicated, and that which has gone to the three sub-moments. Indeed, in the passage, 'Monks, at that time the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, had arisen (uppanna) in the world,' the word 'uppanna' expresses the sense of the past. In the passage, 'An extra robe has arisen (uppanna) for the Venerable Ānanda,' it expresses the sense of being obtained. In the passage, 'Monks, just as a great wind causes a great cloud that has arisen (uppanna) to disappear right then and there,' it expresses the sense of having risen up. In the passage, 'The arisen (uppanna) thought of going is difficult to remove; he causes the evil unwholesome states that have arisen (uppannuppanna) to disappear instantly,' it expresses the sense of not being suppressed. In the passage, 'A practitioner who develops and cultivates the Noble Eightfold Path causes the evil unwholesome states that have arisen (uppannuppanna) to disappear right then and there,' it expresses the sense of not being eradicated. In the passage, 'Is that which is currently arising called arisen (uppanna)? Yes,' it expresses the sense of having gone to the three sub-moments. This word 'uppanna' here should also be understood in the sense of having gone to the three sub-moments. Therefore, in the phrase 'uppannaṃ hoti', it means it has gone to the three sub-moments, it is currently occurring, it is present. This is the summary of the meaning.

The statement 'the mind has arisen' is merely the head (chief) of the teaching. In reality, the mind does not arise alone. Therefore, just as when it is said 'the King has arrived,' it should be understood that he did not come alone by abandoning his retinue, but arrived together with his retinue.
110:
Just as it is known that the King has come with his retinue, so too should it be understood that this mind arises only together with more than fifty wholesome states. However, because it is the precursor, it is simply said 'the mind has arisen.' In truth, in mundane states, the mind is the chief, the mind is the leader, the mind is the precursor. In supramundane states, wisdom (paññā) is the chief, wisdom is the leader, wisdom is the precursor. Because of this, when the Blessed One asks a question in the context of the Vinaya, He does not ask 'What contact, feeling, perception, or volition do you have?' but asks by making the mind the chief: 'Monk, what mind do you have?' And when it is said, 'Blessed One, I have a mind with intent to steal,' He does not say 'There is no offense for one with a contact of intent to steal,' etc., but says, 'Monk, there is no offense for one with a mind of intent to steal.' Not only in the context of the Vinaya, but also when teaching other mundane discourses, He teaches by making the mind the chief. As He said: 'Monks, whatever states are unwholesome, partaking of the unwholesome, belonging to the side of the unwholesome, all those are preceded by mind. Mind arises first among those states.'

'Mind precedes all mental states, mind is their chief, they are mind-made. If with a corrupted mind one speaks or acts, suffering follows him as the wheel follows the hoof of the ox.'

'Mind precedes all mental states, mind is their chief, they are mind-made. If with a pure mind one speaks or acts, happiness follows him like a shadow that never leaves.'

'The world is led by the mind, it is dragged around by the mind; all have come under the sway of this one state, the mind.'

'Monks, by the defilement of the mind, beings are defiled; by the purification of the mind, beings are purified.'

'Monks, this mind is luminous, but it is defiled by adventitious defilements (āgantuka upakkilesa).'
111:
"Householder, when the mind is unprotected, bodily action is also unprotected, verbal action is also unprotected, and mental action is also unprotected. Householder, when the mind is protected... (pe) ... Householder, when the mind is defiled... (pe) ... Householder, when the mind is not defiled... (pe) ... Householder, when the mind is wet (with defilements)... (pe) ... Householder, when the mind is not wet (with defilements), bodily action is also not wet, verbal action is also not wet, and mental action is also not wet" (stated in the Aṅguttara Nikāya).

In this way, when reaching mundane states (lokiya dhamma), it should be understood that the mind is the chief, the mind is the leader, and the mind is the precursor. In these suttas, it should be understood that all are taken for the sake of protecting the suttas (supporting each other) without taking only one or two.

However, when asking about supramundane states (lokuttara dhamma), instead of asking, "Monk, what kind of contact (phassa) have you attained? What kind of feeling (vedanā), what kind of perception (saññā), what kind of volition (cetanā), what kind of mind (citta)?" one asks by making wisdom (paññā) the chief and wisdom the leader: "Monk, what kind of wisdom have you attained? Is it the wisdom of the first path, or the second... (pe) ... the third... (pe) ... or the wisdom of the fourth path?" All wholesome states that have wisdom as their head do not decline. "Monks, what is the purpose of wisdom?" (Majjhima Nikāya). "Monks, for the noble disciple who possesses wisdom, faith follows that wisdom and is well-established; energy follows that wisdom and is established; mindfulness follows that wisdom and is established; concentration follows that wisdom and is established" (Saṃyutta Nikāya). Such suttas should be seen here. Thus, when reaching supramundane states, it should be understood that wisdom is the chief, wisdom is the leader, and wisdom is the precursor. But this teaching is a mundane teaching. Therefore, wishing to teach by making the mind the leader, he said, "A mind has arisen."

"Accompanied by joy" (somanassasahagata) means (a mind) that has reached the state of co-arising, etc., together with joy, which is described as a pleasant and sweet experience. This word "sahagata" is seen in these meanings: (1) identity (tabbhāva), (2) mixed (vokiṇṇa), (3) dependence (nissaya), (4) object (ārammaṇa), and (5) association (saṃsaṭṭha).

Among these meanings, in the passage "This craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust (nandirāgasahagatā)," the meaning of "identity" (tabbhāva) should be understood; it means having the nature of delight and lust (being lust). In the passage "Monks, the investigation accompanied by sloth (kosajjasahagatā), associated with sloth," the meaning of "mixed" (vokiṇṇa) should be understood; here it means mixed with sloth that arises intermittently. "Accompanied by the perception of a skeleton (aṭṭhikasaññāsahagataṃ)..."
112:
"Accompanied by the perception of a skeleton, he develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5, 238) — in this Pali, (the word sahagata) should be understood in the sense of dependence (nissaya). It means (he develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness) obtained by developing the perception of a skeleton depending on the perception of a skeleton. "He is an obtainer of attainments accompanied by form or accompanied by the formless" (Puggalapaññatti 3-5) — in this Pali, (the word sahagata) should be understood in the sense of object (ārammaṇa). It means (the state of attainments) having a material object (such as the earth kasina) or a non-material object (such as the concept of space). "This happiness is accompanied by this rapture, co-nascent, associated, conjoined" (Vibhaṅga 578) — in this Pali, (the word sahagata) should be understood in the sense of association (saṃsaṭṭha). In this term (somanassasahagata) as well, this very sense of association is intended. Indeed, here, the mind associated with joy is called "accompanied by joy" (somanassasahagata).

This word "saṃsaṭṭha" is also seen in many meanings: similarity (sadisa), being wet/affected (avassuta), friendship/intimacy (mittasanthava), and co-nascent (sahajāta). "Excluding the lean and the fat, horses of similar (saṃsaṭṭha) size and color were harnessed" (Jātaka 2, 22, 70) — in this passage, it appears in the sense of similarity (sadisa). "Sisters, you live being wet (saṃsaṭṭha) (with defilements)" (Pācittiya 727) — in this passage, it appears in the sense of being wet (avassuta). "He lives associated (saṃsaṭṭha) with laypeople" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3, 3) — in this passage, it appears in the sense of friendship/intimacy (mittasanthava). "This happiness is associated (saṃsaṭṭha) with this rapture" — in this passage, it appears in the sense of co-nascent (sahajāta). In this term (somanassasahagata) as well, the sense of co-nascent (sahajāta) is intended. Among those states (sahagata, sahajāta), there is no state that is sahagata but not sahajāta, not saṃsaṭṭha, and not sampayutta. However, a state that is sahajāta may or may not be saṃsaṭṭha and sampayutta. When material and mental states arise together, matter is co-nascent (sahajāta) with the mental, but it is not associated (saṃsaṭṭha) and not conjoined (sampayutta). Likewise, the mental with the material, and matter with matter (are sahajāta but not saṃsaṭṭha or sampayutta). But when the mental arises together with the mental, it is invariably accompanied (sahagata), co-nascent (sahajāta), associated (saṃsaṭṭha), and conjoined (sampayutta). Referring to that (mental-to-mental) co-nascent, associated, and conjoined state of being accompanied, it is said "accompanied by joy" (somanassasahagata).

"Associated with knowledge" (ñāṇasampayutta) means associated with knowledge, conjoined in a balanced way through modes such as co-arising (ekuppāda), etc. What should be said regarding this term is the same method already mentioned in the explanation of the Triad of Feeling (Vedanāttika) in the Matika Commentary. Therefore, this (first great wholesome mind) should be understood as associated with knowledge by these characteristics: co-arising (ekuppāda), co-ceasing (ekanirodha), having the same base (ekavatthu), and having the same object (ekārammaṇa). This is an eminent description (ukkaṭṭhaniddesa). In the formless realm (arūpabhūmi), however, association (sampayoga) is obtained even without having the same base (ekavatthukabhāva).

What has been taught by this sequence of words? Among the sense-sphere wholesome states, the Great Wholesome Mind that is accompanied by joy, rooted in three causes (tihetuka), associated with knowledge, and unprompted (asaṅkhārika) has been taught. By the unspecified question "Which states are wholesome?" the wholesome states occurring in the four planes are taken. But by the statement "A sense-sphere wholesome mind has arisen," the wholesome states occurring in the three planes (fine-material, immaterial, and supramundane) are excluded...
113:
By setting aside 'wholesome' in general, only the eight types of sense-sphere wholesome (kāmāvacara kusala) are taken. By the word 'associated with joy' (somanassasahagata), the four associated with equanimity are set aside from those, and only the four associated with joy are taken. By the word 'associated with knowledge' (ñāṇasampayutta), the two disconnected from knowledge are set aside from those, and only the two associated with knowledge are taken. As for the state of being unprompted (asaṅkhārika), although it is not taken by being explicitly mentioned (in the Pali), and even though 'unprompted' is not stated here, it should be understood as unprompted because 'prompted' (sasaṅkhārena) is mentioned later. Indeed, it should be understood that the Fully Enlightened One, having determined from the very beginning to show this Great Consciousness (mahācitta) by classifying it, began this teaching; thus, the conclusion is made here.

Now, to show that same consciousness by way of its object, He said, 'Whether a visible object' (rūpārammaṇan vā) and so forth. When the Blessed One wishes to show immaterial phenomena (arūpadhamma), He shows them by way of base (vatthu), or by way of object (ārammaṇa), or by way of both base and object (vatthārammaṇa), or by way of their own intrinsic nature (sarasabhāva). In such passages as 'eye-contact... mind-contact; feeling born of eye-contact... feeling born of mind-contact; eye-consciousness... mind-consciousness,' immaterial phenomena are shown by way of base. In such passages as 'perception of forms... perception of mental objects; volition regarding forms... volition regarding mental objects,' they are shown by way of object. In such passages as 'Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact... dependent on the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact,' they are shown by way of both base and object. In such passages as 'Monks, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness,' immaterial phenomena are shown by way of their own intrinsic nature. In this context, however, wishing to show them by way of object, He said, 'Whether a visible object' and so forth.

Among those objects, only the visible base (rūpāyatana) of the past, future, and present, produced by the four causes—kamma, consciousness (citta), temperature (utu), and nutriment (āhāra)—is called a visible object (rūpārammaṇa). Only the sound base (saddāyatana) of the past, future, and present, produced by the two causes—consciousness and temperature—is called a sound object (saddārammaṇa). Only the odor base (gandhāyatana) of the past, future, and present, produced by the four causes, is called an odor object (gandhārammaṇa). Only the flavor base (rasāyatana) of the past, future, and present, produced by the four causes, is called a flavor object (rasārammaṇa). Only the tangible base (phoṭṭhabbāyatana) of the past, future, and present, produced by the four causes, is called a tangible object (phoṭṭhabbārammaṇa). The consciousness and mental factors (cetasika) of the past, future, and present, produced by one, two, three, or four causes, or not produced by any cause at all, and likewise those which cannot be said to be produced by one cause and so forth, and the remaining mental bases (dhammāyatana) known as the range of consciousness, are called mental objects (dhammārammaṇa). Those teachers who say that even visible objects and so forth that have not come into the range (of the senses) are mental objects should be refuted by this Sutta. For it was said:
114:
“Friends, these five faculties, having different spheres and different domains, do not experience each other's domain and sphere; the mind (mano) is their resort, and the mind experiences their domain and sphere” (M. Ni. 1.455).

These visible objects and so forth are indeed called domains. Even when they are experienced by the mind, the fact that they remain visible objects and so forth is established. This fact is also established because the knowledge of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa) and so forth have visible objects and so forth as their objects. Visible objects and so forth that have not yet come into the range of the five senses are the objects of the divine eye and so forth, and they do not become mental objects (dhammārammaṇa); the definition of objects should be understood according to the method already mentioned.

Among those objects, each object appears in two doors each. For a visible object strikes the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) and at that very moment appears in the mind-door; the meaning is that it becomes a condition for the vibration of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga-calana). This same method applies to sound, odor, flavor, and tangible objects. Just as a bird coming through the sky and perching on a treetop strikes the branch and its shadow strikes the ground simultaneously—the striking of the branch and the spreading of the shadow occur at the same moment without before or after—so too, the striking of the eye-sensitivity and so forth by present visible objects and so forth, and their appearance in the mind-door due to the ability to vibrate the life-continuum, occur at the same moment without before or after. Then, having interrupted the life-continuum, this Great Consciousness arises toward one of those objects immediately after the thought-process starting from adverting (āvajjana) and ending with determining (votthabbana) that has arisen in the eye-door and so forth.

In the pure mind-door (suddha-manodvāra), however, there is no function of striking the sensitivity. These objects appear only by virtue of what has been seen, heard, smelled, tasted, or touched in the past. How? In this world, a certain person, having circumambulated a Great Stupa (mahācetiya) which is smoothly plastered, adorned with various colors like orpiment and realgar, decorated with various kinds of raised banners and flags, entwined with garlands and floral wreaths, surrounded by rows of lamps, shining with a most delightful splendor, and fully decorated and prepared; having bowed at the sixteen stations with the five-point prostration, and standing with palms joined, looking up and taking joy (pīti) having the Buddha as object. That person, having thus seen the Stupa and generated joy with the Buddha as object, later when he has gone to any other place...
115:
For one who reflects while staying in places suitable for the night or the day, the decorated Mahācetiya appears in the eye-door as if it were present; it is like the time when one is circumambulating and worshipping the stupa. In this way, first, the visible object appears (in the mind-door) by the power of an object previously seen.

Furthermore, for one who has heard the voice of a Dhamma preacher preaching with a sweet tone, or the chanting of a sarabhāṇaka (intoner), and later reflects while staying in any place, that Dhamma talk or the sarabhañña chanting appears as if it were present in the ear-door; it is like the time when one is listening and saying "Sādhu." In this way, the sound object appears (in the mind-door) by the power of an object previously heard.

Furthermore, for one who has obtained fragrant incense or flowers and performed an offering at a seat or at a stupa with a mind focused on the odor object, and later reflects while staying in any place, that odor object appears as if it were present in the nose-door; it is like the time when one is performing the offering. In this way, the odor object appears (in the mind-door) by the power of an object previously smelled.

Furthermore, for one who has shared and consumed excellent food and snacks with fellow Dhamma-farers (sabrahmacārī), and later, when obtaining food such as millet in any place, reflects, "At such a time, I shared and consumed excellent food with fellow Dhamma-farers," that taste object appears as if it were present in the tongue-door; it is like the time when one is consuming it. In this way, the taste object appears (in the mind-door) by the power of an object previously tasted.

Furthermore, for one who has used soft and pleasant-to-touch couches, chairs, rugs, or robes, and later, when sleeping on a miserable bed in any place, reflects, "At such a time, I used soft couches, chairs, rugs, and robes," that tangible object appears as if it were present in the body-door. It is like the time when one is experiencing the pleasant touch. In this way, the tangible object appears (in the mind-door) by the power of an object previously touched. Thus, in the pure mind-door, there is no function of striking the sensitive matter (pasāda). It should be understood that these objects appear (in the mind-door) only by the power of what has been normally seen, heard, smelled, tasted, and touched.
116:
Now, regarding the appearance of objects by the power of what is seen and so on in the normal way, there is also this other method not explicitly mentioned in the Commentary (aṭṭhakathāmuttaka). First, these categories such as 'seen' should be understood as: Diṭṭha (seen), Suta (heard), and Ubhayasambandha (connected to both). Therein, 'Diṭṭha' means an object previously grasped by the power of the five doors. 'Suta' means visible objects and so on that are grasped not by direct experience but by the power of oral tradition (anussava). The object connected to both the seen and the heard is called 'Ubhayasambandha'. Thus, it should be understood that these objects appear in the mind-door by the power of these categories of 'seen' and so on. Therein, the appearance of objects by the power of the 'seen' has already been explained by the five methods above.

Some person hears: "Such is the physical form of the Blessed One produced by extraordinary merit, an extremely sweet voice, the extremely delightful scent of certain flowers in a certain place, the extremely sweet taste of certain fruits, the extremely pleasant touch of certain robes and so on." For that person, without any striking of the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) and so on, those objects appear in the mind-door merely by hearing. Then, that person's mind arises with regard to that form or sound by way of devotion (pasāda). Regarding the odor object and so on, it arises by way of the desire to give to the Noble Ones (ariya), or by way of rejoicing (anumodanā) when seeing others give. In this way, these objects appear in the mind-door by the power of the 'heard' (suta).

For another person, the aforementioned visible objects and so on may have been seen or heard. For him, by the power of the connection between the seen and the heard, without any striking of the eye-sensitivity and so on, those objects appear in the mind-door in such a way as: "Such a physical form will also belong to the Buddha who will arise in the future." Then, this great wholesome mind (mahākusala citta) arises by taking one of those objects as its objective range, in the same manner as described below. In this way, these objects appear in the mind-door by the power of 'connection to both' (ubhayasambandha).

And this description is just a mere indication. The appearance of these objects in the mind-door should be understood in detail by the power of faith (saddhā), preference (ruci), reflection on reasons (ākāraparivitakka), and acceptance of a view after pondering (diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti), and so on. However, because the objects that appear in this way may be true or may be false, this method was not included in the Commentary. Thus, it should be understood that the impulsion (javana) occurring for each object arises in two doors. The javana taking a visible object as its object arises in the eye-door and also in the mind-door. The same method applies to sound objects and so on.

Therein, the javana with a visible object arising in the mind-door is of three types: consisting in giving (dānamaya), consisting in virtue (sīlamaya), and consisting in mental development (bhāvanamaya). Among those, each one is bodily action, verbal action...
117:
Mental action (manokamma) is of three kinds. The same method should be understood regarding sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects.

Among those objects, the great wholesome consciousness (mahākusala citta) that arises first by taking a visible form (rūpārammaṇa) as an object, arises by taking as its object a color that is desirable, lovely, pleasing, and charming, known as a beautiful sign (subhanimitta), from among flowers, garments, or elements of blue, yellow, red, or white color. If it is asked: "Is not such a desirable object a basis for greed? How then does this consciousness become wholesome?" It is answered: It becomes wholesome through the power of determination (niyama), through the power of transformation (pariṇāma), through the power of habitual practice (samudācara), and through the power of reflection (ābhujita). For one who has determined the mind upon performing wholesome deeds, thinking, "I should perform only wholesome deeds"; who has transformed the mind toward performing wholesome deeds by turning away from the occurrence of unwholesome states; who has practiced the habit of wholesomeness through frequent performance; and whose wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra) occurs through such supporting conditions (upanissaya) as living in a suitable locality, associating with good persons, hearing the true Dhamma, and having performed merit in the past—to such a person, wholesome consciousness arises through the power of this determination, transformation, habitual practice, and reflection.

Furthermore, the state of being accompanied by joy (somanassa-sahagata) in this consciousness should be understood by the power of the object. Because it arises in a desirable object (iṭṭhārammaṇa), this consciousness is accompanied by joy. Abundance of faith and so on are also causes here. For those without faith and those with wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi), joy does not arise even upon seeing the physical form of the Tathāgata, which is an extremely desirable object. For those who do not see the benefits in the occurrence of wholesomeness, joy does not arise even when they are performing wholesome deeds at the encouragement of others. Therefore, the state of being accompanied by joy should be understood through the abundance of faith, purity of view, and the seeing of benefits. Moreover, eleven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of rapture (pīti-sambojjhaṅga): recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of virtue (sīla), recollection of generosity (cāga), recollection of deities, recollection of peace (upasama), avoiding coarse persons, associating with refined persons, reflecting on inspiring discourses (suttantas), and being inclined towards that rapture. Through these causes also, the state of being accompanied by joy should be understood. The detail of these will be made clear in the Bojjhaṅga Vibhaṅga.

The state of being associated with knowledge (ñāṇasampayutta) in this consciousness should be understood through kamma, through rebirth (upapatti), through maturity of faculties (indriya-paripāka), and through distance from defilements (kilesa-dūrībhāva). One who...
118:
...preaches the Dhamma to others, teaches blameless arts, crafts, and sciences, makes offerings to a Dhamma-preacher and has them preach, and makes various kinds of offerings after making a prayer, "May I be wise in the future"—for such a person, wholesome consciousness associated with knowledge arises depending on such wholesome kamma. Also, for one born in a world free from ill-will (avyāpajja loka), wholesome consciousness associated with knowledge arises depending on rebirth (upapatti), according to the method: "To that happy one in that realm, the groups of Dhamma flow... monks, the arising of mindfulness is slow, yet that being quickly reaches the distinction (visesa)." Likewise, for those whose faculties have reached maturity, having reached the decade of wisdom (paññā-dasaka), wholesome consciousness associated with knowledge arises depending on the maturity of faculties. For those whose defilements have been suppressed, wholesome consciousness associated with knowledge arises depending on the distance from defilements. This has also been said:
"From yoga (meditation) indeed wisdom is born; from the lack of yoga, wisdom is lost."

Thus, the state of being associated with knowledge should be understood through these causes: kamma, rebirth, maturity of faculties, and distance from defilements.

Furthermore, seven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of investigation of states (dhamma-vicaya-sambojjhaṅga): being inquisitive, making the objects clean, balancing the faculties, avoiding unwise persons, associating with wise persons, reflecting on the conduct of profound knowledge, and being inclined towards that investigation. Through these causes also, the state of being associated with knowledge should be understood. The detail of these will be made clear in the Bojjhaṅga Vibhaṅga.

This consciousness, having arisen associated with knowledge, is called unprompted (asaṅkhārika) because it arises without exertion (payoga) and without premeditation of other means. When it arises taking a charming visible form as an object, it arises in three ways: consisting in giving (dānamaya), consisting in virtue (sīlamaya), or consisting in meditation (bhāvanāmaya).

How? When one obtains one of the flowers of blue, yellow, red, or white color and, reflecting on it by way of its color, worships the Buddha-gem and so on, thinking, "May this be my offering of color (vaṇṇa-dāna)," then it is dānamaya. In this regard, there is this story: It is said that the treasurer Saṅghamitta, upon obtaining a gold-embroidered cloth, thought, "This cloth is of golden color, and the Fully Enlightened One is also of golden color; a cloth of golden color is suitable only for the One of golden color, and it will be our offering of color," and he offered it at the Mahācetiya.
119:
In such a time, it should be understood as dānamaya (merit consisting in giving). When one obtains such an object of offering and honors the Buddha Jewel and so forth, thinking, 'This is my family lineage, this is my family tradition, this is my family heritage, this is my family duty,' then it is sīlamaya (merit consisting in virtue). When, after honoring the Triple Gem with such an object, one contemplates its decay and destruction, thinking, 'This appearance will reach exhaustion, will reach destruction,' then it is bhāvanāmaya (merit consisting in meditation).

Even while it is occurring as dānamaya, when one honors the Triple Gem with one's own hands, it is bodily action (kāyakamma).
