When, in honoring the Triple Gem, one commands one's children, wife, slaves, workers, or people to perform the honoring, it is verbal action (vacīkamma). When one thinks, 'I will give an offering of color (visual object),' based on that aforementioned existing object, it is mental action (manokamma). According to the Vinaya method, it is called dāna by the characteristic of the spoken word, 'I will give, I will do.' According to the Abhidhamma method, however, merit arises from the moment one thinks in the mind, 'I will give,' based on the existing object. It is said that later one will perform what is to be done by body or speech. Thus, dānamaya is threefold by way of bodily, verbal, and mental action.

When one obtains the aforementioned object and honors the Triple Gem with one's own hands based on family lineage and so forth, it is sīlamaya bodily action. When one commands children, wife, and so forth to perform the honoring based on family lineage and so forth, it is verbal action. When one thinks, 'I will give an offering of color,' based on the existing object, thinking, 'This is my family lineage, this is my family tradition, this is my family heritage, this is my family duty,' it is mental action. Thus, sīlamaya is threefold by way of bodily, verbal, and mental action.

When one obtains the aforementioned object, honors the Triple Gem, and contemplates decay and destruction while walking back and forth (caṅkamati), it is bhāvanāmaya bodily action. For one who initiates contemplation by speech, it is verbal action. For one who initiates contemplation only by mind, without moving the limbs of the body or the organs of speech, it is mental action. Thus, bhāvanāmaya is threefold by way of bodily, verbal, and mental action. In this way, the King of Dhamma (the Buddha) showed this merit based on visual objects (rūpārammaṇa) by dividing it into the three bases of meritorious action and the nine doors of action. The same method applies to sound objects (saddārammaṇa) and so forth.
120:
Regarding sounds such as the sound of a drum, this merit arises based on a pleasant sound as the object, according to the three criteria mentioned above. In that offering of sound, it is not possible to pluck out the sound like a lotus root or to place it in the hand like a blue lotus and give it; rather, one is said to give an offering of sound only when giving it together with the object that produces the sound, such as a drum. Therefore, when one thinks, 'I will give an offering of sound,' and performs an offering to the Triple Gem with any kind of musical instrument such as a large drum (bheri) or a mudiṅga drum; or when one has drums and so forth set up, thinking, 'This will be my offering of sound'; or when one gives oil, molasses, and so forth as medicine for the voice to monks who are Dhamma preachers; or when one proclaims the hearing of the Dhamma, chants sarabhañña, preaches the Dhamma, gives a talk to those sitting nearby, or gives a talk of appreciation (anumodanā); then it is dānamaya merit. When one performs this same arrangement by way of family lineage or by way of duty, it is sīlamaya merit. When, after performing all these arrangements, one initiates contemplation, thinking, 'Even if this sound is so great that it reaches the Brahma world, it will reach exhaustion, it will reach destruction,' then it is bhāvanāmaya merit.

Among those, regarding dānamaya: when one takes drums and so forth and performs the offering with one's own hands, or even when setting them up for a permanent offering, one sets them with one's own hands; or when one goes to proclaim the hearing of the Dhamma, or goes to preach the Dhamma or chant sarabhañña, thinking, 'This will be my offering of sound,' then it is bodily action. When one commands, 'Friends, go and perform an offering to the Triple Gem; it will be our offering of sound'; or when one commands, 'Place this large drum, this mudiṅga drum on the pagoda platforms,' thinking, 'This will be my offering of sound'; or when one personally proclaims the hearing of the Dhamma, preaches the Dhamma, or chants sarabhañña, then it is verbal action. When one renounces the existing object with the mind, without moving the limbs of the body or the organs of speech, thinking, 'I will give an offering of sound,' then it is mental action.

Sīlamaya merit is also bodily action for one who performs the offering with one's own hands using drums and so forth, thinking, 'The offering of sound is my family lineage, tradition, and heritage'; or for one who places drums and so forth on pagoda platforms (cetiyangaṇa) with one's own hands; or for one who gives voice-medicine to Dhamma preachers with one's own hands; or for one who goes for the purpose of proclaiming the hearing of the Dhamma, preaching the Dhamma, or chanting sarabhañña as a duty. It is verbal action for one who commands, 'The offering of sound is our family lineage, tradition, and heritage; friends, go and perform an offering to the Buddha Jewel and so forth'; or for one who personally preaches the Dhamma or chants sarabhañña by way of family lineage. For one who thinks, 'The offering of sound is my...'
121:
Thinking, "I will give the gift of sound, which is my family tradition," for one who relinquishes an existing object only with the mind without moving the limbs of the body or the organs of speech, it is a mental action (manokamma).

In the wholesome merit consisting in meditation (bhāvanāmaya), when one contemplates the decay and passing away of sounds while walking to and fro, it is a bodily action (kāyakamma). For one who contemplates with speech without moving the limbs of the body, it is a verbal action (vacīkamma). For one who contemplates the sound-base (saddāyatana) only with the mind without moving the limbs of the body or the organs of speech, it is a mental action (manokamma). Thus, the Buddha, the King of Dhamma, showed the wholesome state having sound as its object, dividing it by way of the three bases of meritorious action and the nine doors of action.

Regarding root-scents and so on, taking a pleasant odor as an object, this wholesome state arises by way of the three rules in the same manner as mentioned below. Among those wholesome states, when one obtains any scent from root-scents and so on, and attending to it by way of scent, offers it to the Buddha-gem and so on, thinking, "This will be my gift of scent," then it is merit consisting in giving (dānamaya). Everything should be understood in detail in the same manner as stated under the gift of color (vaṇṇa-dāna). Thus, the Buddha, the King of Dhamma, showed the wholesome state having odor as its object, dividing it by way of the three bases of meritorious action and the nine doors of action.

Regarding root-tastes and so on, taking a pleasant taste as an object, this wholesome state arises by way of the three rules in the same manner as mentioned below. Among those wholesome states, when one obtains any pleasant object of taste from root-tastes and so on, and attending to it by way of taste, gives and relinquishes it, thinking, "This will be my gift of taste," then it is merit consisting in giving (dānamaya). Everything should be understood in detail in the same manner as stated under the gift of color. However, in the section on merit consisting in virtue (sīlamaya) regarding this taste-object, stories are found in the Great Commentary (Mahā-aṭṭhakathā), beginning with the story of King Duṭṭhagāmaṇī Abhaya, who partook of a delicious taste only after having it offered to twelve thousand monks, reflecting, "It is not our habit to consume without having given to the Saṅgha." This is the distinction. Thus, the Buddha, the King of Dhamma, showed the wholesome state having taste as its object, dividing it by way of the three bases of meritorious action and the nine doors of action.

Regarding the wholesome state having a tangible as its object, the three great elements called the earth-element, the fire-element, and the air-element are known as the tangible-base (phoṭṭhabbārammaṇa). In this context, instead of applying it by way of those elements, it should be applied by way of couches, stools, and so on. Indeed, when one obtains any pleasant tangible object from couches, stools, and so on, and attending to it by way of the tangible, gives and relinquishes it, thinking, "This will be my gift of tangibles," then it is merit consisting in giving (dānamaya). Everything should be understood in detail in the same manner as stated under the gift of color. Thus, the Buddha, the King of Dhamma, showed the wholesome state having a tangible as its object, dividing it by way of the three bases of meritorious action and the nine doors of action.
122:
Regarding the object of mental states (dhammārammaṇa), the six internal bases, the three marks (such as impermanence), the three mental aggregates, the fifteen types of subtle matter, Nibbāna, and concepts—these are the states included in the base of mental states (dhammāyatana) and those not included, which are called mental-state objects (dhammārammaṇa). However, in this context, the meaning should be taken not by way of those internal bases and so on, but by way of the gift of nutriment (ojā-dāna), the gift of drinks (pāna-dāna), and the gift of life (jīvitadāna). For, taking a pleasant mental-state object among nutriment and so on, this wholesome state arises by way of the three rules in the same manner as mentioned below.

Among those types of merit such as giving, when one gives ghee, fresh butter, and so on, thinking, "This will be my gift of nutriment"; when one gives the eight kinds of drinks, thinking, "This will be my gift of drinks"; when one gives food-by-tickets, food-for-the-Saṅgha, and so on, thinking, "This will be my gift of life"; when one gives medicine to sick monks, or has a physician attend to them; when one has nets torn, or has fish-traps destroyed, or has bird-cages destroyed; when one causes release from bonds, or has the drum of non-slaughter beaten; or when one performs other such acts for the sake of protecting life—then it is merit consisting in giving (dānamaya). But when one performs the gift of nutriment, the gift of drinks, and the gift of life by way of a duty, thinking, "These are my family tradition, family lineage, and family custom," then it is merit consisting in virtue (sīlamaya). When one brings about the contemplation of decay and passing away regarding a mental-state object, then it is merit consisting in meditation (bhāvanāmaya).

Even for the wholesome state occurring as merit consisting in giving, when one gives the gift of nutriment, the gift of drinks, and the gift of life with one's own hand, then it is bodily action (kāyakamma). When one gives by commanding one's children, wife, and so on, then it is verbal action (vacīkamma). When one thinks with the mind, "I will give," regarding an existing object by way of the gift of nutriment, the gift of drinks, and the gift of life, without moving the limbs of the body or the organs of speech, then it is mental action (manokamma).

But when one gives an existing object of the aforementioned kind with one's own hand by way of family tradition and so on, then it is bodily action consisting in virtue (sīlamaya-kāyakamma). When one gives by commanding one's children, wife, and so on, by way of family tradition and so on, then it is verbal action (vacīkamma). When one thinks only with the mind, "I will give," regarding an existing object of the aforementioned kind by way of family tradition and so on, then it is mental action (manokamma).

For a person who brings about the contemplation of decay and passing away regarding a mental-state object while walking to and fro, it is bodily action consisting in meditation (bhāvanāmaya-kāyakamma). For a person who brings about the contemplation of decay and passing away with speech without moving the limbs of the body, it is verbal action (vacīkamma). For one who, without moving the limbs of the body or the organs of speech, only with the mind, regarding a mental-state object...
123:
For a person who causes the arising of dissolution and growth (khaya-vaya) in the mental object (dhammārammaṇa) through the mind alone, without moving the limbs of the body or the organs of speech, it is mental action (manokamma). Thus, wholesome action consisting in meditation (bhāvanāmaya-kusala) is of three kinds by way of bodily action, verbal action, and mental action. In this way, the Buddha, the King of Dhamma, showed this wholesome state, which is a mental object, by analyzing it into nine doors of action (kammadvara) by way of the three bases of meritorious action (puññakiriyavatthu). Thus, this great wholesome consciousness (mahākusala-citta) has been explained by way of various objects in various bases. However, this consciousness can also be obtained by way of various objects even in a single base. How? Among the four requisites, six objects are obtained in a robe (cīvara). The color of a newly dyed robe is pleasing and beautiful to look at; this is the visible object (vaṇṇārammaṇa). When used, it makes a sound like 'paṭa-paṭa'; this is the sound object (saddārammaṇa). The smell of the dye, such as black-dye (kāḷakacchaka) etc., in that robe; this is the odor object (gandhārammaṇa). The flavor object (rasārammaṇa) is spoken of by way of the flavor resulting from use. The state of having a pleasant touch in that robe; this is the tangible object (phoṭṭhabbārammaṇa). The pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) that arises depending on the robe is the mental object (dhammārammaṇa). In alms-food (piṇḍapāta), the flavor object is obtained in the primary sense. Thus, by connecting them with various objects in the four requisites, the distinctions of giving (dānamaya) etc., should be understood. Only the object of this consciousness is constant, because it cannot arise without an object. But the door (dvāra) is not constant. Why? Because action (kamma) is not constant. When action is not constant, the door is also not constant.

## Discussion on the Doors of Wholesome Sense-Sphere Action

## Discussion on the Door of Bodily Action

To clarify the meaning of the non-constancy of these doors of action, the discussion on doors (dvārakathā) from the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā is stated here. In that Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, the three actions, three doors of action, five consciousnesses, five doors of consciousness, six contacts, six doors of contact, eight non-restraints, eight doors of non-restraint, eight restraints, eight doors of restraint, ten wholesome courses of action, and ten unwholesome courses of action—this collection of words is called the setting out of the table of contents (mātikā) of the discussion on doors. Although the three actions are mentioned first in that table of contents, setting them aside for a moment, the three doors of action are first analyzed and shown in order. What are those three? They are the door of bodily action, the door of verbal action, and the door of mental action.
124:
In the phrase 'door of bodily action' (kāyakammadvāra), the body (kāya) is of four kinds: the clung-to body (upādinnaka-kāya), the nutriment-produced body (āhārasamuṭṭhāna-kāya), the temperature-produced body (utusamuṭṭhāna-kāya), and the mind-produced body (cittasamuṭṭhāna-kāya). Among those four kinds of bodies, the eight kamma-produced matters (kamma-samuṭṭhāna-rūpa) starting from the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) and ending with the life-faculty (jīvitindriya), as well as the eight matters—the four great elements, color, smell, taste, and nutritive essence—which are produced by kamma alone, are called the clung-to body. Those same eight matters produced by nutriment are called the nutriment-produced body. Those same eight matters produced by temperature are called the temperature-produced body. Those same eight matters produced by the mind are called the mind-produced body.

Among those bodies, the name 'door of bodily action' is not the name of the clung-to body, nor is it the name of the others such as the nutriment-produced body. However, among the eight matters produced by the mind, there is one [called] intimation (viññatti); this is called the door of bodily action. With reference to that matter of intimation, it is said (in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī): 'What is that matter which is bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti)? For one who has a wholesome mind, an unwholesome mind, or an indeterminate mind, in the acts of moving forward, moving backward, looking straight, looking aside, bending, or stretching, there is the stiffening, the thorough stiffening, the state of being thoroughly stiffened of the body, the intimation, the making known, the state of being made known; this matter is called bodily intimation.' When the mind arises with the thought, 'I will move forward, I will move backward,' it produces mind-born matter. At the moment that mind arises, within the groups of eight matters consisting of the earth element, water element, fire element, and air element, and the color, smell, taste, and nutritive essence dependent on them, there is the air element (vāyodhātu) produced by the mind; that air element stiffens, supports, and moves the physical body that is co-nascent with it, causing it to move forward and move backward.

Among those air elements produced by the mind, within the seven javanas in a single mind-door process (manodvāra-vīthi) having one adverting (āvajjana), the air element produced by the first mind (the first javana) is able to stiffen and support the physical body co-nascent with it, but it is not able to move it here and there. The same method applies to the second javana and so forth. However, the air element produced by the seventh mind (the seventh javana), having obtained the support of the air elements produced by the six preceding minds, is able to stiffen, support, move, cause to move forward, cause to move backward, cause to look straight, cause to look aside, cause to bend, and cause to stretch the physical body co-nascent with it. For that reason, going occurs, coming occurs, and going and coming occur. That air element produced by the seventh javana, which occurs many times, brings about the state of being able to say, 'He has gone a league (yojana), he has gone ten leagues.'
125:
For example, in a cart that must be pulled by seven yokes, the oxen harnessed to the first yoke are only able to steady and support the yoke; they cannot make the wheels turn. The same principle applies to the second yoke and so on. However, when oxen are harnessed to the seventh yoke, and a skilled driver sits at the front, takes the reins, and strikes the oxen with a goad starting from the very first one, then all the oxen exert equal force, supporting the yoke and causing the wheels to turn. They bring the cart to a state where it can be said, 'Taking the cart, they have traveled ten leagues, or twenty leagues.' This should be understood in accordance with this analogy.

In that context, the body originated from consciousness (cittasamuṭṭhāna) is not the intimation (viññatti). However, there is a specific alteration of mode (ākāravikāra) capable of being the condition to steady, support, and move the physical body (rūpakāya) that arises together with the air element (vāyodhātu) originated from consciousness; this is called 'intimation' (viññatti). This intimation is not 'purely' originated from consciousness in the same way as the eight types of matter. Nevertheless, just as it is said, 'Monks, aging and death are impermanent, conditioned,' etc. (Saṃ. Ni. 2.20), because aging and death belong to phenomena that are impermanent, so too this is called 'originated from consciousness' because it is the intimation of matter originated from consciousness.

This specific alteration of mode is called 'intimation' (viññatti) because it makes something known (viññāpanato). What does it make known? It makes known a bodily action (kāyikakaraṇa). A person standing before one's eyes raises a hand or a foot, or moves the head or eyebrows; this mode of the hands, etc., is cognizable by the eye (cakkhuviññeyya). However, the intimation itself is not cognizable by the eye; it is cognizable only by the mind (manoviññeyya). Indeed, with the eye, one sees only the color-object (vaṇṇārammaṇa) vibrating by the power of the hand-alterations and so on. But having reflected on the intimation with the mind-door consciousness, one knows, 'I think this person is doing this and that.'

For example, in a forest during the summer at a place where there is water, people tie palm leaves and such to the tops of trees, intending, 'By this sign, people will know the existence of water here.' They set up a flag at the door of a tavern. Or, the wind strikes and moves a tall tree. When fish move inside the water, bubbles rise to the surface. At the edge of the path where a great flood has passed, grass, leaves, and debris are left caught. In these examples, by seeing the movement of palm leaves, flags, or branches, the bubbles, or the debris of grass and leaves, although not seen with the eye, one knows through mind-consciousness: 'There will be water here; there will be liquor; this tree must have been struck by the wind; there will be fish in the water.' Similarly, intimation is not cognizable by the eye, but cognizable only by the mind-consciousness. Indeed, with the eye, by the power of hand-alterations and so on...
126:
...one knows through mind-consciousness, 'The flood must have gone through, covering this much area.' In the same way, intimation is not cognizable by the eye, but cognizable only by the mind. With the eye, one sees only the color-object (vaṇṇārammaṇa) vibrating by the power of hand-alterations and so on. But having reflected on the intimation with the mind-door consciousness, one knows (by understanding the intent), 'I think this person wishes to do this and that.'

This alteration (vikāra) is called intimation (viññatti) not only because it makes something known to others (viññāpanato), but also because it is known by others (viññeyyato). This intimation is evident to others, even down to animals. When creatures such as dogs, foxes, crows, and oxen gathered in various places see the gesture of someone picking up a stick or a stone to strike, they know, 'This person wants to hit us,' and they flee in any direction. There are also times when it is not evident to others who are separated by walls, fences, and so on. Even if it is not evident at that moment, it is still called intimation because it is evident to those who are present.

When the body originated from consciousness (cittasamuṭṭhāna) moves, does the body originated from the other three causes (kamma, temperature, and nutriment) move or not? It moves in the same way. It follows the same course and conforms to it. For example, when water flows, dry sticks, grass, and leaves that have fallen into the water also follow the course of the water; when the water moves, they move; when the water stops, they stop. The completeness of this analogy should be understood. Thus, among the matter originated from consciousness, this intimation should be known as the 'door of bodily action' (kāyakammadvāra).

The volition (cetanā) that is clearly produced at that door, by which one kills a living being, takes what is not given, commits sexual misconduct, or abstains from killing and so on—this volition is called 'bodily action' (kāyakamma). Thus, when there is communication to others (paravādi), the body is called the 'door,' and the volition produced at that door should be classified as bodily action, whether 'wholesome or unwholesome.' If there is no communication to others, it should be classified by adding 'indeterminate' (abyākata) to complete the triad (tika). Among those doors, just as a city gate remains in the place where it was built and does not shift even a finger's breadth here or there, yet the great multitude of people pass through those various gates; in the same way, the door does not move to another door, but the action (kamma) 'moves' (proceeds) because it arises at those respective doors. Therefore, the ancient teachers said:

'Actions proceed at the door; the doors do not move from door to door.
Therefore, actions are distinguished individually by their doors.'
128:
...in the speech-door. Therefore, because it occurs mostly in the body-door, its status as bodily action is established, just as the resorts of forest-dwellers and clumsy maidens are named 'forest-dweller' and so on. In this way, the definition of action is also appropriate.

## The Discussion on the Door of Bodily Action is Finished.

## The Discussion on the Door of Vocal Action

In the discussion on the door of vocal action, 'speech' (vācā) is of three kinds by way of intention (cetanā), abstinence (virati), and sound (sadda). Among those three, the speech mentioned as: "Monks, speech endowed with four factors is well-spoken, not ill-spoken; it is blameless and beyond reproach by the wise" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.213), is called 'speech as intention' (cetanā-vācā). The speech mentioned as: "That which is the avoiding, the abstaining from the four vocal misconducts... pe ... this is called Right Speech" (Vibhaṅga 206), is called 'speech as abstinence' (virati-vācā). The speech mentioned as: "Speech, talk, path of language, utterance, sound, making of sound, speech, breaking of speech" (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 850), is called 'speech as sound' (sadda-vācā).

Among those three types of speech, the name 'door of vocal action' (vacīkammadvāra) is not the name for intention, nor for abstinence. However, there is one vocal intimation (vacīviññatti) that occurs together with sound; this intimation alone is called the 'door of vocal action.' Referring to that vocal intimation, it was said: "What is that materiality which is vocal intimation? That which is the speech, talk, path of language, utterance, sound, making of sound, speech, breaking of speech of one who has a wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate mind—this is called speech. The intimation, the making known, the state of having made known by that speech—this materiality is vocal intimation" (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 636).

For one who thinks, "I will say this, I will say that," there arises what is called 'sound produced by the diffusion of initial application' (vitakkavipphārasadda). In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, it is stated that this sound is not cognizable by ear-consciousness but only by mind-consciousness. However, in the Sutta Commentaries, the sound of those who talk in their sleep or those who are delirious, which arises by the power of the diffusion of initial application, is called 'vitakkavipphārasadda.' It is said that after hearing that sound, one can point out the matter about which the person was thinking when the sound arose, saying, "Your mind was thus, your mind was in such a state," and various stories are also told. In the Paṭṭhāna also, it is stated: "The sound-base produced by mind is a condition for ear-consciousness by way of object-condition." Therefore, there is no such thing as 'sound produced by the diffusion of initial application' that is not cognizable by ear-consciousness, apart from the impact of intimation (viññatti-ghaṭṭanā). "This...
129:
The mind that arises thinking, 'I will say this, I will say that,' produces eight types of matter: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, color, odor, flavor, and nutritive essence. Within these eight types of matter, the earth element originated by the mind arises by striking against the earth element that is clung-to (kamma-born). Along with the striking of these elements, sound arises. This is called sound originated by the mind (cittasamuṭṭhāna-sadda). This sound is not intimation (viññatti). However, there is a certain alteration of mode (ākāra-vikāra) which is the cause for that mind-originated earth element striking the clung-to earth element; this is called vocal intimation (vacī-viññatti). From here on, everything such as 'that vocal intimation is not mind-originated like the eight types of matter' and so forth should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

In this case of vocal intimation as well, upon hearing the voice of someone calling 'Tissa, Datta, Mitta,' and having reflected on the intimation with the mind-door consciousness, one knows the intention: 'I think this person wants me to do such and such.' Like bodily intimation, this vocal intimation is also evident even to animals. For, upon hearing the sound 'Come, go,' even animals know the intention, thinking 'I think this person wants me to do such and such,' and they come or go. However, the section on 'whether it moves the body originated by the three causes or not' is not applicable here. There is also no function of support by the (earth element) originated by preceding minds. That volition (cetanā) which is manifest at that vocal door, by which one speaks falsehood, slanders, speaks harshly, talks frivolously, or abstains from falsehood and so on, is called vocal action (vacī-kamma). From here on, the definition of all actions and the definition of doors should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

## The Discussion on the Door of Vocal Action is Finished.

## Discussion on the Door of Mental Action

In the discussion on the door of mental action, the mind, which is fourfold according to the sense-sphere and so on, is called 'mind' (mano). Among those minds, the sense-sphere mind is of 54 types, the fine-material sphere mind is of 15 types, the immaterial sphere mind is of 12 types, and the supramundane mind is of 8 types, making a total of 89 types. Among these minds, it should not be said that 'such and such a mind is not a mind-door.' Just as it should not be said that 'such and such a volition is not kamma' (for even the volition associated with the fivefold consciousness is described as kamma in the Great Treatise (Mahāpakaraṇa)), likewise, it should not be said that 'such and such a mind is not a mind-door.'
130:
In this matter of the mind-door, there is this inquiry: 'What does this so-called kamma do?' (The answer is:) It is said that it performs accumulating (āyūhana), processing (abhisaṅkharaṇa), massing (piṇḍakaraṇa), volitional activity (cetanā), planning (kappana), and repeated planning (pakappana). If it performs such things as accumulating and so on, what does the volition of the fivefold consciousness accumulate, what does it process, what does it mass, what does it will, what does it plan, and what does it repeatedly plan? (The answer is:) It performs these for the co-nascent (sahajāta) states. For that volition of the fivefold consciousness also accumulates, processes, masses, wills, plans, and repeatedly plans the associated aggregates (sampayuttak-khandha) that are co-nascent with it. Or else, what is the use of such a debate? This statement was made by way of including all minds. The conclusion here is: the twenty-nine types of wholesome and unwholesome minds belonging to the three planes are called the door of mental action (manokamma-dvāra). The volition that arises at that mind-door, by which one takes up covetousness, ill-will, and wrong view, or non-covetousness, non-ill-will, and right view, is called mental action (manokamma). From here on, the classification of all actions and the classification of doors should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. These are the three doors of action (kamma-dvāra).

## The Discussion on the Door of Mental Action is Finished.

## Discussion on Kamma

Now, having set aside the three actions, these doors of action have been shown; starting with those (three actions), the detailed explanation of the matrix (mātikā) of the remaining discussion on doors will be given. For there are three actions: bodily action, vocal action, and mental action. If it is asked, 'What is this kamma?', it is volition (cetanā) and certain states associated with volition. Regarding the nature of volition as kamma, there are these Suttas:

"Monks, I say that volition is kamma. Having willed, one performs kamma through body, speech, or mind."

"Ānanda, when there is the body (bodily intimation), pleasure and pain arise internally due to bodily volition. When there is speech (vocal intimation), pleasure and pain arise internally due to vocal volition. When there is the mind (mind-door), pleasure and pain arise internally due to mental volition."

"Monks, threefold bodily volition is unwholesome bodily action, resulting in suffering, having suffering as its result. Monks, fourfold vocal volition is... [as above]... Monks, threefold mental volition is unwholesome mental action, resulting in suffering, having suffering as its result."
131:
Monks, the three types of bodily volition are wholesome bodily actions that produce happiness and have happy results. Monks, the four types of verbal volition... Monks, the three types of mental volition are wholesome mental actions that produce happiness and have happy results. 

"Ānanda, if this foolish man Samiddhi, when asked thus by the wanderer Pāṭaliputta, were to answer: 'Friend Pāṭaliputta, having performed a volitional action by way of body, speech, or mind that is to be felt as pleasant, one experiences pleasure... having performed a volitional action... that is to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, one experiences neither-pain-nor-pleasure.' Ānanda, answering in this way, the foolish man Samiddhi would be answering the wanderer Pāṭaliputta correctly."

These are the discourses showing the nature of volition as kamma. However, the nature of kamma for states associated with volition is shown by the fourfold kamma (kamma-catukka). It has been said: 

'Monks, these four kammas have been realized and declared by me through my own higher knowledge. Which four? Monks, there is dark kamma with dark results. Monks, there is bright kamma with bright results. Monks, there is dark-and-bright kamma with dark-and-bright results. Monks, there is kamma that is neither dark nor bright, with neither dark nor bright results, which leads to the destruction of kamma. ... Monks, what is the kamma that is neither dark nor bright, with neither dark nor bright results, which leads to the destruction of kamma? These are the seven factors of enlightenment: the enlightenment factor of mindfulness... the enlightenment factor of equanimity. Monks, this is called kamma that is neither dark nor bright, with neither dark nor bright results, which leads to the destruction of kamma. ... Monks, what is the kamma that is neither dark nor bright, with neither dark nor bright results, which leads to the destruction of kamma? It is this Noble Eightfold Path: namely, right view... right concentration. Monks, this is called kamma that is neither dark nor bright, with neither dark nor bright results, which leads to the destruction of kamma.'

Thus, these fifteen states, by way of the factors of enlightenment and the path factors, are shown by the fourfold kamma. Together with these six states—covetousness, ill will, wrong view, non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view—twenty-one states should be understood as states associated with volition.
132:
Among those states associated with volition, when the supramundane path (lokuttara-magga) is developed, it is included in the three types of kamma such as bodily action. When one transgresses and practices immorality through the body (such as killing, etc.), the state that restrains and blocks that bodily immorality is to be known as bodily restraint (kāyika-saṃvara). When one transgresses and practices immorality through speech (such as lying, etc.), the state that restrains and blocks that verbal immorality is to be known as verbal restraint (vācasika-saṃvara). Thus, right action (sammā-kammanta) is called bodily action; right speech (sammā-vācā) is called verbal action. When these two are taken, right livelihood (sammā-ājīva) is also taken because it belongs to the side of right action and right speech. When one transgresses and practices immorality through the mind (such as wrong view, etc.), the state that restrains and blocks that mental immorality is to be known as mental restraint (mānasika-saṃvara). That mental restraint is fivefold by way of right view, right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. These five types are also called mental action. Thus, when the supramundane path is developed, it is included in the three types of kamma.

In this context, there is what is called the coordination of doors (dvāra-saṃsandana). In the bodily and verbal doors, there are actions that reach the stage of movement (copana) but do not reach the course of action (kamma-patha). In the mental door, there are actions that reach the stage of occurrence (samudācāra) but do not reach the course of action. Taking those actions that do not reach the course of action, they are classified only under their respective doors.

Regarding this coordination of doors, this is the method: A hunter, thinking 'I will go to find game,' prepares his bow, twists the bowstring, sharpens his spear, eats his meal, and puts on his clothes. By this much preparation, movement is reached in the bodily door. If that hunter wanders in the forest all day and does not catch even a rabbit or a cat at the end, does this action constitute unwholesome bodily kamma or not? It does not. Why? Because it has not reached the course of action (kamma-patha). However, it should be known as mere bodily misconduct (kāya-duccharita). The same method applies to efforts such as fishing.

In the verbal door as well, if one gives an order, 'Let us go to find game; prepare the bows and so on quickly,' and like the previous method, the hunter who gets nothing in the forest reaches movement in the verbal door, but because it has not reached the course of action, it does not become bodily kamma. It should be known as mere verbal misconduct (vacī-duccharita).

In the mental door, however, the moment the volition to kill arises, it constitutes a breach of the course of action. That breach of the course of action occurs by way of ill will (byāpāda), not by way of killing (pāṇātipāta). Unwholesome bodily kamma originates in the bodily and verbal doors, not in the mental door; likewise for unwholesome verbal kamma. Unwholesome mental kamma, however, originates in all three doors. Likewise, wholesome bodily, verbal, and mental kammas should be understood.
133:
...Unwholesome vocal action (vacīkamma) arises in the body-door (kāyadvāra) and speech-door (vacīdvāra), but not in the mind-door (manodvāra). Specifically, unwholesome mental action (manokamma) arises in all three doors. Wholesome bodily, vocal, and mental actions should be understood in the same way.

How so? In brief, for one who kills a living being with their own hand, takes what is not given, or commits sexual misconduct, the action is bodily action (kāyakamma) only. The door is also the body-door only. Thus, first, unwholesome bodily action arises in the body-door. Covetousness (abhijjhā), ill will (byāpāda), and wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) that arise together with those consciousnesses are either on the side of volition (cetanā) or are unexpressed (avvohārika) because they are not designated as mental action.

For one who gives an order, saying, 'Go, deprive such-and-such a person of life; steal such-and-such a property,' the action is bodily action, but the door is the speech-door. Thus, unwholesome bodily action arises in the speech-door. Covetousness, ill will, and wrong view that arise together with those consciousnesses are either on the side of volition or are unexpressed. This much is the common view of the teachers in the Commentaries.

However, a Vitaṇḍavādī says, 'Unwholesome bodily action also arises in the mind-door.' When told, 'Bring a sutta that was included in the three Councils,' he brought this Kulumba Sutta:

'Furthermore, bhikkhus, here a certain ascetic or brahmin who possesses psychic power and has attained mastery over the mind, looks repeatedly with an evil mind at a fetus in another's womb, thinking, "Oh, may this fetus in the womb not come out safely!" In this way, bhikkhus, there is the destruction (kulumba) of the fetus.'

After citing this sutta, he said: 'Just by thinking in this way with the mind, the fetus in the womb dissolves like a mass of foam. Where is there any movement of the limbs of the body or movement of the organs of speech in this case? Therefore, this unwholesome bodily action arises only in the mind-door.'

The teachers, saying to him, 'We shall weigh the meaning of your sutta,' weighed it as follows: 'You speak of harming others through psychic power. What is called psychic power (iddhi) is of ten kinds: iddhi through resolve (adhiṭṭhāniddhi), iddhi through transformation (vikubbaniddhi), mind-made iddhi (manomayiddhi), iddhi by the diffusion of knowledge (ñāṇavipphāriddhi), iddhi by the diffusion of concentration (samādhivipphāriddhi), noble iddhi (ariyiddhi), iddhi born of the result of kamma (kammavipākajiddhi), the iddhi of a meritorious person (puññavato iddhi), iddhi made of vijjā (vijjāmayiddhi), and [iddhi] due to right effort in various circumstances...'
134:
Psychic power (iddhi) is of ten kinds in the sense of succeeding. Among those ten kinds of iddhi, which one do you mean? He replied, 'I mean the iddhi produced by meditation (bhāvanāmaya).' When asked, 'Can the act of killing another occur through iddhi produced by meditation?' he replied, 'Yes, some teachers say it can happen once.' Just as when a person wishing to strike another throws a pot full of water, the pot breaks and the water is destroyed; similarly, they say the act of killing another can occur once through iddhi produced by meditation, and from then on, that iddhi is lost.

Then, saying to him, 'The act of killing another cannot occur even once or twice through iddhi produced by meditation,' they questioned him as he came to the classification of wholesome, unwholesome, and so on: 'Is bhāvanāmaya-iddhi wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate? Is it associated with pleasant feeling, painful feeling, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling? Is it with initial and sustained thought, with sustained thought only, or without initial and sustained thought? Does it belong to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, or the immaterial sphere?'

One who knows this problem would say: 'Bhāvanāmaya-iddhi is either wholesome or indeterminate. It is associated only with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. It is only without initial and sustained thought. It belongs only to the fine-material sphere.' Then he should be asked: 'In which category among wholesome and so on does the volition of killing (pāṇātipāta-cetanā) fall?' One who knows would say: 'The volition of killing is only unwholesome. It is associated only with painful feeling. It is only with initial and sustained thought. It belongs only to the sense sphere.' 'If that is so, your view does not agree with the Wholesome Triad (Kusala-ttika), nor with the Feeling Triad (Vedanā-ttika), nor with the Initial Thought Triad (Vitakka-ttika), nor with the difference in planes (bhūmantara).'

When asked, 'Then is such a great sutta useless and in vain?' they replied, 'It is not useless; it is just that you do not know its meaning. In the phrase "possessing psychic power and has attained mastery over the mind," bhāvanāmaya-iddhi is not intended; rather, the power mentioned in the Athabbana Veda (vijjāmayiddhi) is intended. Only that power is applicable here. That Athabbana power cannot be performed by bypassing the body-door and speech-door. Those who desire Athabbana power eat saltless food for seven days, spread grass and sleep on the ground, and practice austerities. On the seventh day, they prepare a cemetery ground, stand at the seventh step, wave their hands repeatedly, and recite mantras with their mouths. Only then is their work successful. Similarly, this vijjāmayiddhi cannot be performed by bypassing the body-door and speech-door. Therefore, the conclusion should be reached here that "bodily action does not arise in the mind-door."'
135:
For one who speaks falsehoods and so forth by means of hand gestures (bodily movements), the action is verbal action (vaci-kamma), but the door is the body-door (kāya-dvāra). Thus, unwholesome verbal action also arises at the body-door. Covetousness, ill-will, and wrong view that arise together with those thoughts either belong to the side of volition (cetanā) or are not conventionally designated (abbohārīka) [as mental action].

For one who speaks falsehoods and so forth by uttering words, the action is verbal action and the door is also the speech-door (vaci-dvāra). Thus, unwholesome verbal action arises at the speech-door. Covetousness, ill-will, and wrong view that arise together with those thoughts either belong to the side of volition or are not conventionally designated. This much is known as the common explanation (samānatthakathā) of the teachers.

However, a Vitaṇḍavādī (sophist) says: 'Unwholesome verbal action also arises at the mind-door.' When told, 'Bring a sutta that has been included in the three councils,' he brought this sutta from the Uposathakkhandhaka:

'If a monk, while [the Pātimokkha] is being recited for the third time, remembers and does not reveal an existing offense, it becomes a deliberate lie (sampajāna-musāvāda) for him.'

Having brought this sutta, he said: 'Thus, while remaining silent and not revealing the offense, he falls into another offense. Where is there any movement of the body (kāyaṅga-copana) or movement of speech (vācaṅga-copana) here? This unwholesome verbal action arises only at the mind-door.'

He should be asked: 'Is this sutta one of indirect meaning (neyyattha) or direct meaning (nītattha)?' He says: 'For me, this sutta is of direct meaning.' He should be told: 'Do not say so; let us weigh the meaning of this sutta,' and then asked: 'What offense occurs because of deliberate lying?' If he is knowledgeable, he will say: 'An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) occurs because of deliberate lying.'

Then he should be told: 'The roots of the Vinaya are two: body and speech. The Fully Enlightened One has prescribed all offenses only in these two doors; there is no such thing as prescribing an offense at the mind-door. You are very knowledgeable in the Vinaya indeed, you who prescribe an offense where the Teacher has not prescribed one, who slanders the Fully Enlightened One, and who strikes at the Conqueror's authority (jinacakka)!' After rebuking him with such words, he should be further asked: 'Does deliberate lying arise from action (kiriya) or from non-action (akiriya)?' If he is knowledgeable, he will say: 'From action.' Then he should be asked: 'What action does one who does not reveal an offense perform?' Truly, not seeing any action, he will come to distress.
136:
He should be made to understand by the meaning of that sutta. Here is the meaning: Regarding what was stated as 'it becomes a deliberate lie,' what does that become in terms of an offense? The meaning is 'what offense occurs?' The answer is 'an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) occurs.' It should be understood that this offense of wrong-doing does not occur by the characteristic of lying itself, but according to the words of the Blessed One, it is an offense arising from non-action (akiriya) at the speech-door. This matter is also stated in the Parivāra:

'Without speaking to any human being,
And without uttering a word to others,
One may fall into a verbal offense, but not a bodily one.
This problem has been considered by the wise.'

Thus, it should be understood in this conclusion of the discussion on action (kammakathā) that unwholesome verbal action does not arise at the mind-door.

At another time, when one moves the body with a mind associated with covetousness and performs acts such as taking by the hand; or when one performs acts such as grasping a stick or a weapon with a mind associated with ill-will; or when one performs acts such as preparing seats, worshipping, or saluting with joined palms for deities like Khandha or Siva, thinking 'Khandha, Siva, and others are supreme' with a mind associated with wrong view—at that time, the action is mental action (mano-kamma), but the door is the body-door. Thus, unwholesome mental action arises at the body-door. Here, volition (cetanā) does not receive the designation [of bodily action].

At another time, when one moves the organ of speech with a mind associated with covetousness and thinks or speaks about another's property, 'O, would that what belongs to another were mine!'; or when one says with a mind associated with ill-will, 'May these beings be killed, bound, or destroyed!'; or when one says with a mind associated with wrong view, 'There is no result of giving, no result of offering,' and so forth—at that time, the action is mental action, but the door is the speech-door. Thus, unwholesome mental action arises at the speech-door. Here too, volition does not receive the designation [of verbal action].

At another time, when one stays in seclusion without moving the body or speech and produces thoughts associated with covetousness, ill-will, and wrong view—at that time, the action is mental action and the door is also the mind-door. Thus, unwholesome mental action arises at the mind-door. In this situation, both volition and the states associated with volition arise only at the mind-door. Thus, it should be understood that unwholesome mental action can arise at all three doors.
137:
In the statement, 'Likewise, wholesome bodily, verbal, and mental actions,' this is the method: When someone, for some reason unable to speak, undertakes these precepts—'I refrain from taking life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct'—by means of gestures, then that action is bodily action and the door is also the bodily door. Thus, wholesome bodily action arises at the bodily door. The non-covetousness and so forth associated with those thoughts either belong to the side of volition or are non-conventional (not designated as mental action).

When one undertakes those same precepts by breaking into speech, then the action is bodily action, but the door is the verbal door. Thus, wholesome bodily action arises at the verbal door. The non-covetousness and so forth associated with those thoughts either belong to the side of volition or are non-conventional.

When those precepts are being given and one undertakes them mentally alone—'I refrain from taking life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct'—without moving the limbs of the body or the organs of speech, then the action is bodily action, but the door is the mind door. Thus, wholesome bodily action arises at the mind door. The non-covetousness and so forth associated with those thoughts either belong to the side of volition or are non-conventional.

It should be understood that for one undertaking the four precepts such as 'refraining from false speech' through the body and so forth in the manner already stated, wholesome verbal action arises at the three doors. Here too, non-covetousness and so forth either belong to the side of volition or are non-conventional.

Furthermore, for one who, with thoughts associated with non-covetousness and so forth, moves the limbs of the body to perform acts such as sweeping the courtyard of a pagoda, making offerings of incense and flowers, or worshipping a pagoda, the action is mental action, but the door is the bodily door. Thus, wholesome mental action arises at the bodily door. Here, volition is non-conventional (not designated as bodily action).

For one who, with a thought associated with non-covetousness, moves the organs of speech and thinks without covetousness, 'Oh, may the property and belongings of others not be mine!'; or for one who, with a thought associated with non-ill-will, says, 'May all beings be free from enmity, free from harm, free from suffering, and may they maintain themselves in happiness'; or for one who, with a thought associated with right view, utters such things as 'There is fruit in what is given'—the action is mental action, but the door is the verbal door. Thus, wholesome mental action arises at the verbal door.
138:
Here, volition is non-conventional (not designated as verbal action). But for one who, sitting in seclusion without moving the limbs of the body or the organs of speech, produces thoughts associated with non-covetousness and so forth by mind alone, the action is mental action and the door is also the mind door. Thus, wholesome mental action arises at the mind door. In this case, both volition and the states associated with volition arise only at the mind door.

In cases of taking life (pāṇātipāta) and taking what is not given (adinnādāna) that arise through command (āṇatti), one who says the action is bodily action and the door is also the bodily door by virtue of the action is said to 'protect the action but destroy the door.' In cases of false speech (musāvāda) and so forth that arise through hand gestures (hatthamuddā), one who says the door is the bodily door and the action is also bodily action by virtue of the door is said to 'protect the door but destroy the action.' Therefore, one should not destroy the door while thinking 'I will protect the action,' nor should one destroy the action while thinking 'I will protect the door.' Action and door should be understood only according to the method already stated. Indeed, one who speaks thus destroys neither the action nor the door.

## The Discussion on Action is Finished.

Now, regarding 'five consciousnesses, five doors of consciousness,' and so forth (the decision should be understood). Eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness—these five are called consciousnesses. The eye-consciousness door, ear-consciousness door, nose-consciousness door, tongue-consciousness door, and body-consciousness door—these five are called doors of consciousness. It should be understood that volition arising by virtue of these five doors is neither bodily action nor verbal action, but only mental action. Eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact—these six are called contacts (samphassa). The eye-contact door, ear-contact door, nose-contact door, tongue-contact door, body-contact door, and mind-contact door—these six are called doors of contact.

Eye non-restraint, ear non-restraint, nose non-restraint, tongue non-restraint, sensitive-body non-restraint, moving-body non-restraint, verbal non-restraint, and mental non-restraint—these eight are called non-restraints (asaṃvara). In terms of their nature, these are five states: immorality (dussīlya), lack of mindfulness (muṭṭhassacca), ignorance (aññāṇa), lack of patience (akkhanti), and laziness (kosajja). Among these five states, not even one arises in the thoughts ending with determining (votthabbana) in the five doors; they arise only at the moment of impulsion (javana). Even though they arise in impulsion, they are called non-restraint in the five doors.

Indeed, the contact associated with eye-consciousness is called eye-contact, volition is called mental action, and that thought is called the door of mental action. Here, the fivefold non-restraint...
139: There is none. Contact arising together with the receiving consciousness (sampaticchana) is called mind-contact (manosamphassa); volition is called mental action (manokamma); that consciousness is called the mental action-door (manokammadvāra). Here also, there is no non-restraint (asaṃvara). The same method applies to the investigating (santīraṇa) and determining (votthabbana) consciousnesses. However, contact arising together with impulsion (javana) is called mind-contact; volition is called mental action; that consciousness is called the mental action-door. Non-restraint occurring in this impulsion is called non-restraint of the eye (cakkhu-asaṃvara). The same method applies to the doors of the ear, nose, tongue, and sensitive body. When a mind-door impulsion, having one of the objects such as a visible form, arises without the speech-door but causing movement (copana) known as the pure body-door, then the contact arising together with that consciousness is called mind-contact, and the volition is called bodily action (kāyakamma). That consciousness, however, does not receive the designation 'mind-door'; because movement has arisen, it is not reckoned as the mind-door. Non-restraint occurring here is called non-restraint of the moving body (copanakāya-asaṃvara). When such an impulsion arises without the body-door but causing movement known as the pure speech-door, then the contact arising together with that consciousness is called mind-contact, and the volition is called verbal action (vacīkamma). That consciousness, however, does not receive the designation 'mind-door'; because movement has arisen, it is not reckoned as the mind-door. Non-restraint occurring here is called non-restraint of speech (vācā-asaṃvara). When such an impulsion-consciousness arises without the body or speech doors, occurring only in the pure mind-door, then the contact arising together with that consciousness is called mind-contact, volition is called mental action, and that consciousness is called the mental action-door. Non-restraint occurring here is called non-restraint of the mind (mano-asaṃvara). Thus, by means of these eight types of non-restraint, these eight doors of non-restraint should be understood: the door of eye non-restraint, ear..., nose..., tongue..., sensitive body..., moving body..., speech..., and mind non-restraint. Restraint of the eye, ear..., nose..., tongue..., sensitive body..., moving body..., speech..., and mind are called the eight types of restraint (saṃvara). In terms of their nature, these restraints are these five qualities: virtue (sīla), mindfulness (sati), wisdom (ñāṇa), patience (khanti), and energy (vīriya). Among these five qualities, not even one arises in the consciousnesses ending with determining (votthabbana) in the five doors. They arise only at the moment of impulsion (javana). Even though they arise in impulsion, they are called restraint in the five doors. The arising of all these restraints should be understood in the same way as described for non-restraint, starting with 'contact arising together with eye-consciousness is called eye-contact,' and so on. Thus, by means of these eight types of restraint, these eight doors of restraint should be understood: the door of eye restraint... etc. ...the door of mind restraint.
140: ## Akusalakammapathakathā: Discussion on the Unwholesome Courses of Action Killing (pāṇātipāta), stealing (adinnādāna), sexual misconduct (kāmesumicchācāra), false speech (musāvāda), slanderous speech (pisuṇavācā), harsh speech (pharusavācā), frivolous chatter (samphappalāpa), covetousness (abhijjhā), ill-will (byāpāda), and wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi)—these ten are called the unwholesome courses of action (akusalakamma-patha). Among these ten, the rapid falling (killing) of the life of another is called pāṇātipāta. It is also called pāṇavadha (slaying a being) or pāṇaghāta (striking down a being). In this term pāṇātipāta, 'pāṇa' refers to a 'being' in conventional terms (vohāra), but in the ultimate sense (paramattha), it is the life-faculty (jīvitindriya). The volition of killing (vadhakacetanā) that arises in one of the doors—either the body-door or the speech-door—which produces the effort to cut off the life-faculty of a being, while perceiving that being as a living being, is called pāṇātipāta. Regarding beings without special qualities, such as animals, this act of killing is of less blame (appasāvajja) in the case of small beings and of great blame (mahāsāvajja) in the case of large-bodied beings. Why? Because of the greatness of the effort (payoga). Even when the effort is equal, it is because of the greatness of the object (the being). Among beings with special qualities, such as humans, it is of less blame in the case of those with few qualities and of great blame in the case of those with great qualities. When the body and qualities are equal, it should be understood that the act is of less blame due to the mildness of the defilements and the effort, and of great blame due to their intensity. There are five factors (sambhāra) of that act of killing: a living being, the perception of it as a living being, the intent to kill, the effort to kill, and death resulting from that effort. There are six types of effort (payoga): killing with one's own hand (sāhatthika), by command (āṇattika), by discharging weapons (nissaggiya), by permanent means such as digging pits (thāvara), by magical arts (vijjāmaya), and by psychic power (iddhimaya). If this matter were to be explained in detail, it would become too extensive; therefore, it is not elaborated here. Those who desire such details should look for them in the Vinaya Commentary named Samantapāsādikā. Taking what is not given by the owner is called 'adinnādāna'. It means carrying away, thieving, or stealing the property of another. In this context, 'adinna' (not given) refers to property possessed by another, where the owner can act according to their will and is not liable to punishment or reproach. The volition of theft (theyyacetanā) that produces the effort to take that property, while perceiving it as property possessed by another, is called adinnādāna. This act of stealing is of less blame in the case of inferior property belonging to another and of great blame in the case of superior property. Why? Because of the superiority of the object. When the objects are equal, it is of great blame in the case of property belonging to those with superior qualities. In relation to those with superior qualities, the act is of less blame in the case of property belonging to those with fewer qualities.
141:
There are five factors (sambhāra) of that adinnādāna (taking what is not given). They are: the property of another, the perception of it as another's property, the intention to steal, the effort made, and the taking away by that effort. There are six types of effort (payoga), starting with personal effort (sāhatthika). These efforts occur according to the circumstances through the five types of theft: theft by stealing (theyyāvahāra), theft by force (pasahyāvahāra), concealed theft (paṭicchannāvahāra), theft by design (parikappāvahāra), and theft by switching lots (kusāvahāra). This is a summary here; the detailed explanation is given in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary.

In the term ‘kāmesu micchācāra’, ‘kāmesu’ refers to sexual misconduct. ‘Micchācāra’ is base conduct that is absolutely censurable. By characteristic, sexual misconduct (kāmesu micchācāra) is the volition to transgress forbidden persons (agamaniya-ṭṭhāna) occurring through the body-door with the intention of unwholesome conduct.

In that context, forbidden persons (women) for men are: first, the ten types of women such as those protected by their mother (mātu-rakkhitā), protected by their father, protected by both parents, protected by their brother, protected by their sister, protected by relatives, protected by their clan, protected by fellow practitioners, those betrothed from birth (sārakkhā), and those under penalty (saparidaṇḍā). Then there are the ten types of wives such as those bought with wealth (dhanakkītā), those living together by choice, those living for wealth, those living for clothes, those married by the water-pouring ceremony, those taken after removing the head-pad, slave-wives, worker-wives, those captured in war, and temporary wives. Thus, there are twenty types of women. Among these women, for other men, the twelve types—the two (sārakkhā and saparidaṇḍā) and the ten starting with dhanakkītā—are considered forbidden persons (agamaniya-ṭṭhāna).

That sexual misconduct carries little blame when committed with forbidden persons who lack virtue (sīla), etc. It carries great blame when committed with forbidden persons who are endowed with virtue, etc. There are four factors (sambhāra) of that sexual misconduct: a forbidden object, the intent to associate with that object, the effort to associate, and the acceptance of the union of the organs. There is only one type of effort: personal effort (sāhatthika).

‘Musā’ (falsehood) is a verbal or bodily effort that destroys welfare, preceded by the intent to deceive. The volition that produces bodily or verbal effort to deceive others with the intention of deception is called musāvāda (false speech). Another way: ‘musā’ is an untrue, unreal matter. ‘Vāda’ is making that matter known as if it were true and real. By characteristic, musāvāda is the volition that produces the corresponding intimation (viññatti) of one who wishes to make another understand an unreal matter as real. That musāvāda carries little blame if the welfare it destroys is small, and great blame if the welfare is great. Furthermore...
142:
For laypeople, false speech such as saying 'I do not have it' because of not wanting to give one's own property carries little blame. False speech spoken as a witness to destroy another's welfare carries great blame. For monks, false speech spoken in jest after receiving a little oil or ghee, such as 'Today in the village, oil is flowing like a river,' following the style of ancient metaphors, carries little blame. For those who say they saw what they did not see, false speech carries great blame.

There are four factors (sambhāra) of that musāvāda: an unreal matter, the intent to deceive, the corresponding effort, and another person understanding that meaning. There is only one type of effort: personal effort (sāhatthika). That effort should be understood as performing an act of deceiving another through the body, through something connected to the body, or through speech. If another person understands that meaning through that act, at the very moment of the volition that produces this action, one is bound by the kamma of musāvāda (the course of action is completed). Just as one deceives another through the body, things connected to the body, or speech, so too are those who command another saying 'Speak this,' those who write a message and place it in front, and those who write on walls, etc., saying 'This meaning should be understood thus.' Therefore, in this musāvāda, the efforts known as command (āṇattika), written/dropped (nissaggiya), and permanent (thāvara) are also applicable. However, since they are not directly mentioned in the Commentaries, they should be accepted after careful investigation.

In the terms ‘pisuṇavācā’ (slander), etc., the decision should be understood. Speech by which, when spoken to someone, one makes oneself dear to that person's heart and makes another person empty (hated) is called pisuṇavācā. Speech by which one makes oneself and others harsh, which is itself harsh, not pleasant to the ear, and does not reach the heart, is called pharusavācā (harsh speech). Speaking useless words is called samphappalāpa (frivolous talk). The volition that is the root of those speeches also receives the names pisuṇavācā, etc. In this context of the courses of action (kammapatha), only that volition is intended.

Among those, the volition that produces bodily or verbal effort of one with a defiled mind, either to cause division among others or out of a desire to be dear to them, is called pisuṇavācā. That pisuṇavācā carries little blame if the person divided has little virtue, and great blame if they have great virtue.

There are four factors of that pisuṇavācā: another person to be divided, the intent to cause division with the thought 'These people will be divided' or the desire to be dear with the thought 'Thus I will be dear and trusted,' the corresponding effort, and another person understanding that meaning.
143: "Understanding the meaning" means that as long as others do not understand the meaning, it does not yet constitute a course of action (kammapatha); it only becomes a course of action when they do. The purely harsh intention that originates bodily and vocal efforts which cut to the heart of another (painful as if cutting the vital parts) is called "harsh speech" (pharusavācā). To clarify this harsh speech, there is this story: A boy went to the forest, ignoring his mother's words. Being unable to stop him, the mother cursed him, saying, "May a wild buffalo chase you!" Then, a buffalo indeed appeared before the boy in the forest. The boy made an act of truth: "May the words my mother spoke with her mouth not happen; may only the thought she conceived in her mind happen." The buffalo stood still as if tied right there. Thus, even if it is an effort that cuts to the heart, it is not harsh speech because of the softness of the mind. Parents sometimes say to their children, "May thieves cut you into pieces," yet they do not wish even a lotus petal to fall upon them. Teachers and preceptors also sometimes say to their pupils, "Why do these shameless and reckless ones wander about? Drive them out!" yet they only desire their success in learning and practice. Just as it is not harsh speech when the mind is soft, it is not gentle speech (apharusavācā) just because the words are soft. The words of one who wants to kill, saying "Let this man sleep peacefully," are not gentle speech. Because of the harshness of the mind, it is indeed harsh speech. That harsh speech has little blame if the person targeted has few virtues, and great blame if they have many virtues. Its three factors are: another person to be cursed, an angry mind, and the act of cursing. The unwholesome intention that originates bodily and vocal efforts to communicate what is useless is called "frivolous talk" (samphappalāpa). It has little blame if practiced little, and great blame if practiced much. Its two factors are: preoccupation with useless talk such as the Bharata war or the abduction of Sītā, and the act of telling such stories. If others do not accept that talk, it does not constitute a course of action; it only becomes a course of action when others accept the frivolous talk. Covetousness (abhijjhā) is so called because it covets. It means it proceeds by leaning towards another's goods, being directed towards them. Its characteristic is coveting another's goods, thinking, "Oh, may this of yours be mine!" Like theft (adinnādāna), it has both small and great blame.
144: The factors of that covetousness are two: another's property and diverting it to oneself. Even if greed arises regarding another's property, it does not yet constitute a course of action as long as one does not divert it to oneself, thinking, "Oh, may this be mine!" Ill-will (byāpāda) is so called because it destroys welfare and happiness. It has the characteristic of malice with the desire for another's destruction. Like harsh speech, it has small and great blame. Its factors are two: another being and the thought of their destruction. Even if anger arises regarding another being, it does not yet constitute a course of action as long as one does not think of their destruction, "Oh, may this person be cut off and perish!" Wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) is so called because it sees wrongly by not grasping the truth. It has the characteristic of perverted vision, such as "Natthi dinnaṃ" (There is no fruit of giving), etc. Like frivolous talk, it has small and great blame. Alternatively, uncertain wrong view has little blame, while certain wrong view (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi) has great blame. Its factors are two: the perversion of the object from its actual state and the appearance of it to oneself in that perverted way. Among those wrong views, only the views of nihilism (natthika-diṭṭhi), non-causality (ahetuka-diṭṭhi), and the inefficacy of action (akiriya-diṭṭhi) constitute a course of action, not other views. The decision regarding these ten unwholesome courses of action should be understood through five aspects: by nature (dhamma), by category (koṭṭhāsa), by object (ārammaṇa), by feeling (vedanā), and by root (mūla). Among those five, "by nature" means that in these courses of action, seven are sequentially only the mental factor of intention (cetanā), while the three starting with covetousness are states associated with intention. "By category" means that the seven in sequence and wrong view—these eight—are only courses of action, not roots. Covetousness and ill-will are both courses of action and roots. When covetousness reaches the status of a root, it is the "unwholesome root of greed" (lobha-akusalamūla); ill-will is the "unwholesome root of hatred" (dosa-akusalamūla). "By object" means that killing (pāṇātipāta) has formations as its object because it takes the life faculty as its object. Taking what is not given (adinnādāna) has either beings or formations as its object. Sexual misconduct (micchācāra) has formations as its object by way of touch (phoṭṭhabba); some teachers say it also has beings as its object. False speech (musāvāda) has either beings or formations as its object. Slander (pisuṇavācā) is the same. Harsh speech (pharusavācā) has only beings as its object. Frivolous talk (samphappalāpa) has either beings or formations as its object by way of what is seen, heard, sensed, or cognized. Covetousness is the same. Ill-will has only beings as its object. Wrong view has only formations as its object by way of the states belonging to the three planes.
145:
“By way of feeling” (Vedanāto) means that the killing of living beings (pāṇātipāta) has painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā). Even if kings, upon seeing a thief, laugh and say, “Go, execute him,” their decisive volition (sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā) is associated only with pain. Taking what is not given (adinnādāna) has three feelings. For one who takes with joy upon seeing another's property, there is pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā). For one who takes while trembling with fear, there is painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā). Likewise for one reflecting on the results of the kamma and its consequences (there is painful feeling). For one who takes while remaining in a state of indifference, there is neutral feeling (adukkhamasukha-vedanā/upekkhā). Sexual misconduct (micchācāra) has two feelings by way of pleasant and neutral. However, in the decisive mind, neutral feeling does not occur. False speech (musāvāda) has three feelings in the same way as mentioned for taking what is not given. Slander (pisuṇavācā) is the same. Harsh speech (pharusavācā) has painful feeling. Idle chatter (samphappalāpa) has three feelings. This is because when others are applauding and throwing up their garments, one who is joyful while telling stories such as the abduction of Queen Sītā or the Bhārata war has pleasant feeling. When a person who was previously paid says, “Tell it again from the beginning,” and the speaker tells it with a displeased mind, thinking, “Must I tell these various disconnected stories?”, there is painful feeling. For one who speaks with indifference, there is neutral feeling. Covetousness (abhijjhā) has two feelings by way of pleasant and neutral. Wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) is the same. Ill will (byāpāda) has painful feeling.

“By way of roots” (Mūlato) means that killing has two roots by way of hatred (dosa) and delusion (moha). Taking what is not given has two roots, either by way of hatred and delusion or by way of greed (lobha) and delusion. Sexual misconduct has two roots by way of greed and delusion. False speech has two roots, either by way of hatred and delusion or by way of greed and delusion. Slander and idle chatter are the same. Harsh speech has two roots by way of hatred and delusion. Covetousness has one root by way of delusion. Ill will is the same. Wrong view has two roots by way of greed and delusion.

## The Discussion on Unwholesome Courses of Action is finished.

## The Discussion on Wholesome Courses of Action

The seven abstinences (virati) from killing and so forth, along with non-covetousness (anabhijjhā), non-ill will (abyāpāda), and right view (sammādiṭṭhi), are called the ten wholesome courses of action (kusala-kamma-patha). Among them, the meanings of killing and so forth are just as previously stated. They abstain from killing and so forth by means of this [dhamma], or it abstains by itself; (therefore it is called abstinence/virati). For one who abstains from killing, the abstinence associated with the wholesome mind, which is taught as “at that time there is abstinence from killing,” is of three kinds: abstinence from an encountered situation (sampatta-virati), abstinence by undertaking (samādāna-virati), and abstinence by eradication (samuccheda-virati).

Among these three, for those who have not undertaken precepts, when they reflect on their own birth, age, learning, and so forth, and think, “It is not proper for us to commit the killing of living beings,” and do not transgress against the object that has appeared, the abstinence that arises is to be understood as sampatta-virati. Regarding this sampatta-virati, the story of the lay devotee Cakkana in the island of Sri Lanka is an illustration. When Cakkana was young, his mother fell ill.
146: Abstinence (virati) is so called because it is the act of abstaining from killing and so forth, or the means of abstaining, or simply the state of abstaining. For one who abstains from killing, the abstinence associated with a wholesome mind, which is described in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī as "that which is the avoidance, the abstinence from killing at that time," is of three types: natural abstinence (sampatta-virati), abstinence by undertaking [precepts] (samādāna-virati), and abstinence by eradication (samuccheda-virati). Among these three, natural abstinence (sampatta-virati) should be understood as the abstinence that arises in those who have not yet undertaken precepts, when they reflect on their birth, age, learning, and so forth, thinking, "It is not proper for one such as I to commit such an evil deed," and do not transgress against the object that has come before them. This is like the case of Cakkana Upāsaka in the island of Sīhaḷa. When Cakkana Upāsaka was young, his mother fell ill. The physician said, "It is necessary to obtain fresh hare meat." Therefore, Cakkana's elder brother sent him, saying, "Little brother, go and wander through the fields [to find a hare]." Cakkana went to those fields. At that time, a hare had come to eat the young crops. Seeing Cakkana, it ran swiftly but became entangled in a creeper and cried out "Kiri kiri!" Cakkana went toward the sound, caught the hare, and thought, "I will make medicine for my mother." Then he thought again, "It is not proper for me to deprive another of life for the sake of my mother's life." Then he released it, saying, "Go, enjoy grass and water with the other hares in the forest." When his elder brother asked, "Little brother, did you get a hare?" he told the whole story, and his brother scolded him. Cakkana went to his mother and made an Act of Truth: "Since I was born, I do not recall intentionally depriving any living being of life." At that very moment, his mother was cured of her illness. Abstinence by undertaking (samādāna-virati) should be understood as the abstinence that arises in those who have undertaken precepts, when they do not transgress against the object even by sacrificing their own life, both at the time of undertaking the precepts and thereafter. This is like the Upāsaka living on Uttaravaḍḑhamāna Mountain. It is said that this Upāsaka took the precepts from the Elder Piṅgalabuddharakkhita, who resided at Ambariya Monastery, and was plowing his field. Then his ox was lost.
