While searching for the ox, he climbed Uttaravaḍḑhamāna Mountain. There, a large python caught and coiled around him. He thought, "I will cut off the snake's head with this sharp billhook." Then he thought again, "It is not proper for me to break the precepts I have taken from my venerable teacher." Having thought this up to three times, he decided, "I will sacrifice only my life, but I will not sacrifice the precepts," and threw the sharp billhook on his shoulder into the forest. At that very moment, the python released the Upāsaka and went away. Abstinence by eradication (samuccheda-virati) should be understood as the abstinence associated with the Noble Path (ariya-magga). From the moment that abstinence arises, even the mere thought "I will kill a living being" no longer occurs to the Noble Ones (ariya-puggala). Just as the analysis (vinicchaya) of the ten unwholesome courses of action was understood by five aspects, so should the analysis of these ten wholesome courses of action be understood by five aspects: Dhamma, portion (koṭṭhāsa), object (ārammaṇa), feeling (vedanā), and root (mūla). Among these, the analysis by way of Dhamma is: among these ten wholesome courses of action, the first seven in order can be both volition (cetanā) and abstinence (virati). The last three are only mental factors associated with volition. By way of portion (koṭṭhāsa), the first seven in order are called "courses of action" (kammapatha). The roots are...
147:
Thinking, "I will sacrifice my life, but I will not sacrifice the precept," he threw the sharp bone-handled axe that was on his shoulder into the forest. At that very moment, the great python released that lay devotee and went away.

Abstinence associated with the Noble Path should be known as 'abstinence by eradication' (samuccheda-virati). From the moment that abstinence arises, even the slightest thought of "I will kill a living being" does not arise in Noble Persons (ariya-puggala).

Now, just as the analysis of the unwholesome courses of action was known, so too the analysis of these wholesome courses of action (kusala-kammapatha) should be known by way of these five aspects: (1) by way of state (dhamma), (2) by way of portion (koṭṭhāsa), (3) by way of object (ārammaṇa), (4) by way of feeling (vedanā), and (5) by way of root (mūla).

Therein, the analysis 'by way of state' (dhamma) is as follows: Among these wholesome courses of action, in sequence, the first seven can be either volition (cetanā) or abstinence (virati). The final three are only states associated with volition.

The analysis 'by way of portion' (koṭṭhāsa) is as follows: In sequence, the first seven are only courses of action (kammapatha) and not roots (mūla). The final three are both courses of action and roots. When non-covetousness (anabhijjhā) reaches the level of a root, it becomes the wholesome root of non-greed (alobha-kusalamūla). Non-ill-will (abyāpāda) is the wholesome root of non-hatred (adosa-kusalamūla), and right view (sammā-diṭṭhi) is the wholesome root of non-delusion (amoha-kusalamūla).

The analysis 'by way of object' (ārammaṇa) is as follows: The objects of unwholesome states such as killing living beings are the very objects of these wholesome courses of action. This is because what is called 'abstinence' (veramaṇī) occurs only from the objective field that is to be transgressed. Just as the Noble Path, which has Nibbāna as its object, abandons the defilements, so too these courses of action, which have the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) and so forth as their objects, should be understood to abandon immoralities (dussīlya) such as killing living beings.

The analysis 'by way of feeling' (vedanā) is as follows: All courses of action are either accompanied by pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) or neutral feeling (majjhatta-vedanā). This is because at the level of wholesome states, there is no such thing as painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā).

The analysis 'by way of root' (mūla) is as follows: In sequence, the first seven courses of action have three roots by way of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion for one who abstains with a consciousness associated with knowledge (ñāṇa-sampayutta-citta). For one who abstains with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇa-vippayutta-citta), there are two roots. When non-covetousness occurs with a consciousness associated with knowledge, it has two roots; when it occurs with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge, it has one root. Non-greed itself cannot be its own root. The same method applies to non-ill-will. Right view has only two roots by way of non-greed and non-hatred. These are the ten wholesome courses of action.

## Discussion on the Comparison of Courses of Action

Now, at this point, what is called the comparison of the courses of action (kammapatha-saṃsandana) should be understood. Indeed, non-restraint (asaṃvara) arising by way of the five sense-contact doors (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body) is only unwholesome mental action (manokamma). However, non-restraint arising by way of the mind-contact door (manophassa-dvāra) can be all three types of action. If that non-restraint reaches the point of movement (copana) in the body-door, it is unwholesome bodily action (kāyakamma); if it reaches movement in the speech-door, it is unwholesome verbal action (vacīkamma); if it does not reach movement in either, it is unwholesome mental action. Non-restraint arising by way of the five doors of non-restraint is also only unwholesome mental action. Non-restraint arising by way of the body-door of non-restraint with movement is only unwholesome bodily action; that arising by way of the speech-door of non-restraint is only unwholesome verbal action; that arising by way of the mind-door of non-restraint is only unwholesome mental action. The three types of bodily misconduct are only unwholesome bodily action; the four types of verbal misconduct are only unwholesome verbal action; the three types of mental misconduct are only unwholesome mental action.

Restraint (saṃvara) arising by way of the five sense-contact doors is also only wholesome mental action. This restraint arising by way of the mind-contact door, like non-restraint, can be all three types of action. Restraint arising by way of the five doors of restraint is also only wholesome mental action; restraint arising by way of the body-door of restraint with movement is only wholesome bodily action; restraint arising by way of the speech-door of restraint is only wholesome verbal action; restraint arising by way of the mind-door of restraint is only wholesome mental action. The three types of bodily good conduct are only wholesome bodily action; the four types of verbal good conduct are only wholesome verbal action; the three types of mental good conduct are only wholesome mental action.

Unwholesome bodily action does not arise by way of the five sense-contact doors; it arises only by way of the mind-contact door. Unwholesome verbal action is the same. Unwholesome mental action, however, arises by way of all six sense-contact doors. If that mental action reaches movement in the body-door and speech-door, it becomes unwholesome bodily and verbal action; if it does not reach movement, it is only unwholesome mental action. Just as it does not arise by way of the five sense-contact doors, so too unwholesome bodily action does not arise by way of the five doors of non-restraint; it arises only by way of the body-door and speech-door of non-restraint with movement, and not by way of the mind-door of non-restraint. Unwholesome verbal action also does not arise by way of the five doors of non-restraint; it arises by way of the body-door and speech-door of non-restraint with movement, and not by way of the mind-door of non-restraint. Unwholesome mental action, however, certainly arises by way of the eight doors of non-restraint. The same method should be understood for wholesome bodily action and so forth.
149:
This is the distinction: just as unwholesome bodily and verbal actions do not arise by way of the door of mental non-restraint, these (wholesome bodily and verbal actions) are not like that. Indeed, these (wholesome actions) do arise even at the door of mental restraint for one who undertakes the precepts without moving the bodily or vocal organs.

Among those (doors), the wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara-kusala-citta) arises by way of the three doors of action (kammadvara); it does not arise by way of the five doors of consciousness (viññāṇadvara). By the method, "Whatever feeling arises—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—conditioned by eye-contact," it arises by way of the six doors of contact (phassadvara). It does not arise by way of the eight doors of non-restraint (asaṃvaradvara); it arises by way of the eight doors of restraint (saṃvaradvara). It does not arise by way of the ten courses of unwholesome action (akusalakammapatha); it arises by way of the ten courses of wholesome action (kusalakammapatha). Therefore, whether this consciousness arises by way of the three doors of action, the six doors of contact, the eight doors of restraint, or the ten courses of wholesome action, it is so. When it is said, "A wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere has arisen ... etc. ... (taking) a visible object ... etc. ... or a mental object," everything has been stated.

## The Discussion on Doors is Finished.

Regarding the phrase "yaṃ yaṃ vā panārabbha," the construction is as follows: among the visible objects and so forth mentioned below, it means "beginning with a visible object," or "having made it the object." It arises beginning with an audible object ... etc. ... or a mental object. By this much, it is as if only one of these objects is permitted for this consciousness. This (consciousness) arises for one person at one time beginning with a visible object, and again at another time for another person, it arises beginning with any other object among audible objects and so forth. For this consciousness thus arising, there is no such sequence as: first, in one existence, it arises beginning with a visible object, and later with an audible object. Even among visible objects, there is no such rule as: first a blue object, and later a yellow object.

Thus, to show the state of having all these as objects, the state of having no fixed sequence, and the state of having no fixed rule even among blue, yellow, and so forth despite the lack of sequence, he said, "yaṃ yaṃ vā panārabbha." This is the meaning: it is not just any single one among these visible objects and so forth; rather, it arises beginning with whichever object. Even when it arises thus, it does not occur in a sequence such as "first beginning with a visible object, then an audible object," but arises beginning with whichever object. The meaning is: "It arises by making this or that object among visible objects and so forth, whether in reverse order, in direct order, or by the method of skipping one, skipping two, and so forth." Even among visible objects...
290:
Only view itself is called 'gone to view' (*diṭṭhigata*). It is like the terms 'gone to excrement' (*gūthagata*) or 'gone to urine' (*muttagata*). Alternatively, because there is no essence to be known, it is called *diṭṭhigata* as it is merely the occurrence of view. That which is associated with that view is called 'associated with wrong view' (*diṭṭhigata-sampayutta*).

In that state associated with wrong view, the arising of this wrong seeing (*micchā-dassana*) known as *diṭṭhigata* should be understood as occurring through causes such as unwise attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*), which includes listening to false Dhamma (*asaddhamma-savana*), having bad friends (*akalyāṇamittatā*), and the lack of desire to see the Noble Ones (*ariyānaṃ adassanakāmatā*). It should be understood that this view arises through: listening to false doctrines related to wrong views, preceded by great esteem and exceeding indifference, without investigation; through bad friendship (*akalyāṇamittatā*) characterized by leaning towards bad friends who have fallen into wrong views; through the lack of desire to see the Noble Ones and virtuous persons such as the Buddha; through lack of proficiency in the Noble Dhamma such as the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*); through lack of discipline (*avinaya*) characterized by the failure of restraint (*saṃvara*) in the Noble Dhamma and the Dhamma of virtuous persons, specifically the failure of restraint in the Pātimokkha (*pātimokkha-saṃvara*), restraint of the senses (*indriya-saṃvara*), restraint of mindfulness (*sati-saṃvara*) (here meaning restraint of patience, *khanti-saṃvara*), restraint of knowledge (*ñāṇa-saṃvara*), and restraint of abandonment (*pahāna-saṃvara*) (restraint of energy, *vīriya-saṃvara*); through unwise attention nurtured by those causes; and through devotion to omens of things seen and heard (*diṭṭha-maṅgala*, *suta-maṅgala*), etc. The unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*) nature of that consciousness should be understood in the same way as mentioned below.

In the section on the summary of phenomena (*dhammuddesa-vāra*), 'contact' (*phassa*) refers to the contact that arises together with unwholesome consciousness. The same method applies to feeling (*vedanā*) and so on. Thus, the only difference from the previously mentioned wholesome contact and feeling is that these are merely unwholesome. 'One-pointedness of mind (*cittassa ekaggatā*) occurs' means that even in acts such as killing (*pāṇātipāta*), there is one-pointedness of mind in the sense of non-distraction. This is because people, having concentrated their minds and becoming undistracted, strike the bodies of beings with weapons that do not miss. Those with well-concentrated minds steal the property of others. With a mind of single-minded purpose, they commit sexual misconduct (*micchācāra*). Thus, even in the occurrence of the unwholesome, there is one-pointedness of mind.

Wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*) means improper view, or a distorted view because it is held wrongly. It is also called *micchā-diṭṭhi* because it is a view loathed by the wise as it brings about harm. The same method applies to wrong intention (*micchā-saṅkappa*) and so on. Furthermore, it is called *micchā-diṭṭhi* because one sees wrongly by it, or it sees wrongly itself, or it is merely a wrong seeing. It has the characteristic of unwise conviction (*ayoniso abhinivesa*), the function of misinterpretation (*parāmāsa*), the manifestation of wrong conviction (*micchā-abhinivesa*), and the proximate cause of not desiring to see the Noble Ones. It should be regarded as a supreme fault.
291:
In wrong intention (*micchā-saṅkappa*) and so on, the only difference is the word 'wrong' (*micchā*). The remaining meaning should be understood in the same way as stated in the section on the wholesome.

In the terms 'power of shamelessness' (*ahirika-bala*) and 'power of fearlessness' (*anottappa-bala*), the meaning of 'power' (*bala*) will become clear in the section of definitions (*niddesa-vāra*). As for the other terms: one is 'shameless' (*ahirika*) because one is not ashamed. The state of being shameless is 'shamelessness' (*ahirikaṃ*). That which is not dread (*ottappa*) is 'fearlessness' (*anottappa*). Between these two, shamelessness has the characteristic of not loathing bodily misconduct and so on, or the characteristic of lack of shame (*alajja*). Fearlessness has the characteristic of lack of dread regarding those same bodily misconducts, or the characteristic of lack of fear. Shamelessness itself being a power is the 'power of shamelessness'. Fearlessness itself being a power is the 'power of fearlessness'. This is the summary of the meaning here. The detailed explanation should be understood by way of the opposites of shame (*hiri*) and dread (*ottappa*) mentioned below.

One lusts by it, or it lusts itself, or it is merely lusting; therefore, it is 'greed' (*lobha*). One is deluded by it, or it is deluded itself, or it is merely deluding; therefore, it is 'delusion' (*moha*). Between these two, greed has the characteristic of grasping an object like monkey-glue. It has the function of sticking to an object like a piece of meat thrown onto a hot pan. It manifests in knowledge as being unable to let go, like an oil stain. It has the proximate cause of seeing enjoyment in things that are fetters (*saṃyojaniya-dhamma*). It should be understood that as it grows into the river of craving (*taṇhā-nadī*), it carries beings away to the states of loss (*apāya*), just as a river with a swift current flows into the great ocean.

Delusion has the characteristic of blindness of mind or the characteristic of ignorance. It has the function of non-penetration or the function of covering the true nature of the object. It manifests in knowledge as wrong practice or manifests as darkness. It has unwise attention as its proximate cause. It should be regarded as the root of all unwholesome states.

One covets the wealth of others by it, or it covets itself, or it is merely coveting; therefore, it is 'covetousness' (*abhijjhā*). That covetousness has the characteristic of desiring to make others' wealth one's own. It has the function of seeking in that manner. It manifests in knowledge as being directed towards others' wealth. It has great delight in others' wealth as its proximate cause. Indeed, that covetousness manifests only as being directed towards others' wealth. Moreover, it arises when there is delight in that wealth. It should be regarded as the stretching out of the mind's hand towards others' wealth.

In 'tranquility occurs' (*samatho hoti*) and so on, it is 'tranquility' (*samatha*) because it calms distraction from other tasks. It is 'exertion' (*paggāha*) because it upholds the mind in the occurrence of the unwholesome. It is 'non-distraction' (*avikkhepa*) because it does not allow distraction.
292:
In this (first unwholesome) consciousness, these factors—faith, mindfulness, wisdom, and the six pairs—are not included. Why? Because in a mind devoid of faith, there is no such thing as devotion (pasāda). Therefore, faith is not included first. If it is asked, 'Do those with wrong views not believe in their own teachers?'—they do believe. However, that is not what is called faith; it is merely the acceptance of words. In essence, it is either delusion (moha) lacking investigation or it is wrong view (diṭṭhi). Since there is no mindfulness in a mind devoid of mindfulness, it is not included. If it is asked, 'Can those with wrong views not remember what they have done?'—they can remember. However, that is not what is called mindfulness. It is merely the occurrence of unwholesome consciousness in that mode. Therefore, mindfulness is not included. Then why is it called 'wrong mindfulness' (micchā-sati) in the Suttas? Because unwholesome aggregates are devoid of mindfulness and are the opposite of mindfulness, it is taught there figuratively (pariyāya) for the purpose of completing the factors of the wrong path and wrongness (micchatta). In the literal sense (nippariyāya), however, it does not exist. Therefore, it is not included. Since there is no wisdom in a blindly foolish mind, it is not included. If it is asked, 'Do those with wrong views not have deceptive wisdom?'—they do. However, that is not wisdom; it is called illusion (māyā). In essence, that illusion is just craving (taṇhā). This consciousness is accompanied by distress, and is heavy, burdensome, coarse, rigid, unwieldy, ailing, crooked, and devious. Therefore, the six pairs beginning with tranquility (passaddhi) are not included.

Having shown the thirty-two terms presented in the Pāḷi text by way of the constituents of consciousness through this sequence of words, the text now says 'or whatever other' (ye vā pana) etc., to show the 'or-whatever-other' factors (yevāpanaka). Among them, in all unwholesome consciousnesses, only these ten factors—intention (chanda), decision (adhimokkha), attention (manasikāra), conceit (māna), envy (issā), avarice (macchariya), sloth (thina), torpor (middha), restlessness (uddhacca), and remorse (kukkucca)—are said to be the 'or-whatever-other' factors that appear in the Sutta passages. However, in this specific consciousness, only four factors known as the invariable factors (apaṇṇakanga)—intention, decision, attention, and restlessness—are the 'or-whatever-other' factors.

Among those four, the three beginning with intention should be understood according to the method mentioned below. The only difference is that those mentioned below are wholesome, while these are unwholesome. As for the remaining factor, restlessness (uddhacca), it is the state of being distracted. It has the characteristic of unpeacefulness of mind, like water stirred by the impact of the wind; the function of instability, like a banner or flag fluttering in the wind; the manifestation of turmoil, like ashes flying up when struck by a stone; and it has inappropriate attention (ayoniso manasikāra) to the unpeacefulness of mind as its proximate cause. It should be regarded as the distraction of the mind.

Thus, there are thirty-two factors beginning with contact, and four mentioned by way of the 'or-whatever-other' factors; therefore, in this summary of phenomena (dhammuddesa-vāra), there are thirty-six factors in total. These are the four invariable factors.
293:
Excluding the four invariable factors, there are only thirty-two factors directly appearing in the Pāḷi text. However, by taking the factors not yet included in this summary of phenomena, there are sixteen factors: the group of five starting with contact (phassa-pañcaka), initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), zest (pīti), one-pointedness of mind (ekaggatā), the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya), the life-faculty (jīvitindriya), wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi), lack of shame (ahirika), lack of dread (anottappa), greed (lobha), and delusion (moha). Among these sixteen factors, seven are undivided (avibhattika) and nine are divided (savibhattika). Which are the seven? Contact, perception, volition, sustained application, zest, the life-faculty, and delusion—these seven are undivided. Feeling, consciousness, initial application, one-pointedness of mind, the faculty of energy, wrong view, lack of shame, lack of dread, and greed—these nine are divided.

Among them, six factors are divided into two places, one factor into three places, one factor into four places, and one factor into six places. How? Consciousness, initial application, wrong view, lack of shame, lack of dread, and greed—these six are divided into two places. Among them, consciousness is first called 'consciousness' (citta) when it reaches the group of five starting with contact, and it is called the 'mind-faculty' (manindriya) when it reaches the faculties. Initial application is called 'initial application' (vitakka) when it reaches the jhana factors, and it is called 'wrong intention' (micchā-saṅkappa) when it reaches the path factors. Wrong view is called 'wrong view' (micchā-diṭṭhi) both in the path factors and in the courses of action (kammapatha). Lack of shame is called the 'power of shamelessness' (ahirika-bala) when it reaches the powers, and it is called 'shamelessness' (ahirika) when it reaches the dyad of world-destroyers. The same method applies to the lack of dread (anottappa). Greed is called 'greed' (lobha) when it reaches the roots (mūla), and it is called 'covetousness' (abhijjhā) when it reaches the courses of action. These six factors are divided into two places.

As for feeling (vedanā), it is called 'feeling' when it reaches the group of five starting with contact, 'happiness' (sukha) when it reaches the jhana factors, and the 'faculty of joy' (somanassindriya) when it reaches the faculties. Thus, this single factor is divided into three places.

As for energy (vīriya), it is called the 'faculty of energy' (vīriyindriya) when it reaches the faculties, 'wrong effort' (micchā-vāyāma) when it reaches the path factors, the 'power of energy' (vīriya-bala) when it reaches the powers, and 'exertion' (paggāha) when it reaches the End Dyads (piṭṭhiduka). Thus, this single factor is divided into four places.

As for concentration (samādhi or ekaggatā), it is called 'one-pointedness of mind' (ekaggatā) when it reaches the jhana factors, the 'faculty of concentration' (samādhindriya) when it reaches the faculties, 'wrong concentration' (micchā-samādhi) when it reaches the path factors, the 'power of concentration' (samādhi-bala) when it reaches the powers, and when it reaches the End Dyads, in the second dyad, by way of a single...
294:
... It is called 'calm' (samatha), and in the third dyad, it is called 'non-distraction' (avikkhepa). Thus, this single dhamma is analyzed in six places.

All these dhammas form nine groups by way of the fivefold contact (phassa-pañcaka), the factors of absorption (jhāna-aṅga), the faculties (indriya), the path factors (maggaṅga), the powers (bala), the roots (mūla), the courses of action (kammapatha), the world-destroyers (lokanāsaka), and the concluding dyads (piṭṭhiduka). What should be said in this Summary of Dhammas (Dhammuddessavāra) has already been stated in the exposition of the first wholesome consciousness (pathama-kusala-citta-niddesa).

## The Commentary on the Summary of Dhammas (Dhammuddessavāra-kathā) is finished.

## The Commentary on the Exposition (Niddesavāra-kathā)

In the Exposition (Niddesavāra), within the exposition of one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā-niddesa), first, the two terms 'steadfastness' (saṇṭhiti) and 'fixity' (avaṭṭhiti) are merely synonyms for 'stability' (ṭhiti). However, the statement made in the wholesome exposition (kusala-niddesa) that "it is called fixity (avaṭṭhiti) because it stands having entered and penetrated the object" is not applicable here in this unwholesome exposition (akusala-niddesa). It has already been shown below that one-pointedness of mind is weak in unwholesome consciousness.

The meaning of 'non-shifting' (avisāhāra) as being the opposite of 'shifting' (visāhāra) to various objects occurring by way of restlessness (uddhacca) and doubt (vicikicchā) is also not applicable here. However, it is called 'non-shifting' (avisāhāra) because it does not cause the co-nascent dhammas to shift. It is called 'non-distraction' (avikkhepa) because it does not scatter. The state of a mind that is not shifted by the power of unwholesome one-pointedness of mind is called 'the state of a non-shifted mind' (avisāhaṭamānasatā). It is called 'the power of concentration' (samādhibala) because it does not waver regarding co-nascent dhammas. It should be understood in this unwholesome exposition that it is called 'wrong concentration' (micchāsamādhi) because it is a wrong way of focusing on an object.

In the exposition of the faculty of energy (viriyindriya-niddesa), the method stated below starting with "this energy is an exit for the removal of sense desires" is not applicable here. It should be known as 'the power of energy' (viriyabala) only in the sense of not wavering regarding co-nascent dhammas.

In the exposition of wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi-niddesa), it is called 'wrong view' (micchādiṭṭhi) in the sense of seeing incorrectly. This seeing has gone into views; it is called 'resorting to views' (diṭṭhigata) because it is included within the sixty-two views. The meaning of this has also been stated below. Just like a thicket of grass, a thicket of forest, or a thicket of mountains, view itself is called 'the jungle of views' (diṭṭhigahana) in the sense of being difficult to cross. View itself, in the sense of being accompanied by danger and suspicion...
295:
Wrong view is called 'the wilderness of views' (diṭṭhikantāra) because it is full of danger, like a wilderness frequented by robbers, a wilderness of wild beasts, a sandy wilderness, a waterless wilderness, or a famine-stricken wilderness. It is called 'the thorn of views' (diṭṭhivisūkāyika) in the sense of piercing right view and in the sense of being contrary to it. Indeed, when wrong view arises, it both pierces and opposes right vision (sammā-dassana). It is called 'the agitation of views' (diṭṭhivipphandita) because it is a distorted trembling of view due to sometimes holding the eternalist view (sassata) and sometimes the annihilationist view (uccheda). A person with wrong views cannot stand in a single view but follows sometimes the eternalist view and sometimes the annihilationist view. View itself is called 'the fetter of views' (diṭṭhisaṃyojana) in the sense of binding.

It is called 'a grip' (gāha) because it firmly grasps the object, just as creatures like crocodiles seize a man. It is called 'a standing place' (patiṭṭhāha) because it stands firmly having arisen with great force. Indeed, this dhamma of view grasps by standing firmly due to its powerful occurrence. It is called 'adherence' (abhinivesa) because it strongly attends to things as permanent, etc. It is called 'misapprehension' (parāmāsa) because it touches upon things as permanent, etc., by transcending the true nature of dhammas. It is called 'the wrong path' (kummagga) because it leads to harm and because it is the path to the loathsome woeful states. It is called 'the false path' (micchāpatha) because it is an incorrect road. Just as a person confused about the directions, though taking a road thinking 'this is the road to such-and-such a village,' cannot reach that village, so too a person with wrong views, though taking a view thinking 'this is the path to a happy destination,' cannot reach a happy destination; thus it is 'the false path' (micchāpatha) because it is an incorrect road. It is called 'wrongness' (micchatta) because it is of a false nature. It is called 'a landing-place' (tittha) like a ferry-port because fools wander back and forth within that view. It is called 'the resort of the landing-place' (titthāyatana) because that view is the basis for harm. Or, it is called 'titthāyatana' in the sense of being the place of origin and the dwelling place of sectarians (titthiya). It is called 'the grip of perversion' (vipariyesaggāha) because it grasps in a perverted way. The term 'vipalatthagāha' has the same meaning.

387-388. In the expositions of shamelessness (ahirika) and fearlessness of wrongdoing (anottappa), the meaning should be understood as the opposite of the method stated in the expositions of shame (hiri) and fear of wrongdoing (ottappa). They should be known as 'the power of shamelessness' (ahirika-bala) and 'the power of fearlessness' (anottappa-bala) only in the sense of not wavering regarding co-nascent dhammas.

In the expositions of greed (lobha) and delusion (moha), it is called 'greed' (lobha) because it covets. 'Lubbhana' is the manner of coveting. A mind associated with greed, or a person, is called 'covetous' (lubbhita), and the state of such a person is 'covetousness' (lubbhitatta). It is called 'intense passion' (sārāga) because it is intensely lustful. 'Sārajjanā' is the manner of being intensely lustful. The state of an intensely lustful mind or person is called 'the state of being intensely lustful' (sārajjitatta). In the sense of 'scheming' (abhijjhāyana)...
296:
Abhijjhā (Covetousness). Again, the reason for the word 'greed' (lobha) has already been stated. It is called an unwholesome root (akusalamūla) because it is both unwholesome and a root, or because it is the root of unwholesome states.

It is called non-knowledge (aññāṇa) and non-seeing (adassana) because it is the opposite of knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassana). It is called non-realization (anabhisamaya) because it occurs in the presence of phenomena but does not rightly understand or meet them. Understanding phenomena in accordance [with truth] is called anubodha; because it is the opposite of that, it is called non-understanding (ananubodha). It is called non-enlightenment (asambodha) because it does not understand in conjunction with [the characteristics of] impermanence and so on. It is also called non-enlightenment because it understands what is non-existent and improper. It is called non-penetration (appaṭivedha) because it does not penetrate the Four Noble Truths. It is called non-comprehension (asaṅgāhanā) because it does not grasp even a single phenomenon among form and so on by way of the common characteristics such as impermanence. It is called non-plunging (apariyogāhanā) because it does not plunge into that very phenomenon. It is called improper looking (asamapekkhaṇā) because it does not look [at things] evenly. It is called non-reflection (apaccavekkhaṇā) because it does not reflect based on the nature of phenomena.

Because of perverse activity regarding wholesome and unwholesome actions, or because of the absence of grasping the nature [of things], not even a single action is direct to this [delusion]; or because it does not itself make any action direct, it is called non-direct action (appaccakkhakamma). When this delusion does not arise, the mental continuum would be pure and bright; because this delusion corrupts that pure mental continuum, it is called bad wisdom (dummejjha). It is called folly (bālya) because it is the state of fools. It is called delusion (moha) because it deludes. Intense delusion is pamoha. It is called complete delusion (sammoha) because it deludes all around. It is called ignorance (avijjā) because it is not knowledge, being the opposite of knowledge (vijjā). The meanings of flood (ogha) and yoke (yoga) have already been stated. It is called a latent tendency (anusaya) because it lies dormant in the sense of being firmly established. It is called obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna) because it overwhelms or pervades the mind. Because it does not grasp what is beneficial, it cannot go towards what is beneficial, but rather slips away; thus it is called laṅgī, meaning it slips. Or it is called laṅgī in the sense of being difficult to open. Indeed, just as a door-bolt called a mahāpaligha is difficult to open, so too this delusion is like a door-bolt; thus it is called laṅgī. The remaining words have clear meanings. The Summary Section (Saṅgahavāra) and the Voidness Section (Suññatavāra) should also be understood by way of meaning according to the method already stated below.

## Second Consciousness

In the second consciousness, the word 'with prompting' (sasaṅkhārena) is the distinction. The meaning of that word has also been stated below. Although this consciousness arises for one who, being joyful regarding the six objects, produces greed and misapprehends them by way of 'a being, a being,' and so on, yet because it is prompted (sasaṅkhārika), it arises with effort and with means...
297:
When a young man of good family desires a maiden from a family of wrong view, and they do not give the maiden, saying, 'You are of a different view,' then other relatives say, 'He will do whatever you do,' and cause them to give her. That man approaches the sectarians along with them. At first, he is full of doubt. As time goes by, he thinks, 'The behavior of these people is pleasing,' and he comes to like their doctrine and adopts the wrong view. It should be understood that this [second] consciousness arises at such a time.

Among the remaining (yevāpanaka) states, sloth (thina) and torpor (middha) are predominant here. Therein, the state of being slothful is 'sloth' (thina). The state of being torpid is 'torpor' (middha). It means lack of enthusiasm, shrinking, lack of capability, and exhaustion. Sloth and torpor combined are called 'sloth and torpor' (thina-middha). Therein, sloth has the characteristic of lack of enthusiasm, the function of dispelling energy, and is manifested as sinking. Torpor has the characteristic of unwieldiness (incapability), the function of enveloping [the doors of perception], and is manifested as dejection or as nodding and sleepiness. Both have unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra)—arising from dissatisfaction, laziness, stretching the body, and so on—as their proximate cause.

## Third Consciousness

The third consciousness arises for one who, being joyful regarding the six objects, produces greed but does not misapprehend them (wrongly) by way of 'a being, a being,' and so on, such as for one watching the Nārāyaṇa festival, wrestling matches, boxing matches, dramatic performances, and so on, or for one devoted to listening to pleasing sounds and so on. In this consciousness, there are five invariable factors along with conceit (māna). Therein, it is called 'conceit' (māna) because it is proud. That conceit has the characteristic of loftiness, the function of self-exaltation, is manifested as the desire to fly a banner, has greed disconnected from wrong view as its proximate cause, and should be regarded as being like madness.

## Fourth Consciousness

The fourth consciousness arises in the aforementioned situations, such as when one is spat upon on the head or has dust thrown on one's feet, and one looks around from time to time with effort to avoid that danger; or when royal plays are being performed and the crowd is being cleared, for those who are peeking through various gaps; it arises in such situations.
298:
In this fourth consciousness, however, there are seven *yevāpanaka* states together with sloth and torpor (*thina-middha*). In both (the third and fourth), wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*) is excluded. Setting aside that wrong view, the enumeration of states should be understood by way of the remaining states.

## The Fifth Consciousness

The fifth consciousness arises in a person who, being indifferent towards the six objects by way of feeling, arouses greed and misapprehends them in such ways as "a being, a being," etc. In this fifth consciousness, equanimity (*upekkhā-vedanā*) occurs in the place of joy (*somanassa*), and the term zest (*pīti*) is excluded. All the rest is exactly the same as the first consciousness.

## The Sixth Consciousness and Others

409-412. The sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses should also be understood in the same manner as described for the second, third, and fourth consciousnesses, by changing the feeling and excluding the term zest (*pīti*). In these eight consciousnesses rooted in greed, both types of predominance—predominance of co-nascence (*sahajātādhipati*) and predominance of object (*ārammaṇādhipati*)—are obtained.

## The Ninth Consciousness

The ninth consciousness arises in one who is displeased with the six objects and arouses aversion (*paṭigha*). In the section on the delimitation of the occasion (*samayavavatthānavāra*) for that ninth consciousness, first (the analysis should be understood): a mind that is bad (because it is destroyed by anger), or a mind that is contemptible because of the inferior nature of its feeling, is called *dummana* (bad-minded). The state of being *dummana* is *domanassa* (displeasure). Because it arises together with that displeasure, it is called "accompanied by displeasure" (*domanassasahagata*). Because it strikes against the object with a nature of non-endearedness, it is called *paṭigha* (aversion). Because it is associated with that aversion, it is called "associated with aversion" (*paṭighasampayutta*).

In the enumeration of states (*dhammuddesa*), only the feeling of displeasure (*domanassavedanā*) appears in all three places. There, the term for feeling (*vedanā*) has the meaning already stated. Likewise, the terms pain (*dukkha*) and displeasure (*domanassa*) also have the meanings already stated. By way of characteristics, etc., displeasure (*domanassa*) has the characteristic of experiencing an undesirable object; its function is the enjoyment of the undesirable aspect in its true nature, or in any way; its manifestation is the affliction of the mind; and its proximate cause is invariably the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*).

Just as in the root courses of action (*mūlakammapatha*) for the previous consciousnesses it was stated that "greed occurs" and "covetousness occurs," so here it is stated that "hatred occurs" and "ill-will occurs." There, one offends by means of it, or it offends by itself, or it is merely the act of offending...
299:
Hatred (*dosa*) has the characteristic of fierce anger, like a cobra struck by a stick. Its function is to spread like poison, or its function is to consume its own support like a forest fire consuming its own base (the heart-base or the whole body). It is manifested as a state that destroys oneself and others, like an enemy who has found an opportunity. It should be understood as having the grounds of resentment (*āghātavatthu*), such as doing harm, as its proximate cause, like putrid urine mixed with poison.

By that hatred, the mind is corrupted and reaches a state of putrefaction; or, because it destroys the practice of discipline, the perfection of appearance, and welfare and happiness, etc., it is called ill-will (*byāpāda*). In essence, this ill-will is just hatred. In this ninth unwholesome consciousness, there are 29 terms in the sequence of words. By taking only those not yet taken, there are 14. By way of those 14, the distinction between the group with inflections and the group without inflections should be understood.

Among the *yevāpanaka* states, intention (*chanda*), decision (*adhimokkha*), attention (*manasikāra*), and restlessness (*uddhacca*) are fixed. Among envy (*issā*), avarice (*macchariya*), and remorse (*kukkucca*), they arise in groups of five along with any one of them. Thus, these three states are called unfixed *yevāpanaka* states. Among those three, envy (*issā*) is so called because it envies; it has the characteristic of being jealous of the prosperity of others, its function is dissatisfaction with that very prosperity, its manifestation is turning one's face away from it, and its proximate cause is the prosperity of others. It should be regarded as a fetter (*saṃyojana*). The state of being a miser is avarice (*macchariya*). It has the characteristic of concealing one's own prosperity, whether already attained or to be attained; its function is the inability to bear the sharing of those very things with others; its manifestation is shrinking, or its manifestation is "harsh-jacketedness" (stinginess); and its proximate cause is one's own prosperity. It should be regarded as a deformity of the mind. A contemptible act is *kukata*. The state of that is remorse (*kukkucca*). It has the characteristic of subsequent regret; its function is grieving over what has been done and what has been left undone; its manifestation is repentance; and its proximate cause is what has been done and what has been left undone. It should be regarded as being like slavery. This is the distinction in the section of enumeration (*uddesavāra*).

In the section of detailed exposition (*niddesavāra*), in the exposition of feeling, the unpleasant (*asāta*) should be understood by way of the opposite of the pleasant (*sāta*).

In the exposition of hatred, it is called *dosa* because it offends (*dussati*). *Dussanā* is the manner of offending. *Dussitatta* is the state of the mind being offended. *Byāpatti* is the corruption in the sense of abandoning the natural state. *Byāpajjanā* is the manner of corruption. It is called *virodha* because it opposes. It is called *paṭivirodha* because it opposes again and again. Or this is said by way of the manner of opposition and the manner of repeated opposition. A fierce person is called *caṇḍa* or *caṇḍika*; the state of such a person is fierceness (*caṇḍikka*). Because no well-placed (polite) speech occurs through this hatred, and only ill-spoken (incomplete) speech occurs, it is called *asūropa* (harshness). Indeed, at the time of anger, there is no such thing as complete speech. Even if it occurs to someone, that speech is not to be taken as standard (it is *appamāṇa*).
300:
Other teachers say it is called 'assuropa' because it causes tears to flow, in the sense of producing tears. This is not the reason, because tears also fall when there is joy (somanassa). Because it is the opposite of 'attamanatā' (delight) mentioned below, it is called 'anattamanatā' (displeasure) due to the state of not being delighted. Since this displeasure belongs only to the mind and not to a being, it is said 'of the mind' (cittassa). The remaining meaning in this exposition (niddesa-vāra), as well as in the summary (sangaha-vāra) and the voidness section (suññata-vāra), should be understood in the same way as mentioned below.

## The Tenth Consciousness

The tenth consciousness, being prompted (sa-saṅkhārika), arises in one who is urged by others, or in one who is reminded of the offenses of others, or in one who gets angry by recollecting the offenses of others by oneself.

In this tenth consciousness also, there are twenty-nine terms according to the sequence of words; however, by taking only those not yet taken, there are only fourteen terms. Among the 'or-whatever' (yevāpanaka) states, sloth and torpor (thina-middha) are also obtained. Therefore, in this tenth consciousness, excluding envy (issā), avarice (macchariya), and remorse (kukkucca), there are four constant factors and sloth and torpor—these six. At the time when envy etc. arise, seven 'or-whatever' states arise simultaneously with one of those (envy, etc.). All the remaining meanings in all sections are just the same as the ninth consciousness. In these two types of unpleasant consciousness (domanassa-citta), only the conascent predominance (sahajātādhipati) is obtained, not the object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati). This is because an angry person does not hold any object in high esteem.

## The Eleventh Consciousness

The eleventh consciousness arises at the time of the occurrence of doubt in one who is indifferent (majjhatta) by way of feeling (vedanā) regarding the six objects. In the definition of the occasion (samaya-vavatthāna) of that consciousness, the term 'associated with doubt' (vicikicchā-sampayutta) is new. Its meaning is: 'associated with doubt,' thus 'associated with doubt.' In the summary of states (dhammuddesa), only the term 'doubt occurs' (vicikicchā hoti) is the distinction.

In that term, the meaning should be understood: it is called 'vicikicchā' because it is devoid of 'cikicchā' (remedy/knowledge). Or, one who investigates the nature of things with this doubt becomes weary (kicchati/kilamati); because of that state of weariness, it is called 'vicikicchā.' That doubt has the characteristic of uncertainty, or the characteristic of wavering 'is it this or that?'. It has the function of mental agitation regarding various objects. It manifests as indecision, or it manifests as taking a non-definitive (two-sided) view. It has unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) as its proximate cause. It should be regarded as a factor that creates an obstacle to practice.

Here, there are twenty-three terms according to the sequence of words. By taking only those not yet taken, there are fourteen terms. By means of those terms, the decision regarding the groups with and without grammatical inflections should be understood. Only two states, attention (manasikāra) and restlessness (uddhacca), are the 'or-whatever' (yevāpanaka) states.
301:
In the explanation of one-pointedness of mind (cittassekaggatā-niddesa) of the Niddesa-vāra, because this (consciousness associated with doubt) is weak, and because there is only the mere occurrence and stability in this consciousness, the single term 'stability' (ṭhiti) of the mind is mentioned, without mentioning terms such as 'steadfastness' (saṇṭhiti). For that very reason, in the Uddesa-vāra also, the 'faculty of concentration' (samādhindriya) and so on are not mentioned.

In the explanation of doubt (vicikicchā-niddesa), it is called 'kaṅkhā' in the sense of doubting. It is called 'kaṅkhāyanā' because it leads to doubting. Indeed, the preceding doubt is said to lead to (bring about) the succeeding doubt. Or, this is stated by way of its mode. The consciousness possessed of doubt is called 'kaṅkhāyita' because it occurs in the mode of doubting. The state of that consciousness is 'kaṅkhāyitatta'. 'Vimati' means it is just doubt (not wisdom). 'Vicikicchā' has the meaning already stated. It is called 'dveḷhaka' because it wavers in two ways in the sense of shaking. It is called 'dvedhāpatha' because it is like a two-way path, as it obstructs practice. Because it occurs as 'is this permanent or is it impermanent?' etc., and is unable to stay in a single mode, it stays all around; thus it is 'saṃsaya' (uncertainty). Because it is unable to grasp a single side, it is not a one-sided grasp; thus it is 'anekāṃsagāha' (not taking one side). Because it is unable to decide, it retreats from the object; thus it is 'āsappanā' (slipping away). Because it is unable to plunge in, it moves all around; thus it is 'parisappanā' (wavering around). Because it is unable to plunge in thoroughly, it is 'apariyogāhanā' (not plunging in). Because it is unable to proceed towards the object by way of decision, it is 'thambhitatta' (rigidity); the meaning is the state of stiffness of the mind. For doubt, having arisen, makes the mind stiff. Indeed, when this doubt arises, it is as if it scratches the mind while taking the object; therefore, it is called 'manovilekha' (mental scratching). The remaining words have clear meanings in all sections.

## The Twelfth Consciousness

In the definition of the occasion of the twelfth consciousness, it is called 'associated with restlessness' (uddhacca-sampayutta) because it is conjoined with restlessness. This consciousness, being neutral towards the six objects by the power of feeling, is unsettled. In the summary of states (dhammuddessa) of this twelfth consciousness, in the place of 'doubt', it is stated 'there is restlessness' (uddhaccaṃ hoti). In the sequence of words, there are twenty-eight terms. By taking the unique terms, there are fourteen. By means of those terms, the arrangement of the groups with and without grammatical inflections should be understood. Only two, decision (adhimokkha) and attention (manasikāra), are the 'or-whatever' (yevāpanaka) states.

In the explanation of restlessness (uddhacca-niddesa) of the Niddesa-vāra, 'of the mind' (cittassa) means it does not belong to a being or a person (it belongs only to the mind). 'Uddhacca' is the mode of being unsettled. It is called 'avūpasama' because there is no calm. Of the mind...
302:
It is called cetaso vikkhepa (distraction of mind) because it casts the mind onto various objects. The state of the mind's wavering is called 'bhantattaṃ cittassa'; it is like a wavering vehicle, a wavering ox, and so on. By this term, wavering within a single object alone is intended. In fact, restlessness (uddhacca) wavers on a single object, while doubt (vicikicchā) wavers on various objects. The remaining words in all sections should be understood in the same manner as previously explained below.

Now, the miscellaneous decision regarding these two types of consciousness will be presented. If it is asked, 'How many types of consciousness are there that roll upon an object?', it should be said, 'Only these two.' Among those two, consciousness associated with doubt (vicikicchā-sahagata) rolls certainly; however, consciousness associated with restlessness (uddhacca-sahagata), having obtained decision (adhimokkha), rolls while pausing and staying because it has found a footing. For example, when two stones—one round and one square—are rolled and released in a sloping place, the round stone rolls certainly, while the square stone rolls by pausing and staying; this illustration should be understood as complete in this way. Even among all twelve unwholesome consciousnesses, the distinctions such as 'inferior' (hīna) and so on are not shown, because all unwholesome consciousnesses are certainly inferior. Although conascent predominance (sahajātādhipati) may be obtained, it is also not shown according to the method previously demonstrated. Since there is no wisdom in these unwholesome consciousnesses, there is no such thing as predominance of investigation (vīmaṃsādhipati). In the last two types of consciousness, the remaining predominances also do not exist. Why? Because they do not arise by making any of the conascent states like desire (chanda) etc., the leader, and also because it is prohibited in the Paṭṭhāna.

When kamma is accumulated by these twelve unwholesome consciousnesses, excluding the consciousness associated with restlessness (uddhacca-sahagata), only the remaining eleven types of consciousness lead to rebirth (paṭisandhi). It might be asked: if even the consciousness associated with doubt (vicikicchā-sahagata), which is weak due to the lack of decision (adhimokkha), can lead to rebirth, why does the consciousness associated with restlessness (uddhacca-sahagata), which is strong due to having decision (adhimokkha), not lead to it? The answer is: because it is not a state to be abandoned by vision (dassana - the Path of Stream-entry). If it were to lead to rebirth, it would appear in the Dassana-pahātabba-pada-vibhaṅga; however, it does not appear there. Therefore, excluding that consciousness associated with restlessness, only the remaining eleven lead to rebirth. Among those eleven unwholesome consciousnesses, if kamma is accumulated by any one of them, rebirth occurs in the four woeful planes (apāya) through that volition (cetanā). Among the unwholesome resultant consciousnesses, it takes rebirth with the rootless mind-consciousness-element associated with equanimity (ahetuka-manoviññāṇadhātu-upekkhāsahagata). The other one (restlessness-associated) would also give rebirth in these four woeful planes. However, since that does not happen, it does not appear in the Dassana-pahātabba-pada-vibhaṅga.

## The explanation of the term 'Akusalā Dhammā' is finished.
303:
## The Term Abyākata
## Rootless Wholesome Resultant (Ahetuka-kusala-vipāka)

Now, in order to analyze and show the term abyākata (indeterminate), the section beginning with 'Which states are indeterminate?' is commenced. That abyākata is of four kinds: resultant (vipāka), functional (kiriya), matter (rūpa), and nibbāna. Among those four, resultant indeterminate; within resultant indeterminate, wholesome resultant; within wholesome resultant, limited resultant (kāmāvacara-vipāka); within limited resultant, rootless; within rootless, the fivefold sense-consciousness; and within the fivefold sense-consciousness, eye-consciousness (is intended to be analyzed). To show the arising of that eye-consciousness solely by the power of the uncommon kamma-condition, excluding common conditions such as doors and objects, it is said: 'Because of having done wholesome kamma of the sense-sphere', and so on. In that text, 'katattā' means because of the reason of 'having been done.' 'Upacitattā' means because of the reason of 'having been accumulated' or 'having been increased.' It is called eye-consciousness because it is the consciousness of the eye which is the cause, or consciousness that proceeds from the eye, or consciousness that is dependent on the eye. In the case of ear-consciousness and so on that follow, the same method should be understood.

Among those consciousnesses, eye-consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing visible forms depending on the eye-base. It has the function of having only the visible form as its object. It manifests to knowledge as the state of being directed towards the visible form. It has the ceasing of the functional mind-element (five-door adverting) which takes the visible form as its object as its proximate cause. The ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness that follow also depend on the ear-base and so on, and have the characteristic of cognizing sounds and so on. They have the function of having only sounds and so on as their objects. They manifest to knowledge as the state of being directed towards sounds and so on. They have the ceasing of the functional mind-elements which take sounds and so on as their objects as their proximate causes.

In this eye-consciousness, there are 10 terms according to the sequence of terms. By way of taking what has not yet been taken (aggahitaggahaṇa), there are 7 terms. Among those 7, five are without classification, and two are with classification. Among those two, consciousness (citta) reaches classification in two places: by way of the pentad of contact and by way of the faculties (indriya). Feeling (vedanā) reaches classification in only three places: by way of the pentad of contact, the factors of absorption (jhānaṅga), and the faculties. The groups (rāsi) are also only these three. In the 'or-whatever' (yevāpanaka) states, however, there is only one: attention (manasikāra).

In the section of exposition (niddesavāra), eye-consciousness is called 'paṇḍara' (luminous/white) by way of its physical base. Wholesome consciousness is called paṇḍara because of its own purity. Unwholesome consciousness is called paṇḍara as a natural result of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). Resultant consciousness is paṇḍara because its physical base is pure.

In the exposition of one-pointedness of mind (cittassekaggatā-niddesa), only the single term 'stability of mind' (cittassa ṭhiti) is mentioned. This is because in this weak consciousness, only the mere stability of its occurrence is obtainable here.
304: (This eye-consciousness) is not capable of reaching the state of stability and steadfastness (saṇṭhiti avaṭṭhiti). In the Summary Section (saṅgahavāra), the Jhana factors and Path factors are not extracted. Why? Because Jhana is constrained by initial thought (vitakka), and the Path is constrained by roots (hetu). In a mind that naturally lacks initial thought, Jhana factors cannot be obtained; and in a rootless mind, Path factors cannot be obtained. Therefore, in this (eye-consciousness), both are not extracted. Here, the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) is also analyzed as having only four factors (contact, volition, one-pointedness, and life faculty). The Section on Emptiness (suññatavāra) is just as usual. The explanations (niddesa) of ear-consciousness and so on should also be understood in this same way. Specifically, the distinction here is that 'equanimity' (upekkhā) is analyzed in eye-consciousness and so on, while 'pleasure' (sukha) is analyzed in body-consciousness. This distinction should be understood as being due to the force of impact (between the object and the sensitive material). In the four doors such as the eye-door, only derived matter (upādārūpa) strikes derived matter. When derived matter strikes derived matter, the friction of the impact is not strong. It is like placing four balls of cotton on four anvils and striking them with other balls of cotton; it is merely a touch. The feeling remains in a neutral (upekkhā) state. In the body-door, however, the external object of the great essentials (mahābhūta) strikes the internal body-sensitivity (kāyapasāda) and hits the great essentials that are the basis of that sensitivity. Just as when one places a ball of cotton on an anvil and strikes it with a sledgehammer, the hammer cuts through the cotton and hits the anvil, making the friction of the impact very strong. In a desirable (iṭṭha) object, body-consciousness accompanied by pleasure (sukha) arises; in an undesirable (aniṭṭha) object, body-consciousness accompanied by pain (dukkha) arises. The bases, doors, and objects of these five types of consciousness are fixed. There is no shifting of the base and so on here. Wholesome-resultant eye-consciousness, taking the eye-sensitivity as its base, performs the function of seeing with regard to desirable and neutral-desirable visible-form objects of fourfold origin, and arises as a result while stationed at the eye-door. Ear-consciousness and so on, taking the ear-sensitivity and so on as their bases, perform the functions of hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching with regard to desirable and neutral-desirable sounds and so on, and arise while stationed at the ear-door and so on. Here, sound (saddārammaṇa) is produced by only two causes (consciousness and temperature). In the explanation of the mind-element (manodhātu), the mind itself is an element (dhātu) because of its nature of being empty and not a being. That mind-element has the characteristic of cognizing visible forms and so on immediately after eye-consciousness and so on. It has the function of receiving (sampaṭicchana) visible forms and so on. It manifests as such a state. Its proximate cause is the passing away of eye-consciousness and so on. In this Summary of States (dhammuddesa), there are twelve terms.
305: By taking what has not yet been taken, there are nine (terms). Among those nine terms, seven are without classification and two are with classification. The two called decision (adhimokkha) and attention (manasikāra) are the 'whatever-other' (yevāpanaka) states. In the explanation of initial thought (vitakka), it is placed having reached (the sense of) directing onto the object (abhiniropana). Specifically, because this receiving mind is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, it is not called right intention (sammā-saṅkappa) or wrong intention (micchā-saṅkappa). Although obtainable in the Summary Section, the Jhana factor is not extracted because it has fallen into the stream of the fivefold consciousness. As for the Path factor, it is simply not obtainable, so it is not extracted. The Section on Emptiness is just as usual. The base of this receiving mind is fixed; it is only the heart-base (hadayavatthu). The doors and objects are not fixed. Among those bases and objects, even if the doors and objects change, the occasion (ṭhāna) is only one. In truth, this mind performs only the function of receiving (sampaṭicchana). Indeed, this mind arises as a result by being the receiver of the five objects at the five doors. When wholesome-resultant eye-consciousness and so on have ceased, it receives those very visible forms and so on that have reached the occasion immediately after that eye-consciousness and so on. ## In the explanations of the mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu), the term 'joy' (pīti) is additional in the first mind-consciousness-element. The feeling is also the feeling of mental pleasure (somanassa). Indeed, this first mind-consciousness-element arises only with a desirable object, which is why it is a feeling of mental pleasure. The second mind-consciousness-element arises with a neutral-desirable object. Therefore, in that second mind-consciousness-element, there is a feeling of equanimity (upekkhā). The terms are just the same as in the explanation of the mind-element. In both types of mind-consciousness-element, the Jhana factors are not extracted because they have fallen into the stream of the fivefold consciousness. The Path factors are not extracted because they are not obtainable. All the rest should be understood according to the method already stated. Specifically, by way of characteristics and so on, this rootless resultant mind-consciousness-element, which is of two kinds, should be understood as having the characteristic of cognizing the six objects. It has the function (rasa) of investigating (santīraṇa), registration (tadārammaṇa), rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), death (cuti), and life-continuum (bhavaṅga) as appropriate. It manifests (paccupaṭṭhāna) to knowledge as having those functions of investigating and so on. Its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) is the heart-base (hadayavatthu). Among those two mind-consciousness-elements, the first mind-consciousness-element arises as a result in two occasions. Indeed, that first mind-consciousness-element arises as a result at the five doors, performing the function of investigating on that very object, after the resultant mind-element—which arose immediately after wholesome-resultant eye-consciousness and so on at the five doors—has received that object and ceased. Furthermore, when there is a strong object (an extremely great or clear object) at the six doors, it arises as a result by becoming registration (tadārammaṇa). How does it arise as a result? Just as when a boat is going across a fierce current, the water is parted and follows the boat for a short distance before flowing back according to the current; in the same way, when a strong object at the six doors appears and entices, the impulsion (javana) runs. When that impulsion has run, it is the turn of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). But this mind, without giving the turn to the life-continuum, takes the object taken by the impulsion and occurs for one or two thought-moments...
306:
It descends only into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). This simile should be expanded even in the case of a herd of cattle crossing a river. Thus, because this mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) re-takes the very object taken by the impulsion (javana), it arises as a resultant called registration (tadārammaṇa).

The second mind-consciousness element performs its resultant function in five positions. How? Firstly, in the human world, it performs the function of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) at the moment of conception for those who are born blind, born deaf, born mute, born insane, as well as for hermaphrodites and eunuchs. After the rebirth-linking consciousness has ceased, it performs the function of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) throughout the duration of life. It also functions as investigating (santīraṇa) in the five-sense-door process (pañcadvāravīthi) regarding moderately desirable objects; as registration (tadārammaṇa) in the six doors regarding powerful objects; and as death (cuti) at the time of passing away. Thus, it performs its resultant function in these five positions.

## The two mind-consciousness elements are finished.

## Explanation of the Eight Great Resultant Consciousnesses

Now, to show the eight great resultant consciousnesses (mahāvipāka), the text begins with: "Which states are indeterminate (avyākata)?" and so on. In that Pali text, only the method is shown, and all the sections (vāra) are abbreviated. The meaning of those sections should be understood according to the method already mentioned below. To show the specific distinction in these great resultants, it is said: "Non-greed is an indeterminate root (avyākatamūla)," and so on. What has not been said should be understood as follows: The divisions of the doors of action (kammadvāra), the paths of action (kammapatha), and the bases of meritorious action (puññakiriyavatthu) mentioned in the sensuous-sphere wholesome (kāmāvacara kusala) do not exist in these resultants. Why? Because they do not produce intimation (viññatti), they are not states that produce further resultants (avipākadhamma), and they do not occur as meritorious actions such as giving (dāna).

Compassion (karuṇā) and appreciative joy (muditā), which are mentioned among the "or-whatever" (yevāpanaka) states, do not exist in the resultants because they take beings as their object. This is because the sensuous-sphere resultants (kāmāvacara vipāka) have exclusively limited (paritta/sensuous) objects. Not only are compassion and appreciative joy absent, but the abstinences (virati) also do not exist here. For it is said: "The five precepts are exclusively wholesome (kusala)."

The arrangement of the unprompted (asaṅkhārika) and prompted (sasaṅkhārika) in these resultants should be understood by way of the wholesome and by way of the distinction of conditions. The resultant of unprompted wholesome is exclusively unprompted, and the resultant of prompted wholesome is prompted. Furthermore, a resultant produced by powerful conditions is unprompted, while one produced by other conditions is prompted. Even in the classification of inferior and so on, these resultants are not called inferior (hīna), medium (majjhima), or superior (paṇīta) because they are not produced by inferior, medium, or superior desire (chanda) and so forth. However, the resultant of an inferior wholesome deed is inferior.
307:
The resultant of a medium wholesome deed is called medium (majjhima). The resultant of a superior wholesome deed is called superior (paṇīta). Predominant factors (adhipati) also do not exist in these great resultants. Why? Because they are not to be produced by making desire (chanda) and so forth the leader. All the rest is exactly as described for the eight wholesome consciousnesses.

Now, the positions where these eight great resultant consciousnesses perform their functions should be understood. They perform their resultant functions in four positions: rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), life-continuum (bhavaṅga), death (cuti), and registration (tadārammaṇa). How? Firstly, among humans and the sensuous-sphere deities (kāmāvacara deva), they perform the function of rebirth-linking at the moment of conception for meritorious persons who are double-rooted (duhetuka) or triple-rooted (tihetuka). After the rebirth-linking has passed, during the course of existence (pavatti), they function as the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) for sixty years, eighty years, or even for an incalculable (asaṅkhyeyya) lifespan; as registration (tadārammaṇa) in the six doors regarding powerful objects; and as death (cuti) at the time of passing away. Thus, they perform their functions in four positions.

Among those eight great resultants, all Omniscient Bodhisattas, when taking their final rebirth, take rebirth with the first great resultant consciousness which is accompanied by joy, triple-rooted, and unprompted (somanassasahagata tihetuka asaṅkhārika mahāvipāka). That rebirth-linking consciousness is the result of the preliminary stage of the meditation on loving-kindness (mettā-pubbabhāga). Although the rebirth-linking granted by that kamma lasts for an incalculable period, it undergoes change (shortening of life) due to the influence of time (and external causes). However, the Elder Mahāsīva said: "The equanimity-rooted (upekkhāsahagata) is more powerful than the joy-rooted (somanassasahagata). Therefore, Bodhisattas take rebirth with the equanimity-rooted consciousness. Those who take rebirth with equanimity-rooted consciousness have great aspirations. Even regarding divine objects, they are not frivolous (not overly attached), like the Elder Tipitaka Cūḷanāga and others." But in the Commentary, this is rejected, saying: "This is merely the Elder's wishful thinking; this view is not correct," and it is stated: "The practice of welfare (hitūpacāra) toward beings is powerful in Omniscient Bodhisattas. Therefore, they take rebirth with the sensuous-sphere wholesome resultant consciousness that is accompanied by joy, triple-rooted, and unprompted, which is the result of the preliminary stage of loving-kindness."

## Discussion on the Extraction of Resultants (Vipākuddhārakathā)

Now, the table of contents (mātikā) for the Discussion on the Extraction of Resultants should be set forth. Firstly, the Elder Tipitaka Cūḷanāga said: "From a single wholesome volition (kusala cetanā), sixteen resultant consciousnesses arise. Within this, there is a twelve-fold path (by way of triple-rooted rebirth) and an eight-fold rootless group (by way of rootless rebirth)." But the Elder Mahādatta, a resident of Moravāpī, said: "From a single wholesome volition, twelve resultant consciousnesses arise. Within this, there is a ten-fold path and an eight-fold rootless group." The Elder Tipitaka Mahādhammarakkhita said: "From a single wholesome volition, ten resultant consciousnesses arise, and within this, there is the eight-fold rootless group."
308:
In this context, what is known as the Sāketa Question (Sāketa-pañha) is taken. It is said that while lay devotees in the city of Sāketa were sitting in a rest house, they raised a question but were unable to decide: "When kamma is accumulated with a single volition, does only one rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) occur, or do various rebirth-linkings occur?" They approached the Elders who were proficient in Abhidhamma and asked them. The Elders explained, "Just as only one sprout emerges from a single mango seed, so too, only one rebirth-linking occurs."

Then, on another day, they raised another question and being unable to decide, asked the Elders again: "When kamma is accumulated with various volitions, do various rebirth-linkings occur, or does only one rebirth-linking occur?" The Elders explained, "Just as many sprouts emerge when many mango seeds are planted, so too, many rebirth-linkings occur."

Furthermore, in this context, what is known as the Exposition on Predominance (Ussada-kittana) is taken. For these beings, greed (lobha) may be predominant, and hatred (dosa) and delusion (moha) may also be predominant. Non-greed (alobha), non-hatred (adosa), and non-delusion (amoha) may also be predominant. What determines the predominance of these traits in those beings? The previous cause (pubba-hetu) determines it. Diversity occurs at the very moment of kamma accumulation (kammāyūhana-kkhaṇa). How?

For someone who, at the moment of kamma accumulation, greed is strong and non-greed is weak, while non-hatred and non-delusion are strong and hatred and delusion are weak; for that person, the weak non-greed cannot overcome greed, but the strong non-hatred and non-delusion can overcome hatred and delusion. Therefore, when that person is born by the power of the rebirth-linking given by that kamma, they will be a greedy person, yet they will live happily, be free from anger, and possess sharp wisdom like a diamond (vajirūpama-ñāṇa).

For someone who, at the moment of kamma accumulation, greed and hatred are strong and non-greed and non-hatred are weak, while non-delusion is strong and delusion is weak; that person, following the previous method, will be both greedy and malicious, yet they will possess sharp wisdom like a diamond, like the Elder Dattābhaya.

For someone who, at the moment of kamma accumulation, greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are strong and the others (non-greed, hatred, and delusion) are weak; that person, following the previous method, will be both greedy and slow, yet they will live happily and be free from anger.

Likewise, for someone who, at the moment of kamma accumulation, all three—greed, hatred, and delusion—are strong and non-greed and the others are weak; that person, following the previous method, will be greedy, malicious, and deluded.
309:
For someone who, at the moment of kamma accumulation, non-greed, hatred, and delusion are strong and the others are weak; that person, following the previous method, will have few defilements and remain steady even upon seeing divine objects, yet they will be malicious and slow-witted.

For someone who, at the moment of kamma accumulation, non-greed, non-hatred, and delusion are strong and the others are weak; that person, following the previous method, will not be greedy and will live happily, yet they will be slow-witted.

Likewise, for someone who, at the moment of kamma accumulation, non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are strong and the others are weak; that person, following the previous method, will not be greedy and will be wise, yet they will be malicious and prone to anger.

For someone who, at the moment of kamma accumulation, all three—non-greed and the others—are strong and greed and the others are weak; that person, like the Elder Mahāsaṅgharakkhita, will be free from greed, free from anger, and wise.

In this context, what is known as the Exposition on Roots (Hetu-kittana) is also taken. Triple-rooted kamma (tihetuka-kamma) gives triple-rooted, double-rooted, and rootless (ahetuka) results (vipāka). Double-rooted kamma does not give triple-rooted results, but gives the other double-rooted and rootless results. Through triple-rooted kamma, rebirth-linking is either triple-rooted or double-rooted, but not rootless. Through double-rooted kamma, rebirth-linking is either double-rooted or rootless, but not triple-rooted. Unprompted (asaṅkhārika) wholesome kamma gives both unprompted and prompted (sasaṅkhārika) results. Prompted wholesome kamma also gives both prompted and unprompted results. Feeling (vedanā) should be changed by the object. Registration (tadārammaṇa) should be determined by impulsion (javana).

Now, in the doctrines of various Elders, the sixteen paths and so forth should be understood. For one who has taken rebirth-linking with the first great resultant consciousness (mahāvipāka-citta) which is similar to the first sense-sphere wholesome consciousness (kāmāvacara-kusala), and has emerged from the womb and reached the state of being capable of practicing restraint or non-restraint; when a 'desirable object' comes into range at the eye-door, before the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is adverted by the functional mind-element (kiriya-manodhātu), there is no measure of the objects that have passed by. Why is this so? It is because of the weakness of the object. This is one void turn (moghavāra).

If, however, the life-continuum is adverted; when the life-continuum is adverted by the functional mind-element, in the interval before reaching the determining (votthabbana) stage, either at the eye-consciousness or at the receiving (sampaṭicchana) stage...
310:
The possibility of returning and sinking back while staying at the investigation stage (santīraṇa) does not exist. By the power of the determining consciousness (votthabbana), however, one or two consciousnesses arise while staying there. Beyond that, having obtained repetition (āsevana) and staying in the position of impulsion (javana), it descends again into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). This also happens only because of the weakness of the object. This occurrence (vāra) is obtained at the time of saying, 'It is as if I saw, it is as if I heard,' and so on. This is the second void occurrence (moghavāra).

For another person, when the life-continuum is adverted by the functional mind-element (kiriya-manodhātu), the process consciousnesses (vīthicitta) arise, and impulsion (javana) impels. At the end of the impulsion, it is the turn of the registration (tadārammaṇa). Even before that registration arises, it descends into the life-continuum. Here is an analogy: Just as when a dam is built in a river and the water is directed toward a large canal, the water goes and fills the fields on both banks, and the excess water escapes through crab holes and so on, and descends back into the river itself; so should this be understood.

In this analogy, the time the water flows in the river is like the time of the life-continuum process. The time of building the dam is like the time of adverting the life-continuum by the functional mind-element. The time the water flows in the large canal is like the arising of the process consciousnesses. Filling the fields on both banks is like the impulsion. The excess water escaping through crab holes and so on and descending back into the river is like descending back into the life-continuum after the impulsion has impelled, even before the registration has arisen. Thus, there is no counting the number of consciousnesses that descend into the life-continuum. This also happens only because of the weakness of the object. This is the third void occurrence (moghavāra).

If, however, a strong object (balavārammaṇa) comes into the range of the senses, and the life-continuum is adverted by the functional mind-element, eye-consciousness and so on arise. In the position of impulsion, the first sense-sphere wholesome consciousness (kāmāvacara-kusala-citta) becomes the impulsion, impels for six or seven times, and then gives the turn to the registration.
