When the registration is established, the same great resultant consciousness (mahāvipāka-citta) similar to that impulsion is established. This consciousness receives two names: 'root life-continuum' (mūlabhavaṅga) because it is similar to the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-citta), and 'registration' (tadārammaṇa) because it takes the object taken by the impulsion. In this place, the four resultant consciousnesses—eye-consciousness, receiving (sampaṭicchana), investigation (santīraṇa), and registration (tadārammaṇa)—come into the count.

When the second wholesome consciousness becomes the impulsion, then only the second resultant consciousness similar to it is established as the registration. This consciousness also [receives] two names...
311:
(The second great resultant consciousness) receives the names. Because it is not similar to the rebirth-linking consciousness, it is called 'adventitious life-continuum' (āgantukabhavaṅga), and as in the previous method, it is called 'registration' (tadārammaṇa). Together with this second great resultant consciousness, the four consciousnesses that occurred previously become five.

When the third great wholesome consciousness becomes the impulsion, then the third great resultant consciousness similar to it is established as the registration. This consciousness also, in the same way as mentioned, receives the two names 'adventitious life-continuum' and 'registration'. Together with this third great resultant consciousness, the previous five consciousnesses become six.

When the fourth great wholesome consciousness becomes the impulsion, then the fourth great resultant consciousness similar to it is established as the registration. This consciousness also, in the same way as mentioned, receives the two names 'adventitious life-continuum' and 'registration'. Together with this fourth great resultant consciousness, the previous six consciousnesses become seven.

When a 'desirable-neutral object' (iṭṭhamajjhattārammaṇa) comes into the range of that eye-door, there also the three void occurrences are obtained in the same way as mentioned. However, because the feeling changes according to the object, in that desirable-neutral object, the investigation consciousness accompanied by equanimity (upekkhāsahagata-santīraṇa) arises. At the end of the four great wholesome impulsions accompanied by equanimity, only the four great resultant consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity are established as the registration. These four consciousnesses also, in the same way as mentioned, receive the two names 'adventitious life-continuum' and 'registration'. They are also called 'back life-continuums' (piṭṭhibhavaṅga). Thus, these five consciousnesses together with the previous seven become twelve. In this way, there are twelve in the eye-door, and twelve each in the ear-door and so on, making sixty in total. Thus, when kamma is accumulated by a single volition (cetanā), sixty resultant consciousnesses arise. However, by taking what has not yet been taken, there are twelve in the eye-door, and with the four—ear, nose, tongue, and body-consciousness—they become sixteen.

In this place, they take the mango analogy (ambopama). Briefly: A man is sleeping with his head covered at the foot of a fruiting mango tree. Then a ripe mango, being released from its stalk, falls to the ground with the sound 'thud', as if brushing against the man's ear. That man, waking up because of that sound, opens his eyes and looks. Then, stretching out his hand, he takes the fruit, squeezes it, smells it, and eats it.

In that analogy, the time the man is sleeping at the foot of the mango tree is like the time of being endowed with the life-continuum. The time the ripe mango is released from its stalk and falls, brushing against the ear, is like the time the object strikes the sensitive matter (pasāda). Because of that sound...
312:
It is the time when the functional mind-element (kiriya-manodhātu) turns the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), like the time of waking up. It is the time when eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa) performs the function of seeing, like the time of opening the eyes and looking. It is the time when the resultant mind-element (vipāka-manodhātu) receives the object, like the time of stretching out the hand and taking. It is the time when the resultant mind-consciousness-element (vipāka-manoviññāṇadhātu) investigates the object, like the time of taking and kneading. It is the time when the functional mind-consciousness-element (kiriya-manoviññāṇadhātu) determines the object, like the time of smelling. It is the time when the impulsion (javana) experiences the essence of the object, like the time of consuming.

What does this analogy show? The impact of the object on the sensitive material (pasāda) is the only function. When there is an impact on the sensitive material, the turning of the life-continuum by the functional mind-element, the mere seeing by eye-consciousness, the mere receiving of the object by the resultant mind-element, the mere investigation of the object by the resultant mind-consciousness-element, and the mere determination of the object by the functional mind-consciousness-element are their respective functions. In truth, it shows that only the impulsion (javana) experiences the essence of the object.

In this regard, there is no doer (kattā) or instigator (kāretā) who commands, "You, become the life-continuum; you, the adverting; you, the seeing; you, the receiving; you, the investigating; you, the determining; you, the impulsion."

In this context, five types of laws (niyāma) are recognized: the law of seeds (bīja-niyāma), the law of physical order (utu-niyāma), the law of kamma (kamma-niyāma), the law of nature (dhamma-niyāma), and the law of the mind (citta-niyāma). Among these five, the shoot of a chickpea plant pointing north, a right-winding creeper encircling a tree from the right, sunflowers facing the sun, the māluva-creeper heading only towards a tree, and the presence of a hole at the top of a coconut—such giving of results by various seeds according to their nature is called the law of seeds (bīja-niyāma). The simultaneous blooming, fruiting, and sprouting of various trees at their respective times is called the law of physical order (utu-niyāma). Three-rooted kamma gives three-rooted, two-rooted, or rootless results. Two-rooted kamma gives two-rooted or rootless results, but does not give three-rooted results. Thus, the giving of results by various kammas according to their nature is called the law of kamma (kamma-niyāma).

In another way, the law of kamma also exists by way of results resembling the kamma. To illustrate this, they tell this story: In the time of the Fully Enlightened Buddha, in a gate-village of Sāvatthī...
313:
(The village) caught fire. From that fire, a burning ring of grass rose up and caught the neck of a crow flying in the sky. That crow fell to the ground crying out and died. In the great ocean, a ship also came to a standstill, unmoving. Seeing no obstruction beneath, they drew lots for the "unlucky one" (kāḷakaṇṇi). The lot fell into the hand of a laywoman who was the wife of the sailor. Then they said, "Let us not all perish because of this one woman; let us throw her into the water." The sailor said, "I cannot bear to see this woman floating in the water," and so he had a pot of sand tied to her neck and had her thrown in. At that very moment, the ship sped away like a released arrow. A monk was living in a cave when a large mountain peak collapsed and blocked the cave entrance. On the seventh day, it moved away by itself. While the Fully Enlightened Buddha was residing at the Jetavana monastery and preaching the Dhamma, these three incidents were reported to him at once. The Teacher said, "This was not done by others; it is only the kamma performed by themselves," and he brought forth the past to show it, saying:

In a past life, when the crow was a human, he was unable to tame a vicious ox, so he tied a bundle of straw to its neck and set it on fire. The ox died from that fire. Now, that kamma does not allow him to escape even while flying in the sky. That woman was also a woman in a past life. A dog became very familiar with her and would follow her when she went to the forest and return with her. People mocked her, saying, "Now our dog-huntress has gone out." Being distressed by that mockery and unable to stop the dog, she tied a pot of sand to its neck and threw it into the water. That kamma did not allow her to escape in the middle of the ocean. That monk was also a cowherd in a past life. He blocked the hole where an iguana had entered with a handful of broken branches. Then, on the seventh day, he came and opened it himself. The iguana came out trembling. Out of compassion, he did not kill it. That kamma did not allow that monk, who was sitting inside the mountain cave, to escape. Combining these three stories, he spoke this verse:

"Not in the sky, nor in the middle of the ocean,
Nor by entering a mountain cleft,
There is no place found on earth
Where, staying there, one might escape from evil kamma."
(Dhp. 127)
314:
This order is also known as the Order of Kamma (kamma-niyāma). Other such stories should also be told.

Furthermore, the shaking of the ten thousand world systems at the time when the Bodhisattas take rebirth-linking, when they emerge from their mother's womb, when they realize the Four Noble Truths, when the Blessed One turns the Wheel of Dhamma, when he relinquishes the life-force, and when he attains Parinibbāna, is called the Order of Nature (dhamma-niyāma).

When an object strikes the clear sensitive matter (pasāda), there is no doer (kattā) or instigator (kāretā) who commands, "You, become adverting... You, become impulsion." Rather, by their own nature, from the moment the object strikes the sensitive matter, the functional mind-element (kiriya-manodhātu) adverts to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga); the eye-consciousness performs the function of seeing; the resultant mind-element performs the function of receiving (sampaṭicchana); the resultant mind-consciousness-element performs the function of investigating (santīraṇa); the functional mind-consciousness-element performs the function of determining (vōṭṭhabbana); and the impulsion (javana) experiences the taste of the object. This process is called the Order of Mind (citta-niyāma). This Order of Mind is what is intended here.

When kamma is accumulated by prompted triple-rooted wholesome consciousness (tihetuka-kusala), or by unprompted or prompted wholesome consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity, the same method should be understood for the rebirth-linking taken by resultant consciousnesses similar to that kamma. Specifically, in the combination of the two [consciousnesses] accompanied by equanimity, the occurrence by way of a "desirable-neutral object" (iṭṭhamajjhatta-ārammaṇa) should be shown first, and later the occurrence by way of a "desirable object" (iṭṭha-ārammaṇa).

In this way, there are twelve [resultants] in each door, making a total of sixty (samasaṭṭhi). By taking what has not been taken [counting unique instances] (aggahitaggahaṇa), sixteen resultant consciousnesses arise.

In this context, the "Simile of the Five Sugarcane-Pressing Machines" is cited. It is said that at the time of pressing sugarcane, eleven experts in sugarcane-pressing machines set out from a village. Seeing a sugarcane field and knowing its ripeness, they approached the owner of the field and said, "We are experts in sugarcane-pressing machines." The owner replied, "I have been looking for you," and took those eleven men to the sugarcane shed. There, they prepared the pressing machine and said, "We are eleven people; it is proper to have one more; please hire someone for a wage." The owner of the sugarcane field said, "I myself will be the companion," and after filling the shed with sugarcane, he became their companion. They performed their respective duties and...
315:
When the molasses cooker had finished cooking the sugarcane juice, and the molasses binder had finished shaping it, and the owner of the sugarcane field had weighed and distributed the shares, they each took their own share, handed the sugarcane shed back to the owner, and in this same manner, they worked in four other sheds and then departed.

In this simile, the five sensitive matters (pasāda-rūpa) should be understood as the five sugarcane sheds. The five objects should be understood as the five sugarcane fields. The eleven resultant consciousnesses should be understood as the eleven traveling machine experts. The five types of consciousness (viññāṇa) should be understood as the five owners of the sugarcane fields. In the first shed, the time when the twelve people, including the owner, worked together and took their shares is like the time when the eleven resultant consciousnesses work together with eye-consciousness to perform their respective functions regarding a visible object at the eye-door. The time when the shed is handed back to the owner is like the eye-consciousness not performing the transition of doors. The time when the twelve people worked together and took their shares in the second, third, fourth, and fifth sheds is like the time when the eleven resultant consciousnesses work together with body-consciousness to perform their respective functions regarding a tangible object at the body-door. The time when the shed is handed back to the owner is like the body-consciousness not performing the transition of doors. Thus far, the section (vāra) stating that triple-rooted rebirth-linking occurs due to triple-rooted kamma has been explained. As for the double-rooted rebirth-linking that occurs due to that [same] triple-rooted kamma, it is included as hidden.

Now, the section stating that double-rooted rebirth-linking occurs due to double-rooted kamma will be explained. When kamma is accumulated by a double-rooted unprompted consciousness accompanied by joy, for one whose rebirth-linking is taken by a similar double-rooted resultant consciousness, when a 'desirable object' comes into range at the eye-door according to the method already mentioned, three void turns (moghavāra) occur. At the end of the double-rooted unprompted impulsion accompanied by joy, a registration (tadārammaṇa) occurs which is similar to it and is called the original life-continuum (mūla-bhavaṅga). At the end of a prompted impulsion, a registration occurs which is similar to it and is called the adventitious life-continuum (āgantuka-bhavaṅga). Regarding a 'desirable-neutral object', at the end of the two impulsions accompanied by equanimity, two such registration consciousnesses arise. Here, by counting eight in each door, forty consciousnesses occur. However, by taking what has not been taken (aggahitaggahaṇa), there are twelve: eight at the eye-door, and forty [total] across ear, nose, tongue, and body consciousnesses. In this way, when kamma is accumulated by a single volition...
316:
Twelve resultant consciousnesses (vipākacittāni) arise. The mango simile and the discussion on the five laws (niyāma) are just as before. The same method should be understood for one whose rebirth (paṭisandhi) is taken by a resultant consciousness similar to the remaining three two-root (duhetuka) consciousnesses. In this regard, according to the simile of the machine-pullers, there are seven machine-pullers. When they have prepared the machine in that situation, the application should be understood according to the method already mentioned, making the owner of the sugarcane field the eighth. Thus far, the section (vāra) stating that two-root rebirth occurs due to two-root kamma has been explained.

Now, the discussion on rootless (ahetuka) rebirth will be told. When kamma is accumulated by any one of the four two-root wholesome consciousnesses, it cannot be said that the rebirth of one whose rebirth is taken by the rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity, which is a wholesome resultant, is similar to the kamma. This is because the kamma is two-root while the rebirth is rootless. When a desirable-neutral object (iṭṭhamajjhattārammaṇa) comes into the range of the eye-door of such a person who has reached maturity, the three void sections (moghavāra) should be understood just as in the previous method. At the conclusion of the impulsion (javana) of any one of the four two-root wholesome consciousnesses, a rootless consciousness stands as registration (tadārammaṇa). That consciousness receives two names: 'original life-continuum' (mūlabhavaṅga) and 'registration' (tadārammaṇa). Thus, in this eye-door, eye-consciousness, receiving (sampaticchana), and investigating (santīraṇa) accompanied by equanimity arise. Since registration is also accompanied by equanimity, by taking one out of those two—investigating and registration—the consciousnesses that enter the count are only three.

However, in the case of a desirable object (iṭṭhārammaṇa), both investigating and registration are accompanied by joy (somanassa). Taking one of those two and adding it to the previous three, they become four. Thus, by making four for each of the five doors, it should be understood that twenty resultant consciousnesses arise when kamma is accumulated by a single volition (cetanā). By the method of 'taking what has not been taken' (aggahitaggahaṇa), there are four in the eye-door, and four each for ear, nose, tongue, and body consciousnesses, making eight. This is called the 'Rootless Eight' (ahetukaṭṭhaka). This group is taken in the human realm.

In the four woeful states (apāya), it is obtained during the course of existence (pavatti). For instance, when the Elder Mahāmoggallāna created a lotus in hell and sat on the pericarp of the lotus to preach the Dhamma to the denizens of hell, while those denizens of hell were looking at the Elder, wholesome resultant eye-consciousness arose. While listening to the sound, ear-consciousness; when smelling the scent of the robes of the Elder who had come after staying for the day-abiding in a sandalwood forest, nose-consciousness; when water was given by making it rain to extinguish the fires of hell, tongue-consciousness; and when a gentle breeze was made to blow, body-consciousness arose. Thus, eye-consciousness and so forth...
317:
...five, one receiving (sampaticchana), and two investigating (santīraṇa) consciousnesses—thus the Rootless Eight (ahetukaṭṭhaka) is obtained. Even though Nagas, Garudas, and Petas with mansions (vimānika peta) take rebirth through unwholesome kamma, wholesome resultants ripen during the course of existence (pavatti). Likewise, in the case of the auspicious elephants, horses, etc., of a wheel-turning monarch (even though they take rebirth through unwholesome kamma, wholesome resultants ripen during the course of existence). This is the sequence of discussion concerning 'desirable objects (iṭṭhārammaṇa) and desirable-neutral objects (iṭṭhamajjhattārammaṇa)' by way of wholesome impulsion (javana).

In the case of a 'desirable object', when the four unwholesome consciousnesses accompanied by joy (somanassa) impel, the rootless wholesome resultant consciousness accompanied by joy becomes the registration (tadārammaṇa). In the case of a 'desirable-neutral object', when the four consciousnesses associated with greed and accompanied by equanimity impel, the rootless wholesome resultant consciousness accompanied by equanimity becomes the registration. The statement that 'registration is determined by impulsion' should be understood as being said with reference to wholesome impulsion. If registration arises immediately after an impulsion accompanied by displeasure (domanassa), what consciousness arises? The rootless unwholesome resultant mind-consciousness-element arises.

What factor determines this impulsion for the sake of the wholesome or the unwholesome? It is indeed the advertence (āvajjana) that adverts and the determining (votthabbana) that determines. When there is wise (yoniso) advertence and wise determining, it is impossible for the impulsion to be unwholesome. When there is unwise (ayoniso) advertence and unwise determining, it is also impossible for the impulsion to be wholesome. It should be understood that only when both are done wisely does the impulsion become wholesome, and if done unwisely, it becomes unwholesome.

Regarding how registration occurs for one with doubt or restlessness in the case of a 'desirable object': whether there is doubt or not, or restlessness or not, only the rootless wholesome resultant consciousness accompanied by joy becomes the registration. In the case of a 'desirable-neutral object', the 'rootless wholesome resultant consciousness accompanied by equanimity' becomes the registration. This is the view of the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita, which explains the meaning concisely in this matter. When an impulsion accompanied by joy occurs, five registrations should be sought. When an impulsion accompanied by equanimity occurs, six should be sought.

Then, when one with a rebirth accompanied by joy attains jhāna during the course of existence and later falls away from jhāna due to negligence, reflecting, "My sublime state has perished"...
318:
When displeasure (*domanassa*) arises by the power of remorse (*vippaṭisāra*), what registration (*tadārammaṇa*) arises then? For, in the *Paṭṭhāna*, it is forbidden for displeasure to follow joy (*somanassa*), and for joy to follow displeasure. Is it not also forbidden in that same *Paṭṭhāna* for registration to occur when *javana* arises with a sublime state (*mahaggata*) as its object? The equanimity-accompanied rootless mind-consciousness element (*upekkhāsahagata ahetuka manoviññāṇadhātu*), whether a resultant of wholesome or unwholesome, arises; what is its adverting (*āvajjana*)? (It is answered:) Just as there is no function of adverting in the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and the adverting consciousness, so there is no function of adverting in this consciousness.

Let those *bhavaṅga* and adverting consciousnesses arise because of their own inclination, practice, and habitual occurrence; but how does this (equanimity-accompanied rootless mind-consciousness element) arise? (It is asked). Just as the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception arises as the proximity-condition for cessation (*nirodha*), and for one emerging from cessation, the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), the noble path (*ariyamagga*), and the fruition consciousnesses immediately following the path arise (even without inclination, etc.), even so, though there is no adverting, it arises by the power of inclination, practice, and habitual occurrence. Indeed, consciousness can arise without adverting, but it cannot arise without an object. If so, what is the object of that consciousness? It is one of the limited states (*parittadhamma*) such as visible forms. It should be understood that whichever of those limited states appears at that moment, this consciousness arises based on that object.

Now, for the purpose of clarifying all these types of consciousness, this miscellaneous method (*pakiṇṇakanaya*) is stated:

The spider's thread, the doorkeeper, the village boy, the mango, the sugarcane press,
The blind man, the cripple, the grasping of the object, and by way of strong dependence.

In those analogies, 'the spider's thread' means: a spider that waits on a path to eat spreads its thread in five directions, makes a web, and lies in the middle. When an insect, a grasshopper, or a fly hits the thread spread in the first direction, the spider moves from its place of rest, goes along the thread, drinks the juice of that insect, and returns to lie in that same place. It does the same when the thread is hit in the second direction and so on.

In that analogy, the five sensitive matters (*pasāda*) are like the threads spread in five directions. The mind is like the spider lying in the middle. The moment the object strikes the sensitive matter is like the moment the insect hits the thread. The moment the life-continuum is turned by the functional mind-element (*kiriyamanodhātu*) after taking the object that struck the sensitive matter is like the movement of the spider lying in the middle. The occurrence of the cognitive process (*vīthicitta*) is like the going along the thread. At the head...
319:
...piercing (the insect's head) and drinking the juice is like the moment the *javana* impels (experiences) the object. Returning and lying in the middle is like the mind occurring based only on the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*).

What does this analogy illustrate? It illustrates that when an object strikes the sensitive matter, the mind based on the heart-base arises before the mind based on the sensitive matter. It also shows that a single object appears at two doors (the sense-door and the mind-door).

In the 'Doorkeeper' (*dovārika*) analogy: A king is asleep in bed. His attendant sits massaging his feet. A deaf doorkeeper stands at the door. Three guards stand in order. Then a villager from the border brings a gift and knocks on the door. The deaf doorkeeper does not hear the sound. The foot-massaging attendant gives a signal. Because of that signal, (the doorkeeper) opens the door and looks. The first guard takes the gift and gives it to the second; the second gives it to the third; the third presents it to the king. The king enjoys the gift.

In that analogy, the *javana* should be understood as the king. The adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*) as the foot-massaging attendant. The eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*) as the deaf doorkeeper. The three cognitive processes starting from receiving (*sampaṭicchana*) should be understood as the three guards. The villager bringing the gift and knocking on the door is like the object striking the sensitive matter. The moment the foot-massager gives the signal is like the moment the functional mind-element turns the life-continuum (*āvajjana*). The moment the deaf doorkeeper opens the door due to the signal is like the moment the eye-consciousness performs the function of seeing the object. The moment the first guard takes the gift is like the moment the resultant mind-element receives (*sampaṭicchana*) the object. The moment the first guard gives it to the second is like the moment the resultant mind-consciousness element investigates (*santīraṇa*) the object. The moment the second guard gives it to the third is like the moment the functional mind-consciousness element determines (*vavatthāpana*) the object. The moment the third guard presents it to the king is like the moment the determining consciousness (*votthabbana*) hands it over to the *javana*. The moment the king enjoys it is like the moment the *javana* experiences the flavor of the object.

What does this analogy illustrate? The function of the object is merely to strike the sensitive matter; the function of the functional mind-element is merely to turn the life-continuum; the functions of eye-consciousness and so on are merely seeing, receiving, investigating, and determining. However, it illustrates that only the *javana* definitely experiences the flavor of the object.
320:
Regarding the word ‘Gāmillo’ (the village boys): Many village boys were playing in the dust in the middle of the street. Among those boys, a kahāpaṇa coin struck the hand of one boy. That boy said, ‘What is this that has struck my hand?’ Then one boy said, ‘This is something white.’ Another boy grasped it firmly along with the dust. Another boy said, ‘This is flat and square.’ Yet another boy said, ‘This is a kahāpaṇa.’ Then, he took that kahāpaṇa and gave it to his mother. The mother used it for [making] jewelry (such as bracelets or strings).

In this simile, the time when many boys are sitting and playing in the middle of the street should be understood as the occurrence of the bhavaṅga-mind. The time when the kahāpaṇa strikes the hand should be understood as the time when the object strikes the sensitive matter (pasāda). The time when he says, ‘What is this?’ should be understood as the time when the bhavaṅga is adverted by the functional mind-element (kiriya-manodhātu) taking that object. The time when he says, ‘This is white’ should be understood as the time when the function of seeing is accomplished by eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa). The time when he grasps it firmly along with the dust should be understood as the time when the object is received by the resultant mind-element (vipāka-manodhātu). The time when he says, ‘This is flat and square’ should be understood as the time when the object is investigated by the resultant mind-consciousness element (vipāka-manoviññāṇadhātu). The time when he says, ‘This is a kahāpaṇa’ should be understood as the time when the object is determined (marked) by the functional mind-consciousness element (kiriya-manoviññāṇadhātu). The time when the mother uses it for an object should be understood as the javana experiencing the taste of the object.

What does this simile illustrate? It illustrates that the functional mind-element adverts the bhavaṅga without seeing (the object); the resultant mind-element receives it without seeing; the resultant mind-consciousness element investigates it without seeing; the functional mind-consciousness element determines it without seeing; and the javana experiences the taste of the object without seeing. In reality, it illustrates that only eye-consciousness accomplishes the function of seeing.

The phrase ‘Ambō kōliyakēna ca’ is said in reference to the mango simile and the sugarcane field owner simile mentioned below.

Regarding the phrase ‘Jaccandho pīṭhasappī ca’ (the born-blind and the lame): Both of them were sitting in a rest house at the city gate. Between the two, the lame man said, ‘O blind one, why are you wandering around here withered and without food or drink? Such-and-such a place is well-supplied with alms-food and has plenty of food and drink. Is it not fit to go there and live happily?’ (The blind man replied,) ‘On your part, you have told me; but for you, why is it not fit to go there and live happily?’ (The lame man said,) ‘I have no legs to go.’ (The blind man also said,) ‘I too have no eyes to see.’ ‘If that is so, let your legs be mine, and let my eyes be yours,’ saying thus, both of them...
321:
Accepting by saying "Very well," the born-blind man took the lame man upon his shoulders. That lame man, sitting on the shoulders of the blind man, embraced the other's head with his left hand and, with his right hand, directed the way, saying, "In this place, a tree root stands blocking the path; in this place, there is a stone; leave the left and take the right; leave the right and take the left." In this way, it was as if the blind man had legs and the lame man had eyes; by joining together, both went to their desired place and lived happily.

In this simile, the blind man is like the material body (rūpakāya), and the lame man is like the immaterial body (arūpakāya). Just as the blind man, without the lame man, is unable to bring about the activity of going to another place, so too should it be understood that the material body, without the immaterial (mental) states, is incapable of reaching the state of taking, grasping, or moving. Just as the lame man, without the blind man, cannot bring about the activity of going to another place, so too should it be understood that in the five-constituent realm (pañcavokāra-bhava), the immaterial states do not occur without the material body. Just as the two, by joining together, go to their desired place and live happily, so too should it be understood that the material and immaterial phenomena (rūpārūpa-dhamma), by being associated with one another, have the capacity to occur in all activities. This problem is explained by way of the five-constituent existence.

"Visayaggāho ca" means the eye takes the object of visible form. The ear and so forth take the objects of sound and so forth.

"Upanissayamatthaso" means by way of strong dependence (upanissaya) and by way of purpose/result (attha). Therein, eye-consciousness arises together with its associated states due to four conditions: the eye being unimpaired, visible forms coming into range, the presence of light, and having attention as a cause. Therein, even the eye of a dead person is called "impaired." Even in a living person, an eye that has ceased, or an eye that is unable to be a condition for eye-consciousness because it is obstructed and afflicted by bile, phlegm, or blood, is called an "impaired eye." One that is able (to be a condition) is called an "unimpaired eye." This same method applies to the ear and so forth. However, even if the eye is unimpaired, if the external visible object does not come into range, eye-consciousness does not arise. Even if that object comes into range, if there is no dependence on light, it does not arise. Even if there is light, if the functional mind-element (kiriya-manodhātu) does not advert the bhavaṅga, it does not arise. It arises only when there is adverting. Eye-consciousness that arises in this way arises only together with its associated states. Thus, eye-consciousness arises having obtained these four conditions (this is slightly different from Majjhima Nikāya, Paṇṇāsa Pāḷi, 1, 306).
322:
Ear-consciousness (sotaviññāṇa) arises together with associated states due to these four causes: the non-destruction of the ear (sotapasāda), sounds coming into the range of the sense, dependence on space (ākāsa), and the presence of attention (manasikāra). Among these causes, 'dependence on space' means it arises only when the support of the space element (ākāsadhātu) is obtained, and it cannot occur without it. Indeed, ear-consciousness cannot occur for a person whose ear canal is blocked. The remaining meanings should be understood in the same way as the previous method. Just as in this ear-consciousness, the same applies to the subsequent nose-consciousness and so on. However, I shall state the specific distinctions.

Nose-consciousness (ghānaviññāṇa) arises together with associated states due to four causes: the non-destruction of the nose (ghānapasāda), odors coming into the range of the sense, dependence on air (vāyo), and the presence of attention. Among these causes, 'dependence on air' means nose-consciousness arises only when air enters the nostril; it means it does not arise in the absence of that air.

Tongue-consciousness (jivhāviññāṇa) arises together with associated states due to four causes: the non-destruction of the tongue (jivhāpasāda), tastes coming into the range of the sense, dependence on liquid (āpo), and the presence of attention. Among these causes, 'dependence on liquid' means it arises only when the water element (āpodhātu) that moistens the tongue is obtained, and it cannot occur without it. Indeed, for a person with a dry tongue, tongue-consciousness does not arise even if dry food is placed on the tongue.

Body-consciousness (kāyaviññāṇa) arises together with associated states due to four causes: the non-destruction of the body (kāyapasāda), tangible objects (phoṭṭhabba) coming into the range of the sense, dependence on earth (pathavī), and the presence of attention. Among these causes, 'dependence on earth' means it arises only when the support of the earth element (pathavīdhātu), which is a cause for the body-sensitivity, is obtained, and it cannot occur without it. In fact, at the body-door, an external great essential (mahābhūta) as an object strikes the internal body-sensitivity and impinges upon the great essentials that are the causes of that sensitivity.

Mind-consciousness (manoviññāṇa) arises together with associated states due to four causes: the non-destruction of the mind (bhavaṅga-citta), mental objects (dhammārammaṇa) coming into the range of the sense, dependence on the base (hadayavatthu), and the presence of attention. Among these causes, 'mind' refers to the life-continuum mind (bhavaṅga-citta). Even if that life-continuum mind has ceased, or if it occurs weakly without being able to be a cause for the adverting consciousness (āvajjana-citta), it is called 'destroyed' (sambhina). Only when it is capable of being a cause for the adverting consciousness is it called 'non-destroyed' (asambhina). 'Mental objects coming into the range of the sense' means the mental objects become manifest. 'Dependence on the base' means it arises only when the support of the heart-base (hadayavatthu) is obtained, and it cannot occur without that base. This problem also...
323:
...is stated with reference to the realm of five-constituent existence (pañcavokārabhava). 'Due to the cause of attention' (manasikārahetuka) means that the functional mind-consciousness element (kiriya-manoviññāṇadhātu) arises only when the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is adverted to. This is first the explanation of 'dependence' (upanissaya) in the phrase 'by way of the meaning of dependence' (upanissayamatthaso).

By way of meaning, the eye has the function of seeing, the ear has the function of hearing, the nose has the function of smelling, the tongue has the function of tasting, the body has the function of touching, and the mind has the function of cognizing. Therein, seeing is the purpose (function) of that eye. Because that seeing is to be accomplished by that eye, it is called 'for the purpose of seeing' (dassanatthaṃ). The same method applies to the remaining terms. By this much, in the tradition of the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga, the sixteen-fold path is completed along with the twelve-fold path and the eight rootless states (ahetuka).

Now, there is the discussion of the twelve-fold path in the tradition of the Elder Mahādatta, a resident of Moravāpī. Therein, the Sāketa problem, the showing of the excess (ussada), and the showing of the cause (hetu) are already well-known. This Elder, seeing a fault in the unprompted (asaṅkhārika) and prompted (sasaṅkhārika) states, said: "An unprompted kamma gives only an unprompted result, not a prompted one. A prompted kamma also gives only a prompted result, not an unprompted one." This Elder does not state the fixity of mind by way of impulsion (javana), but states the fixity of feeling by way of the object. For that reason, in the extraction of resultants (vipāka) in his tradition, what is called the twelve-fold path arises. The ten-fold path and the eight rootless states are also included herein.

Therein, this is the method: When kamma is accumulated with a triple-rooted unprompted consciousness associated with joy (somanassa-sahagata tihetuka asaṅkhārika citta), for one who has taken rebirth with a similar resultant consciousness and has grown up, when a very desirable object comes into the range of the eye-door, three void turns (moghvāra) occur according to the method mentioned below. For that person, when registration (tadārammaṇa) is established at the end of one of the thirteen impulsions—four associated with joy from the wholesome (kusala), four from the unwholesome (akusala), and five from the functional (kiriya)—either a triple-rooted or a double-rooted unprompted consciousness associated with joy is established. Thus, in that person's eye-door, there are five consciousnesses counted as: three consciousnesses starting with eye-consciousness, and two registrations.

By changing the feeling by way of the object, at the end of one of the twelve impulsions associated with equanimity (upekkhā)—four from the wholesome, four from the unwholesome, and four from the functional—either a triple-rooted unprompted resultant associated with equanimity or a double-rooted unprompted resultant arises as registration (tadārammaṇa). Thus, in that person's eye-door, one investigating consciousness (santīraṇa) associated with equanimity and these two registrations, making three...
324:
The consciousnesses that come into counting arise. These, together with the five previous ones, are eight. In the ear-door and so on, there are also eight each; thus, when kamma is accumulated by a single volition (cetanā), a total of forty consciousnesses arise. However, by taking what has not yet been taken, there are eight in the eye-door and four in the ear-consciousness and so on, making twelve. Therein, the state of original bhavaṅga, the state of adventitious bhavaṅga, and the explanation of the mango simile (ambopama) should be understood in the manner already stated.

Even when kamma is accumulated by a three-rooted prompted wholesome consciousness accompanied by joy, or when kamma is accumulated by three-rooted unprompted or prompted consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity, the method is the same. Therein, the machine simile (yantopama) is also evident in this section. By this much, the section stating that "three-rooted rebirth occurs through three-rooted kamma" has been explained. The section stating that "two-rooted rebirth occurs through three-rooted kamma" has proceeded in a hidden manner.

Now, the explanation of two-rooted rebirth occurring through two-rooted kamma will be given. For one who has taken rebirth with a similar resultant consciousness through kamma accumulated by a two-rooted unprompted consciousness accompanied by joy, when a desirable object comes into range at the eye-door upon reaching maturity, the three void turns (moghavāra) occur in the manner already stated. For a two-rooted person, there is no functional impulsion (javana-kiriya). Therefore, at the end of the impulsion by any one of these eight consciousnesses—four accompanied by joy from the wholesome and four from the unwholesome—a two-rooted unprompted registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa) accompanied by joy arises. Thus, for that person, there are three consciousnesses such as eye-consciousness and this one registration consciousness, making four consciousnesses that come into counting. But in the case of a moderately desirable object, at the end of the impulsion by any one of the eight consciousnesses—four accompanied by equanimity from the wholesome and four from the unwholesome—a two-rooted unprompted registration consciousness accompanied by equanimity arises. Thus, for that person, there are the investigating consciousness (santīraṇa) accompanied by equanimity and this registration consciousness, making two consciousnesses that come into counting. These, together with the four previous ones, are six. In the ear-door and so on, there are also six each; thus, when kamma is accumulated by a single volition, a total of thirty consciousnesses arise. However, by taking what has not yet been taken, there are six in the eye-door and four in the ear-consciousness and so on, making ten. The explanation of the mango simile is evident. It is stated that the machine simile is not applicable here.
325:
The same method should be understood when kamma is accumulated by a two-rooted prompted wholesome consciousness accompanied by joy, or when kamma is accumulated by two-rooted unprompted or prompted consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity. By this much, the section stating that "two-rooted rebirth occurs through two-rooted kamma" has been explained.

Furthermore, the section stating that "rootless rebirth occurs" should be understood as follows: When kamma is accumulated by the four consciousnesses dissociated from knowledge from the wholesome, and when rebirth is taken by the rootless mind-consciousness element which is a wholesome resultant accompanied by equanimity, it should not be said that "rebirth is similar to kamma." Starting from these words "four from the wholesome," the sequence of the occurrence of consciousness in the case of a desirable object and a moderately desirable object should be understood by the method already stated below. The reason is that in the view of this Elder, a collective impulsion (piṇḍajavana) occurs. All the remaining words, such as "Who determines this impulsion for the sake of the wholesome or for the sake of the unwholesome?" should be understood in the manner already stated below. By this much, in the view of Elder Mahādatta, a resident of Moravāpī, the Twelvefold Path (dvādasakamagga) is completed along with the Tenfold Path (dasakamagga) and the Rootless Octad (ahetukaṭṭhaka).

## Now, the explanation of the Tenfold Path in the view of Elder Mahādhammarakkhita follows.

In that explanation of the Tenfold Path, the descriptions of the Sāketa questions and the protuberances (ussada) are just as usual. However, in describing the roots (hetu), this is the distinction: Three-rooted kamma gives three-rooted resultants, two-rooted resultants, and rootless resultants. Two-rooted kamma does not give three-rooted resultants, but gives the others. Through three-rooted kamma, rebirth is only three-rooted; it is not two-rooted or rootless. Through two-rooted kamma, rebirth is two-rooted or rootless; it is not three-rooted. Unprompted kamma gives only unprompted resultants, not prompted. Prompted kamma also gives only prompted resultants, not unprompted. Feeling (vedanā) should be changed according to the object. The impulsion that occurs is only the collective impulsion (piṇḍajavana). The consciousnesses should be described from the beginning.

Therein, this is the explanation: A certain person accumulates kamma with the first wholesome consciousness and takes rebirth with the first resultant consciousness only. This is rebirth similar to kamma. When that person reaches maturity and a "desirable object" comes into range at the eye-door, the three void turns (moghavāra) occur in the manner already stated. Then, for that person, at the end of any one of the thirteen impulsions accompanied by joy mentioned below, the first resultant consciousness itself...
326:
At that time, the registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa) arises. That consciousness receives two names: 'original life-continuum' (mūlabhavaṅga) and 'registration' (tadārammaṇa). Thus, for that person, there are four types of consciousness that come into counting: the three beginning with eye-consciousness and this one registration consciousness.

In the case of a desirable-neutral (iṭṭhamajjhatta) object, at the end of any of the twelve neutral impulsion (upekkhāsahagata-javana) mentioned below, a neutral, triple-rooted, unprompted consciousness arises as registration. It receives two names: 'adventitious life-continuum' (āgantukabhavaṅga) and 'registration' (tadārammaṇa). Thus, for that person, there are two types of consciousness that come into counting: the neutral investigating consciousness (upekkhāsahagata-santīraṇa) and this one registration consciousness. When these are added to the previous four, they become six. Thus, when kamma is accumulated by a single volition, thirty types of consciousness arise in the five doors. However, by taking the remainder, there are ten: six in the eye-door and four each in the ear-consciousness and so on. The rule of the mango simile (ambopama) is just as usual.

Even when kamma is accumulated by the second, third, and fourth wholesome consciousnesses, there are just this many resultant consciousnesses. The same method applies when accumulated by the four neutral consciousnesses. Here, however, the desirable-neutral object should be shown first. Later, the feeling should be changed with the desirable object. The rule of the mango simile is just as usual. The machine simile (yantopama) is not obtained. Starting from the words, "When kamma is accumulated by any of the four consciousnesses dissociated from knowledge from the wholesome," everything should be explained in detail and the eight rootless ones (ahetukaṭṭhaka) should be mentioned. With this much, the ten-fold path (dasakamagga) together with the eight rootless ones in the view of Elder Mahādhammarakkhita is finished.

Among these three elders, whose view should be accepted? Not exclusively any one person's. Rather, what is appropriate in the views of all should be accepted. In the first view, the arrangement of prompted (sasaṅkhāra) and unprompted (asaṅkhāra) is intended by way of the distinction of conditions (paccayabheda). Therefore, in this view, taking the prompted resultant arisen from weak conditions of unprompted wholesome, and the unprompted resultant arisen from strong conditions of prompted wholesome, and discarding the functional impulsions that could be obtained, and determining the registration by the wholesome impulsion and the feeling by the object, the sixteen-fold path (soḷasakamagga) is stated by way of the trainee (sekha) and the worldling (puthujjana). Here, the fact that only the rootless resultant is shown as registration at the end of an unwholesome impulsion is because it is not shown elsewhere. Therefore, the rooted resultant mentioned in those places and everything mentioned here are indeed obtainable. Herein, this is the method: when an unwholesome impulsion occurs occasionally in the midst of wholesome impulsions, at the end of the wholesome impulsion, it is just like what has been practiced...
327:
...at the end of an unwholesome impulsion, a rooted registration (sahetuka-tadārammaṇa) is appropriate. When only unwholesome impulsions occur continuously, then a rootless registration (ahetuka-tadārammaṇa) is appropriate. Thus, the appropriate meaning in the first view should be accepted.

In the second view, however, the arrangement of prompted and unprompted is intended by way of the wholesome. Therefore, in this second view, taking only the unprompted resultant of the unprompted wholesome and only the prompted resultant of the prompted wholesome, without determining the registration by the impulsion, the twelve-fold path (dvādasakamagga) is taught by way of the collective impulsion (piṇḍajavana) that should arise for all trainees (sekha), non-trainees (asekha), and worldlings (puthujjana). In this second view, at the end of a triple-rooted impulsion, a triple-rooted registration is appropriate. Although it is not taught by analyzing that at the end of a double-rooted impulsion there is a double-rooted registration, and at the end of a rootless impulsion there is a rootless registration, thus the appropriate meaning in the second view should be accepted.

In the third view also, the arrangement of unprompted and prompted is intended only by way of the wholesome. According to the statement, "Triple-rooted kamma gives triple-rooted resultant, double-rooted resultant, and rootless resultant," for one with a triple-rooted unprompted rebirth-linking, an unprompted double-rooted registration should also occur. Without showing that which should occur, the registration that is just similar to the root of the productive kamma (janakakamma) is shown. Such showing does not agree with the previously mentioned view that states the productive root. It is stated only for the purpose of clarifying the ten-fold path. However, the other unprompted double-rooted registration is also obtainable. Thus, the appropriate meaning in the third view should also be accepted. All this discussion on registration (tadārammaṇakatha) is spoken with reference only to the resultant of the kamma that produces rebirth-linking. Because of the teaching, "The rooted life-continuum is a condition for the rootless life-continuum by way of proximity-condition (anantarapaccaya)," a rooted resultant registration also arises for one with a rootless rebirth-linking by way of various kammas. The arrangement of its occurrence will become clear in the Great Treatise (Mahāpakaraṇa).

## The Discussion on Sense-sphere Wholesome Resultant is finished.

## Discussion on Fine-material and Immaterial-sphere Resultant

Now, to show the Fine-material-sphere resultant and so on, it begins again with "Which are the states that are indeterminate?" and so forth. In that context, because the sense-sphere resultant is sometimes similar to its own wholesome and sometimes dissimilar, it is not analyzed by making it follow the wholesome. However, just as the shadows of elephants, horses, mountains, etc., are similar to the elephants and so on, the fine-material and immaterial-sphere resultants are only similar to their own wholesome. Therefore, they are analyzed by making them follow the wholesome. And sense-sphere kamma, when...
328:
Sense-sphere kamma gives results from time to time. However, fine-material and immaterial sphere kammas give results only in the second existence without any obstacle; thus, they are classified according to the sequence of the wholesome. The rest should be understood in the same way as stated in the section on the wholesome. This, however, is the distinction: the differences such as the mode of progress (paṭipadā) and the states of being inferior, superior, or medium are to be understood in these resultants by way of the attainment of jhāna (jhānāgamana). Since these are not produced by making any one of the factors such as desire (chanda) the predominant one, they are exclusively without predominant influence (niradhipatika).

## The Discussion on the Resultants of the Fine-material and Immaterial Spheres is finished.

## The Discussion on the Supramundane Resultant

The supramundane resultant is also classified according to the sequence of the wholesome because of its similarity to the wholesome. Since the wholesome of the three planes accumulates and increases the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) by way of death and rebirth, it is said therein, 'because of being done, because of being accumulated.' However, the supramundane state destroys that very round accumulated by that wholesome, and it does not itself accumulate the round by way of death and rebirth. Therefore, in this supramundane resultant, instead of saying 'because of being done, because of being accumulated,' it is said 'because of being done, because of being developed.'

Regarding terms such as 'void' (suññata), the Path first acquires its name through three reasons: by way of arrival (āgamana), by way of its own quality (saguṇa), and by way of its object (ārammaṇa); this has been explained in detail below in the section on the wholesome. Among those reasons, according to the Suttanta method, it acquires a name by way of its own quality and by way of its object. This is because that is a figurative teaching (pariyāya-desanā). The Abhidhamma discussion, however, is an abstract teaching (nippariyāya-desanā). Therefore, here in the Abhidhamma, it does not acquire a name by way of its own quality or its object, but only by way of arrival (āgamana). Arrival alone is the leader (dhura). That arrival is of two kinds: arrival through insight (vipassanāgamana) and arrival through the Path (maggāgamana). Between these two, in the context of the Path, arrival through insight is the leader; in the context of the Fruit, arrival through the Path is the leader; this has also been stated below.

Among those, this is the context of the Fruit; therefore, it should be understood that here arrival through the Path is the leader. That Path, having acquired the name 'void' (suññata) by way of arrival, is also called 'signless' (animitta) and 'undirected' (appaṇihita) by way of its own quality and its object. Therefore, standing in the position of arrival itself, it gives the three names to its own Fruit. How? This 'Void Path' (suññata-magga), which has acquired its name solely by way of pure arrival, standing in the position of arrival itself, giving the name to its own Fruit as 'void'...
329:
...assigned the name. The 'void-signless Path' (suññata-animitta-magga), standing in the position of arrival itself, when giving the name to its own Fruit, assigns the name 'signless' (animitta). The 'void-undirected Path' (suññata-appaṇihita-magga), standing in the position of arrival itself, when giving the name to its own Fruit, assigns the name 'undirected' (appaṇihita). These three names are obtained in this manner only in the Fruit consciousness that occurs immediately after the Path, not in the Fruit Attainment (phala-samāpatti) enjoyed at a later time. At a later time, however, one is able to contemplate with the three insights such as impermanence. When one is thus able, three Fruits known as signless, undirected, and void arise by way of the insight from which one has just emerged. For those Fruits, those very insights such as the contemplation of impermanence, which have formations as their object, are called 'conformity knowledge' (anuloma-ñāṇa).

The same method stated for the Void Path applies to the Undirected Path as well. This 'Undirected Path' (appaṇihita-magga), which has acquired its name by way of pure arrival, standing in the position of arrival itself, when giving the name to its own Fruit, assigns the name 'undirected'. The 'undirected-signless Path' (appaṇihita-animitta-magga), standing in the position of arrival itself, when giving the name to its own Fruit, assigns the name 'signless'. The 'undirected-void Path' (appaṇihita-suññata-magga), standing in the position of arrival itself, when giving the name to its own Fruit, assigns the name 'void'. These three names are also obtained in this manner only in the Fruit consciousness that occurs immediately after the Path, not in the Fruit Attainment enjoyed at a later time. Thus, in this Exposition of Resultants (Vipāka-niddesa), the resultant consciousnesses should be understood as being triple the wholesome consciousnesses.

Just as the wholesome of the three planes are unable to make their own resultant a predominant factor (adhipati), it is not that the supramundane wholesome are unable to do so (i.e., they are able). Why? Because for the wholesome of the three planes, the time of exertion (āyūhana-kāla) is one, and the time of ripening (vipaccana-kāla) is another. Because of this difference in time, those wholesome of the three planes are unable to make their own resultant a predominant factor. As for the supramundane wholesome, they obtain the resultant immediately after the Path without fail and without delay, while that faith, that energy, that mindfulness, that concentration, and that wisdom have not yet subsided. Because they give results immediately after the Path, they are able to make their own resultant a predominant factor.

For example, just as in the place where a small fire has passed, the state of heat is extinguished and becomes nothing as soon as the fire is extinguished, but a great, blazing mass of fire...
330:
Just as when a great fire is extinguished and the ground is smeared with cow dung, the state of heat remains unappeased, so too, in the wholesome actions of the three planes (tebhūmaka-kusala), the moment of performing the kamma is one, and the moment of the result (vipāka) is another. That mundane wholesome action is like the time when the heat is extinguished in a small fireplace. Therefore, that wholesome action is unable to cause its own result to be obtained as a predominant factor (adhipati). In the supramundane (lokuttara), however, before that faith... before that wisdom is appeased (before its power ceases), the fruit (phala) arises immediately after the path (magga). Therefore, it should be understood that such supramundane wholesome action is able to cause its own result to be obtained as a predominant factor. Thus, the ancient teachers said: "Excluding the supramundane result, there is no predominant factor (adhipati) in the remaining results."

In explaining the fourth fruit, the faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya) is the faculty of the Arahat whose task of knowledge regarding the Four Truths is completed. Alternatively, it is called a faculty because it accomplishes the state of governance within the associated states (sampayutta-dhamma) of those who have completed their tasks regarding the Four Truths, having known and penetrated the Four Truths. In the Niddesa section as well, "aññātāvīnaṃ" means of those who remain having known. "Dhammānaṃ" means within the associated states. "Aññā" means knowing; "paññā" and "pajānanā" etc., have the same meanings as previously stated. "Maggaṅgaṃ maggapariyāpannaṃ" means a factor of the path occurring in the fruit, and it is included in the path of the fruit.

Furthermore, there is this miscellaneous decision regarding this supramundane result: one faculty goes to one place, one goes to six places, and one goes to one place. Specifically, the faculty of "I shall know the unknown" (ananya-taññassāmītindriya) goes to one place, the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga). The faculty of higher knowledge (aññindriya) goes to six places: the three lower fruits and the three higher paths. The faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya) goes to one place, the fruit of Arahatship (arahatta-phala). Since there are eight faculties each in all paths and fruits in terms of meaning, sixty-four supramundane faculties are spoken of. However, according to the Pali text, by making them nine each, there are seventy-two. Just as it is called a path factor (maggaṅga) in the path, it is also called a path factor in the fruit. Just as it is called an enlightenment factor (bojjhaṅga) in the path, it is also called an enlightenment factor in the fruit. Just as it is called abstinence and refraining (arati virati) at the moment of the path, it is also called abstinence and refraining at the moment of the fruit. Therein, the path is called the path because of its very nature as a path; the fruit, however, is called the path by way of derivation from the path (due to its similarity to the path). It is also appropriate to call them fruit-factors (phalaṅga) and included in the fruit (phalapariyāpanna). In the path, it is a factor of one who is awakening, thus it is a factor of enlightenment (sambojjhaṅga); in the fruit, it is a factor of one who has awakened, thus it is a factor of enlightenment. In the path, it is abstinence and refraining by way of cutting off the object (ārammaṇa-viramaṇa). In the fruit, however, it occurs by way of abstinence and refraining.

## The Discussion on Supramundane Result is finished.
331:
## Description of Unwholesome Resultants

Following this supramundane resultant are the unwholesome resultant consciousnesses—the five sense-consciousnesses: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness; one mind element (manodhātu); and one mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu). These seven types of consciousness are similar to the wholesome resultant consciousnesses mentioned below, both in terms of the Pali text and their meaning.

Indeed, those wholesome resultant consciousnesses have wholesome kamma as their cause, while these unwholesome resultant consciousnesses have unwholesome kamma as their cause. Those wholesome resultants occur in pleasant (iṭṭha) and neutral-pleasant (iṭṭhamajjhatta) objects, while these unwholesome resultants occur in unpleasant (aniṭṭha) and neutral-unpleasant (aniṭṭhamajjhatta) objects. In those wholesome resultants, body-consciousness is accompanied by pleasure (sukhasahagata), but in these unwholesome resultants, it is accompanied by pain (dukkhasahagata). In those wholesome resultants, the mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity (upekkhāsahagata) ripens in five places, beginning with the rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) of those born blind, etc., among humans. In these unwholesome resultants, however, when kamma is accumulated by the eleven types of unwholesome consciousness, it ripens by taking one of the objects among kamma, kamma-nimitta, or gati-nimitta, and becomes rebirth-linking in the four woeful planes. From the second moment of consciousness onwards, it ripens in only five places: as the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) throughout the lifespan; as the investigating consciousness (santīraṇa) in the five-sense-door process having unpleasant and neutral-unpleasant objects; as the registering consciousness (tadārammaṇa) in the six doors when the object is powerful; and as the death consciousness (cuti) at the time of dying.

## The Description of Unwholesome Resultants is finished.

## Description of Functional Indeterminate

## Mind Element Consciousness

Now, in order to analyze and show the functional indeterminate (kiriyābyākata), the teaching begins with "Again, which states are indeterminate?" and so on. In that context, "kiriyā" (functional) means mere action. Indeed, among all functional consciousnesses, that which does not reach the state of impulsion (javana) is like a wind-flower (vātapuppha) which bears no fruit. That which has reached the state of impulsion is also fruitless, like the flower of a tree whose roots are severed. However, because it occurs by way of accomplishing various functions, it is mere action. Therefore, it is called "functional" (kiriyā). In the phrases "neither wholesome nor unwholesome" etc., it should be understood as "not wholesome" because of the absence of wholesome roots (kusala-hetu), and "not unwholesome" because of the absence of unwholesome roots. Wise attention (yoniso...)
332:
Because of the absence of wholesome and unwholesome causes, namely wise attention and unwise attention, they are called 'neither wholesome nor unwholesome.' Because of the absence of the productive cause (janaka-hetu) known as wholesome or unwholesome, they are also not kamma-resultants (vipāka).

In this functional mind-element as well, in the description of one-pointedness of mind, only 'occurrence and persistence' (pavatti-ṭṭhiti) is obtained. In these seventeen types of consciousness—namely, the ten types of fivefold sense-consciousness, the three mind-elements, the three mind-consciousness-elements, and the consciousness accompanied by doubt—because they are weak, terms such as 'stability' (saṇṭhiti) and 'steadfastness' (avaṭṭhiti) are not obtained. Everything else, except for the place of arising, should be understood in the same way as stated in the description of the resultant mind-element. That resultant mind-element arises immediately after the fivefold sense-consciousness. However, this functional mind-element arises before all other consciousnesses during the time of the thought process (vīthi) that experiences an object at the five doors. How? In the eye-door, when any visible object—whether extremely desirable, moderately desirable, undesirable, or extremely undesirable—strikes the eye-sensitivity, this consciousness arises, taking that object, acting as the precursor by way of advertence (āvajjana), and turning the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). The same method applies to the ear-door and so on.

## The Functional Mind-element is finished.

## Functional Mind-consciousness-elements

'Mind-consciousness-element has arisen... and so on... accompanied by joy'—this consciousness is not shared with others; it is unique to the Arahant. It is obtained at all six doors. For, at the eye-door, seeing a place suitable for right effort (sammappadhāna), an Arahant becomes joyful with this consciousness. At the ear-door, having reached a place where goods are distributed, and seeing many people making a great noise and seizing them with great greed, he becomes joyful with this consciousness, thinking: 'Such frivolous greed and craving have been abandoned by me.' At the nose-door, when worshipping a shrine with scents or flowers, he becomes joyful with this consciousness. At the tongue-door, having received delicious alms-food, and after sharing and consuming it, he becomes joyful with this consciousness, thinking: 'Indeed, the duties of hospitality (sāraṇīyadhamma) have been fulfilled by me.' At the body-door, when performing the duties of proper conduct (abhisamācārika-vatta), he becomes joyful with this consciousness, thinking: 'Indeed, the duty at the body-door has been fulfilled by me.' Thus, it is obtained at the five doors.
333:
At the mind-door, however, [the consciousness of the smile] arises based on past and future objects. Indeed, the Tathāgata manifested a smile after reflecting on causes performed in the past, such as in the times of the youth Jotipāla, King Maghadeva, and the ascetic Kaṇha. That reflection is the function of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). At the conclusion of the occurrence of those two knowledges, this consciousness of the smile (hasituppāda) arises, producing joy. Regarding the future, he manifested a smile after reflecting: 'Tantissara, who has a voice like a drum, will become a Paccekabuddha.' That also is the function of the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of omniscience. At the conclusion of the occurrence of those two knowledges, this consciousness arises, producing joy.

In the Niddesa-vāra, however, because this consciousness is stronger than the remaining rootless consciousnesses, one-pointedness of mind is established as the power of concentration (samādhi-bala), and energy as the power of energy (vīriya-bala). But in the Uddesa-vāra, because it is not stated as 'there is the power of concentration, there is the power of energy,' these two are not called 'powers' in the sense of a full power. This is because, being rootless, they lack firm stability, and thus the sense of 'power' is not complete. Furthermore, because it is 'neither wholesome nor unwholesome,' it is not established as a power. Since it is not a power in the primary sense, it is also not stated in the Saṅgaha-vāra that 'two powers arise.' Everything else should be understood in the same way as stated in the description of the rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy.

The consciousness accompanied by equanimity (mind-door advertence) is common to all sentient beings with minds in the three planes of existence; there is no one with a mind for whom it does not arise. When it arises, it becomes 'determining' (votthabbana) at the five doors and 'advertence' (āvajjana) at the mind-door. Even the six unique knowledges (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa) take only the object grasped by this consciousness. This consciousness is called the 'great elephant' consciousness because of its great scope; there is no such thing as 'no object' for this consciousness. If it is asked, 'Which is the non-omniscient knowledge that follows the course of omniscient knowledge?', it should be said, 'It is this consciousness.' The rest here should be understood in the same way as stated for the previous consciousness. Specifically, because that previous consciousness was accompanied by zest (pīti), the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) was analyzed as having nine factors. Here, because it is without zest, it has eight factors (aṭṭhaṅgika).
334:
Now, the eight great wholesome consciousnesses themselves become functional (kiriya) when they arise in an Arahant. Therefore, those functional consciousnesses should be understood in the same way as stated in the description of the wholesome (kusala-niddesa).

At this point, the consciousnesses that produce smiling should be summarized. If it is asked, 'How many are there?', it is said there are thirteen. For worldlings (puthujjana) smile with eight types of consciousness: four wholesome types accompanied by joy and four unwholesome types accompanied by joy. Learners (sekha) smile with six types of consciousness: four wholesome types accompanied by joy and two unwholesome types accompanied by joy that are dissociated from wrong view. Arahants smile with five functional types of consciousness accompanied by joy.

## Fine-material and Immaterial Sphere Functional Consciousness

In the descriptions of the fine-material and immaterial sphere functional consciousness, 'abiding in happiness in the present life' (diṭṭhadhamma-sukhavihāra) means simply abiding in happiness in this very life, in this very existence. Among those attainments, as long as an Arahant has not yet entered an attainment that was produced during his time as a worldling, it remains wholesome; but at the time of entering it, it becomes functional. However, an attainment produced during his time as an Arahant is functional only. Everything else should be understood in the same way as stated in the description of the wholesome, as they are similar.

## In the Commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī called the Atthasālinī,
## the Discussion on the Chapter on the Arising of Consciousness is finished.
## The section on the Indeterminate (abyākata), however, is not yet finished.
## The Explanation of the Chapter on the Arising of Consciousness is finished.
335:
## 2. Rūpakaṇḍa
## Uddesavaṇṇanā
Now, in order to show the analysis of the Rūpakaṇḍa (Section on Matter), it begins with "Which are the states that are indeterminate (avyākata)?" and so forth. Among those indeterminate states, although resultant indeterminates (vipāka-avyākata) and functional indeterminates (kiriya-avyākata) have been fully analyzed below in the Cituppādakaṇḍa, matter-indeterminates and Nibbāna-indeterminates have not yet been taught. Wishing to show the fourfold indeterminates together in order to teach those (matter and Nibbāna), the Blessed One said, "Those states which are resultants of wholesome and unwholesome states," and so forth. In that statement, "of wholesome and unwholesome" refers to the wholesome and unwholesome states belonging to the four planes.

Thus, first, the resultant indeterminates are shown by encompassing them in two terms: wholesome resultants and unwholesome resultants. Since those resultant indeterminates are either entirely of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara) or belong to one of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) and so on, he shows those same resultant indeterminates by way of the different planes, starting with "sense sphere." Since those resultant indeterminates are also the aggregate of feeling... etc... the aggregate of consciousness, he shows them again by way of the four associated mental aggregates.

Having thus shown the resultant indeterminates by three methods—by way of wholesome and unwholesome, by way of the different planes, and by way of the associated aggregates—he then, wishing to show the functional indeterminates, said, "Which states are functional," and so forth. There, it should be said, "sense sphere, fine-material sphere, immaterial sphere, aggregate of feeling... etc... aggregate of consciousness." However, since they have already been taken below, he merely indicates the method and leaves them out. Now, wishing to show the indeterminates that have not yet been analyzed, he said, "All matter and the unconditioned element." In that statement, by the term "all matter," twenty-five types of matter and ninety-six portions of matter are to be understood as included without remainder. By the term "unconditioned element," Nibbāna is included without remainder. With this, the term "indeterminate states" is concluded.

In that context, why is this question "What is all matter?" taken? Below, matter as indeterminate was taught in brief. Now, to show that matter-indeterminate in detail by way of ones, twos, threes, fours... etc... elevens, this question is taken. The meaning of that statement is: of those two terms mentioned as "All matter and the unconditioned element," "What is meant by 'all matter'?" Now, wishing to show that matter, he said, "The four..."
336:
He spoke the words, "The four great essentials (mahābhūta) and..." and so forth. In that statement, "four" is a numerical delimitation. By such delimitation, he prevents the idea of there being fewer or more of those great essentials. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of conjunction. By that word "ca," he conjoins "derivative matter" (upādā-rūpa), meaning that not only the four great essentials are matter, but there is other matter as well.

In this term "mahābhūta," the nature of being a great essential should be understood through reasons such as great manifestation and so forth. Indeed, these are called "great essentials" because of: great manifestation, similarity to a great being (such as a magician or an ogress), being maintained by great effort, great transformation, and being great entities. Among those reasons, "because of great manifestation" means that these great essentials manifest greatly in both the non-clung-to continuity (anupādinnaka-santāna, inanimate) and the clung-to continuity (upādinnaka-santāna, animate). Their great manifestation in the non-clung-to continuity should be understood thus: One world-system (cakkavāḷa) is 1,203,450 yojanas in length and breadth.

In circumference, it is altogether
3,610,350 yojanas.

This earth is said to be
240,000 yojanas in thickness.

The water supporting that earth
is 480,000 yojanas in thickness
and rests on air.

The air supporting that water
stands in space for 960,000 yojanas;
this is the stability of the world.

In this world-system thus established,
the king of mountains, Sineru, the best of mountains,
stands submerged in the great ocean for 84,000 yojanas
and rises above the water by that same amount.
337:
By half the measure of that Sineru, in order,
submerged and rising, divine,
and adorned with various jewels,

Yugandhara, Isadhara, Karavīka, Sudassana,
Nemindhara, Vinataka, and the broad Assakaṇṇa;
these seven great mountains stand around Sineru.
They are the abodes of the Great Kings,
frequented by devas and yakkhas.

The Himavā mountain is 500 yojanas high.
It is 3,000 yojanas in length and breadth.
It is adorned with 84,000 peaks.

The Rose-apple tree (Jambu) called Naga, by whose power the Rose-apple Island (Jambudīpa) is famous, has a trunk circumference of fifteen yojanas. The length of the main branches spreading out from the trunk is fifty yojanas each. It is one hundred yojanas wide in diameter and its height is also one hundred yojanas.

The dimensions of that Rose-apple tree are the same as the Citra-pāṭali tree of the Asuras, the Simbali tree of the Garuḷas, the Kadamba tree in Aparagoyāna, the Kappa tree in Uttarakuru, the Sirīsa tree in Pubbavideha, and the Pāricchattaka tree in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Therefore, the ancient teachers said:

"The Pāṭali, Simbali, Jambu, the Pāricchattaka of the devas,
the Kadamba, the Kappa tree, and the Sirīsa is the seventh."

The Cakkavāḷa stone mountain is submerged in the ocean for 82,000 yojanas. It rises upwards by that same amount. That Cakkavāḷa mountain stands surrounding the entire world-element like a wall.

In the clung-to continuity (animate) as well, great bodies manifest by way of the bodies of fish, turtles, devas, asuras, and so forth. For it was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, there are in the great ocean beings with bodies one hundred yojanas long," and so forth.
338:
Regarding the phrase 'Mahābhūtasāmaññato' (By similarity to great illusions/beings): Just as a magician shows water, which is not a gem, as a gem; or shows a clod of earth, which is not gold, as gold; and just as he himself, though neither an ogre (yakkha) nor a bird, displays the appearance of an ogre or a bird; in the same way, these great elements, though not blue themselves, display derived matter (upādā-rūpa) that is blue. Though not yellow, not red, and not white themselves, they display derived matter that is white. Because of this similarity to a magician, they are called 'Great Elements' (Mahābhūta).

Furthermore, just as when ogres and such great beings seize a creature, they are found neither inside nor outside that creature, yet they cannot exist without depending on it; in the same way, these material phenomena are found neither inside nor outside one another, yet they cannot exist without depending on one another. Because of this inconceivable nature, similar to ogres and such great beings, they are also called 'Great Elements'.
