Just as the great beings known as ogresses (yakkhinī) conceal their terrifying nature with pleasing colors, shapes, and movements to deceive beings; in the same way, these material phenomena in the bodies of women and men conceal their own characteristics, such as harshness and roughness, with pleasing skin-complexion, pleasing shapes of limbs great and small, and pleasing movements of hands, feet, fingers, eyebrows, and eyes, thereby deceiving the foolish. They do not allow their true nature to be seen. Because of this deceptive sense, similar to the great beings known as ogresses, they are also called 'Great Elements'.

Regarding 'Mahāparihārato' (By great maintenance): This is because they must be nurtured and protected by great requisites. These material phenomena are called 'Great Elements' because they are maintained by vast amounts of food, clothing, and so on, which must be provided day after day. Alternatively, they are 'Great Elements' because they are beings (bhūta) that require great maintenance.

Regarding 'Mahāvikārato' (By great alteration): This is because of the great alterations of the elements. These material phenomena, whether karmically acquired (upādinnaka) or not karmically acquired (anupādinnaka), undergo great alterations. Among them, the greatness of alteration in non-karmically acquired matter becomes evident at the time of the dissolution of the world-cycle (kappa-vuṭṭhāna). The alteration of karmically acquired matter becomes evident at the time of the disturbance of the elements (dhātu-kkho-bha). As it is said:

When the world is consumed by the element of fire (tejo-dhātu),
The flames rise from the earth and race up to the Brahma-world.

When the world is destroyed by the raging waters,
A hundred thousand crores of world-systems (cakkavāḷa) melt away.
339:
When the world is destroyed by the disturbance of the wind element (vāyo-dhātu), a hundred thousand crores of world-systems are scattered and destroyed.

Just as a body bitten by a 'wood-mouth' (kaṭṭhamukha) snake becomes stiff, so too, due to the disturbance of the earth element (pathavī-dhātu), that body becomes truly stiff as if bitten by a wood-mouth snake.

Just as a body bitten by a 'putrid-mouth' (pūtimukha) snake becomes putrid, so too, due to the disturbance of the water element (āpo-dhātu), that body becomes truly putrid as if bitten by a putrid-mouth snake.

Just as a body bitten by a 'fire-mouth' (aggimukha) snake becomes burning hot, so too, due to the disturbance of the fire element (tejo-dhātu), that body becomes truly burning hot as if bitten by a fire-mouth snake.

Just as a body bitten by a 'weapon-mouth' (satthamukha) snake becomes shredded, so too, due to the disturbance of the wind element (vāyo-dhātu), that body becomes truly shredded as if bitten by a weapon-mouth snake.

Because they are elements (bhūta) with such great alterations, they are called 'Great Elements' (Mahābhūta).

Regarding 'Mahantabhūtattā ca' (And because of being great entities): These elements are 'great' because they must be grasped with great effort, and they are 'elements' because they exist (vijjamāna). Thus, they are called 'Great Elements' because of their greatness and their existence. They are called 'Great Elements' for reasons such as their great manifestation.

In the phrase 'Catunnañca mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya rūpaṃ' (Matter derived from the four great elements), the genitive case (sixth case) carries the sense of the accusative (second case). It means matter that exists by depending on the four great elements without leaving them. The phrase 'This is called all matter' refers to these four great elements and the twenty-three types of derived matter (upādā-rūpa) mentioned in sequence, making a total of twenty-seven varieties of what is called 'all matter'.

## Ekavidharūpasaṅgaho (The Onefold Summary of Matter)

Now, in order to show that matter in detail, the Teacher sets forth the matrix (mātikā) by means of eleven summaries, starting with the 'onefold' (ekavidha), and states: "All matter is not a root (na hetu)," and so on.

In that context, the term 'all matter' (sabbaṃ rūpaṃ) should be joined with all subsequent terms as follows: "All matter is not a root," "All matter is rootless (ahetuka)," and so forth. These forty-three terms, starting with 'not a root', are briefly indicated. Among those forty-three terms, forty terms are taken from the matrix in sequence, and at the end, three terms are outside the matrix (mātikā-mutta). Thus, the definition of the Pali text in the first summary should be understood. The same method applies to the second summary and the others.
340:
## Twofold Summary of Matter
In this twofold summary of matter, there is this method: In the second summary (the twofold summary), there are first 104 dyads (dukas). Among those 104 dyads, the fourteen dyads mentioned at the beginning, such as "There is matter that is derived (upādā); there is matter that is not derived (no-upādā)," are called the Miscellaneous Dyads (pakiṇṇaka-duka) because they lack mutual connection. Following that, the twenty-five dyads, such as "There is matter that is the physical base (vatthu) of eye-contact," are called the Base Dyads (vatthu-duka) because they occur by way of investigating the base and the non-base. Following that, the twenty-five dyads, such as "There is matter that is the object (ārammaṇa) of eye-contact," are called the Object Dyads (ārammaṇa-duka) because they occur by way of investigating the object and the non-object. Following that, the ten dyads, such as "There is matter that is the eye-base (cakkhāyatana)," are called the Base Dyads (āyatana-duka) because they occur by way of investigating the base and the non-base. Following that, the ten dyads, such as "There is matter that is the eye-element (cakkhudhātu)," are called the Element Dyads (dhātu-duka) because they occur by way of investigating the element and the non-element. Following that, the eight dyads, such as "There is matter that is the eye-faculty (cakkhundriya)," are called the Faculty Dyads (indriya-duka) because they occur by way of investigating the faculty and the non-faculty. Following that, the twelve dyads, such as "There is matter that is bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti)," are called the Subtle Matter Dyads (sukhumatara-rūpa-duka) because they occur by way of investigating subtle matter and non-subtle matter. This is the definition of the Pali text in the second summary.

## Threefold Summary of Matter
In the third summary (the threefold summary), there are 103 triads (tikas). Among those triads, one internal dyad (ajjhattika-duka) from the fourteen miscellaneous dyads taught in the second summary is combined with the remaining thirteen dyads in this way: "Whatever matter is internal matter, that matter is derived matter. Whatever matter is external matter, there is matter that is derived and there is matter that is not derived." The thirteen triads established in this manner are called the Miscellaneous Triads (pakiṇṇaka-tika). Following that, that same internal dyad is combined with the remaining dyads, and the remaining triads are established in this way: "Whatever matter is external matter, that matter is not the base of eye-contact. Whatever matter is internal matter, there is matter that is the base of eye-contact and there is matter that is not the base of eye-contact." The names and numbers of those triads should be understood by way of those base dyads and so forth. This is the definition of the Pali text in the third summary.

## Fourfold and Other Summaries of Matter
In the fourth summary (the fourfold summary), there are twenty-two tetrads (catukkas). Among those tetrads, without considering the matrix (mātikā) taught in this text as the very last one, namely, "There is matter that is derived; there is matter that is not derived"...
341:
...it is established. However, the remaining tetrads are established by considering (the matrix).

How are they established? Taking each of the first three dyads among the miscellaneous dyads in this twofold summary, and combining them with five dyads each in this way: "Whatever matter is derived matter, there is matter that is clung-to (upādiṇṇa) and there is matter that is not clung-to (anupādiṇṇa)," fifteen tetrads based on the three dyads are established at the beginning.

Now, there is the tetrad containing the visible dyad (sanidassana-duka). That visible dyad does not enter into combination with the dyads that follow it, such as "Whatever matter is visible matter, there is matter that is with impact (sappaṭigha) and there is matter that is without impact (appaṭigha)," nor with the dyads that precede it, such as "There is derived matter and there is non-derived matter," because of the absence of meaning, the absence of order, and the absence of distinction. Indeed, what is called visible matter does not exist as matter without impact or as non-derived matter; therefore, it does not enter into combination due to the absence of meaning. In visible matter, there is indeed clung-to matter and non-clung-to matter, but such visible matter does not enter into combination due to the absence of order. The reason is that all dyads are combined only with subsequent dyads. This is the order here. With preceding dyads, there is an absence of order. If it is argued, "The absence of order is not a reason when there is meaning; therefore, it should be combined with terms such as 'clung-to' (upādiṇṇa)," it should be said that it is not combined because of the absence of distinction. The reason is that terms such as "clung-to" have already been combined with this visible dyad. In such a combination, even if one says, "Clung-to matter is visible matter" or "Visible matter is clung-to matter," there is no difference; thus, it does not enter into combination due to the absence of distinction. Therefore, without considering that fourth visible dyad, six tetrads are established by combining two dyads each that are suitable for combination with the three subsequent dyads such as "There is matter with impact," in this way: "Whatever matter is matter with impact, there is matter that is a faculty (indriya) and there is matter that is not a faculty. Whatever matter is matter without impact, there is matter that is a faculty and there is matter that is not a faculty."

Just as this fourth dyad does not enter into combination, so too the first (derived) dyad does not enter into combination with that fourth dyad. Why? Because non-derived matter (no-upādā-rūpa) is always invisible matter (anidassana-rūpa). When that first dyad is combined with the fourth dyad in this way: "Whatever matter is non-derived matter, there is matter that is visible and there is matter that is invisible," it does not enter into combination. Therefore, bypassing that fourth dyad, it is combined with the fifth dyad. In this way, it should be understood which dyad enters into combination with which dyad, and which does not. This is the definition of the Pali text in the fourth summary. From here on, the seven summaries, such as the fivefold summary (pañcavidha-sangaha), are distinct and unmixed. Thus, the definition of the Pali text in the entire matrix should be understood.
342:
## Commentary on the Exposition of the Singlefold Classification of Matter

Now, to explain the meaning of that Mātikā by analysis, the passage beginning with "All matter is not a cause" (sabbaṃ rūpaṃ na hetumeva) is undertaken. Why is there no question here such as "What is all that matter which is not a cause?" It is because there is no distinction (differentiation).

Indeed, just as in the dyads (dukas) and so on, there is a distinction such as "there is derived matter (upādā-rūpa) and there is non-derived matter (no-upādā-rūpa)," in this passage beginning with "All matter is not a cause," there is no such distinction as "cause and non-cause" or "with-cause (sahetuka) and without-cause (ahetuka)." Therefore, it is analyzed directly without posing a question. In that passage, "all" (sabba) means the whole, without remainder. "Matter" (rūpa) is the exposition of the general characteristic (sāmañña-lakkhaṇa) which shows the nature of being deformed or affected by opposing conditions such as cold and heat. "Not a cause indeed" (na hetumeva) is the exposition of the negation of cause along with emphasis (avadhāraṇa).

In that context, there are four types of causes: root-cause (hetu-hetu), condition-cause (paccaya-hetu), predominant-cause (uttama-hetu), and common-cause (sādhāraṇa-hetu). Among these, the causes mentioned as "three wholesome roots, three unwholesome roots, and three indeterminate roots" are called 'root-causes'. The cause mentioned as "Monks, the four great elements are the cause, the four great elements are the condition for the designation of the form aggregate (rūpakkhandha)" is called 'condition-cause'. The cause mentioned as "Wholesome and unwholesome [kamma] are predominant in their own result-producing stage; a desirable object is predominant in the stage of wholesome result; an undesirable object is predominant in the stage of unwholesome result" is called 'predominant-cause'.

How is this explained? When it is said, "He understands as it really is the result of the undertaking of kammas—past, future, and present—by way of cause and by way of root," and "This is the cause, this is the condition for formations (saṅkhāras), namely, ignorance (avijjā)," ignorance is called 'common-cause' because it is a common condition for formations and pervades the state of being a condition. Indeed, just as the essence of earth and the essence of water are conditions for both sweet and non-sweet tastes, so too ignorance is the common condition (sādhāraṇa-paccaya) for both wholesome formations and unwholesome formations. In this context, however, only the 'root-cause' (hetu-hetu) is intended. Thus, wishing to negate the status of being a cause for matter, as found in the Mātikā "States that are causes, states that are not causes," the Buddha said, "Not a cause indeed."

By this method, the exposition of negation and the exposition of non-negation in all terms should be understood. The word-meaning (vacanattha) of all terms has already been stated in the Commentary on the Mātikā.

In the term "with conditions indeed" (sappaccayam-eva), matter born of kamma has only kamma as its condition; matter born of nutriment and so on has only nutriment and so on as its condition. Thus, by way of the four conditions of matter already mentioned...
343:
...the meaning should be understood by way of [the four conditions]. The term "matter indeed" (rūpam-eva) negates the state of being immaterial (arūpī) mentioned in the Mātikā "Material states, immaterial states."

"Arisen [known] by six consciousnesses" (uppannaṃ chahi viññāṇehi) means that only present matter is to be known by the six consciousnesses, such as eye-consciousness. Specifically, the reference to being "arisen" (uppanna) is taken with respect to eye-consciousness and the others. Indeed, those consciousnesses—eye-consciousness and so on—do not know the past or the future. Mind-consciousness (manoviññāṇa), however, knows both the past and the future. That mind-consciousness is included here because it falls into the stream of these five consciousnesses (pañcavivññāṇasota) and thus proceeds as one that has fallen into the stream. Because of the sense of perishing after having arisen, it is "impermanent indeed" (aniccam-eva). Because it has the nature of being oppressed by decay, it is "overcome by decay indeed" (jarābhibhūtam-eva). Or, because decay is evident in the material body (rūpa-kāya), it is also said to be "overcome by decay indeed."

In the phrase "Thus is the summary of matter by the singlefold method" (evaṃ ekavidhena rūpasaṅgaho), the word 'vidhā' is seen in the senses of pride (māna), form (saṇṭhāna), and portion or group (koṭṭhāsa). In passages such as "The pride 'I am better' is a vidhā; the pride 'I am equal' is a vidhā," pride is called 'vidhā'. In passages such as "What kind (kathaṃvidhaṃ) of virtuous person do they speak of? What kind of wise person do they speak of?", form or manner is called 'vidhā'. The meaning of the term 'kathaṃvidha' is "of what form/manner". In passages such as "The object of knowledge by one portion (ekavidhena), the object of knowledge by two portions," a portion or group is called 'vidhā'. Here also, only 'portion' is intended.

The word 'summary' (saṅgaha) is also of four kinds by way of common nature (sajāti), common origin (sañjāti), common action (kiriya), and number (gaṇana). Among these, the summary that appears in such passages as "Let all those of the warrior caste (Khattiyas) come; let all Brahmins, all merchants, all laborers come," and "Friend Visākha, Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood—these states are grouped (saṅgahitā) in the Virtue Aggregate (sīlakkhandha)," is called 'summary by common nature' (sajāti-saṅgaha). For here, all states reach a single grouping by way of their nature, just as in the case where it is said, "Let those of the same birth come."

The summary that appears in such passages as "Let all Kosalans come; let all Magadhans, all Bhārukacchakans come," and "Friend Visākha, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration—these states are grouped in the Concentration Aggregate (samādhikkhandha)," is called 'summary by common origin' (sañjāti-saṅgaha). For here, all states reach a single grouping by way of their place of origin or residence, just as in the case where it is said, "Let those born and raised in the same place come."

The summary that appears in such passages as "Let all elephant-riders come; let all horse-riders, all charioteers come," and "Friend Visākha, Right View and Right Intention—these states are grouped in the Wisdom Aggregate (paññākkhandha)," is called 'summary by common action' (kiriya-saṅgaha).
344:
All these (such as the elephant-rider, etc., and the factors like right view, etc.) reach a single inclusion by performing their respective functions. "In what way is the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) counted as an aggregate? The eye-base is counted as the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha). If the eye-base is counted as the aggregate of matter, because of such counting, it should certainly be said that 'the eye-base is included within the aggregate of matter'" (Kathāvatthu 471). Such an inclusion is called 'gaṇanasaṅgaha' (inclusion by counting). In this context (of the term 'ekavidharūpasaṅgaha'), it is this gaṇanasaṅgaha that is intended. Here, the meaning is the counting of matter as a single portion. This method should be understood in all cases (such as duvidharūpasaṅgaha, etc.).

## Description of the Dyads (Dukaniddesavaṇṇanā)

## Discussion on the Classification of Derived Matter (Upādābhājanīyakathā)

Now, in the duvidhasaṅgaha and so forth, because of the existence of the distinction "there is matter that is derived (upādā) and there is matter that is not derived (no-upādā)," the Buddha spoke the words beginning with "katamaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ upādā" (what is that matter which is derived?), showing the classification of terms preceded by a question. Among those, it is called 'upādā' because it is derived or it clings. The meaning is that it arises by taking hold of and not letting go of the great essentials (mahābhūta), depending upon them. Now, wishing to show that derived matter by way of its divisions, he spoke the words beginning with "cakkhāyatanaṃ."

Having thus briefly pointed out the twenty-three kinds of derived matter, and wishing again to describe that same derived matter in detail, he spoke the words beginning with "katamaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ cakkhāyatanaṃ." In that context, the eye is of two kinds: the fleshly eye (maṃsacakkhu) and the wisdom eye (paññācakkhu). Among these, the wisdom eye is of five kinds: the Buddha-eye (buddhacakkhu), the all-seeing eye (samantacakkhu), the knowledge-eye (ñāṇacakkhu), the divine-eye (dibbacakkhu), and the Dhamma-eye (dhammacakkhu). Among these five, the eye mentioned in the passage, "Bhikkhus, when I was looking at the world with the Buddha-eye, I saw beings with little dust in their eyes... beings difficult to instruct" (Majjhima Nikāya 1.283), is called the Buddha-eye. The eye mentioned in the passage, "The all-seeing eye is said to be the knowledge of omniscience," is called the all-seeing eye. The eye mentioned in the passage, "The eye arose, the knowledge arose" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.1081), is called the knowledge-eye. The eye mentioned in the passage, "Bhikkhus, I saw with the divine-eye, which is purified" (Majjhima Nikāya 1.284), is called the divine-eye. The knowledge described as the three lower paths in the passage, "Right in that very seat, the dustless, stainless Dhamma-eye arose" (Majjhima Nikāya 2.395), is called the Dhamma-eye.

The fleshly eye is also of two kinds: the sensitive eye (pasādacakkhu) and the composite eye (sasambhāracakkhu). Among these two, that which is situated in the eye-socket, delimited below by the eye-socket bone, above by the brow bone, on both sides by the corners of the eye, inside by the brain, and outside by the eyelashes...
345:
The lump of flesh that is the eye is a mass of flesh delimited (by the eye-socket bone, brow bone, corners of the eye, brain, and eyelashes). Briefly, it has a collection of fourteen constituents (sambhāra): the four elements, color, smell, taste, nutritive essence, originating fluid (sambhava), shape, life (jīvita), gender (bhāva), body-sensitivity (kāyapasāda), and eye-sensitivity (cakkhupasāda).

In detail, the four elements and the six factors depending on them—color, smell, taste, nutritive essence, shape, and originating fluid—become forty because they are produced by the four origins (samuṭṭhāna). The four factors—life, gender, body-sensitivity, and eye-sensitivity—are produced solely by kamma. Thus, by way of these forty-four types of matter, there is a collection of forty-four constituents (sambhāra).

In the world, although people recognize the white, large, wide, and broad eye as 'the eye,' they do not recognize the actual eye-sensitivity (cakkhupasāda); they only recognize the physical base of the sensitivity as the eye. That lump of flesh is situated in the eye-socket and is connected to the brain by a sinew-thread. In that lump of flesh, there are white, black, and red colors. There are also the elements of earth, water, fire, and air. It is white due to the abundance of phlegm, black due to the abundance of bile, and red due to the abundance of blood. It is stiff due to the abundance of the earth element, it is as if trickling due to the abundance of the water element, it is hot due to the abundance of the fire element, and it moves due to the abundance of the air element. This is called the composite eye (sasambhāracakkhu).

Furthermore, the sensitivity (pasāda) that depends on and is connected to this composite eye, and which is derived from the four great essentials, is called the sensitive eye (pasādacakkhu). That eye-sensitivity is situated in the center of the black circle, which is surrounded by the white circle, in the region of the pupil where the reflection of the bodies of those standing in front appears. It pervades the seven layers of the eye, just as oil poured onto seven layers of cotton pervades those layers. It remains receiving the assistance of the four elements which perform the functions of supporting, binding, maturing, and moving, just as a young prince is tended by four nurses who perform the functions of carrying, bathing, dressing, and fanning. It is supported by temperature, consciousness, and nutriment; it is protected by life (jīvita); it is surrounded by color, smell, taste, and so forth. In size, it is only about the head of a louse, and it stands fulfilling the role of the base (vatthu) and door (dvāra) for eye-consciousness and so forth as appropriate.

Regarding this matter, the General of the Dhamma (Venerable Sāriputta) also said:
'That eye-sensitivity by which one sees forms,
It is small and subtle,
Comparable to the head of a louse.'

It is called 'cakkhāyatana' because it is both the eye (cakkhu) and a base (āyatana). In the phrase "that eye which is the sensitivity derived from the four great essentials," here too, the genitive case (sāmivacana) stands in the sense of the accusative case (upayoga). The four...
346:
The meaning is the sensitive matter (pasāda-rūpa) that arises depending on the four great elements. By this (Pali), only the sensitive eye (pasāda-cakkhu) is taken, and the remaining composite eye (sasambhāra-cakkhu) is excluded. In the Indriyagocara Sutta, it is stated: "The sensitive matter arising depending on one great element is included and supported by the remaining three great elements in the earth element, and by the water element, the fire element, and the air element." Also, in the Catuparivatta Sutta, it is stated: "The sensitive matter arising depending on two great elements is included and supported by the remaining two great elements in the earth element and the water element, and by the fire element and the air element." These statements are spoken in a figurative sense (pariyāya). This Suttanta discourse is indeed a figurative teaching (pariyāya-desanā). The sensitive matter that arises depending on the four great elements is simply the sensitive matter of each one or of two among those four; it is by this figurative method that the teaching appears in those Suttas. Abhidhamma, however, is called the non-figurative teaching (nippariyāya-desanā). Therefore, in this (Abhidhamma), it is stated: "the sensitive matter arising depending on the four great elements."

Because it is grasped by foolish people as "This body is my self (attā)," the body or the collection of the five aggregates is called "attabhāva" (individual existence). Because it is included in that individual existence or depends on it, it is called "attabhāva-pariyāpanna." Because it cannot be seen by eye-consciousness, it is called "anidassana" (invisible). Because impingement (striking) occurs here (with the visible object), it is called "sappaṭigha" (reactive).

The summary meaning of the terms beginning with "yena" (by which) is as follows: By which eye, as an instrument, this being saw in the past, or sees in the present, or will see in the future, this visible form of the described nature; if that being were to have an unimpaired eye, then he would see the visible form that has come into range; or he saw the past visible form with the past eye, sees the present visible form with the present eye, will see the future visible form with the future eye; if that visible form were to come into the range of the eye, he would see that visible form with the eye—this statement here is a hypothetical statement (parikappa-vacana). This state is called "cakkhu" (eye) in the sense of leading the act of seeing. It is called "cakkhāyatana" (eye-base) in the sense of being a place of origin and meeting. It is called "cakkhudhātu" (eye-element) in the sense of being empty of self and not a being. It is called "cakkhundriya" (eye-faculty) because it exercises lordship in the characteristic of seeing. It is called "loka" (world) in the sense of crumbling and disintegrating. It is called "dvāra" (door) in the sense of being an entrance. It is called "samudda" (ocean) in the sense of being insatiable. It is called "paṇḍara" (white/pure) in the sense of being pure. It is called "khetta" (field) in the sense of being the place where contact and so on arise. It is called "vatthu" (base) in the sense of being the support for those same states. It is called "netta" (guide) because it leads the individual existence while showing the even and the uneven. For that same reason...
347:
This state is also called "nayana" (leading) because it leads the individual existence while showing the even and the uneven. It is also called "the near shore" (orima-tīra) because it is included in the states of the three planes (sakkāya) that exist in the ultimate sense. This phenomenon is also like an "empty village" (suñña-gāma) because it is common to many and because it has no owner.

By this much, it should be understood that by combining the fourteen names beginning with "cakkhu" with the four terms beginning with "passi vā" (or saw), the four methods of determining the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) are taught. How? Herein, by which invisible and reactive eye one saw a visible and reactive form, or saw... (and so on) ...it is also called an empty village; this visible form is the eye-base—this is one method. In the same way, the remaining methods should also be understood.

Now, because a visible form impinges on the sensitive eye even when one does not wish to look, such as during a lightning flash, the second exposition (niddesa-vāra) is begun to show that manner. In that second exposition, "yamhi cakkhumhi" means "in which eye" as the location (adhikaraṇa). "Rūpaṃ" is a term in the nominative case. Among those terms, "paṭihanyi vā" expresses the past sense, "paṭihanyati vā" the present sense, "paṭihanyissati vā" the future sense, and "paṭihanye vā" the hypothetical (parikappa) sense. A past visible form is said to have impinged on a past eye. A present visible form is said to be impinging on a present eye. A future visible form is said to be about to impinge on a future eye. If that visible form were to come into the range of the eye, that visible form would impinge on the eye—this is the hypothesis (parikappa) here. In terms of reality, however, only the visible form that is actually impinging on the sensitive matter is called "paṭihanyati" (impinges). Here too, the four methods of determination should be understood just as in the previous method.

Now, because the eye impinges on the visible form for one who, wishing to look of his own accord, directs the eye towards the visible form, the third exposition (niddesa-vāra) is begun to show that manner. That exposition is clear in its meaning. Here, the eye is said to impinge on the visible form only while receiving the object. Here too, the four methods of determination should be understood just as in the previous method.

Following this, ten expositions (vāra) are shown: five by way of showing the arising of the states beginning with contact as the fifth (phassa-pañcamaka), and five by way of showing their arising in connection with the object. In those expositions, "cakkhuṃ nissāya" means depending on the eye, making it a condition. "Rūpaṃ ārabbha" means concerning the visible object, depending on it, or in reference to it. By this statement, regarding the states such as contact which have the sensitive eye as their base...
348:
By way of the prenascence condition (purejāta-paccaya), the state of visible-data object (rūpārammaṇa) being a condition for the states included in the eye-door impulsion cognitive process (cakkhudvāra-javana-vīthi) through the object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati) and object-decisive support (ārammaṇūpanissaya) conditions is shown. In the remaining five cycles (vāra), the state of being a condition is shown merely by the object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) in the sense that 'this state has visible data as its object' (rūpārammaṇa). Just as in the first three cycles, in these ten cycles also, the four methods of determination (vavatthāpana-naya) should be understood. Thus, in order to show the eye (cakkhu) extracted in the question 'What is that rūpa-cakkhāyatana?' as 'This is that eye' in various ways, the thirteen sections of exposition (niddesavāra)—the former three and these ten—are shown. It should be understood that since four methods of determination appear in each of these thirteen cycles, they are shown as being adorned with fifty-two methods.

The same method applies to the expositions of the ear-base (sotāyatana) and so on that follow. However, the following distinction should be understood: It is called the ear (sota) because it hears. That ear is situated inside the physical ear-hole (sasambhāra-sota) in a place shaped like a finger-ring, covered with fine red hairs; it is assisted by the aforementioned types of elements (dhātu), supported by temperature (utu), mind (citta), and nutriment (āhāra), protected by the life-faculty (āyu/jīvitindriya), and surrounded by color and so on; it exists fulfilling the state of being the base (vatthu) and door (dvāra) as appropriate for ear-consciousness and so on.

It is called the nose (ghāna) because it smells. That nose is situated inside the physical nose-hole in a place shaped like a goat's hoof; having the aforementioned assistance, support, protection, and surroundings, it exists fulfilling the state of being the base and door as appropriate for nose-consciousness and so on.

It is called the tongue (jivhā) in the sense of licking flavors. That tongue is situated above the middle of the physical tongue in a place shaped like the tip of a lotus petal; having the aforementioned assistance, support, protection, and surroundings, it exists fulfilling the state of being the base and door as appropriate for tongue-consciousness and so on.

As far as there is clung-to matter (upādinnaka-rūpa) in this body, the body-base (kāyāyatana) exists everywhere, like oil in a layer of cotton; having the aforementioned assistance, support, protection, and surroundings, it exists fulfilling the state of being the base and door as appropriate for body-consciousness and so on. This is the distinction here. The remaining variations in the Pali text and the meaning should be understood in the same way as stated in the exposition of the eye (cakkhu-niddesa). Specifically, in place of the word 'eye' (cakkhu), the word 'ear' (sota) and so on appear; in place of the word 'visible data' (rūpa), the word 'sound' (sadda) and so on appear; and in place of words like 'sees', words like 'hears' and so on appear.
349:
Due to the absence of these two words, 'netta' and 'nayana', there are twelve names each (for the ear, etc.). The rest of the text is exactly the same as what was stated in all places (in the exposition of the eye).

In that regard, there might be a question: 'If the body-base (kāyāyatana) exists everywhere where there is clung-to matter (upādinnaka-rūpa/kammaja-rūpa) in this body, like oil in cotton, then would there not be a confusion of characteristics (lakkhaṇa-sammissatā)?' The answer is: 'No, there would not.' 'Why?' 'Because one type of matter does not exist in another group (kalāpa).' 'If so, do you mean that the body-base does not exist everywhere?' If asked thus, the answer is: 'In the ultimate sense (paramattha), it indeed does not exist everywhere. However, because it is not possible to show the distinction by separating them individually, it is stated thus. For example, although visible data (rūpa), flavor (rasa), and so on are said to be pervasive with one another because they cannot be separated like grains of sand, in the ultimate sense, flavor does not exist in visible data. If it did, then by grasping visible data, flavor would also be grasped. In the same way, the body-base in the ultimate sense does not exist everywhere, yet it is not the case that it does not exist everywhere, because of the inability to separate it. Thus, it should be understood that there is no confusion of characteristics in this matter.'

Furthermore, the non-confusion of these (eye, etc.) should be understood by the determination of their characteristics and so on. Among them, the eye (cakkhu) has the characteristic of sensitivity of the great elements (mahābhūta) susceptible to the impact of visible data; or it has the characteristic of sensitivity of the great elements originated by kamma based on the desire to see. It has the function (rasa) of drawing in visible data. It has the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) of being the support for eye-consciousness. It has the great elements originated by kamma based on the desire to see as its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna).

The ear (sota) has the characteristic of sensitivity of the great elements susceptible to the impact of sound; or it has the characteristic of sensitivity of the great elements originated by kamma based on the desire to hear. It has the function of drawing in sounds. It has the manifestation of being the support for ear-consciousness. It has the great elements originated by kamma based on the desire to hear as its proximate cause.

The nose (ghāna) has the characteristic of sensitivity of the great elements susceptible to the impact of odors; or it has the characteristic of sensitivity of the great elements originated by kamma based on the desire to smell. It has the function of drawing in odors. It has the manifestation of being the support for nose-consciousness. It has the great elements originated by kamma based on the desire to smell as its proximate cause.

The tongue (jivhā) has the characteristic of sensitivity of the great elements susceptible to the impact of flavors; or it has the characteristic of sensitivity of the great elements originated by kamma based on the desire to taste. It has the function of drawing in flavors. It has the manifestation of being the support for tongue-consciousness. It has the great elements originated by kamma based on the desire to taste as its proximate cause.
350:
Kāya (body-sensitivity) has the characteristic of clarifying the great elements (mahābhūta) that are susceptible to being struck by tangible objects (phoṭṭhabba). Or, it has the characteristic of clarifying the great elements produced by kamma, which has the desire to touch as its root cause. Its function is to draw [consciousness] towards tangible objects. It manifests as the state of being the support for body-consciousness. Its proximate cause is the great elements born of kamma, which has the desire to touch as its root cause.

Some teachers, however, say: "The sensitivity of the great elements where the fire element (tejo) is predominant is called the eye (cakkhu); the sensitivities of the great elements where the air (vāyo), earth (pathavī), and water (āpo) elements are respectively predominant are the ear (sota), nose (ghāna), and tongue (jivhā); the body (kāya) is the sensitivity of all great elements." Other teachers say: "The sensitivity of the great elements where fire is predominant is the eye; the sensitivities of the great elements where space (ākāsa), air, water, and earth are respectively predominant are the ear, nose, tongue, and body." These teachers should be told: "Bring forth a Sutta as evidence." They will certainly not find such a Sutta.

Some teachers here state the reason: "Because they are supported by visible forms (rūpa), etc., which are the qualities of fire, etc." These teachers should also be asked: "Who says that visible forms, etc., are the qualities of fire, etc.?" In the case of material phenomena that are inseparable, it is impossible to say, "This rupa is the quality of this element, and that rupa is the quality of that element."

If those teachers should say: "Just as you accept the functions of earth, etc., such as supporting, due to the predominance of those respective elements in various material groups, so too should it be accepted that visible forms, etc., are the qualities of those elements because the predominance of visible forms, etc., is seen in groups where fire, etc., are predominant." To those teachers, it should be said: "We would accept this if the smell in cotton, where the earth element is predominant, were stronger than the smell in liquor, where the water element is predominant; or if the color of cold water were inferior to the color of hot water, where the fire element is predominant."

However, since neither of these is the case, abandon this speculation about the distinction of these elements which are the support. Just as in a single kalāpa (material group) where there is no distinction [of elements], the color, taste, etc., of the elements are different from one another, so too should it be understood that eye-sensitivity, etc., are different from one another even though there is no other distinguishing cause.

What then is that cause which is unique to each? Kamma alone is the cause of their distinction. Therefore, their distinction is due to the distinction of kamma, not due to the distinction of the elements. For if there were a distinction of elements, sensitivity (pasāda) would not even arise. The ancients said: "Sensitivity belongs to equal elements, not to unequal ones." Among these [senses] which are distinct due to the distinction of kamma, the eye and the ear take objects that have not reached them (asampatta-visaya), because they are the cause of consciousness in objects that are not attached to their own support.
351:
The nose, tongue, and body take objects that have reached them (sampatta-visaya). Why? Because they are the cause for the arising of consciousness in objects that are attached to the great elements which are their own support, or through the power of the great elements that are the support of smell and taste.

In the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), however, it is said: "An object is called 'reached' simply because it has come into the range (āpātha)." The color of the moon and sun disks, which are situated forty-two thousand yojanas above, strikes the eye-sensitivity. Although that color appears while standing at a distance, it is still called 'reached.' Because it takes such an object, the eye is said to have a 'reached' object. The bodily movements of those cutting trees or laundrymen washing clothes at a distance are visible even from afar. Sound also comes through a succession of elements, strikes the ear, and gradually reaches the point of being determined.

In that Commentary, although it is said that an object is 'reached' because it has come into the range, the color of the moon disk, etc., does not reach the eye but appears while remaining at a distance. If sound also came gradually, a sound produced far away would be heard only after a long time. And because it comes by successive striking, if it strikes the ear, one would not be able to know that it is a sound from such-and-forth a direction. Therefore, those eye and ear [senses] have only 'not-reached' objects.

These faculties are like snakes, etc. Just as a snake does not delight in a clean place sprinkled with cow-dung water and swept, but delights and attains one-pointedness of mind only when it enters and lies in a rubbish heap, a grass thicket, a pile of leaves, or an anthill; even so, the eye, having an uneven disposition, does not delight in smooth golden walls and such, and does not even wish to look at them, but delights only in pictures variegated with floral designs and the like. In such places, not being satisfied with looking with the eyes, people even wish to look with their mouths open.

A crocodile also, when it comes out, does not see what is to be caught and moves about with its eyes closed. Only when it dives into water about a hundred fathoms (lan) deep and lies in a hole does its mind become one-pointed and it sleeps peacefully. Similarly, the ear, desiring a hole or cavity, depends on space (ākāsa) and has its disposition only within the ear-hole. The space of the ear-hole alone is the condition for hearing sound. Open space is also suitable. When chanting is done inside a cave, the sound does not break through the roof of the cave to go outside, but goes out through the doors and windows, striking through a succession of elements, and reaches the ear-sensitivity.
352:
At that time, those staying at the back of the cave know, "A monk of such a name is reciting."

In this case, [the ear] has a reached object (sampaṭṭagocara). If it is asked, "Does this ear have a reached object?" the answer should be, "Yes, it has a reached object." If an objection is raised, "If that is so, when drums and such are beaten in the distance, the knowledge 'a sound in the distance' would not occur," [the answer is], "It is not that it does not occur; it certainly does. For when the sound strikes the ear-sensitivity (sotapasāda), the mode of knowing occurs as 'a sound in the distance,' 'a sound nearby,' 'a sound on that bank,' or 'a sound on this bank.' This is just the nature of things (dhammatā)." (It is said), "What is the use of this nature? Wherever there is an opening, hearing occurs from that place. Just as seeing the moon, sun, etc., this ear has only a non-reached object (asampaṭṭagocara)."

A bird also does not delight in a tree or on the ground. Only when it flies into the open sky, passing the distance of one or two stone-throws, does it attain a concentrated mind. In the same way, the nose (ghāna) also desires the sky; it has the smell depending on the wind as its object. Indeed, at the beginning of the rainy season, cows sniff the ground repeatedly and then face the sky to inhale the wind. Furthermore, even when holding a mass of perfume with the fingers to smell it, if one does not inhale the wind, one cannot know the scent of that perfume.

A domestic dog also, while wandering outside, finds no safety and is oppressed by stone-throwing and such. Only when it enters the village, scratches the ashes in the fireplace, and lies down does it find comfort. In the same way, the tongue (jivhā) also desires the village; it has the taste depending on the water-element (āpo-dhātu), which is saliva, as its object. Indeed, even after developing monk's practice throughout the three watches of the night, one must enter the village in the early morning taking the bowl and robes. Furthermore, without moistening dry food with saliva, one cannot know its taste.

A jackal also, while wandering outside, finds no delight. Only when it eats human flesh in a cemetery and lies down does it find comfort. In the same way, the body (kāya) also desires clung-to matter (upādinnaka-rūpa); it has the tangible (phoṭṭhabba) depending on the earth-element (pathavī-dhātu) as its object. Indeed, beings who do not find other clung-to matter lie down placing their head on their own palm. The internal and external earth-element of this body is the cause for grasping the object. Indeed, whether on a well-spread bed or with fruits placed in the hand, without sitting or pressing, one cannot know the state of hardness or softness.
353:
The internal and external earth-element is the cause (condition) for this body-sensitivity (kāyaprasāda) to know the tangible object (phoṭṭhabbārammaṇa). By defining the characteristics and so forth in this way, the unmixed state of these [eye-sensitivity, etc.] should also be understood. Indeed, the characteristic (lakkhaṇa), function (rasa), manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna), proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna), field (gocara), inclination (ajjhāsaya), and support (nissaya) of eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) are distinct; those of ear-sensitivity (sota-pasāda) and so forth are also distinct. Therefore, the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) and so forth are certainly unmixed.

Furthermore, this analogy should also be understood regarding their unmixed state: Just as when banners of five colors are hoisted, the shadows appear as if they are continuous, yet the shadow of each banner is certainly not mixed with the others; and just as when a wick is made of five-colored cotton and a lamp is lit, the flame appears as if it is continuous, yet the individual flame of each cotton fiber is certainly not mixed with the others; in the same way, although these five bases (āyatana) are collected in a single individual existence (attabhāva), they are certainly not mixed with one another. Not only are these five bases unmixed, but the remaining types of matter (rūpa) are also certainly unmixed.

In this body, there are three parts: the lower body, the middle body, and the upper body. Among these three, from the navel downwards is called the lower body (heṭṭhimakāya). In that lower body, there are 44 types of matter: the body-decad (kāya-dasaka), the sex-decad (bhāva-dasaka), 8 octads produced by nutriment (āhāra-samuṭṭhāna), 8 octads produced by temperature (utu-samuṭṭhāna), and 8 octads produced by mind (citta-samuṭṭhāna). From above the navel up to the throat (gullet) is called the middle body (majjhimakāya). In that middle body also, there are 54 types of matter: the body-decad, the sex-decad, the heart-decad (vatthu-dasaka), and 3 octads such as those produced by nutriment. Above the throat is called the upper body (uparimakāya). In that upper body, there are 84 types of matter: the eye-decad (cakkhu-dasaka), the ear-decad (sota-dasaka), the nose-decad (ghāna-dasaka), the tongue-decad (jivhā-dasaka), the body-decad, the sex-decad, and 3 octads such as those produced by nutriment.

Among those types of matter, the eye-decad (cakkhu-dasaka) is so called by virtue of the ten types of produced matter (nipphanna-rūpa) that are strictly inseparable: the four great essentials (mahābhūta) which are the causes of eye-sensitivity, color (vaṇṇa), smell (gandha), taste (rasa), nutritive essence (ojā), life-faculty (jīvitindriya), and eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda). In this way, the remaining [decads] should also be understood. Among those types of matter, the matter in the lower body is unmixed with the matter in the middle and upper bodies. The matter in the remaining two parts of the body is also certainly unmixed with the others. Just as in the evening, the shadow of a mountain and the shadow of a tree appear as if they are continuous, yet they are not mixed with each other; in the same way, although the 44, 54, and 84 types of matter in these parts of the body appear as if they are continuous, they are certainly not mixed with one another.
354:
## Explanation of the Base of Visible Forms (Rūpāyatana-niddesa-vaṇṇanā)

In the description of the base of visible forms (rūpāyatana-niddesa), color itself is called 'vaṇṇanibhā'. Alternatively, it is called 'nibhā' because it shines. The meaning is that it is evident to eye-consciousness. It is called 'vaṇṇanibhā' because color itself is radiant. It is called 'sanidassana' (visible) because it exists along with the state of being seen. The meaning is that it is to be seen by eye-consciousness. It is called 'sappaṭigha' (with impingement) because it exists along with impingement. The meaning is that it produces the impact of impingement.

Among the colors such as blue (nīla), the color similar to the ummā flower is blue (nīla). The color similar to the kaṇikāra flower is yellow (pītaka). The color similar to the bandhujīvaka flower is red (lohitaka). The color similar to the morning star (osadhitārakā) is white (odāta). The color similar to charcoal is black (kāḷaka). The color similar to the slightly red sinduvāra or karavīra buds is madder-colored (mañjiṭṭhaka).

In the Jātaka verse, "O General Sumukha, who has a complexion like the color of gold, if you wish, you may go," although 'hari' refers to gold, in this context of the description of the base of visible forms, 'hari' refers to a dark green or tawny color because 'jātarūpa' (gold) is mentioned in a subsequent term. These seven colors are shown by their own nature without reference to an object.

'Harivaṇṇa' means having the color of green grass. 'Ambaṅkuravaṇṇa' means having a color similar to a mango sprout. These two are shown by reference to objects. The twelve terms such as long (dīgha) and so on are shown by way of conventional usage (vohāra). Such conventional usage is of two kinds: that established by comparison (upanidhāyasiddha) and that established by configuration (sannivesasiddha). Long, short, and so on are established by mutual comparison. Round, circular, and so on are established by a particular configuration.

In that regard, that which is higher or longer in comparison to the low or short (rassa) is called 'long' (dīgha). That which is lower or shorter in comparison to that long one is called 'short' (rassa). That which is smaller in comparison to the thick or large (thūla) is called 'minute' (aṇu). That which is larger in comparison to that minute one is called 'large' (thūla). A wheel-like shape is 'round' (vaṭṭa). An egg-like shape is 'circular' (parimaṇḍala). That which is possessed of four sides is 'square' (caturamsa). The same method applies to six-sided shapes and so on. 'Ninna' means low-lying, and 'thala' means elevated.

In that regard, although long and so on can be known by touch, blue and so on cannot be known in that way; therefore, 'long' is not a visible form (rūpāyatana) in the literal sense. The same applies to 'short' and so on. However, it should be understood that in this description of the base of visible forms, the collection of colors that stands in such and such a shape, depending on the collection of the four great elements (mahābhūta) that have such and such a shape as long or short, is spoken of by the conventional terms 'long' and 'short'.

Shadow and sunlight are mutually delimited. Likewise, light and darkness are also mutually delimited. The four such as clouds (abbha) and mist (mahikā) are shown only by way of objects. Therein, 'abbha' is a cloud. 'Mahikā' is frost or mist. By these four terms, the colors of clouds and so on are shown. By the radiance of the moon's disk and so on, the light-colors of those respective objects are shown.

Therein, the distinction of the objects such as the moon's disk should be understood as follows: The mansion of the moon deity, which is made of jewels, covered with silver, and is forty-nine leagues in length and breadth...
355:
...is called the moon's disk (candamaṇḍala). (It is made of jewels inside and covered with silver outside, being 49 leagues in length and breadth.) The mansion of the sun deity, which is made of gold, covered with crystal, and is fifty leagues in length and breadth, is called the sun's disk (suriyamaṇḍala). The mansions of various deities, which are made of the seven kinds of jewels and are seven, eight, ten, or twelve leagues in length and breadth respectively, are called the stars (tārakā).

Among those (moon and sun), the moon is below and the sun is above; the interval between the two is one league. From the lower edge of the moon to the upper edge of the sun, it is one hundred leagues. On both sides, the constellations and stars travel. Among these three, the moon has a slow movement, the sun has a fast movement, and the constellations and stars have the fastest movement of all. Sometimes they are in front of the moon and sun, and sometimes they are behind.

'Ādāsamṇḍala' (mirror-disk) means a mirror made of bronze. 'Maṇi' (gem) refers to various kinds of rubies such as the jotirasa, excluding the beryl (veḷuriya). 'Saṅkha' (conch) refers to the sea-conch. 'Muttā' (pearl) refers to sea-pearls and other pearls. 'Veḷuriya' (beryl) refers to a gem the color of bamboo. 'Jātarūpa' (gold) refers to gold that has a color like that of the Teacher (the Buddha). The Teacher is of golden hue, and gold is like the hue of the Teacher. 'Rajata' (silver) refers to currency (kahāpaṇa)—all those that are used in trade such as copper tokens (lohamāsaka), wooden tokens (dārumāsaka), and lac tokens (jatumāsaka) are to be included here.

By the phrase "or whatever other [color]" (yaṃ vā panaññampi), visible forms that are not directly mentioned in the Pali text, such as the colors of mats, old clothes, mushrooms, and so on, are included. All of these are included in the 'yevāpanaka' states.

Thus, although visible form (rūpa) is divided by way of blue and so on, all visible forms are undivided by way of characteristics and so on. For all this visible form has the characteristic of impinging on the eye (cakkhupaṭihanana-lakkhaṇa), the function (rasa) of being the objective field of eye-consciousness, the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) as the resort of that same eye-consciousness, and the four great elements as its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna). Just as this is so, all derived matter (upādārūpa) also [has the four great elements as proximate cause]. Where there is a distinction, I shall mention it there. The rest should be understood in the same manner as stated in the description of the eye-base (cakkhāyatana-niddesa).

The only difference is that in the eye-base description, the eye was mentioned first, whereas here, visible form is mentioned first. There, fourteen names such as 'cakkhuṃ p'etaṃ' were given, while here, only three names such as 'rūpaṃ p'etaṃ' are given. The rest is exactly the same. Just as thirteen cycles (vāra) were stated to define the eye by adorning it with four methods each, here too they are stated in the same way.

In the description of the sound-base (saddāyatana-niddesa), 'bherisadda' (sound of a drum) refers to the sound of a large drum or a struck drum. The sounds of the mudiṅga, conch, and paṇava are also sounds produced depending on the mudiṅga and so on. The sound known as song (gīta) is...
356:
The sound of singing is called gītasadda. The sound of other musical instruments such as the lute (vīṇā), which are bound with strings, is called vāditasadda. Sammasadda refers to the sounds of gongs, bronze gongs, cymbals, and the sound of wooden clappers. Pāṇisadda is the sound of hand-clapping. Sattānaṃ nigghosasadda is the shouting sound of many people gathered together where individual words and syllables are not distinct. Dhātūnaṃ sannighātasadda refers to sounds such as trees rubbing against each other, the tinkling of small bells, the striking of stone gongs, and so on. The sound of the blowing wind is called vātasadda. The sound of flowing or splashing water is called udakasadda. The sound of human conversation and so forth is called manussasadda. Excluding human sound, all other sounds are called amanussasadda. With these two terms, all sounds are encompassed. Even so, sounds not directly mentioned in the Pāḷi text, such as the sound of splitting bamboo or tearing cloth, should be understood as included in the yevāpanaka section.

Thus, although sound is divided into various types such as the sound of a drum, it is undifferentiated in terms of its characteristics and so forth. All sound has the characteristic of impinging on the ear-sensitivity (sotapasāda), the function of being the objective field of ear-consciousness (sotaviññāṇa), and it manifests as the resort of that same ear-consciousness. The rest should be understood in the same way as stated in the Exposition on the Eye-base (Cakkhāyatananiddesa). Here too, thirteen sections (vāra) adorned with four methods each are mentioned. Since their meaning can be understood by the method already stated, they are not elaborated further.

In the Exposition on the Smell-base (Gandhāyatananiddesa), mūlagandha is the smell that arises depending on some kind of root. The same method applies to heartwood-smell (sāragandha) and so on. The smell of raw or poorly cooked vegetables and so forth is called āmakagandha (raw smell). The smell of fish scales, putrid meat, rancid ghee, and so forth is called vissagandha (fishy smell). Sugandha is an agreeable smell. Duggandha is a disagreeable smell. With these two terms, all smells are encompassed. Even so, all smells not directly mentioned in the Pāḷi text, such as the smell of mold or the smell of cloth, should be understood as included in the yevāpanaka section.

Thus, although smell is divided into various types such as root-smell, it is undifferentiated in terms of its characteristics and so forth. All smell has the characteristic of impinging on the nose-sensitivity (ghānapasāda), the function of being the objective field of nose-consciousness (ghānaviññāṇa), and it manifests as the resort of that same nose-consciousness. The rest should be understood in the same way as stated in the Exposition on the Eye-base. Here too, thirteen sections adorned with fifty-two methods are mentioned. They are clear in meaning.
357:
In the Exposition on the Taste-base (Rasāyatananiddesa), mūlarasa is the taste that arises depending on some kind of root. The same method should be understood for the taste of stems (khandharasa) and so on. Ambila refers to sour buttermilk and so forth. Madhura refers strictly to cow's milk, ghee, and so forth. Honey, however, is associated with an astringent taste; if kept for a long time, it tends to become astringent. Molasses is associated with a salty taste; if kept for a long time, it tends to become salty. As for ghee, even if its color and smell fade after being kept for a long time, its taste does not fade; therefore, that ghee alone is strictly of sweet taste. Tittaka refers to neem leaves and so forth. Kaṭuka refers to ginger, black pepper, and so forth. Loṇika refers to sea salt and so forth. Khārika refers to eggplant, bamboo shoots, and so forth. Lambila refers to jujube, emblic myrobalan, wood-apple juice, and so forth. Kasāva refers to yellow myrobalan and so forth. All these tastes are taught by way of their physical bases (vatthu). However, it should be understood that in this exposition, the taste itself arising from those various bases is taught by names such as ambila (sourness) and so forth. Sādu is an agreeable taste, and asādu is a disagreeable taste. With these two terms, all tastes are encompassed. Although all are included by these two terms, tastes not directly mentioned in the Pāḷi text, such as the taste of a clod of earth, the taste of a wall, the taste of old cloth, and so forth, should also be understood as included in the yevāpanaka section.

Thus, although taste is divided into types such as root-taste, it is undifferentiated in terms of its characteristics and so forth. All taste has the characteristic of impinging on the tongue-sensitivity (jivhāpasāda), the function of being the objective field of tongue-consciousness (jivhāviññāṇa), and it manifests as the resort of that same tongue-consciousness. The rest should be understood in the same way as stated in the Exposition on the Eye-base. Here too, thirteen sections adorned with fifty-two methods are mentioned.

In the Exposition on the Female Faculty (Itthindriyaniddesa), the word 'yaṃ' is a term expressing the cause (karaṇa). The meaning here is: the cause by which the female appearance (itthiliṅga) and so forth occur in a woman. Among those, 'liṅga' refers to the shape. The shape of a woman's hands, feet, neck, chest, and so forth is not like that of a man. The lower body of women is distinct (broad), while the upper body is indistinct (narrow). The hands and feet are small; the face is also small. 'Nimitta' refers to the sign for recognition. The breasts of women are distinct; there is no beard or mustache on the face. The way of tying the hair and wearing clothes is also not like that of men. 'Kutta' refers to behavior. When women are young, they play with small winnowing baskets and pestles, they play with ornate dolls, and they play at spinning thread with clay pots and vessels. 'Ākappo' refers to the manner of walking and so forth. When women walk, they walk in an indistinct manner; when standing, lying down, sitting, eating, or drinking, they also act in an indistinct manner. Even if it is a man, if he is seen to be indistinct (having feminine manners)...
358:
People say: "She walks like a woman, stands, lies down, sits, chews, and eats like a woman."

'Itthattā' means 'itthibhāva' (the state of being a woman); both have the same meaning, referring to the nature of a woman. This female state is born of kamma and arises at rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). However, the female marks (itthilinga) and so forth arise during the course of existence (pavatti) based on the female faculty (itthindriya). For example, just as when there is a seed, based on the seed and because of the seed, a tree grows, becomes endowed with branches and foliage, fills the sky, and stands; similarly, when there is the female faculty called itthibhāva, the female marks and so forth arise. The female faculty is like the seed. Like the tree that grows based on the seed and stands filling the sky, the female marks and so forth arise during the course of existence based on the female faculty. Among these, the female faculty is not cognizable by the eye; it is cognizable only by the mind. The female marks and so forth are cognizable by both the eye and the mind.

Regarding the statement "This matter is the female faculty": unlike the eye-faculty (cakkhundriya) etc., which also occur in men, this faculty belongs exclusively to women by rule; hence it is called 'female faculty' (itthindriya).

The same method applies to the male faculty (purisindriya). Male marks (purisalinga) etc. should be understood as the opposite of female marks. The shape of a man's hands, feet, neck, chest, etc., is not like a woman's. Men's upper bodies are distinct (broad), and their lower bodies are not distinct (not broad). Hands and feet are large, the face is large, the chest muscles are distinct (prominent), and beards and mustaches appear. The way of tying hair and wearing clothes is not like women's. In childhood, they play with small carts and plows, build sand embankments and dig "ponds," and their movements etc. are distinct (bold). Even if it is a woman, if her movements are seen to be bold, people say, "She walks like a man," etc. The rest is similar to what was said about the female faculty.

In this context, the female faculty has the characteristic of femininity (itthibhāva-lakkhaṇa), the function of manifesting as "this is a woman," and the manifestation of being the cause for female marks, signs, behavior, and deportment. The male faculty has the characteristic of masculinity (purisabhāva-lakkhaṇa), the function of manifesting as "this is a man," and the manifestation of being the cause for male marks, signs, behavior, and deportment. Both these faculties arose during the course of existence (pavatti) for the first beings of the aeon. In later times, they arise at rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). Even if arisen at rebirth-linking, they can fluctuate or change during the course of existence.
359:
The shape of the neck, chest, etc., is not like a woman's. Indeed, the upper body of men is distinct and clear, while the lower body is not distinct (not clear). Hands and feet are large, the face is large, the chest muscle is distinct, and beards and mustaches appear. Tying hair and wearing clothes are not like women's. In childhood, they play with small carts and plows. They build sand embankments, call them ponds, and dig them. Movements etc. are distinct (bold). Indeed, even if it is a woman, if her movements are seen to be bold, they say, "She walks like a man," etc. The rest is similar to what was said about the female faculty.

Between these two, the female faculty has the characteristic of femininity (itthibhāva), which is the cause for the knowledge "this person is a woman" and the term "woman." It has the function of showing the state of being a woman. It manifests in knowledge as the cause of female organs, signs, behavior, and gait. Because the name "woman" and the knowledge "woman" arise due to this state, it is called itthibhāva. The male faculty likewise has the characteristic of masculinity (purisabhāva), which is the cause for the knowledge "this person is a man" and the term "man." It has the function of showing the state of being a man. It manifests in knowledge as the cause of male organs and behavior. Both these state-matters (bhāva-rūpa) arose during the course of existence for the first beings of the aeon; for later beings, they arise at rebirth-linking. The state-matter arisen at rebirth-linking can change or transform (sex change) during the course of existence. It should be noted that the state-matter arisen during the course of existence can also change during the course of existence.

For this reason, it was said (in the Pārājika Pali): "At that time, the female marks appeared on a certain monk. At that time, the male marks appeared on a certain bhikkhunī."

Between these two sexes, the male sex is superior and the female sex is inferior. Therefore, the male sex disappears due to powerful unwholesome kamma, and the female sex is established due to weak wholesome kamma. When the female sex disappears, it disappears due to weak unwholesome kamma, and the male sex is established due to powerful wholesome kamma. Thus, it should be understood that both sexes disappear due to unwholesome kamma and are established due to wholesome kamma.

Does a person with both sexes (ubhatobyañjanaka) have one faculty or two? Only one. For a female-hermaphrodite, it is the female faculty; for a male-hermaphrodite, it is the male faculty. If asked: "In that case, the second organ would not exist. The faculty is said to be the cause of the organ. Since that person lacks the [second] faculty, [how can they have the organ]?" The answer is: "For that person, the faculty is not the cause of the [second] organ." "Why?" "Because it is not always present." When a female-hermaphrodite develops a lustful mind (rāgacitta) toward another woman, only then does the male organ become manifest, while the female organ remains hidden and concealed. The same applies to the other type (male-hermaphrodite) regarding the other organ (female organ).

If the faculty were the cause of the second organ for them, both organs would exist at all times. But they do not. Therefore, it should be understood that the faculty is not the cause of that organ. Only the lustful mind, accompanied by kamma, is the root cause here. Because such a person has only one faculty, a female-hermaphrodite can both become pregnant herself and cause another to become pregnant. It should be understood that a male-hermaphrodite can cause another to become pregnant but cannot become pregnant himself.

Regarding the explanation of the life faculty (jīvitindriya), what needs to be said was already mentioned below in the section on the immaterial life faculty (arūpa-jīvitindriya). The only difference is that there it was said "of those immaterial states," whereas here, being the material life faculty (rūpa-jīvitindriya), it is said "of those material states." Its characteristics etc. should be understood as follows: The life faculty has the characteristic of maintaining co-nascent kamma-born material phenomena. It has the function of making them proceed (persist). It manifests as the establishing of those very phenomena. Its proximate cause is the material phenomena that are to be maintained.
360:
## Exposition of Bodily Intimation
In the exposition of bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti), regarding the term 'kāyaviññatti': firstly, it is called 'intimation' (viññatti) because the intention is known through this [phenomenon], as the bodily movements of animals making their own state known to humans, or humans to animals, are grasped accordingly. It is also called 'intimation' because it is itself known by following the bodily movements. The body itself, referred to as 'movement' in such discourses as 'Restraint by the body is good' (kāyena saṃvaro sādhu), is called 'bodily intimation' because it makes [the intention] known. Furthermore, it is called 'bodily intimation' because it is the cause for making the intention known through bodily movement, and because it is itself known in that manner through the body.

Regarding the phrases such as 'of a wholesome consciousness' (kusala-cittassa vā), [intimation arises] for one with a wholesome consciousness by way of the nine wholesome consciousnesses, namely, the eight sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses and one direct-knowledge (abhiññā) consciousness; for one with an unwholesome consciousness by way of the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses; and for one with an indeterminate consciousness (abyākata-citta) by way of the eleven functional consciousnesses, namely, the eight great functional consciousnesses, the two rootless functional consciousnesses, and the one fine-material functional consciousness that has reached direct-knowledge. Consciousnesses other than these mentioned do not produce intimation. Since intimation arises through only these many consciousnesses for learners (sekha), those beyond training (asekha), and worldlings (puthujjana), it is shown 'by way of cause' (hetuto) through these three phrases according to the wholesome and so forth.

Now, in order to show it 'by way of result' (phalato) through six phrases, the words beginning with 'of one advancing' (abhikkamantassa vā) are stated. Indeed, advancing and so forth are called the results of intimation because they occur by the power of intimation. Therein, 'of one advancing' (abhikkamantassa) refers to the state of one who carries the body forward. 'Of one retreating' (paṭikkamantassa) refers to the state of one who carries the body back. 'Of one looking straight' (ālokentassa) refers to the state of one who looks directly. 'Of one looking away' (vilokentassa) refers to the state of one who looks here and there. 'Of one bending' (samiñjentassa) refers to the state of one who contracts the joints. 'Of one stretching' (pasārentassa) refers to the state of one who extends the joints.

Now, in order to show it 'by way of nature' (sabhāvato) through six phrases, the words beginning with 'the stiffening of the body' (kāyassa thambhanā) are stated. Therein, 'of the body' (kāyassa) refers to the physical body. It is called 'stiffening' (thambhanā) because it supports the body and makes it rigid. That same 'thambhanā' is stated as 'santhambhanā' (strengthening/supporting) by adding a prefix. Alternatively, a more powerful stiffening is called 'santhambhanā'. 'The state of being supported' (santhambhitattaṃ) means the condition of being supported. It is called 'intimation' (viññatti) by way of the power to make [the intention] known. 'Intimating' (viññāpanā) is the mode of making known. 'The state of being intimated' (viññāpitattaṃ) is the condition of having been made known. All other things that should be said here should be understood as already stated below in the Discussion on Doors (Dvārakathā). The same applies to vocal intimation.
361:
The meaning of the term 'vocal intimation' (vacīviññatti) and its explanatory terms was not mentioned in that Discussion on Doors (Dvārakathā). That meaning should be understood as follows: it is called 'intimation' (viññatti) because the intention is known by this mode, as the speech of animals making their own state known to humans, or humans to animals, is grasped according to the sequence of speech. It is also called 'intimation' because it is itself known by following the sequence of speech. Speech itself, which makes the intention known as mentioned in 'Restraint by speech is good' (sādhu vācāya saṃvaro) and so forth, is 'vocal intimation' because it is the intimation. It is also called 'vocal intimation' because it is the cause for making the intention known through the sound of speech, and because it is itself known in that manner through speech. Among the terms such as 'vācā' and 'girā', it is called 'vācā' (speech) because it is spoken. It is called 'girā' (utterance) because it is uttered. 'Vyappatha' (distinctive phrasing) is a specific variation of a sentence. It is called 'vyappatha' because it is both a sentence and a path (means) for those who wish to know the meaning and those who wish to make it known. It is called 'udīraṇa' because it is pronounced. It is called 'ghosa' because it is sounded. It is called 'kamma' because it is performed. It is called 'ghosakamma' (sound-action) because the sound itself is the thing performed. It means the sound produced by various distinct modes. The distinction of speech is called 'vacībheda' (vocal articulation). To show that this distinction is not a destruction but merely speech that has reached a specific distinction to make the meaning known, it is stated as 'vācā vacībheda'. By all these terms, only 'sound-speech' (sadda-vācā) is shown. Now, in order to show that intimation by way of nature in three modes through the power of terms such as 'viññatti' which have the meanings stated below in connection with that speech, the words beginning with 'that which is intimation by that speech' (yā tāya vācāya viññatti) are stated. That statement is very clear in meaning as it follows the method already stated below.

Now, to avoid confusion regarding the consciousnesses that produce intimation, this miscellaneous (pakiṇṇaka) summary should be understood: thirty-two, twenty-six, nineteen, and sixteen. Thirty-two consciousnesses produce matter (rūpa), support the postures (iriyāpatha), and generate both types of intimation. Twenty-six consciousnesses do not generate intimation alone, but perform the other two (producing matter and supporting postures). Nineteen consciousnesses produce matter only, and do not perform the other two. Sixteen consciousnesses do not perform even one of these three.

Among those consciousnesses, the thirty-two are those already mentioned below: 8 sense-sphere wholesome, 12 unwholesome, 10 functional consciousnesses, the direct-knowledge consciousness of learners and worldlings, and the direct-knowledge consciousness of Arahants. The twenty-six are: 5 fine-material wholesome, 5 fine-material functional, 4 immaterial wholesome, 4 immaterial functional, 4 path consciousnesses, and 4 fruit consciousnesses. The nineteen are: 11 sense-sphere wholesome resultants, unwholesome resultants...
362:
When life-continuum (bhavaṅga) consciousness occurs, the limbs and members seem to sink or go in. Similarly, when the 32 and 26 types of consciousness that cause awakening occur, the limbs do not sink or go in. In fact, when those types of consciousness occur, the limbs remain firm in their usual posture. This should be noted. Consciousnesses produce the two types of intimation (viññatti). 26 types of consciousness produce only intimation, but do not produce posture and matter. 19 types of consciousness produce only matter, but do not produce posture and intimation. 16 types of consciousness do not produce any of the three: matter, posture, or intimation.

Among those, the 32 types are: 8 wholesome consciousnesses of the sense sphere, 12 unwholesome consciousnesses, 10 functional consciousnesses, the direct-knowledge (abhiññā) consciousness of trainees (sekha) and worldlings (puthujjana), and the direct-knowledge consciousness of Arahants. The 26 types are: 5 wholesome and 5 functional consciousnesses of the fine-material sphere, 4 wholesome and 4 functional consciousnesses of the immaterial sphere, 4 path consciousnesses, and 4 fruition consciousnesses. The 19 types are: 11 resultant consciousnesses of the sense sphere, 2 unwholesome resultants, 1 functional mind-element, and 5 resultant consciousnesses of the fine-material sphere. The 16 types are: 10 types of fivefold sense-consciousness (dve-pañcavijñāṇa), the rebirth-linking consciousness of all beings, the death consciousness of Arahants, and 4 resultant consciousnesses in the immaterial realm. These sixteen types of consciousness do not produce even one of the following: matter, posture, or intimation. Many other types of consciousness arising in the immaterial realm also do not produce matter because there is no occasion for matter. The consciousnesses that produce bodily intimation also produce vocal intimation.

## Exposition of the Space Element
In the exposition of the space element (ākāsadhātu-niddesa), the decision should be understood. That which cannot be scratched, cut, or destroyed is called space (ākāsa). Space itself is called 'gone to space' (ākāsagata), like 'gone to saliva' (kheḷagata), etc. Or, it is called 'gone to space' because it is known as a place that cannot be scratched. It is called 'agha' because it cannot be struck. It is called 'vivara' (fissure) because of the sense of a hole or cavity. 'Vivara' itself is 'gone to fissure' (vivaragata).
