It refers to the space element that is not touched by the four great essentials. In terms of characteristics, etc., the space element has the characteristic of delimiting matter (rūpa-pariccheda). It has the function of showing the boundaries of matter (rūpa-pariyantappakāsana). It manifests as the boundaries of matter (rūpa-mariyāda), or it manifests as the state of untouched holes and gaps (asamphuṭṭhabhāva chiddavivara-bhāva). It has delimited matter (paricchinna-rūpa) as its proximate cause. Because of that space element, it becomes evident in delimited matter that 'this is above, this is below, this is across.'

Following this, the expositions of lightness of matter (rūpassa lahutā), etc., should be understood in the same way as mentioned for lightness of mind (cittassa lahutā), etc. Lightness of matter has the characteristic of non-sluggishness (adandhatā). It has the function of dispelling the heaviness of matter (garubhāva-vinodana). It manifests as the state of being able to change quickly (lahuparivattitā). It has light matter as its proximate cause. Malleability of matter (rūpassa mudutā) has the characteristic of non-rigidity (athaddhatā). It has the function of dispelling the rigidity of matter (thaddhabhāva-vinodana). It manifests as non-opposition to all activities (avirodhitā). It has soft matter as its proximate cause. Wieldiness of matter (rūpassa kammaññatā) has the characteristic of being suitable for bodily actions (sarīrakiriyānukūla-kammaññabhāva). It has the function of dispelling unsuitability for work (akammaññatā-vinodana). It manifests as the state of non-weakness (adubbalabhāva). It has wieldy matter as its proximate cause.

These three do not abandon each other. Nevertheless, the lightness and non-sluggishness of matter, like the matter of a healthy person, is called 'lightness of matter' (rūpassa lahutā). The softness and compliance in all activities, like well-tanned leather, is called 'malleability of matter' (rūpassa mudutā).
363: ...which arises from a cause that is the opposite of the disturbance of elements causing rigidity, is 'softness of matter' (rūpassa-mudutā). The state of readiness of materiality, like well-refined gold, which is the mode of being suitable for bodily actions, arising from a cause that is the opposite of the disturbance of elements making it unsuitable for bodily actions, is 'readiness of matter' (rūpassa-kammaññatā). Thus the distinction between these should be known. These three (lightness, softness, readiness) cannot perform actions by themselves; nutriment and so on perform them. Indeed, yogis say: 'Today we have obtained suitable food; our body is light, soft, and ready.' 'Today we have obtained suitable climate; today our mind is one-pointed, our body is light, soft, and ready.' In the exposition of integration (upacaya) and continuity (santati), 'of the bases' (āyatanānaṃ) refers to the eleven material bases. 'Accumulation' (ācaya) means arising (nibpatti). The integration of that materiality is the initial arising of the bases that arise again and again; it means growth (vaḍḍhi). The integration of materiality is the continuity of materiality; the growth of materiality thus integrated, in the period of its further occurrence, is called the continuity of materiality; it means occurrence (pavatti). It should be understood that the time when water emerges in a small well dug on a riverbank is like accumulation (ācaya), which is arising; the time when it becomes full is like integration (upacaya), which is growth; and the time when it overflows and flows along is like continuity (santati), which is occurrence. In this way, what is being said? By 'base', 'accumulation' is said; by 'accumulation', 'base' is said. To say 'accumulation' is to say 'base'. In this way, what is being said? The accumulation, integration, arising, and growth of the four types of continuity-materiality are being said. In meaning, both of these are just synonyms for the materiality of birth (jāti-rūpa). However, because of the diversity of modes and for the sake of those to be taught, the teaching was given with the headings 'integration' and 'continuity'. Since there is no difference in meaning here, it was said in the exposition: 'That which is the accumulation of the bases is the integration of materiality; that which is the integration of materiality is the continuity of materiality.' And since both of these are just synonyms for the materiality of birth, here the integration of materiality has the characteristic of accumulation (ācaya); its function is to make materiality emerge from the past towards the future...
364: (The matter of accumulation, upacaya) has the manifestation of handing over those material phenomena as if saying, 'These are material phenomena,' or it has the manifestation of the state of fullness. Its proximate cause is accumulated matter. The continuity (santati) of matter should be understood as having the characteristic of the successive occurrence of material phenomena; its function is to link them together without interruption; its manifestation is non-interruption; its proximate cause is matter that is being linked together. In the description of jaratā, it is called jarā (old age) by way of aging and decaying. This term 'jarā' in this description is the indication of its nature (sabhāva-niddesa). The mode of aging is jīraṇatā. The three terms beginning with khaṇḍicca (brokenness) are descriptions of the function after the lapse of time. The last two terms are descriptions of the natural state (pakati-niddesa). Indeed, this old age is shown by its nature through the term 'jarā'; therefore, this is its description of nature (sabhāva-niddesa). It is shown by its mode through the term 'jīraṇatā'; therefore, this is its description of mode (ākāra-niddesa). It is shown through the term 'khaṇḍicca' because of the function of causing the state of brokenness in teeth and nails after the lapse of time. It is shown through the term 'pālicca' because of the function of causing the state of greyness in hair and body hair. It is shown through the term 'valittacatā' because of the function of causing the state of wrinkledness in the skin by causing the flesh to wither. Therefore, these three terms beginning with 'khaṇḍicca' are descriptions of the function after the lapse of time. Through those terms, by showing these alterations such as broken teeth, grey hair, and wrinkled skin, 'evident old age' (pākaṭa-jarā) is shown. Indeed, just as the path taken by water or fire is evident through the breaking and scattering of grass and trees or through charring, yet that path is not the water or fire itself; even so, the path taken by old age is evident in teeth etc., by way of brokenness etc. It can be grasped even by opening the eyes, yet brokenness etc. are not old age itself. Indeed, old age is not cognizable by eye-consciousness. However, through the terms 'decay of life' (āyuno saṃhāni) and 'ripening of the faculties' (indriyānaṃ paripāko), it is shown by way of the natural state (result) known as the exhaustion of life and the ripening of the eye-faculty etc., which are very evident only after the lapse of time. Therefore, these last two terms should be understood as descriptions of the natural state (pakati-niddesa). Therein, because the life of one who has reached old age wanes, old age is called 'decay of life' by way of metaphorical usage (phalūpacāra). And because the faculties such as the eye, which were very clear in youth and capable of easily grasping even subtle objects, become ripe, disturbed, and unclear upon reaching old age, and are unable to grasp even gross objects, it is also called 'ripening of the faculties' by way of metaphorical usage. All this old age thus described is of two kinds: evident (pākaṭa) and concealed (paṭicchanna). Therein, old age in material phenomena is called evident old age (pākaṭa-jarā) because of the visibility of brokenness etc. in teeth and so on.
365: In mental phenomena (nāma), however, it is called concealed old age (paṭicchanna-jarā) because such alteration is not seen. Again, it is also of two kinds: interval-less (avīci) and with intervals (savīci). Therein, the old age of gems, gold, silver, coral, the moon, the sun, etc.; the old age of living beings in the stages of life such as the 'slow decade' (manda-dasaka) etc.; and the old age of non-living things such as flowers, fruits, and sprouts, is called interval-less old age (avīci-jarā) because the difference in color etc. is difficult to perceive in between; the meaning is continuous old age. In other cases besides those, old age should be understood as old age with intervals (savīci-jarā) because the difference in color etc. is easy to perceive in between. By way of characteristics etc., the old age (jaratā) of matter has the characteristic of ripening of material phenomena; its function is to lead [towards destruction]; its manifestation is the disappearance of newness even when the nature has not disappeared; its proximate cause is matter that is ripening, like the state of old grain. In the description of impermanence (aniccatā), it is called khaya (exhaustion) by way of reaching exhaustion, vaya (vanishing) by way of reaching vanishing, and bheda (breakup) by way of breaking up. Or else, because matter reaches that state and is exhausted, vanishes, and breaks up, it is called 'khaya' because it is exhausted therein, 'vaya' because it vanishes therein, and 'bheda' because it breaks up therein. By expanding the term with a prefix, bheda is called 'paribheda'. It is called 'anicca' (impermanent) because it is not permanent in the sense of non-existence after having been. The state of that impermanence is 'aniccatā'. It is called 'antaradhāna' (disappearance) because matter disappears therein. Indeed, reaching death, matter disappears and goes to invisibility. Not only matter, but all five aggregates as well. Therefore, this very characteristic of the impermanence of the five aggregates should be understood. By way of characteristics etc., the impermanence (aniccatā) of matter has the characteristic of complete breakup; its function is to make [matter] sink; its manifestation is exhaustion and vanishing; its proximate cause is matter that is breaking up. Birth (jāti) was taken below, and old age (jarā) was also taken; in this place, death (maraṇa) is taken. These three things are like enemies with raised swords to these beings. For example, three enemies might wander seeking an opportunity against a man. Among them, one might say, 'Let the task of taking him out of the house and into the forest be mine.' The second says, 'Let the task of striking him and felling him to the ground when he reaches the forest be mine.' The third says, 'Let the task of cutting off his head with a sword from the time he falls to the ground be mine.' These things such as birth etc. are of such a nature. Here, birth is like the enemy who takes him out and into the forest, because it causes him to be born in various places. Like the enemy who strikes and fells him to the ground when he reaches the forest is...
366:
Aging (jarā) makes the arisen aggregates weak, dependent on others, and prone to lying on a couch (like an enemy who fells one). Death (maraṇa), like an enemy who cuts off the head of one lying on the ground with a sword, brings the aggregates that have reached old age to the end of life.

In the explanation of nutriment as morsels (kabaḷīkārāhāra): it is called 'kabaḷīkāra' because it is made into balls or morsels. It is called 'āhāra' because it is brought in (swallowed). The meaning is that it is swallowed after being made into morsels. Alternatively, it is called 'āhāra' because it brings about form (rūpa). Having thus extracted the name by way of the physical substance (vatthu), it is again mentioned as "boiled rice, bread-cakes," etc., to show its divisions by way of substance. The twelve items starting from boiled rice and ending with molasses are the substances of nutriment intended here. Roots, fruits, and so on, which are not directly mentioned in the Pāḷi, are included in the "whatever else" (yevāpanaka) group.

Now, to show those roots, fruits, etc., according to their functions, it is said: "in whatever region," and so on. Among those terms, 'mukhāsiya' (mouth-eatable) is so called because it is eaten with the mouth. 'Dantavikhādana' (tooth-chewable) is so called because it is chewed with the teeth. 'Galajjhoharaṇīya' (throat-swallowable) is so called because it is swallowed through the throat. Now, to show the substance by way of its function, it is said: "distending the belly." For that substance, whether roots and fruits or boiled rice and bread-cakes, when swallowed, distends the belly. This is its function. After showing the nutriment together with its substance by all the preceding terms, it is now said: "by which nutritive essence (ojā) beings subsist," to show the nutritive essence alone that has been produced.

What is the function of the substance here? What is the function of the nutritive essence? They are the removing of danger and the preservation [of life]. The substance can remove danger but cannot preserve; the nutritive essence can preserve but cannot remove danger. Only when both are combined can they both preserve and remove danger. What is this "danger" (parissaya)? It is the kamma-born heat (kammaja-tejo). When there is no substance such as boiled rice in the belly, the kamma-born heat rises and burns the stomach lining, making one say, "I am hungry, give me food." When food is eaten, it lets go of the stomach lining and burns the substance (food). Then the being attains composure of mind.

For example, a shadow-ogre (chāyā-rakkhasa) catches someone who enters the shadow, binds them with divine shackles, and enjoys himself in his abode; when hungry, he comes and bites the person's head. That person cries out because of the bite. Hearing that cry, people come from all directions, thinking, "There is someone in distress here." That ogre catches all who come...
367:
...and devours them, enjoying himself in his abode. The completeness of this simile should be understood thus: The kamma-born heat (kammaja-tejo) is like the shadow-ogre who catches and eats those who enter the shade. The stomach lining (udarapaṭala) is like the being bound with divine shackles. The substance (vatthu) such as boiled rice is like the people who arrive later. The kamma-born heat's seizing of the stomach lining when free from the substance of nutriment is like the ogre descending (from the tree) and biting the head. The time of saying "Give me food" is like the time the bitten person cries out. The composure of mind when the kamma-born heat lets go of the stomach lining and seizes the substance of nutriment is like the time the ogre, hearing the cry as a sign, catches and devours all who arrive and enjoys himself in his abode.

Among those substances of nutriment, the nutritive essence (ojā) is weak in gross substances and powerful in subtle substances. Having eaten millet-rice and the like, one becomes hungry in a moment. For one who remains after drinking ghee and the like, he does not desire rice for the whole day. In this matter of nutriment, grossness and subtleness should be understood by comparison. Compared to the nutriment of crocodiles, the nutriment of peacocks is subtle. It is heard that crocodiles swallow stones, and those stones dissolve upon reaching their bellies. Peacocks eat creatures like snakes and scorpions. Compared to the nutriment of peacocks, the nutriment of hyenas (taracchā) is subtle. It is heard that they eat horns and bones that have been discarded for three years. Those horns and bones become as soft as tubers and roots just by being moistened with their saliva. Compared to the nutriment of hyenas, the nutriment of elephants is subtle. They eat various tree branches and the like. Compared to the nutriment of elephants, the nutriment of wild cattle (gavaya), elks (gokaṇṇa), and deer is subtle. They eat various leaves and the like that lack heartwood. Compared to their nutriment, the nutriment of cattle is subtle. They eat fresh and dry grass. Compared to their nutriment, the nutriment of rabbits is subtle. Compared to the nutriment of rabbits, the nutriment of birds is subtle. Compared to the nutriment of birds, the nutriment of border-dwellers is subtle. Compared to the nutriment of border-dwellers, the nutriment of village headmen is subtle. Compared to the nutriment of village headmen, the nutriment of kings and great ministers is subtle. Compared to their nutriment, the nutriment of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) is subtle. Compared to the nutriment of a Universal Monarch, the nutriment of earth-bound deities (bhumma-deva) is subtle. Compared to the nutriment of earth-bound deities, the nutriment of the Devas of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājika) is subtle. Thus, as far as...
368: The nutriment of the Paranimmita-vasavatti devas should be expanded upon. Their nutriment reaches the ultimate point of subtlety. By way of characteristics, etc., nutriment as edible food (kabaḷīkāra āhāra) should be understood as having the characteristic of nutritive essence (ojā), the function of bringing forth the eightfold materiality of which nutritive essence is the eighth, the manifestation of supporting (the physical body), and the proximate cause of the physical substance that is to be swallowed after being made into a bolus. In the description of non-clinging (no-upādā), just as derived materiality (upādā-rūpa) is only that which is clung to (dependent on the great elements) and is not clung to by other materiality, so too this (great element) is only that which is not clung to by other materiality; therefore, it is called non-clinging (no-upādā). It is called 'tangible' (phoṭṭhabba) because it is to be touched. The meaning is that it is to be known by touching. Because it is both tangible and a base, it is called the tangible base (phoṭṭhabbāyatana). Because it is the water element and is an element (dhātu) in the sense of being a non-sentient, empty nature, it is called the water element (āpo-dhātu). Now, since three types of materiality are to be known by touching, in order to show them by classification, it is said: 'What is the tangible base? It is the earth element,' and so on. Among those elements, the earth element (pathavī-dhātu) has the characteristic of hardness, the function of being a foundation, and the manifestation of receiving (conascent states). The fire element (tejo-dhātu) has the characteristic of heat, the function of maturing, and the manifestation of providing softness. The air element (vāyo-dhātu) has the characteristic of supporting, the function of moving, and the manifestation of leading (the group of elements). The previously mentioned water element (āpo-dhātu) has the characteristic of flowing, the function of increasing or filling, and the manifestation of cohesion. It should be understood that each of these elements has the remaining three great elements as its proximate cause. 'Hard' (kakkhaḷa) means stiff or firm. 'Soft' (muduka) means not stiff, but tender. 'Smooth' (saṇha) means fine or polished. 'Rough' (pharusa) means coarse. 'Pleasant touch' (sukha-samphassa) means a desirable tangible object that is a cause for pleasant feeling. 'Unpleasant touch' (dukkha-samphassa) means an undesirable tangible object that is a cause for painful feeling. 'Heavy' (garuka) means weighty. 'Light' (lahuka) means not weighty, meaning very light. In this (description of the tangible base), the earth element alone is classified by the terms 'hard, soft, smooth, rough, heavy, and light.' In the Sutta which says, 'When this body is accompanied by life, heat, and consciousness, it is lighter, softer, and more workable,' the reference is also made only to the earth element that has reached the state of being light and soft. By the two terms 'pleasant touch' and 'unpleasant touch,' all three great elements (earth, fire, and air) are classified. For the earth element has both pleasant touch and unpleasant touch. Likewise, the fire element and the air element have both pleasant touch and unpleasant touch. Among those three, the earth element which is a pleasant touch...
369: When a young child with soft and tender hands massages the feet, one repeatedly experiences the pleasure (of the earth element) and causes the child to continue, saying, 'Massage more, dear; massage more, dear.' In cold weather, when one brings a charcoal brazier and warms the body, one repeatedly experiences the pleasure of the fire element which is a pleasant touch and causes another to continue, saying, 'Warm me more, dear; warm me more, dear.' In hot weather, when a well-behaved youth fans one with a fan, one repeatedly experiences the pleasure of the air element which is a pleasant touch and causes the youth to continue, saying, 'Fan me more, dear; fan me more, dear.' However, when a child with rough and stiff hands massages the feet, it is as if the bones are breaking. At that time, one reaches the state of having to say, 'Go away!' In hot weather, if a charcoal brazier is brought, one must say, 'Take it away!' In cold weather, if one is fanned with a fan, one must say, 'Go away, do not fan!' In this way, the state of being a pleasant touch and the state of being an unpleasant touch of those elements should be understood. The thirteen sections (vāra) adorned with the fourfold methods, which are taught by the method beginning with 'That tangible which is non-informative and with impact (anidassana-sappatigha),' should be understood in the same way as taught below in the sections on the visible base (rūpāyatana), etc. Do these three great elements come into focus (the field of experience) simultaneously or not? They do. Do these great elements that have come into focus in this way strike the body-sensitivity (kāya-pasāda) or not? They do. Does body-consciousness (kāya-viññāṇa) arise by taking those great elements as an object simultaneously or not? It does not. The taking of an object occurs either by the power of attention (ābhujita) or by the power of predominance (ussada). Between those two, it should first be understood by the power of attention (ābhujita). When a bowl is filled with alms-food and brought, for a person who takes a grain of rice and tests whether it is hard or soft, although the fire element and air element are also present in that rice, he attends only to the earth element. For a person who dips his hand into hot water to test it, although the earth element and air element are also present in that water, he attends only to the fire element. In hot weather, for a person standing by an open window letting the wind strike his body, when a gentle breeze blows, although the earth element and fire element are also present in that wind, he attends only to the air element. This is called taking an object by the power of attention.
370:
A person who slips, or hits a tree with their head, or bites a pebble while eating—even though fire and air elements are present in that slipping etc., they take only the earth element (pathavīdhātu) as an object by way of predominance. One who steps on fire—even though earth and air elements are present in that fire, they take only the fire element (tejodhātu) as an object by way of predominance. When a strong wind strikes the ear-canal and causes deafness—even though earth and fire elements are present in that wind, they take only the air element (vāyodhātu) as an object by way of predominance. For one who takes any element as an object, body-consciousness (kāyaviññāṇa) does not arise simultaneously at all points. When a person is pricked with a bundle of needles, the body is struck at once. However, in whatever place the body-sensitivity (kāyapasāda) is predominant, there body-consciousness arises. Also, in whatever place the friction of impact is strong, there it arises first. When a wound is being washed with a chicken feather, the fibers strike the body-sensitivity. However, in whatever place the sensitivity is predominant, there alone body-consciousness arises. Thus, one takes an object by way of predominance. And body-consciousness is said to arise by way of predominance.

How does the shifting of the mind from one object occur? It occurs in two ways: by way of intention (ajjhāsaya) or by way of the intensity of the object (visayādhimatta). In the case of honoring a monastery etc., a person who goes with the intention, "I will worship various shrines and images, and I will look at the carved and painted artworks," having worshipped or seen one, directs the mind to worship or see another, and indeed goes to worship and see it; this is called shifting by way of intention.

One who stands looking at the Great Shrine (Mahācetiya), which is like the peak of Mount Kelāsa, but later, when all kinds of musical instruments are played, lets go of the visible object and shifts to the sound object. When flowers or perfumes with a pleasing scent are brought, they let go of the sound object and shift to the odor object. This is called shifting by way of the intensity of the object.

In the explanation of the water element (āpodhātu-niddesa), "āpo" is a term indicating its nature. Āpo itself is āpogata (the state of water). By way of its cohesive power, it is called sineha (viscosity/cohesion); sineha itself is sinehagata.
371:
The binding of matter refers to the state of binding of the primary elements (bhūtarūpa) such as the earth element. Indeed, the water element (āpodhātu) binds and coheres things like iron masses, making them into a single lump. Because they are bound by that water element, those iron masses etc. are called "bound" (baddha). The same principle applies to stone mountains, palm seeds, elephant tusks, bull horns, and so on. The water element alone binds all these and makes them into a single mass. Only because they are bound by the water element do they become a single mass.

When the earth element serves as the support for the remaining elements, does it do so by touching or without touching? And when the water element binds the remaining elements, does it bind by touching or without touching? The earth element serves as the support for the water element without touching it, but it serves as the support for the fire and air elements by touching them. The water element, however, binds the earth element as well as the fire and air elements without touching them. If it were to bind by touching, it would become the sense-base of tangibility (phoṭṭhabbāyatana).

The same principle applies to the fire and air elements in performing their respective functions regarding the remaining elements. The fire element burns the earth element by touching it. However, that earth element does not burn by becoming hot itself. If it were to burn by becoming hot, it would be called the characteristic of heat (the fire element). It heats the water element without touching it. That water element, while being heated, does not become hot itself. If it were to become hot, it would be called the characteristic of heat. It heats the air element by touching it. That air element, while being heated, does not become hot itself. If it were to become hot, it would be called the characteristic of heat. The air element supports the earth element by touching it; likewise, it supports the fire element by touching it, but it supports the water element without touching it.

When sugarcane juice is boiled and made into a mass of molasses, does the water element become hard? It does not. For its characteristic is flowing (paggaraṇa). The earth element has the characteristic of hardness (kakkhaḷa). It is simply that the water element has decreased and it has taken on the state of the predominant earth element. That molasses gives up its state of existing in the form of liquid, but it does not give up its characteristic. Even when a mass of molasses melts, the earth element does not melt. This is because the earth element has the characteristic of hardness and the water element has the characteristic of flowing. It is simply that the earth element has decreased and it has taken on the state of the predominant water element. That molasses gives up its state of existing in the form of a solid mass, but it does not give up its characteristic.
372:
For the four great elements, there is only change in mode; there is no such thing as change in characteristic. The absence of change in characteristic is shown by the Aṭṭhānaparikappa Sutta. It is said: "It may be, Ānanda, that the four great elements—the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element—might change, but there can be no change in the noble disciple who is possessed of unwavering confidence in the Buddha" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.76).

The meaning in this sutta is: Ānanda, the earth element, which has the characteristic of hardness, might change and become the water element, which has the characteristic of flowing; but for the noble disciple, there is no such thing as change. Thus, in this sutta, the "supposition of the impossible" (aṭṭhānaparikappa) is presented.

In the subsequent explanations of clung-to matter (upādinna-rūpa) and so on, the meaning of terms like "clung-to" should be understood according to the method already stated in the Mātikā-kathā. The eye-base (cakkhāyatana) and others have been detailed below. Here, I shall only mention the specific points.

In the explanation of clung-to matter, the eye-base and others are mentioned because they are definitely clung-to. Since the visible-data base (rūpāyatana) and others can be both clung-to and not clung-to, they are first shown briefly as "or whatever else" (yaṃ vā pana) and then detailed by the method "the visible-data base due to kamma having been performed" and so on. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all "vā-panaka" (those mentioned as "or whatever else") sections.

Why are "decay" (jaratā) and "impermanence" (aniccatā) not included in both the explanations of "due to kamma having been performed" and "not due to kamma having been performed," but only in the explanations of not clung-to matter and so on? In the phrase "not due to kamma having been performed," production by causes other than kamma is included. In the phrase "due to kamma having been performed," only production by kamma is included. These two types of matter (decay and impermanence) arise neither from kamma nor from any other matter-producing cause; therefore, they are not included. Their non-arising will be made clear later. However, in the sections on not clung-to matter and so on, by the mere taking of the name "not clung-to," only production by kamma is excluded, while production by other causes is not prohibited. Therefore, it should be understood that they are included in those places.

In the explanation of mind-produced matter (cittasamuṭṭhāna-niddesa), the two—bodily intimation (kāya-viññatti) and vocal intimation (vacī-viññatti)—are mentioned because they become manifest depending on the great elements which are definitely mind-produced.
373:
In the ultimate sense (paramattha), only the great elements which are the support of that intimation (viññatti) are mind-produced, because they depend on that mind. Just as the decay and death of impermanent matter are called impermanent, so too these two types of intimation are called mind-produced (cittasamuṭṭhāna).

The same method applies to the explanation of "co-nascent with mind" (cittasahabhū). These two types of intimation are mentioned because they are manifest as long as the mind exists. However, they do not arise together with the mind in the same way as the great elements co-nascent with the mind, or as volition (cetanā) and so on.

The same method applies to "following the mind" (cittānuparivatti). These two types of intimation are said to follow the mind only because they are manifest as long as the mind exists.

"Gross" (oḷārika) means thick because it is taken by way of impact (saṅghaṭṭana) due to being an objective basis. Subtle (sukhuma) matter should be understood as the opposite of what has been said.

"Distant" (dūra) means that which is difficult to perceive because it cannot be taken by way of impact; thus, even if it stands near, it is called "distant." The other type (gross matter), however, is called "near" (santika) even if it stands far away, because it is easy to perceive as it can be taken by way of impact. The explanations of the eye-base and so on should be understood in detail according to the method stated below. This is the specific point regarding the twofold summary of matter. The threefold summary is quite clear in meaning.

## Catukkaniddesa-vaṇṇanā
At the end of the fourfold summary, because there is no difference in the latter terms such as "seen" (diṭṭha) and so on, the text states "the visible-data base is seen, the sound-base is heard," etc., without asking questions from the beginning. Therein, the visible-data base is called "seen" (diṭṭha) because it can be looked at and seen with the eye. The sound-base is called "heard" (suta) because it can be known by hearing with the ear. The three bases starting with the odor-base are called "sensed" (muta) in the sense that they are to be known by reflection, because they are taken by reaching them with the nose, tongue, and body. They are also called "muta" because they are the cause for the arising of consciousness through contact. However, all matter is called "cognized by the mind" (manasā viññāta) because it is to be known by the mind-consciousness.
374:
## Explanation of the Section on the Groups of Five

In the Pañcavidhasaṅgahaniddesa (Explanation of the Fivefold Summary), kakkhaḷa means hardness or rigidity. The rough nature itself is called kharagata; it means roughness. The remaining two terms are also descriptions that point to the intrinsic nature. Ajjhatta means internal, occurring within oneself. Bahiddhā means external, occurring outside. Upādinna (clung-to) does not mean only matter produced by kamma (kammasamuṭṭhāna). In fact, without distinction, it refers to all matter existing in the body by the term upādinna. Indeed, whether the matter in the body is upādinna (kamma-born) or anupādinna (not kamma-born), all of it is called upādinna by virtue of being grasped, clung to, and generally misapprehended by craving and views.

Tejogata refers to the matter characterized by heat that is inherent in all fire elements; or, because fire itself has reached the state of fire, it is called tejogata. Usmā is the mode of heat. Usmāgata is reaching the state of heat. This is simply a name for the mode of heat. Usuma is intense heat. Because usuma itself has reached the state of usuma, it is called usumagata.

By virtue of moving incessantly, it is called vāyo. Because vāyo itself has reached the state of vāyo, it is called vāyogata. Thambhitatta (distension) is the supportive and rigid state of matter, like the rigidity of lotus stalks or leather bags filled with air.

## Explanation of the Section on the Groups of Six, etc.

972-4. Since there is no difference in the final terms of the three summaries starting from the groups of six, the explanation is given from the beginning without asking questions. In that explanation, because it can be known by eye-consciousness, it is called cakkhuviññeyya (cognizable by the eye). ... Because it can be known by mind-consciousness, it is called manoviññeyya (cognizable by the mind). Because it can be known by the three types of mind-element, it is called manodhātuvinñeyya. In this context of 'all matter' (sabbaṃ rūpaṃ), it is said 'all matter' because there is not a single type of matter that is not to be known by the mind-consciousness element. Indeed, when the Perfectly Enlightened One reaches the Abhidhamma, there is no place where a method should be applied that He has not applied. This also is a place where a method should be applied because there is no state of even a single type of matter being unknowable by the mind-consciousness element; therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to show the method, said 'all matter'.

Sukhasamphassa (pleasant contact) refers to tangible matter that is a cause for obtaining pleasant feeling. Dukkhasamphassa (painful contact) refers to tangible matter that is a cause for obtaining painful feeling. Here too, this method is given because of the existence of pleasure and pain caused by tangible objects.
375:
## Explanation of the Section on the Groups of Nine, etc.

In the Navaka (Group of Nine), the method is given because of the existence of matter called faculties (indriyarūpa). In the Dasaka (Group of Ten), the method is given because of the impinging (sappaṭigha) and non-impinging (appaṭigha) nature of that same faculty-matter. In the Ekādasaka (Group of Eleven), the eleven and a half (or eleven along with others) bases (āyatana) are analyzed. The sections of explanation (niddesavāra) for those bases should be understood in detail according to the method mentioned below. In all other remaining parts, the meaning is clear.

## Miscellaneous Discussion

In order to avoid confusion regarding these matters, this 'Miscellaneous' (Pakiṇṇaka) should be understood: Combination (Samodhāna), Origination (Samuṭṭhāna), Produced (Parinipphanna), and Conditioned (Saṅkhata).

Among those, 'Combination' (Samodhāna) means: all this matter, by way of combination, consists of twenty-five items: eye-base ... nutritive essence, tangible-base, and water-element. That matter, together with heart-base matter (vatthurūpa), should be understood as being twenty-six in number. There is no other matter besides this. However, some teachers say, 'There is matter called torpor (middharūpa)'. Those teachers should be refuted by reciting verses such as 'You are indeed a Sage, the Awakened One; you have no hindrances,' and stating that there is no such thing as torpor-matter. Other teachers say there are twenty-seven types of matter including strength-matter (balarūpa), twenty-eight including production-matter (sambhavarūpa), twenty-nine including birth-matter (jātirūpa), and thirty including disease-matter (rogarūpa). Those teachers should also be rejected by showing the non-existence of those items like strength-matter as separate entities. Indeed, when the wind-element (vāyodhātu) is taken, strength-matter is already taken; there is no strength-matter other than the wind-element. With the water-element (āpodhātu), production-matter is taken; with integration (upacaya) and continuity (santati), birth-matter is taken; and when decay (jaratā) and impermanence (aniccatā) are taken, disease-matter is already taken. There is no other disease-matter. Even the affliction such as ear disease exists, that affliction is merely an element arising from uneven causes. Since there is no other disease in that affliction, there are only twenty-six types of matter by way of combination.

'Origination' (Samuṭṭhāna) means: How many matters have how many origins? Ten matters have one origin, one matter has two origins, three matters have three origins, nine matters have four origins, and two matters do not arise from any origin at all.

Among those matters, these eight matters—eye-sensitivity ... life-faculty—arise certainly from kamma alone. The pair of body-intimation and vocal-intimation arises certainly from the mind.
376:
There are ten types of matter that have a single origin (ekasamuṭṭhāna). Sound is called 'matter with two origins' (dvisamuṭṭhāna) because it arises due to temperature (utu) and consciousness (citta); there is one such type. Among these sounds, non-vocal sound (aviññāṇaka-sadda) arises from temperature, and vocal sound (saviññāṇaka-sadda) arises from consciousness. The three types of matter beginning with lightness (lahutā), however, are called 'matter with three origins' (tisamuṭṭhāna) because they arise from temperature, consciousness, and nutriment (āhāra). The remaining nine types of matter are called 'matter with four origins' (catusamuṭṭhāna) because they arise from kamma as well as from those three: temperature, consciousness, and nutriment.

Decay (jaratā) and impermanence (aniccatā), however, are called 'matter not produced by any cause' because they do not arise from even one of these four origins. Why is this? Because they do not come into being anew. Indeed, decay and impermanence are not newly produced. Why? Because they are the state of maturation and breaking of matter that has already been produced. It must certainly be admitted that matter which has arisen must age and break. Indeed, matter or mind that has arisen is never seen to be without exhaustion. In fact, as long as it has not yet broken, the maturation of that matter is evident; this is established. In the phrase 'because they are the state of maturation and breaking of matter that has already been produced,' if decay and impermanence were themselves newly produced, then they too would have their own maturation and breaking. But maturation does not mature again, nor does breaking break again; therefore, because they are the maturation and breaking of produced matter, these two are not newly produced.

In this matter, an objection might be raised: Just as in the descriptions (niddesa) beginning with 'because of being performed by kamma,' it is admitted that birth (jāti) arises through the words 'the accumulation of matter (upacaya), the continuity of matter (santati),' so too let maturation mature and let breaking break (i.e., let them be newly produced). In that description, it is not admitted that 'birth arises.' Because of the state of the first new arising of phenomena produced by causes such as kamma, birth is admitted only as a conventional term for having those causes. In the ultimate sense (paramattha), birth is not newly produced. Indeed, birth is merely the first arising of matter that is in the process of arising.

In this matter, another objection might be raised: Just as birth is the new arising of certain phenomena and thus receives the designation of having those causes and the designation of new arising, so too let maturation and breaking be the maturation and breaking of certain phenomena and receive the designation of having those causes and the designation of new arising. If this were so, it would have to be said that these two, decay and impermanence, are also types of matter originating from kamma and so on. Maturation and breaking do not receive those designations. Why? Because they do not exist at the moment of the productive condition's (janaka-paccaya) influence. Indeed, the influence of productive conditions exists only at the moment of arising (uppāda-kkhaṇa) of the phenomenon to be produced, and not beyond that. Since birth is clearly present at the moment of the phenomenon newly produced by those productive conditions, it receives the designation of having those causes and the designation of new arising, because it exists at that moment. The other two (decay and impermanence) do not exist at that moment, so it must be said that they are not newly produced. 'Monks, decay and death (jarāmaraṇa) are impermanent, conditioned (saṅkhata), and dependently arisen (paṭiccasamuppanna)' (as taught in the Saṃyutta Nikāya).
377:
If it is said that because decay and death (jarāmaraṇa) appear in the Pāli Canon, these two also arise—no, because they are taught figuratively (pariyāya). In that Pāli text, because they are the decay and death of phenomena that are dependently arisen, they are called 'dependently arisen' by way of a figurative method. If it is said that if they are taught figuratively in this way, then these three beginning with birth (jāti), because they do not arise, are non-existent like a rabbit's horn (sasavisāṇa), or permanent like Nibbāna—no, because their occurrence is connected to a support. When the supporting matter such as the earth element is present, the three beginning with birth are evident; therefore, they are not non-existent. When those supporting matters are absent, they are not evident; therefore, they are not permanent. It was solely to refute such wrong attachments that it was taught: 'Monks, decay and death are impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen.' By these and other methods, it should be understood that those two types of matter, decay and impermanence (death), do not originate from any cause.

Furthermore, in the word 'origin' (samuṭṭhāna), this other meaning should also be understood. Its matrix (mātikā) is: kamma-born matter (kammaja), kamma-conditioned matter (kammapaccaya), kamma-conditioned temperature-originated matter; nutriment-originated matter (āhārasamuṭṭhāna), nutriment-conditioned matter (āhārapaccaya), nutriment-conditioned temperature-originated matter; temperature-originated matter (utusamuṭṭhāna), temperature-conditioned matter (utupaccaya), temperature-conditioned temperature-originated matter; consciousness-originated matter (cittasamuṭṭhāna), consciousness-conditioned matter (cittapaccaya), and consciousness-conditioned temperature-originated matter.

Among these, the eight types of matter beginning with eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda), together with the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu), are called 'kamma-born matter.' Hair, beard, elephant tusks, horse tails, yak tails, and so on are called 'kamma-conditioned matter.' The Wheel-treasure, the gardens and mansions of the devas, and so on are called 'kamma-conditioned temperature-originated matter.'

The pure octad (suddaṭṭhaka) kalāpa arising from nutriment is called 'nutriment-originated matter.' The nutriment that is consumed is a condition for both sequences of matter: for nutriment-originated matter and for kamma-born matter (clung-to matter/upādinnarūpa). It assists as a productive cause (janaka) for nutriment-originated matter, and as a maintaining cause (anupālaka) for kamma-born matter. Kamma-born matter thus maintained by nutriment is called 'nutriment-conditioned matter.' Freckles, black spots, sores, and so on that arise in one who travels in the heat after consuming unsuitable nutriment are called 'nutriment-conditioned temperature-originated matter.'

The pure octad kalāpa arising from temperature is called 'temperature-originated matter.' The temperature within that temperature-originated matter produces another octad; this is called 'temperature-conditioned matter.' The temperature within that other octad also produces yet another octad; this is called 'temperature-conditioned temperature-originated matter.' In this way, temperature can strike and produce up to three successive sequences of matter. It cannot do so beyond that. This meaning should also be illustrated with non-clung-to (inorganic/anupādinnaka) matter. A cloud is called 'temperature-originated matter.' Due to temperature...
378:
It is called a stream of rainwater. Furthermore, when it rains, seeds sprout, the earth releases its scent, mountains appear dark green, and the ocean increases; this materiality, such as the scent of the earth arising from seeds due to rain, is called 'materiality originated from temperature having temperature as a support' (utupaccaya-utusamuṭṭhāna).

The pure octad (suddhaṭṭhaka) originated from consciousness is called 'consciousness-originated' (cittasamuṭṭhāna). This pre-nascent body-materiality, of which it is said, "The post-nascent states of consciousness and mental factors are a condition for this pre-nascent body by way of post-nascent condition," is called 'consciousness-conditioned' (cittapaccaya). Materiality such as elephants, horses, chariots, and various arrays of armies shown in the sky and firmament by knowledge-bearers (vidyādharas) and those possessed of psychic power is called 'materiality originated from temperature having consciousness as a condition' (cittapaccaya-utusamuṭṭhāna).

Regarding 'produced' (parinipphanna), fifteen types of materiality are called produced (parinipphanna), and ten types are called non-produced (aparinipphanna). If they were non-produced, they would be called unconditioned (asaṅkhata). However, the variation in the body produced by those eighteen types of produced materiality is called 'bodily intimation' (kāyaviññatti); the variation in speech is called 'vocal intimation' (vacīviññatti); the space or cavity is called 'space element' (ākāsadhātu); the state of lightness is 'lightness' (lahutā); the state of softness is 'malleability' (mudutā); the state of readiness for work is 'wieldiness' (kammaññatā); the initial arising is 'integration' (upacaya); the subsequent repeated arising is 'continuity' (santati); the mode of maturing and aging is 'decay' (jaratā); and the mode of breaking up after having come to be is 'impermanence' (aniccatā). All materiality is indeed produced (parinipphanna) and indeed conditioned (saṅkhata).

## In the Commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī named Atthasālinī,
## the Explanation of the Section on Materiality is finished.
379:
## 3. The Summary Section (Nikkhepakaṇḍa)
## Discussion on the Summary of Triads (Tikanikkhepakathā)
To this extent, the Wholesome Triad (Kusala Tika) has been detailed by way of the method of word-by-word analysis of all wholesome and other states, starting with "Which states are wholesome?" Since this method of analysis for the Wholesome Triad has been stated, this same method applies to the remaining triads and dyads. Just as the method of analysis is noted by the wise in this Wholesome Triad, so too in all triads and dyads, the wise can note the method of analysis in sequence, such as: "Which states are associated with pleasant feeling? At a time when sense-sphere wholesome consciousness accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge has arisen, having a visible object... pe... or whatever other immaterial states there are at that time that have arisen dependently, excluding the aggregate of feeling—these states are associated with pleasant feeling."

Therefore, setting aside that detailed exposition, the Summary Section (Nikkhepakaṇḍa) is undertaken to show the analysis of states taught in all triads and dyads by another method that is neither too brief nor too detailed. The Section on the Arising of Consciousness (Cittuppādakaṇḍa) is a detailed exposition, while the Commentary Section (Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa) is a brief exposition. This Summary Section, however, is brief in comparison to the Section on the Arising of Consciousness and detailed in comparison to the Commentary Section; thus, it possesses the nature of being both brief and detailed. It should be known as the 'Summary Section' (Nikkhepakaṇḍa) because it is taught by setting aside the detailed exposition and for the reasons stated below. For it has been said:

By way of root, and also by way of aggregate,
By way of door, and also by way of plane,
By way of meaning, by way of state (dhamma),
By way of name, and also by way of gender (liṅga),
Because it is taught by setting these down, it is called 'Summary' (Nikkhepa).

This Summary Section is taught by setting down by way of root (mūla) in the manner: "There are three wholesome roots." It is taught by way of aggregate (khandha) as: "The aggregate of feeling associated with those roots," and by way of door (dvāra) as: "Bodily action originated by those roots." Action occurring at the body-door is called 'bodily action' (kāyakamma). It is taught by setting down by way of plane (bhūmi) as: "In the plane of happiness, in the sense-sphere." It should be known as being taught by setting down by way of meaning, state, name, and gender, because it is taught by the power of meaning, state, name, and gender in various places.
380:
In this Exposition of the Wholesome Section (Kusala-pada-niddesa), first, the word 'three' is a term defining the numerical count. These states are called 'wholesome' (kusala) and they are also 'roots' (mūla); therefore, they are 'wholesome roots' (kusalamūla). Alternatively, they are called roots in the sense of being the cause (hetu), the supporting condition (paccaya), the origin (pabhava), the producer (janaka), the source (samuṭṭhāna), and the generator (nibbattaka) of wholesome states; thus, they are wholesome roots. Having shown this by way of meaning, the Teacher now speaks of 'non-greed (alobha), non-hatred (adosa), and non-delusion (amoha)' to show them by way of name. To this extent, since there is no wholesome state that is free from a root, the King of Dhamma (the Buddha) showed the wholesome states of the four planes by exhaustively encompassing them within these three roots.

'Associated with that' means the states associated with non-greed and the others. Among those, in the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) associated with non-greed, non-hatred and non-delusion are also included in the count of the aggregate of mental formations associated with non-greed. The same method applies to the association by way of the remaining two (non-hatred and non-delusion). Thus, the King of Dhamma again showed the wholesome states of the four planes by exhaustively encompassing them by way of the four aggregates associated with them. 'Originated by that' means the states originated by non-greed and the others. By this method also, the King of Dhamma showed those same wholesome states of the four planes by exhaustively encompassing them by way of the three doors of action (kammadvāra). Thus, first, the wholesome states have been shown by exhaustively encompassing them in three instances.

The same method applies to the unwholesome (akusala). Since not even a single mind among the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses is free from a root, the King of Dhamma showed them by exhaustively encompassing them by way of roots. Since there is no unwholesome state beyond the four aggregates associated with them, He showed those same twelve unwholesome consciousnesses by exhaustively encompassing them by way of the four aggregates. Because the occurrence of these unwholesome consciousnesses is evident by way of bodily action and so on, the King of Dhamma showed them by exhaustively encompassing them by way of the doors of action.

In this Exposition of the Unwholesome, in the statement beginning with 'and the defilements (kilesa) that stand in the same place as those,' the decision (viniicchaya) should be understood. Standing in a single consciousness or in a single person is called 'standing in one' (ekaṭṭha). Among these, standing in a single consciousness is called 'co-nascent standing in one' (sahajekaṭṭha). Standing in a single person is called 'standing in one regarding abandonment' (pahānekaṭṭha). Because they stand in one place together with greed and so on, or with other states mentioned in various places, they are called 'standing in the same place as those' (tad-ekaṭṭha).

Regarding such standing, in the Triad of the Defiled (Saṅkiliṭṭha-ttika): 'Which states are defiled and subject to defilement? The three unwholesome roots—greed, hatred, and delusion—and the defilements that stand in the same place as those.' In the Triad of the Inferior (Hīna-ttika): 'Which states are inferior? The three unwholesome roots—greed, hatred, and delusion—and the defilements that stand in the same place as those.' 'Which states are unwholesome? The three unwholesome roots—greed, hatred, and delusion—and the defilements that stand in the same place as those...'
381:
In this Wholesome Triad (Kusala-ttika); and in the Cluster of Defilements (Kilesa-gocchaka): 'Which states are defilements? The three unwholesome roots—greed, hatred, and delusion—and the defilements that stand in the same consciousness as those roots'; and in the Couplet of Things with Conflict (Saraṇa-duka): 'Which states are with conflict? The three unwholesome roots—greed, hatred, and delusion—and the defilements that stand in the same consciousness as those roots'—in these many instances, the sense of 'co-nascent standing in one' (sahajekaṭṭha) is intended.

However, in the Triad of Things to be Abandoned by Vision (Dassanena-pahātabba-ttika): 'These three fetters and the defilements that stand in the same person as those fetters by way of being abandoned together'; and in the Triad of Things having Roots to be Abandoned by Vision (Dassanena-pahātabba-hetuka-ttika): 'These three fetters and the defilements abandoned together with those fetters'; and again in that same place: 'The three fetters—personality view, doubt, and adherence to rules and rituals—these states are to be abandoned by vision; the greed, hatred, and delusion abandoned together with them are the roots to be abandoned by vision; the defilements abandoned together with them and the aggregate of feeling... p... the aggregate of consciousness associated with those states, and the bodily action, verbal action, and mental action originated by those states—these states are those having roots to be abandoned by vision'; and in the Analysis of Right Strivings (Sammappadhāna-vibhaṅga): 'Therein, which are the evil unwholesome states? The three unwholesome roots—greed, hatred, and delusion—and the defilements abandoned together with those roots'—in these many instances, it should be understood that the sense of 'standing in one regarding abandonment' (pahānekaṭṭha) is intended.

The exposition of the indeterminate (abyākata) term is quite clear in its meaning. In this triad, it is said that the three characteristics, the three designations, the space obtained by removing a kasina, the open sky, the space which is the object of the sphere of nothingness, and the attainment of cessation are not obtained.

In the Exposition of the Triad of Feeling (Vedanā-ttika-niddesa), in the phrase 'in the ground of pleasure' (sukhabhūmiyaṃ): just as when one says 'copper-colored soil' or 'black soil,' only the copper-colored or black soils themselves are meant, so too, pleasant feeling itself is called 'the ground of pleasure.' Just as when one says 'sugarcane ground' or 'rice ground,' the places where sugarcane and rice arise are meant, so too, the consciousness which is the place where pleasure arises is called 'the ground of pleasure.' Here, the consciousness which is the place where pleasure arises is intended. Since that pleasant feeling occurs either in the sense sphere (kāmāvacara) or in the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) and so on, the phrase 'in the sense sphere' and so on is stated to show the varieties of that pleasure. 'Excluding pleasant feeling' means excluding that pleasant feeling which exists in the ground of pleasure. 'Associated with that' means associated with that excluded pleasant feeling. In the remaining two terms as well, the meaning should be understood by this same method.
382:
In this Triad of Feeling (Vedanā-ttika), this group of states—namely the three feelings, all matter, and Nibbāna—is also not obtained. This is because this triad is free from those states not obtained in the Triad of Wholesome States (Kusala-ttika) and from these three groups starting with the three feelings. Whatever should be said regarding the subsequent Triads and Dyads, both in terms of text and meaning, has already been stated in the order of terms in the Matika-katha and in the description (Niddesa) of terms such as 'wholesome' (kusala). I shall speak only where there is a specific distinction.

Among those, first in the Triad of Result (Vipāka-ttika): although material phenomena, like mental phenomena, have kamma as their cause (samuṭṭhāna), they do not resemble kamma because they do not take an object (anārammaṇattā). Therefore, only mental phenomena, which take an object, are called 'result' (vipāka) because they resemble kamma, just as a fruit resembles its seed. Indeed, when rice seed is sown, although sprouts, leaves, etc., emerge, they are not called 'rice fruit' (grain). Only when the ear of rice is ripe and matured is the rice, which resembles the seed, called 'rice fruit'. Sprouts, leaves, etc., are merely said to be 'produced from the seed' because they arise from it. Similarly, it is appropriate to call matter 'kamma-born' (kammaja) or 'clung-to' (upādinna).

In the Triad of Clung-to (Upādinna-ttika), although the aggregates of an Arahant become the object for the grasping (upādāna) of others who say, 'Our maternal uncle thera, our paternal uncle thera,' the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna are not grasped and not misapprehended; thus they are only 'unclung-to' (anupādinna). Just as a large iron ball heated all day does not provide a place for flies to land, these states, due to their intense brilliance, do not become objects for grasping through craving, conceit, or views. Therefore, it is said: 'These states are unclung-to and not-graspable (anupādinna-anupādāniya).'

The same method should be understood for the Triad of Undefiled and Not-defiling (Asaṃkiliṭṭha-asaṃkilesika).

In the Triad of Initial Application (Vitakka-ttika), sustained application (vicāra) arising together with initial application, along with those states not obtained in the Triad of Wholesome States, are also not obtained.

In the Triad of Accompanied by Rapture (Pītisahagata-ttika), states such as rapture (pīti), having given the state of being accompanied by rapture to their co-nascent states, themselves become those who turn back. In this triad, two...
383:
...consciousness accompanied by displeasure (domanassa-sahagata), body-consciousness accompanied by pain (dukkha-sahagata), neutral feeling (upekkhā-vedanā), matter, and Nibbāna—these states are also not obtained (in this triad). In fact, this triad is said to be free from the states not obtained in the Triad of Wholesome States and from these five groups (koṭṭhāsa).

In the Triad of Things to be Abandoned by Vision (Dassanena-pahātabba-ttika), 'fetters' (saṃyojana) means bonds (that bind to the three realms). 'Personality belief' (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) is the view regarding the group (kāya) known as the five aggregates, which exists in the sense of being real (sati). Or, it is called 'sakkāya-diṭṭhi' because it is a view regarding that group of five aggregates which is itself real. The view that assumes and adheres to the idea that 'one can be purified by virtue (sīla), one can be purified by vows (vata), one can be purified by virtue and vows,' which are not causes for purification, is called 'adherence to rites and rituals' (sīlabbata-parāmāsa).

The word 'idha' (here) is an indeclinable (nipāta) used to indicate a location (desa). In some places, this word 'idha' is used in reference to the world (loka). As it is said: 'A Tathāgata arises here in the world.' In some places, it refers to the Dispensation (sāsana). As it is said: 'Monks, only here is there a recluse (Sotāpanna), here a second recluse (Sakadāgāmi).' In some places, it refers to a place (okāsa). As it is said:
'Standing right here, I who have become a deva,
Have gained the Dhamma, and have gained life again;
Know thus, O dear one.'
In some places, it is used merely as an expletive to fill the verse (padapūraṇa). As it is said: 'Monks, I here would be one who has eaten and is satisfied.' In this context, however, it should be understood as referring to the world.

In the phrase 'uninstructed worldling' (assutavā puthujjana), one is known as 'uninstructed' (assutavā) due to the absence of learning (āgama) and realization (adhigama). For one who lacks the study (uggaha), inquiry (paripucchā), and investigation (vinicchaya) regarding the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), dependent origination (paccayākāra), foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), etc., there is no 'learning' (āgama) which prevents wrong views. Because the Path and Fruition to be attained through practice have not been attained, there is no 'realization' (adhigama). Such a person is known as 'uninstructed' due to the absence of learning and realization. This person—

Is called a 'worldling' (puthujjana) because of many reasons,
Is called a 'worldling' because of being included among the many,
Is called a 'worldling' because of being a person separate from the Noble Ones.

Indeed, he is a worldling because of reasons such as generating many and various defilements. As it is said: 'They are worldlings because they generate many defilements. They are worldlings because they have many unabandoned personality beliefs. They are worldlings because they look up to the faces of many teachers. They are worldlings because they have not emerged from many destinations (gati). They are worldlings because they perform many volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra)...'
384:
What is meant by 'worldlings' (puthujjanas)? They are called worldlings because they are carried away by various floods (oghas). They are called worldlings because they are tormented by various burnings (santāpas). They are called worldlings because they are scorched by various fevers of defilements (pariḷāhas). They are called worldlings because they are attached to, greedy for, obsessed with, infatuated by, immersed in, clinging to, and oppressed by the many five cords of sensual pleasure (kāmagunas). They are called worldlings because they are obstructed, hindered, closed in from below, closed in from above, covered, and overturned by the many five hindrances (nīvaraṇas)—thus it is stated in the Mahāniddesa. 

Alternatively, they are called worldlings because they are included among the many people who have exceeded the count [of those who can be saved], who have turned their backs on the Dhamma of the Noble Ones, and who practice base conduct. Alternatively, a worldling is one who is counted as separate and distinct from the Noble Ones who are endowed with qualities such as virtue (sīla) and learning (suta). Thus, regarding the two types of worldlings intended by the phrase 'an uninstructed worldling':

"The Buddha, the kinsman of the Sun, has taught two kinds of worldlings:
The blind worldling is one, and the virtuous worldling is the other."

Among these two kinds of worldlings, it should be understood that the 'blind worldling' (andhaputhujjana) is intended here.

In the phrases such as 'one who does not see the Noble Ones' (ariyānaṃ adassāvī), the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha are called 'Noble Ones' (ariyas) because they are far from defilements, because they do not lead beings into harmful practices, because they lead them into beneficial practices, and because they are to be approached by the world including the devas. Alternatively, in this context, only the Buddhas are intended as 'Noble Ones'. As it is said: "Monks, in the world with its devas... the Tathāgata is called the Noble One."

In the term 'virtuous persons' (sappurisas), however, the Paccekabuddhas and the disciples of the Tathāgata should be understood as 'virtuous persons'. They are called 'virtuous persons' because they are excellent men endowed with supramundane qualities. Alternatively, all these individuals are referred to by both terms. For the Buddhas are both Noble Ones and virtuous persons; the Paccekabuddhas and the disciples of the Buddha are likewise. As it is said:

"He who is grateful and appreciative, who is wise,
Who has good friends and is firm in devotion,
Who respectfully performs the duties for one in distress,
Such a person is called a virtuous man (sappurisa)."
385:
"Having good friends and being firm in devotion"—by these words, the disciple of the Buddha is referred to. By qualities such as gratitude, the Paccekabuddhas and the Buddhas are referred to.

Now, the person who does not habitually see those Noble Ones and does not show respect when seeing them should be understood as "one who does not see the Noble Ones." There are two types: one who does not see with the eye and one who does not see with knowledge. Of these two, the one who does not see with knowledge is intended here. Indeed, even if one sees the Noble Ones with the fleshly eye (māṃsacakkhu) or the divine eye (dibbacakkhu), it is as if they are not seen. This is because those eyes can only perceive the appearance and cannot perceive the state of being a Noble One. Even domestic dogs, jackals, and so on see the Noble Ones with their eyes, but they cannot be called "seers of the Noble Ones."

In this regard, there is this story: It is said that an elderly monk who was the attendant of an Arahant elder residing on Cittalapabbata was walking for alms with the elder one day. While following behind, carrying the elder's bowl and robes, he asked, "Venerable sir, what are the Noble Ones like?" The elder replied, "Friend, some elderly monk in this Dispensation, even while carrying the bowl and robes of the Noble Ones, performing all the major and minor duties, and traveling together with them, still does not know the Noble Ones. Friend, the Noble Ones are thus difficult to know." Even when told this, that monk did not understand. Therefore, seeing with the eye is not "seeing"; only seeing with the eye of knowledge is "seeing." As the Blessed One said: "Vakkali, what is the use to you of seeing this foul body? Vakkali, he who sees the Dhamma sees me." Therefore, even if one sees with the eye, if one does not see with knowledge the characteristics such as impermanence (anicca) seen by the Noble Ones, does not attain the Dhamma attained by the Noble Ones, and does not see the qualities that make one a Noble One or the state of being a Noble One, he should be understood as "one who does not see the Noble Ones."

"Unskilled in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones" (ariyadhammassa akovido) means one who is not proficient in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones, which is divided into the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and so forth. Regarding "undisciplined in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones" (ariyadhamme avinīto):

Discipline is of two kinds, and each of these is fivefold;
Because of the absence of that discipline, this person is called "undisciplined".

This discipline (vinaya) is of two kinds: the discipline of restraint (saṃvara-vinaya) and the discipline of abandonment (pahāna-vinaya). In these two kinds of discipline, each is further divided into five. The discipline of restraint is fivefold: restraint by virtue (sīla-saṃvara), restraint by mindfulness (sati-saṃvara), restraint by knowledge (ñāṇa-saṃvara), restraint by patience (khanti-saṃvara), and restraint by energy (vīriya-saṃvara). The discipline of abandonment is also fivefold: abandonment by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna), abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna), abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna), abandonment by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi-pahāna), and abandonment by escape (nissaraṇa-pahāna).
386:
Among those (disciplines), 'He is endowed, fully endowed with this restraint of the Pātimokkha'—this is restraint by virtue (sīla-saṃvara). 'He guards the eye faculty, he attains restraint in the eye faculty'—this is restraint by mindfulness (sati-saṃvara).

Ajita, whatever streams there are in the world,
Mindfulness is their obstruction.
I call it the restraint of the streams;
By wisdom they are shut off.

This is called restraint by knowledge (ñāṇa-saṃvara). 'He is one who endures cold and heat'—this is restraint by patience (khanti-saṃvara). 'He does not tolerate (endure) an arisen sensual thought'—this is restraint by energy (vīriya-saṃvara). All this restraint is called 'restraint' (saṃvara) because it blocks and prevents bodily misconduct and so on that should be restrained and removed according to their respective natures, and it is called 'discipline' (vinaya) because it removes them. Thus, first, it should be understood that 'discipline of restraint' (saṃvara-vinaya) is of five kinds.

Furthermore, in the insight knowledges such as the discernment of mentality-materiality, there is the abandoning of various disadvantages (defilements) by each insight knowledge because they are opposites, just as darkness is abandoned by the light of a lamp. That is to say: the abandoning of personality belief (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) by the discernment of mentality-materiality; of the views of no-cause and wrong-cause by the grasping of conditions; of doubt (vicikicchā) by the knowledge of overcoming doubt which occurs subsequent to that; of the obsession of 'I' and 'mine' by the comprehension of groups; of the perception of the path in what is not the path by the discernment of path and non-path; of the view of annihilation by the vision of arising; of the view of eternity by the vision of passing away; of the perception of fearlessness in what is fearful by the vision of fear; of the perception of gratification by the vision of danger; of the perception of delight by the contemplation of disenchantment; of the desire not to be liberated by the knowledge of desire for deliverance; of the lack of equanimity by the knowledge of equanimity; of the state of being contrary to the stability of Dhamma and Nibbāna by the knowledge of conformity; and of the grasping of the signs of formations by the change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa). This is called 'abandoning by substitution of opposites' (tadaṅga-pahāna).

The abandoning of various hindrances and other states by concentration, consisting of access and absorption, by preventing their occurrence, just as moss on the surface of water is pushed aside by hitting it with a pot—this is called 'abandoning by suppression' (vikkhambhana-pahāna). 'Because of the development of the four noble paths...'
387:
...for the purpose of abandoning the views in one's own continuity by one who possesses the respective path,' and so on—the abandoning of the group of defilements belonging to the side of origination by way of absolute non-occurrence as stated in the manner (of the Dhammasaṅgaṇī) is called 'abandoning by cutting off' (samuccheda-pahāna). The tranquilization of defilements at the moment of fruition is called 'abandoning by tranquilization' (paṭippassaddhi-pahāna). Nibbāna, which has abandoned all conditioned things because of its escape from all conditioned things, is called 'abandoning by escape' (nissaraṇa-pahāna). All this abandoning is called 'abandoning' (pahāna) in the sense of giving up, and 'discipline' (vinaya) in the sense of removing (wrong occurrence). Therefore, it is called 'discipline of abandoning' (pahāna-vinaya). Or else, it is called 'discipline of abandoning' because that respective discipline (removal) occurs for the person who possesses that respective abandoning. Thus, it should be understood that 'discipline of abandoning' is also of five kinds.

Thus, this discipline, which is of two kinds in brief and ten kinds in detail, does not exist for the uninstructed worldling because his restraint is broken and because the things to be abandoned have not yet been abandoned. Because of the absence of that discipline, he is called 'undisciplined' (avinīta). In the passage, 'one who does not see the good persons, who is unskilled in the Dhamma of the good persons, who is undisciplined in the Dhamma of the good persons,' it should be understood in this same way. In terms of meaning, these terms have no difference. As it is said: 'Those who are Noble Ones (Ariyas) are themselves the Good Persons (Sappurisas); those who are Good Persons are themselves the Noble Ones. That which is the Dhamma of the Noble Ones is itself the Dhamma of the Good Persons; that which is the Dhamma of the Good Persons is itself the Dhamma of the Noble Ones. That which is the Discipline of the Noble Ones is itself the Discipline of the Good Persons; that which is the Discipline of the Good Persons is itself the Discipline of the Noble Ones. Whether called Noble One or Good Person, Dhamma of the Noble Ones or Dhamma of the Good Persons, Discipline of the Noble Ones or Discipline of the Good Persons—all these have one meaning, the same nature, the same part, and are of that very kind.'

'He regards form as self' means that here, a certain person regards form as self: 'What is form, that is I; what is I, that is form.' He regards form and self as non-dual. 'Just as when a lamp is burning, one regards the flame and the color as non-dual, thinking: what is the flame, that is the color; what is the color, that is the flame,' even so, here a certain person regards form as self. Thus, he sees with the vision of (wrong) view that form is self. Or else, taking 'the formless is self,' he regards the self as possessing form, like a tree possessing a shadow. Or else, taking 'only the formless is self,' he regards form as being in the self, like a scent in a flower.
388:
In the view "the self is in form," one takes mentality alone as "self" and regards the self as being in form, like a gem in a casket. The same method should be understood for feeling and the others.

Among those [twenty views], by the phrase "one regards form as self," only pure form is called "self." In these seven instances: "the self possessing form," "form in the self," "the self in form," "one regards feeling as self," "...perception as self," "...volitional formations as self," and "...consciousness as self," mentality is called "self." In the twelve instances—three for each of the remaining four aggregates—such as "the self possessing feeling," "feeling in the self," and "the self in feeling," the "self consisting of a mixture of form and mentality" is spoken of.

Among those, in these five instances: "one regards form as self," "...feeling as self," "...perception as self," "...volitional formations as self," and "...consciousness as self," the view of annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi) is spoken of. In the remaining fifteen instances, the view of eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi) is spoken of. Thus, in this context, there are fifteen views of existence (bhava-diṭṭhi) and five views of non-existence (vibhava-diṭṭhi). It should be understood that all these views obstruct the Path, but they do not obstruct [rebirth in] heaven; they are abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry.

"One doubts the Teacher" means one doubts either the physical body of the Teacher, or his qualities, or both. One who doubts the physical body doubts: "Does the physical body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man really exist or not?" One who doubts his qualities doubts: "Does the Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) capable of knowing the past, future, and present really exist or not?" One who doubts both doubts: "Does the Buddha, the Savior of the world, who is endowed with the perfection of a physical body beautified by the eighty minor marks and a fathom-wide radiance, and who stands having penetrated the Omniscient Knowledge capable of knowing all knowable things, really exist or not?" For this person, because of doubting either the physical body or the qualities, it is called doubting both.

"Vicikicchati" means being fatigued due to the inability to decide on an object. "Nādhimuccati" means not obtaining a decision on that very object. "Na sampasīdati" means being unable to become clear by making the mind free from turbidity, or not having faith in the qualities.

In the passage "one doubts the Dhamma," etc., one who doubts: "Do the four Noble Paths that abandon the defilements exist or not? Do the four Fruits of Recluseship where defilements are stilled exist or not? Does the Great Nibbāna, the Deathless, which is the object and condition for the Paths and Fruits, exist or not?" or one who doubts: "Is this Dhamma leading out [of Saṃsāra] or not?" [doubts] the Dhamma...
389:
...doubts the Saṅgha. One who doubts: "Does this Jewel of the Saṅgha, consisting of the four pairs of persons established in the Paths and the four pairs of persons established in the Fruits, exist or not?" or one who doubts: "Has this Saṅgha practiced well or practiced wrongly?" or one who doubts: "Is there a result and fruit of gifts given to this Jewel of the Saṅgha or not?" is said to doubt the Saṅgha.
