One who doubts: "Do the three trainings exist or not?" or one who doubts: "Is there a benefit due to the practice of the three trainings or not?" is said to doubt the training.

The past aggregates, elements, and bases are called the "beginning" (pubbanta). The future ones are called the "end" (aparanta). Therein, one who doubts regarding the past aggregates, etc., "Did they exist in the past or not?" is said to doubt the beginning. One who doubts regarding the future ones, "Will they exist in the future or not?" is said to doubt the end. One who doubts regarding both is said to doubt the beginning and the end. One who doubts: "Does the twelve-linked round of conditions exist or not?" is said to doubt the dependently arisen phenomena through specific conditionality (idappaccayatā-paṭiccasamuppanna). Herein, this is the word-definition: the conditions for these [phenomena] such as aging and death are "idappaccaya" (this-condition). The state of these "this-conditions" is "idappaccayatā" (specific conditionality). Or, the "this-conditions" themselves are "idappaccayatā"; this is a designation for birth (jāti) and so on. Because they arise depending on and arriving at various conditions in birth and so on, they are called "dependently arisen" (paṭiccasamuppanna). This is the meaning: one doubts both specific conditionality and dependently arisen phenomena.

"By precepts" (sīlena) refers to cow-habits and the like. "By vows" (vatena) refers to cow-vows and the like. "By precepts and vows" (sīlabbatena) refers to both. "Purity" (suddhi) means purity from defilements, or Nibbāna itself which is the ultimate purity. "Sharing the same state" (tadekaṭṭha) here emphasizes the state of being abandoned together. In this Pali text, only two defilements appear: the defilement of wrong view and the defilement of doubt. However, these eight—greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing—do not appear directly. But they should be brought in and shown. For here, when wrong view and doubt are abandoned, all those—greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing—that lead to the planes of misery are also abandoned, as they share the same state of abandonment (pahānekaṭṭha). However, the state of sharing the same co-arising (sahajekaṭṭha) should be brought in and shown. By the Path of Stream-entry, five consciousnesses are abandoned: four associated with wrong view and one associated with doubt. Therein, when the two unprompted consciousnesses associated with wrong view are abandoned, the defilements co-arising with them—greed, delusion, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing—are abandoned by way of sharing the same state of co-arising (sahajekaṭṭha). The remaining defilement of wrong view and defilement of doubt are abandoned by way of sharing the same state of abandonment (pahānekaṭṭha). Also, when the prompted consciousnesses associated with wrong view are abandoned, the greed co-arising with them...
390:
Delusion, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing—these defilements are abandoned by way of existing together in the same thought-arising (sahajekaṭṭha) [with wrong view]. The remaining defilements of wrong view (diṭṭhi) and doubt (vicikicchā) are abandoned by way of existing in the same person (pahānekaṭṭha) in terms of abandonment. Thus, the teachers showed this sahajekaṭṭha by bringing it in, saying that sahajekaṭṭha is obtained only within pahānekaṭṭha.

'Associated with that' (taṃsampayutta) refers to the states associated with those eight defilements that exist in the same person (pahānekaṭṭha). Alternatively, by way of analysis, the state of being associated with each individual defilement should be shown, such as 'associated with that greed' or 'associated with that hatred.' Among those defilements, when greed (lobha) is taken, the group of defilements included in the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha)—namely delusion, conceit, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing—is called 'associated with greed.' When hatred (dosa) is taken, the group of defilements—namely delusion, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing—is called 'associated with hatred.' When delusion (moha) is taken, the group of defilements—namely greed, hatred, conceit, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing—is called 'associated with delusion.' When conceit (māna) is taken, the group of defilements arising together with that conceit—namely greed, delusion, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing—is called 'associated with conceit.' In this manner, the connection should be made as 'associated with that' (taṃsampayutta) for states associated with that sloth, that restlessness, that shamelessness, and that fearlessness of wrongdoing. 'Originated by that' (taṃsamuṭṭhānaṃ) means originated by that greed... originated by that fearlessness of wrongdoing.

In the phrase 'these states are to be abandoned by vision' (dassanena pahātabba), 'vision' (dassana) refers to the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga); the meaning is that they are to be abandoned by that Path of Stream-entry. If it is asked, 'Why is the Path of Stream-entry called vision?' the answer is, 'Because of seeing Nibbāna for the first time.' If it is asked, 'Does not the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) see it first?' the answer is, 'It is not that it does not see it; it does see it. However, even though it sees it, it cannot perform the required task because it does not abandon the fetters (saṃyojana); therefore, it should not be said that it "sees."' A person from the countryside serves as an illustration here: even if he sees the king in some place, if he cannot complete his business by presenting a gift, he says, 'Even to this day, I have not yet seen the king.'

'The remaining greed' (avaseso lobho) refers to the greed remaining after what is abandoned by vision. The same method applies to hatred and delusion. In truth, only those defilements leading to states of woe (apāyagamanīya) are abandoned by vision. This is stated to show the other defilements apart from those leading to states of woe. 'Existing in the same place' (tadekaṭṭhā) refers to the five defilements that exist in the same person, either because of association with those three defilements mentioned in the Pāḷi or because of being abandoned [along with them]. The phrase 'neither by vision nor by development' (neva dassanena na bhāvanāya) refers to the fetters, etc...
391:
...it is said with reference to the fact that they are not to be abandoned by those paths. Furthermore, in such passages as: 'By the cessation of kamma-formative consciousness (abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa) through the knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry, those mental and physical phenomena (nāmarūpa) that would have arisen in the beginningless cycle of saṃsāra, except for seven lives, cease here [in those seven lives],' the abandonment of wholesome states and so on is also permitted. It should be understood that this is said with reference to the explanation that those states which would have arisen because those paths were not developed are [now] abandoned because the defilements which are their strong dependence conditions (upanissayapaccaya) have been abandoned.

In the Triad of States with Roots to be Abandoned by Vision (dassanenapahātabbahetuka-tika), after concluding with 'these states have roots to be abandoned by vision,' and then showing the states to be abandoned starting with 'the three fetters,' it is stated in order to show the roots (hetu) and the states with roots (sahetuka) by way of their existing in the same thought-arising or in the same person as those abandoned states. Among those roots and states with roots, regarding the roots to be abandoned by vision: delusion associated with greed is 'with roots' (sahetuka) because of greed; delusion associated with hatred is 'with roots' because of hatred; and greed and hatred are 'with roots' because of delusion. Therefore, these are included in the term 'states with roots to be abandoned by vision.' However, delusion associated with doubt (vicikicchā), because it lacks any other associated root, is a root only and is not 'with roots.' To show the abandonment of that delusion associated with doubt, it is said, 'these states are roots to be abandoned by vision.'

In the second clause, to show the abandonment of delusion associated with restlessness (uddhacca), it is said, 'these states are roots to be abandoned by development' (bhāvanāya pahātabbahetū). For that [delusion associated with restlessness] makes the states associated with itself 'with roots' and becomes the 'back-turner' (piṭṭhivaṭṭaka). Like the delusion associated with doubt, because it lacks any other associated root, it does not fall under the term 'states with roots to be abandoned.' In the third clause, the inclusion of 'unwholesome' (akusala) again in 'the remaining unwholesome states' is done to encompass the delusions associated with doubt and restlessness. For those, lacking an associated root, are not called 'states with roots to be abandoned.'

In the Triad of Limited Objects (parittārammaṇa-tika), 'having started' (ārabbha) means having made an object. Whether they themselves are limited (paritta) or exalted (mahaggata), states that arise having made limited states their object are called 'having limited objects.' States that arise having made exalted states their object are called 'having exalted objects.' States that arise having made immeasurable (appamāṇa) [supramundane] states their object are called 'having immeasurable objects.' Furthermore, those [states that take such objects] can themselves be limited, exalted, or immeasurable.
392:
## Micchattattika
In the Triad of Wrongness (Micchattattika), 'actions with immediate result' (ānantarika-kamma) refers to those states that yield their fruit without any obstacle; this is a designation for matricide (mātughātaka-kamma) and so forth. Indeed, if any one of those actions is committed, no other action is able to block it and create an opportunity for its own ripening. Even if one were to build golden pagodas as large as Mount Sineru, or construct a monastery with a jeweled wall as vast as the universe and, having filled it, offer the four requisites for life to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, that wholesome kamma would still be unable to block the ripening of these ānantarika-kammas. 'Fixed wrong view' (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi) refers to any one of the view of non-causality (ahetuka-vāda), the view of non-action (akiriya-vāda), or nihilism (natthika-vāda). A person firmly holding such a wrong view cannot be made to realize the Dhamma even by a hundred or a thousand Buddhas.

## Maggārammaṇattika
In the Triad of Path as Object (Maggārammaṇattika), 'based on the Noble Path' means taking the Supramundane Path (lokuttara-magga) as an object. Those states of the path-object triad are both limited (paritta) and exalted (mahaggata).

## Maggahētuka-niddesa
In the Exposition of Path as Cause (Maggahētuka-niddesa), by the first method, the state of being 'accompanied by cause' (sahetuka) of the aggregates associated with the path is shown by way of the cause acting as a condition. By the second method, the state of being accompanied by cause of the remaining path factors is shown by way of the cause known as Right View (sammādiṭṭhi), which is the path itself. By the third method, it should be understood that the state of being accompanied by cause of Right View is shown by way of the causes arising within the path.

'Making it predominant' means making it an object-predominant (ārammaṇādhipati). And those states are only limited (paritta) states. For noble disciples (ariyasāvaka), object-predominance is obtained at the time of reflecting on their own path with high esteem. However, a noble disciple reflecting on another's path with the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa), even while holding it in high esteem, does not hold it in such high esteem as the path they have personally realized. If it is asked, 'Seeing the Tathāgata performing the Twin Miracle (yamaka-pāṭihāriya), does one hold His path in high esteem or not?', the answer is: one does, but not in the same way as one's own path. An Arahant holds nothing in high esteem except the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna. Here too, this is the meaning. 'Predominance of investigation' (vīmaṃsādhipateyya) is stated to show conascent-predominance (sahajātādhipati). For one developing the path by making desire (chanda) the chief, desire is called the predominant, not the path. The remaining states are also called 'having desire as predominant,' not 'having path as predominant.' The same method applies to consciousness (citta). But for one developing the path by making investigation (vīmaṃsā/wisdom) the chief, it is both the predominant and the path. The remaining states are then called 'having path as predominant.' The same method applies to energy (vīriya).
393:
In the Exposition of the Triad of Arisen (Uppannattika-niddesa), 'born' (jāta) refers to states that have been produced or have attained their own nature. 'Become' (bhūta) and so forth are merely synonyms for them. Indeed, states that are 'born' are called 'become' because they have reached the state of existence. They are called 'well-born' (sañjāta) because they are born from the combination of conditions. They are called 'produced' (nibbatta) because they have reached the characteristic of production. With the addition of a prefix to the word, they are called 'fully produced' (abhinibbatta). They are called 'manifested' (pātubhūta) because they have appeared clearly. They are called 'arisen' (uppanna) because they have reached the three sub-moments above the previous limit. With a prefix, they are called 'fully arisen' (samuppanna). They are called 'uprisen' (uṭṭhita) because they stand above the previous limit by the nature of production alone. They are called 'well-uprisen' (samuṭṭhita) because they stand above the previous limit due to the combination of conditions. The reason for stating 'arisen' again should be understood according to the method mentioned below. 'Included in the portion of the arisen' (uppannāṃsena saṅgahitā) refers to states that are counted within the category of the arisen. The statement 'matter, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness' is a demonstration of the intrinsic nature of these arisen states. The exposition of the second term (un-arisen/anuppanna) should be understood by the method of negation already mentioned. The exposition of the third term (about to arise/uppādī) has a clear meaning.

This triad is shown by completing it through the power of two periods: the present and the future. The result (vipāka) of a kamma that has gained an opportunity is of two kinds: that which has reached the moment (khaṇappatta) and that which has not reached it (appatta). Therein, that which has reached the moment is called 'arisen' (uppanna). That which has not reached the moment—whether it arises immediately after a thought or after the passing of a hundred thousand aeons—is not called 'non-existent' (not anuppanna) because of its nature of having a certain condition; it is called 'born' (jāta) as 'states about to arise' (uppādino dhammā). For example: 'Poṭṭhapāda, the self consisting of perception, which is called the formless life-continuum, just stands (exists). Even so, other perceptions arise and other perceptions cease for this person.' In this Pali passage, although the original formless life-continuum perception has ceased while sense-sphere perception is occurring in the formless realm, it will definitely arise when the sense-sphere perception ceases. Therefore, the self known as the formless life-continuum is not counted as 'non-existent' but is called 'just standing.' Similarly, the result of a kamma that has gained an opportunity is of two kinds... it is not called 'non-existent' because of its nature of having a certain condition; it is called 'born' as 'states about to arise.'

If all wholesome and unwholesome kamma that has been accumulated were to give results, there would be no opportunity for others. That accumulated kamma is of two kinds: kamma with certain result (dhuva-vipāka) and kamma with uncertain result (adhuva-vipāka). Therein, the five ānantarika-kammas, the eight attainments (samāpatti), and the four Noble Paths are called 'kamma with certain result.' That kamma may have reached the moment or not yet reached it. Therein, that which has reached the moment is called 'arisen.' That which has not yet reached it is called 'un-arisen.' Its result—whether it arises immediately after a thought or after a hundred thousand aeons—is not called 'un-arisen' because of its nature of having a certain condition; it is called 'born' as 'states about to arise.' The Path of the Bodhisatta Metteyya is called 'un-arisen,' but its Fruit is called 'born' as 'states about to arise.'
394:
In the exposition of the Past Triad, 'past' refers to those things that have passed through the three sub-moments. 'Niruddha' (ceased) refers to those that have reached cessation. 'Vigata' (vanished) refers to those that have reached destruction or have disappeared. 'Vipariṇata' (transformed) refers to those that have undergone change by abandoning their natural state. They are called 'atthaṅgata' (disappeared) because they have reached destruction, which is termed cessation. 'Abbhatthaṅgata' is the term expanded by the power of a prefix. Because they have disappeared after arising, they are said to have 'arisen and vanished.' The reason for mentioning the word 'past' again has already been stated below. The same method should be understood for the 'future' and so on that follow. 'Gathered by the past portion' means those that are counted within the past category. What are those past things? They are: form (rūpa), feeling (vedanā), perception (saññā), mental formations (saṅkhāra), and consciousness (viññāṇa). The same method should be understood for the future and so on that follow.

In the exposition of the Past Object Triad, in the phrase 'taking past things as objects' and so on, only the limited (paritta) and the sublime (mahaggata) states should be understood. Indeed, those limited and sublime states arise by taking the past and so on as objects.

In the exposition of the Internal Triad, by the two words 'of those and those,' the Blessed One includes all beings without exception. Both terms 'internal' (ajjhatta) and 'individual' (paccatta) are designations for what is internal to oneself. 'Niyata' (personal) refers to those things arisen within one's own continuity. 'Pāṭipuggalika' (individual-specific) refers to those things belonging to each individual separately. 'Upādinna' (clung-to) refers to those things residing in the bodies of beings. Whether those things are born of kamma or not, they are called 'upādinna' here by way of being grasped, held, and touched.

'Of other beings' (parasattānaṃ) refers to the states of beings other than oneself. 'Of other persons' (parapuggalānaṃ) is a synonym for that same 'other beings.' The rest is just as stated below. 'Both of those' (tadubhayaṃ) means both of those types.

In the first factor of the Internal Object Triad, the limited and sublime states should be understood. In the second factor, the immeasurable (appamāṇa) states should also be understood. In the third factor, only the limited and sublime states should be understood. The immeasurable states, however, sometimes do not take the external as an object and sometimes do not take the internal as an object. The exposition of the Triad with Visibility (Sanidassana-ttika-niddesa) is clear in its meaning.

## Discussion on the Summary of Dyads (Duka-nikkhepa-kathā)

Among the dyads, in the exposition of non-hatred (adosa), it is called 'metti' (friendship) by way of loving. The mode of loving is 'mettāyanā' (loving). The state of a mind that has gone with mettā and is endowed with mettā...
395:
...is 'mettāyitatta' (the state of having loved). It is called 'anuddā' (compassion) because it protects and pities beings; the meaning is that it protects. The act of protecting is 'anuddāyanā.' The state of a mind that brings about protection is 'anuddāyitatta.' It is called 'hitesitā' (seeking welfare) by way of seeking benefit. It is called 'anukampā' (compassion) by way of supporting and protecting. By all these aforementioned terms, only mettā that has reached access concentration (upacāra) or absorption concentration (appanā) is meant. By the remaining terms, the mundane and supramundane state of non-hatred (adosa) is taught.

In the exposition of non-delusion (amoha), 'knowledge of suffering' (dukkhe ñāṇaṃ) is the wisdom that knows the truth of suffering. The same method applies to the origin of suffering and so on. Among these knowledges of the truth of suffering, etc., the knowledge of suffering occurs in hearing, examining, penetrating, and reviewing. The same applies to the origin of suffering. However, regarding the truth of cessation, it occurs only in hearing, penetrating, and reviewing. The same applies to the truth of the path (paṭipadā). 'In the past' (pubbante) means in the past portion. 'In the future' (aparante) means in the future portion. 'In the past and future' (pubbantāparante) means in both of those. 'Knowledge of things that are dependently originated through specific conditionality' (idappaccayatā paṭiccasamuppannesu dhammesu ñāṇaṃ) is the knowledge of both the causes and the caused things, such as: 'This is the cause, this is the effect; depending on this cause, this effect arises.'

In the exposition of greed (lobha), the meaning of the terms not yet mentioned below is as follows: It is called 'rāga' (lust) by way of being stained. It is called 'sārāga' (intense lust) in the sense of strong staining. It is called 'anunaya' (fawning) because it repeatedly leads beings towards sense objects. It is called 'anurodha' (compliance) because it desires; the meaning is desiring. In any existence whatsoever, beings delight through this craving, or it delights by itself; therefore, it is called 'nandī' (delight). That delight is also 'nandī-rāga' because it is both delight and lust in the sense of staining. Between 'nandī' and 'nandī-rāga,' the craving that arises once for a single object is called 'nandī.' The craving that arises repeatedly is called 'nandī-rāga.' 'Intense lust of the mind' (cittassa sārāgo) means that the greed called 'sārāga' below, in the sense of strong staining, is not the intense lust of a being, but the intense lust of the mind alone.

It is called 'icchā' (wish) because one wishes for objects through this craving. It is called 'mucchā' (infatuation) because beings are infatuated and bewildered by this craving in the form of thick defilement. It is called 'ajjhosāna' (cleaving) by way of grasping after swallowing and finishing. It is called 'gedha' (greed) because beings are greedy and reach greed through this craving; or it is called 'gedha' because of its thick nature. In the phrase 'gedhaṃ vā pavanasandaṃ,' it is mentioned in the sense of being thick. The subsequent term is expanded by the power of a prefix. Greed in every aspect is 'paligedha' (entanglement). It is called 'saṅga' (attachment) because one clings through this craving; or it is 'saṅga' in the sense of clinging. It is called 'paṅka' (mire) in the sense of sinking. It is called 'ejā' (motion/craving) by way of pulling. Indeed, it is said, 'Ejā pulls this man for the production of this or that existence.' It is called 'māyā' (deceit) because of its deceptive nature. Beings in the round of rebirth...
396:
It is called janikā because of its nature to produce. It is said: “Craving gives birth to a person; his mind runs to and fro [between births].” It is called sañjananī because it causes beings to be born in the round of existence, connecting them with suffering. It is called sibbinī because of its nature to sew together. This craving sews together beings in the round of existence by way of death and rebirth, just as a tailor sews old rags together; therefore, it is called sibbinī due to its nature of sewing. It is called jālinī because it has a net of various diverse objects, or because it has a net known as the vibration and preoccupation of craving.

It is called saritā because it draws and carries away, like a river with a swift current. Alternatively, it is called saritā because of its moist nature. It is said: “Flowing and lubricated are the joys of a person.” Here, the meaning is: moist by the power of lust, and sticky by the power of joy associated with lust. It is called visattikā because it is extensive. It is called visattikā because it spreads. It is called visattikā because it is vast and wide. It is called visattikā because it endures. It is called visattikā because it causes deviation. It is called visattikā because it removes the mind from renunciation. It is called visattikā because it brings suffering like poison. It is called visattikā because it is like the root of suffering which is like poison. It is called visattikā because it has the result of suffering which is like poison. It is called visattikā because it consumes only suffering which is like poison. Alternatively, that craving is called visattikā because it is spread out and extensive in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects, as well as in families and groups. It is called sutta because it leads to misfortune and ruin, like a thread that binds dust. It is said: “Monks, suttaka is a name for delight and lust (nandīrāga).” It is called visaṭā because of its nature of being spread out in forms and so on. It is called āyūhinī because it causes beings to strive for the sake of obtaining various objects. It is called dutiyā (companion) because it does not allow one to become weary [of saṃsāra], acting like a friend. This craving does not allow beings to become weary in the round of existence; it makes them delight in whatever place they reach, like a beloved companion. Therefore, it is said:

“A man with craving as his companion,
Wandering for a long time in saṃsāra,
Undergoing this state and that state,
Does not transcend the round of existence.”

It is called paṇidhi by way of aspiration. It is called bhavanetti (the conduit to existence), like a rope of existence. By this craving, beings are pulled to whatever place they desire, like oxen bound by a rope at the neck. It is called vana because it desires, frequents, and clings to various objects. Or, it is called vana because it begs. When the word is expanded by a consonant, it is called vanatha. Because of its nature to produce disadvantageous suffering and because of its nature to obstruct...
397:
It is called vana because it is like a forest; this is a name for strong craving. Craving that is stronger than that vana is called vanatha because of its sense of being more dense. Therefore, it is said:

“Monks, cut down the forest [of craving], not the tree.
From the forest, fear is born.
Having cut down both the forest and the undergrowth (vanatha),
Be monks who are free from the forest.”

It is called santhava by way of intimacy or association; it means connection. That santhava is of two kinds: intimacy through craving and intimacy through friendship. Here, intimacy through craving is intended. It is called sineha by way of stickiness. It is called apekkhā because it looks for [objects] by way of creating attachment. It is also said: “O Great King, these eighty-four thousand cities, headed by the royal capital of Kusāvatī, are your cities. Produce desire in these cities; make an expectation (apekkhā) in life.” Here, the meaning is “create attachment.” It is called paṭibandhu because it binds to various objects. Or, it is called paṭibandhu because it is a separate relative in the sense of a kinsman. In the sense of being constantly relied upon, there is no relative for beings equal to craving.

It is called āsā because it overwhelms objects or because it consumes them. The meaning is: because of overwhelming and because of consuming without reaching satisfaction. It is called āsīsanā by way of longing. The state of one who longs is āsīsitattaṃ. Now, to show the place where that craving arises, “desire for forms” (rūpāsā) and so on are mentioned. In those words like rūpāsā, taking the meaning of āsā as longing, longing for forms is rūpāsā. Thus, the nine terms should be understood. Among these, the first five are spoken of by way of the five cords of sensual pleasure. The sixth is spoken of by way of greed for requisites; this is especially for monks. The three after that are spoken of for laypeople by way of objects that cannot be satisfied. For there is nothing more dear to those laypeople than wealth, children, and life. It is called jappa because it makes beings mutter, “This is mine, this is mine,” or “This was given to me by such a person, this was given.” The next two terms are words expanded by prefixes. After that, because it begins to analyze in another manner, it is called jappa again. The manner of muttering is jappanā. The state of being muttered is jappitattaṃ. It is called lolupa because it plunders or pulls at objects again and again. The state of being lolupa is loluppa. The manner of loluppa is loluppāyanā. The state of one possessed of loluppa is loluppāyitattaṃ.
398:
Puccchañjikatā refers to that craving which wanders about wavering, like a dog wagging its tail at places where gains are expected; it is a name for that wavering craving. One is called 'Sādhukāma' because of desiring good and pleasant objects. The state of being such a Sādhukāma is called 'Sādhukamyatā'. Lust that arises in inappropriate instances, such as towards one's mother or maternal aunt, is called 'Adhammarāga' (unrighteous lust). Greed that arises with great force even in appropriate instances is called 'Visamalobha' (unbalanced greed). Alternatively, according to the teaching 'Rāgo visamaṃ' etc., the lustful desire (chandarāga) that arises in either appropriate or inappropriate instances should be understood as 'Adhammarāga' due to its unrighteous nature, and as 'Visamalobha' due to its uneven nature.

'Nikanti' is attachment by way of desiring objects. The mode of desiring is 'Nikāmanā'. 'Patthanā' is by way of longing. 'Pihanā' is by way of yearning. Intense longing is 'Sampatthanā'. Craving for the five cords of sensual pleasure is 'Kāmatanhā'. Craving for existence in the fine-material and immaterial realms is 'Bhavatanhā'. Craving for non-existence, known as annihilation, is 'Vibhavatanhā'. Craving specifically for fine-material existence is 'Rūpatanhā'. Craving for immaterial existence is 'Arūpatanhā'. Lust accompanied by the view of annihilation is 'Diṭṭhirāga'. Craving for cessation (annihilation) is 'Nirodhatanhā'. Craving for visible forms is 'Rūpatanhā'. Craving for sounds is 'Saddatanhā'. The same method applies to craving for smells and so on. Terms such as 'Ogha' (floods) have the meanings already stated.

It is called 'Āvaraṇa' (obstruction) because it blocks wholesome states. It is called 'Chādana' (covering) by way of its concealing nature. It is called 'Bandhana' (bondage) because it binds beings to the round of suffering (saṃsāra). It is called 'Upakkilesa' (defilement) because it approaches the mind and stains it. It is called 'Anusaya' (latent tendency) because it lies dormant with strength. It is called 'Pariyuṭṭhāna' (obsession/outbreak) because it overwhelms the mind when it arises; it means it takes possession of the course of wholesome conduct by not allowing it to arise. Just as in the phrases 'Robbers took possession of the road, fools took possession of the road' etc., it means they seized the road; similarly here, it should be understood as 'Pariyuṭṭhāna' due to the sense of seizing. It is called 'Latā' (creeper) because it entwines like a vine. In the passage 'The creeper arises and stands,' this craving itself is called 'Latā'. It is called 'Veviccha' (diversified desire) because it desires various objects. It is called 'Dukkhamūla' (root of suffering) because it is the root of the suffering of the round. It is called 'Dukkhanidāna' (source of suffering) because it is the cause of that suffering. It is called 'Dukkhappabhava' (origin of suffering) because that suffering originates from this craving. It is called 'Pāsa' (snare) because it binds like a snare. Because it is the snare of Māra, it is 'Mārapāsa'. It is called 'Baḷisa' (fishhook) because it is like a fishhook, being difficult to swallow. Māra's...
399:
...fish-hook is 'mārabalisa'. Beings overcome by craving cannot transcend the realm of Māra; Māra exercises power over them. For this reason, it is called 'māraviṣaya' (Māra's domain). Craving itself is a river, 'taṇhānadī', in the sense of flowing. Craving itself is a net, 'taṇhājāla', in the sense of overwhelming. Just as dogs bound by a leather leash (gaddula) are led wherever one wishes, so too beings bound by craving are called 'gaddula' because they are firmly bound. Craving itself is the leash, 'taṇhāgaddula'. Craving itself is the ocean, 'taṇhāsamudda', in the sense of being difficult to fill.

In the exposition of hatred (dosa-niddesa), 'He has done me harm' means 'He has caused me lack of benefit.' In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all phrases. 'Resentment in improper places' (aṭṭhānāghāta) means anger without cause—for instance, some people get angry saying, 'The rain falls too much,' or 'It does not rain,' or 'The sun is too hot,' or 'It is not hot.' They get angry when the wind blows, and also when it does not blow. Being unable to sweep, they get angry at the Bodhi leaves. Being unable to robe themselves, they get angry at the wind. Having tripped, they get angry at the tree stump. With reference to such groundless anger, it is said, 'Resentment arises in improper places.' In that regard, among the nine grounds mentioned below, because resentment arises in relation to beings, it constitutes a course of action (kammapatha). However, resentment in improper places (aṭṭhānāghāta) arises in relation to formations (saṅkhāra) and thus does not constitute a course of action. It is called 'cittassa āghāta' (resentment of the mind) because it arises harassing the mind. Hatred stronger than that is 'paṭighāta'. It is 'paṭigha' (repugnance) by way of repeatedly striking. It is 'paṭiviroဓော' (opposition) because it opposes. It is 'kopa' (anger) by way of being angry. 'Pakopa' and 'sampakopa' are terms intensified by prefixes. It is 'dosa' (hatred/corruption) by way of corrupting. 'Padosa' and 'sampadosa' are terms intensified by prefixes. 'Cittassa vyāpatti' (malice of mind) means the corruption of the mind, a state of perversion. It is called 'manopadosa' (mental corruption) because it arises destroying the mind. It is 'kodha' (wrath) by way of being angry. The act of being angry is 'kujjanā'. The state of being angry is 'kujjitatta'.

Now, to show the method mentioned in the exposition of unwholesome states (akusala-niddesa), 'dosa dussanā' etc. is stated. Therefore, the terms stated here such as 'such resentment of the mind... kujjitatta' should be connected here as being the same 'dosa' mentioned below by the method of 'dosa dussanā' etc. Only when connected in this way is the fault of repetition (punaruttidosa) avoided. Exposition of delusion (moha-niddesa), exposition of non-delusion (amoha-niddesa)...
400:
(The exposition of delusion) should be understood by the method opposite to the method already stated in the exposition of non-delusion. In every aspect, however, this exposition of delusion will become clear in the Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā.

"Those states which are associated with causes along with those states" (tehi dhammehi ye dhammā sahetukā) means that other root-causes (hetu) or non-root-causes (na-hetu) that arise together with those root-cause states are called "associated with causes" (sahetuka). In the case of the term "without causes" (ahetuka), the same method applies. Here, a root-cause is called a root-cause (hetu) itself, and when three or two [root-causes] arise together, it is also called "associated with causes" (sahetuka). However, delusion (moha) associated with doubt (vicikicchā) and restlessness (uddhacca) is called a root-cause but is "without causes" (ahetuka). In the exposition of the dyad of states associated with root-causes (hetu-sampayutta-duka-niddesa), the same method should be understood.

In the exposition of the conditioned dyad (saṅkhata-duka-niddesa), referring to the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) mentioned in the previous dyad, the singular expression "that very state which..." (yo eva so dhammo) is used. However, in the previous dyad, because the question was raised in the plural, the plural "these states are without conditions" (ime dhammā appaccayā) is used in accordance with the context of the question. In "these states are with a visible object" (ime dhammā sanidassanā), etc., the same method should be understood.

In the exposition of the dyad of 'cognizable by some' (kenaci viññeyya-duka-niddesa), "cognizable by the eye" (cakkhu-viññeyyā) means states to be known by eye-consciousness. In the remaining terms, the same method should be understood. Here, "cognizable by some" (kenaci viññeyya) means states to be known by any one [consciousness] among eye-consciousness, etc., such as eye-consciousness or ear-consciousness. "Not cognizable by some" (kenaci na viññeyya) means states not to be known by that very eye-consciousness or ear-consciousness. Since it was stated below that "if the meaning is such, it becomes a dyad because of the difference in meaning of the two terms," this dyad "those states which are cognizable by the eye are not those states cognizable by the ear" is not possible. However, taking the meaning that "visible form is cognizable by the eye, but sound is not cognizable by the eye," it should be understood that "those states which are cognizable by the eye are not those states cognizable by the ear, or those states which are cognizable by the ear are not those states cognizable by the eye" is a single dyad. Thus, it should be understood that twenty dyads are analyzed by making each faculty (indriya) a root and forming four dyads for each.

Is it not the case that there are no "states cognizable by some mind-consciousness and not cognizable by some"? Is that why dyads are not taught here? It is not that they do not exist; they are not taught because they cannot be defined by a limit. Just as there is a definition for states that are "not cognizable by eye-consciousness," there is no such definition for mind-consciousness; therefore, dyads are not taught here.
401:
There is this meaning: "some states are cognizable by some mind-consciousness and not cognizable by some." Therefore, although it is not stated (in the Mātikā), it should be understood according to what is applicable (yathālābhavasena). Indeed, among the sense-sphere states (kāmāvacara-dhamma) that come under the designation of mind-consciousness, first of all, sense-sphere states themselves are cognizable by some (sense-sphere states) and not cognizable by some. By those very sense-sphere states, states of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), etc., are also cognizable by some and not cognizable by some. By fine-material sphere states, sense-sphere states are cognizable by some and not cognizable by some. By those very fine-material sphere states, fine-material sphere states, etc., are also cognizable by some and not cognizable by some. By immaterial-sphere states (arūpāvacara), however, sense-sphere states, fine-material sphere states, and supramundane (apariyāpanna) states are not cognizable at all. But immaterial-sphere states are cognizable by some (immaterial-sphere states) and not cognizable by some. And among those, only some are cognizable and some are not. By supramundane states, sense-sphere states, etc., are not cognizable at all. But supramundane states, because they are not cognizable by Nibbāna, are cognizable by some (supramundane states) and not cognizable by some. And among those supramundane states, because they are not cognizable by the Paths and Fruits (magga-phala), only some are cognizable and some are not (this should be understood according to what is applicable).

In the exposition of taints (āsava-niddesa), lust (rāga) occurring in the five strands of sensual pleasure is called the taint of sensuality (kāmāsava). Desire and lust (chanda-rāga) occurring in the fine-material and immaterial existences, attachment to jhāna (jhāna-nikanti), lust associated with the view of eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi), and longing by the power of existence are called the taint of existence (bhavāsava). The sixty-two views are called the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava). Ignorance (aññāṇa/moha) regarding the eight instances is called the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava). To avoid confusion regarding the taints mentioned in various Pali passages, the classifications such as one-fold (ekavidha), etc., should be understood. In reality, by nature, these taints are one-fold (ekavidha) in the sense of being long-stored (cira-pārivāsiya). In the Vinaya Pali, however, they appear as two-fold (duvidha): "for the restraint of taints belonging to the present life, and for the warding off of taints belonging to the future life." In the Saḷāyatana-vagga of the Suttas, they appear as three-fold (tividha): "Friends, these taints are three: the taint of sensuality, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance." In the Nibbedhika-pariyāya Sutta, they appear as five-fold (pañcavidha): "Bhikkhus, there are taints that lead to hell, there are taints that lead to the animal realm, there are taints that lead to the realm of hungry ghosts, there are taints that lead to the human world, and there are taints that lead to the world of devas." In the Āhuneyya Sutta of the Book of the Sixes: "There are taints to be abandoned by restraint (saṃvara), there are taints to be abandoned by using (paṭisevanā), there are taints to be abandoned by enduring (adhivāsanā), there are taints to be abandoned by avoiding (parivajjanā), ..."
402:
“There are taints (āsavas) to be abandoned by dispelling; there are taints to be abandoned by development,” thus they are mentioned in six ways (in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Book of Sixes). In the Sabbāsava Sutta, they are mentioned in seven ways along with those to be abandoned by the path of stream-entry (dassana). In this Abhidhamma, however, these taints are mentioned in four ways, such as the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava) and so forth. Among these, the definition (vacanattha) is as follows: The taint that arises in the five cords of sensual pleasure is called ‘kāmāsava’. The taint that arises in the two types of existence—fine-material existence and immaterial existence—by way of both kamma-existence and rebirth-existence is called ‘bhavāsava’. Wrong view itself is a taint, thus it is called ‘diṭṭhāsava’. Ignorance itself is a taint, thus it is called ‘avijjāsava’.

‘Kāmesu’ refers to the five cords of sensual pleasure. ‘Kāmacchanda’ is the desire (chanda) known as sensuality; it is not the desire to act (kattukamyatā-chanda), nor is it the desire for the Dhamma (dhamma-chanda). Sensuality itself is lust (rāga) by virtue of wanting and attachment, thus it is called ‘kāmārāga’. Sensuality itself is delight (nandī) by virtue of wanting and rejoicing, thus it is called ‘kāmanandī’. In this way, understanding the meaning of sensuality in all contexts, it should be known as ‘kāmataṇhā’ due to the sense of craving, ‘kāmasineha’ due to the sense of attachment, ‘kāmapariḷāha’ due to the sense of burning, ‘kāmamucchā’ due to the sense of infatuation, and ‘kāmajjhosāna’ due to the sense of being swallowed and finished. ‘Ayaṃ vuccati’ refers to the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava) as analyzed by these eight terms.

‘Bhavesu bhavachando’ refers to the desire that arises solely by way of longing for existence in the fine-material and immaterial realms; this is called ‘bhavachanda’. The remaining terms should also be understood in this same manner.

‘Sassato loko’ (The world is eternal) and so forth describes the varieties of wrong view (diṭṭhi) through ten modes. Among those ten, in the phrase ‘sassato loko’, taking the five aggregates as the ‘world’, the view that arises in one who holds that “this world is permanent, stable, and eternal” is the wrong view occurring by way of the mode of grasping it as ‘eternal’. ‘Asassato’ (The world is not eternal) is the wrong view occurring by way of the mode of grasping annihilation in one who holds that very world “is cut off and perishes”. ‘Antavā’ (The world is finite) is the wrong view occurring by way of the mode of grasping that “the world is finite” in one who has attained a limited kasina—the size of a winnowing tray or a pot lid—and takes the mental and material phenomena occurring within that attainment as the world, grasping it as ‘finite’ by the limit of the kasina’s boundary. That view can be both eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi) and annihilationism (ucchedadiṭṭhi). For one who has attained an extensive kasina, taking the mental and material phenomena occurring within that attainment as the world...
403:
...and grasping it as ‘infinite’ by the limit of the kasina’s boundary, this is the wrong view occurring by way of the mode of grasping that “the world is infinite” (anantavā loko). That view can also be both eternalism and annihilationism.

The view “the soul is the same as the body” (taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīraṃ) is annihilationism occurring by way of the mode of grasping that “the soul also perishes” when the body perishes, because the body, which is subject to breaking up, is itself grasped as the ‘soul’. In the second phrase (“the soul is different from the body”), because a soul other than the body is grasped, it is eternalism occurring by way of the mode of grasping that “the soul is not cut off” even when the body perishes. In sentences such as “the Tathāgata exists after death,” a being is called ‘Tathāgata’. For one who holds that this being exists after death, it is the first eternalism. For one who holds that he does not exist, it is the second annihilationism. For one who holds that he both exists and does not exist, it is the third partial-eternalism (ekaccasassatadiṭṭhi). For one who holds that he neither exists nor does not exist, it is the fourth eel-wriggling view (amarāvikkhepadiṭṭhi). “These states are taints” means that by combining this kāmāsava and bhavāsava through the power of lust, these states are called taints—three in brief and four in detail.

Does the desire and lust (chandarāga) that arises for the mansions, wish-fulfilling trees, and ornaments of the Brahmas constitute kāmāsava or not? It does not. Why? Because lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure has already been abandoned here (in the Brahma realms). However, when reaching the Root Group (hetugocchaka), it is called the root of greed (lobha-hetu). When reaching the Tie Group (ganthagocchaka), it is called the bodily tie of covetousness (abhijjhā-kāyagantha). When reaching the Defilement Group (kilesagocchaka), greed is called a defilement (kilesa). Does lust associated with wrong view constitute kāmāsava or not? It does not; it is only called lust for views (diṭṭhirāga). Therefore, it was said: “Gifts given to a person who is infatuated with lust for views are not of great fruit, nor of great benefit” (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.129).

These taints should be presented both by the sequence of defilements and by the sequence of the paths. By the sequence of defilements, kāmāsava is abandoned by the path of non-returning (anāgāmimagga), bhavāsava by the path of arahantship (arahattamagga), diṭṭhāsava by the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga), and avijjāsava by the path of arahantship. By the sequence of the paths, diṭṭhāsava is abandoned by the path of stream-entry, kāmāsava by the path of non-returning, and both bhavāsava and avijjāsava by the path of arahantship.

Among the fetters (saṃyojana), in the description of conceit (māna-niddesa), the conceit “I am superior” (seyyohamasmi) is the conceit that arises in the sense of being excellent, as in “I am better.” “I am equal” (sadisohamasmi)...
404:
Conceit (māna) refers to the conceit that arises in the sense of equality, such as 'I am equal to him' (sadisāmāna). Conceit of inferiority (hīnamāna) refers to the conceit that arises in the sense of being low, such as 'I am inferior.' Thus, these three types of conceit—conceit of superiority (seyyamāna), conceit of equality (sadisāmāna), and conceit of inferiority (hīnamāna)—arise in three types of persons. Indeed, for a superior person, three types of conceit arise: 'I am superior,' 'I am equal,' and 'I am inferior.' The same applies to an equal person and an inferior person. Among these, for a superior person, only the conceit of superiority is a factual conceit (yāthāvamāna), while the other two are non-factual conceits. For an equal person, only the conceit of equality is a factual conceit, while the other two are non-factual conceits. For an inferior person, only the conceit of inferiority is a factual conceit, while the other two are non-factual conceits. What is shown by this statement? It shows that three types of conceit arise for a single individual. However, in the Khuddakavatthu Vibhaṅga, in the first Mānabhājanīya, it is taught that one type of conceit arises for three types of persons.

It is called māna because it performs the function of uplifting and puffing oneself up. The two terms maññanā and maññitatta are words indicating the mode and the nature of conceit. It is called unnati (elevation) because of the sense of rising upwards. When conceit arises in someone, it elevates that person; it is called unnamo (uplifting) because it lifts and holds them up. It is called dhaja (banner) in the sense of flaunting over others. It is called sampaggāho (uplifting) because it lifts the mind from all sides. Among many banners, a very high banner is called ketu (standard). Conceit, as it arises repeatedly, is called ketu because it is like a high standard among banners due to its sense of being very high in relation to subsequent conceits. The desire for conceit that is high like a very high standard is ketukamyā, and the state of that desiring mind is ketukamyatā (desire for a standard). That ketukamyatā is a state of the mind, not of a self (atta). Therefore, it is said, 'Ketukamyatā is a state of the mind.' Indeed, a mind associated with conceit desires conceit that is high like a very high standard. The state of that conceit-associated mind is also called ketukamyatā. This is what is meant by conceit known as ketu.

In the explanation of envy (issā), 'envy regarding others' gain (lābha), honor (sakkāra), reverence (garukāra), respect (mānana), salutation (vandanā), and veneration (pūjanā)' means the mental state characterized by intolerance and dissatisfaction with the prosperity of others, thinking 'What is the use of this for them?' Among these, gain (lābha) means obtaining the four requisites such as robes. Indeed, an envious person is intolerant of another's gain, not wishing for it, thinking 'What is the use of this gain for him?' Honor (sakkāra) means obtaining those same requisites in a good and excellent manner. Reverence (garukāra) means the act of respecting, making it a heavy matter. Respect (mānana) means showing affection with the mind. Salutation (vandanā) means paying homage with the five limbs. Veneration (pūjanā) means worshipping with scents, flowers, and so on. It is called issā because of the act of envying. The mode of envying is issāyanā. The state of being envious is issāyitatta. Usūyā and so on are synonyms for envy (issā).
405:
The characteristic of dissatisfaction (intolerance) of this envy (issā) should be shown in both laypeople and monks. Indeed, a certain layperson, depending on his own effort (manly vigor) through some means of livelihood such as farming or trade, obtains a good cart, a vehicle drawn by elephants or horses, or a jewel. Another person, not wishing for his gain, is dissatisfied with that gain. Thinking, 'When will this person fall away from this prosperity and wander about as a poor person?' he rejoices when that person, for some reason, falls away from that prosperity. Among monks also, a monk whose mind is oppressed by envy, seeing the prosperity of gain and so on that has arisen for another monk depending on his learning, scriptural study, and so on, thinks, 'When will this monk fall away from these gains and so on?' and rejoices when he sees that monk fall away for some reason. Thus, the characteristic of dissatisfaction with another's prosperity is to be known as 'envy' (issā).

In the explanation of stinginess (macchariya), it is said, 'There are five types of stinginess: stinginess regarding dwellings (āvāsamacchariya), etc.,' in order to show stinginess according to the object. Among those five, stinginess regarding a dwelling (place) is āvāsamacchariya. The same method applies to the remaining terms.

A dwelling (āvāsa) means the entire monastery (ārāma), a precinct (pariveṇa), a single room, or places for the night and places for the day, etc. Those living in such monasteries live happily and obtain requisites easily. A certain monk does not wish for the arrival of another monk who is accomplished in duties and loves virtue. Even if he arrives, he thinks, 'May he leave quickly.' Such stinginess is called 'stinginess regarding dwellings' (āvāsamacchariya). However, for a monk who does not wish for the stay of bad monks who cause quarrels and so on, it is not called stinginess regarding dwellings.

Family (kula) means both supporter families and relative families. For a monk who does not wish for another monk to visit such a family, there is 'stinginess regarding families' (kulamacchariya). However, a monk who does not wish for a wicked person to visit is not called stingy. This is because that wicked monk acts to destroy the faith of those families. Only a monk who does not wish for the visit of a monk capable of protecting their faith is called stingy.

Gain (lābha) means the obtaining of the four requisites. For a monk who, when another virtuous monk obtains that gain, thinks, 'May he not obtain it,' there is 'stinginess regarding gains' (lābhamacchariya). But seeing someone who destroys things given out of faith, or ruins them through non-use or improper use, or does not give to another even when it is rotting, [and thinking] 'If this person does not get this...'
406:
"May another virtuous person receive it, may they come to enjoy it"—for one who thinks thus, there is no such thing as stinginess (macchariya).

Appearance (vaṇṇa) refers to both physical appearance (sarīravaṇṇa) and the appearance of virtues (guṇavaṇṇa). Among these two, a person stingy regarding physical appearance does not wish to speak when it is said, "Another is pleasing to look at, is beautiful." One who is stingy regarding the appearance of virtues does not wish to speak of another's merits in terms of virtue, ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), practice (paṭipadā), or conduct (ācāra).

Dhamma refers to the Dhamma of learning (pariyattidhamma) and the Dhamma of realization (paṭivedhadhamma). Among these, the noble disciples (ariyasāvaka) are not stingy regarding the Dhamma of realization; they desire that the world including the devas realize the Dhamma they themselves have realized. They wish, "May others know" that realization. Stinginess regarding the Dhamma (dhamma-macchariya) occurs only in the scriptural Dhamma (tantidhamma). A person endowed with that dhamma-macchariya does not wish others to know the secret texts or the sequence of commentaries (aṭṭhakathā) that they know. If someone does not give after examining the person to support the Dhamma, or after examining the Dhamma to support the person, this person is not called one who is stingy with the Dhamma (dhamma-maccharī).

In that regard, some persons are frivolous; at times they become a monk, at times a brahmin, and at times a Nigantha. If a bhikkhu does not give, thinking, "This person will destroy and disturb the subtle and profound Dhamma, the scriptures handed down in succession," this is called not giving after examining the person to support the Dhamma. If someone does not give, thinking, "This Dhamma is subtle and profound; if this person learns it, they will proclaim some other path and fruit, making themselves prominent, and will be ruined," this is called not giving after examining the Dhamma to support the person. If someone does not give, thinking, "If this person learns this Dhamma, they will be able to destroy our doctrine," this person is called one who is stingy with the Dhamma (dhamma-maccharī).

Among these five types of stinginess, due to stinginess regarding dwellings (āvāsa-macchariya), one is first reborn as a yakkha or a peta and wanders about carrying the sweepings of that monastery on one's head. Due to stinginess regarding families (kula-macchariya), upon seeing others giving gifts or paying honor to that family, one thinks, "Alas, this family of mine is ruined," and blood gushes from the mouth, bloody diarrhea occurs, and the intestines come out in pieces. Due to stinginess regarding gains (lābha-macchariya), being stingy with gains belonging to the Saṅgha or a group and using them as if they were personal property, one is reborn as a yakkha, a peta, or a great python. Due to stinginess regarding physical appearance and the appearance of virtues, and stinginess regarding the scriptural Dhamma...
407:
By praising only one's own virtues and speaking of the faults of others, saying, "What virtue does this person have?", and mentioning various faults, and not giving even a little of the scriptural Dhamma (pariyattidhamma) to anyone, one becomes ill-favored and a drooling mute (one who can only utter "a, a, a").

Furthermore, due to stinginess regarding dwellings, one is cooked in the Iron House Hell (Lohageha). Due to stinginess regarding families, one becomes one with few gains. Due to stinginess regarding gains, one is reborn in the Excrement Hell (Gūthaniraya). Due to stinginess regarding appearance, in every life where one is reborn, one is not beautiful. Due to stinginess regarding the Dhamma, one is reborn in the Embers Hell (Kukkulaniraya).

Stinginess is called macchera because of the act of being stingy (maccharāyana). The manner of being stingy is maccharāyanā. The state of being endowed with stinginess is maccharāyitatta. It is called viviccha because one does not wish for all one's prosperity to spread to others, thinking, "May it be for me alone, not for another." The state of that viviccha is veviccha; this is a name for mild stinginess. One who is disrespectful in giving is called kadariya. The state of such a person is kadariyaṃ; this is a name for harsh stinginess. A person endowed with that stinginess even prevents others who are giving to others. As it is said:

The loathsome miserly person (kadariya) of evil thoughts,
Of wrong view and disrespectful,
Prevents even the giving of food
To those who are begging.

One is called katukañcuka because upon seeing a beggar, the mind shrinks with a stinging sensation like a mote in the eye. The state of such a person is katukañcukatā. Another way: katukañcukatā is called "taking rice with a ladle" (kaṭacchuggāha). Just as one who takes rice from a pot full to the brim takes it only with the tip of a curved ladle and cannot take it fully, so too the mind of a stingy person shrinks. When that mind shrinks, the body also shrinks in the same way, recoils, and turns back, unable to expand; thus stinginess is called "katukañcukatā".

"The state of the mind being clutched" (aggahitattaṃ cittassa) means the state where the mind is held back and clutched as if blocked, not expanding in performing benefits for others through giving and so forth. Because a stingy person does not wish to give their own property to others but wishes to take the property of others, they have the characteristic of hiding their own prosperity by way of the occurrence: "May this wonderful thing be for me alone, not for another."
408:
Or it should be understood as having the characteristic of grasping one's own possessions (attasampatti). The meaning of the remaining words in this cluster (gocchaka) is clear.

Furthermore, these fetters (saṃyojana) should be brought [for explanation] according to the sequence of defilements (kilesa-paṭipāṭi) and the sequence of paths (magga-paṭipāṭi). According to the sequence of defilements: the fetters of sensual lust (kāmarāga) and ill-will (paṭigha) are abandoned by the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmimagga); the fetter of conceit (māna) by the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga); wrong view (diṭṭhi), doubt (vicikicchā), and adherence to rites and rituals (sīlabbataparāmāsa) by the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga); the fetter of lust for existence (bhavarāga) by the Path of Arahantship; envy (issā) and avarice (macchariya) by the Path of Stream-entry; and ignorance (avijjā) by the Path of Arahantship. According to the sequence of paths: wrong view, doubt, adherence to rites and rituals, envy, and avarice are abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry; sensual lust and ill-will by the Path of Non-returning; conceit, lust for existence, and ignorance by the Path of Arahantship.

In the Cluster of Ties (ganthagocchaka), it is called a 'bodily tie' (kāyagantha) because it ties the mental group (nāmakāya) to the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) by means of death and rebirth. Adherence to 'this is the truth' (idaṃsaccābhinivesa) is so called because it wrongly attends [to things] in this manner: 'The world is eternal; only this view of mine is true, other views are futile,' even rejecting the Dhamma taught by the Omniscient Buddha. Since there is a distinction between covetousness (abhijjhā) and sensual lust (kāmarāga), in the word-analysis (padabhājana) of the bodily tie of covetousness, it is not said, 'Whatever desire for sense pleasures (kāmacchanda) or sensual lust (kāmarāga) there is in sense pleasures,' but rather it is said, 'Whatever lust (rāga) or intense lust (sārāga) there is,' and so on. By this teaching, it should be understood that what was said below—'The desire and lust (chandarāga) for the celestial mansions of the Brahmas is not the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), but when it reaches the Cluster of Ties, it becomes the bodily tie of covetousness'—is well stated. The same method applies to the Cluster of Defilements (kilesagocchaka) that follows. In the phrase 'excluding adherence to rites and rituals' (ṭhapetvā sīlabbataparāmāsaṃ), since adherence to rites and rituals does not wrongly attend [to things] in the manner of 'only this is the truth,' but rather wrongly attends in the manner of 'purity comes through rites,' etc., even though it is a form of wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi), the Buddha said 'excluding' because He wished to set it apart.

In the explanation of sloth and torpor (thina-middha-niddesa) in the Cluster of Hindrances (nīvaraṇagocchaka), 'unhealthiness of mind' (cittassa akallatā) means the state of the mind being sick. For a sick person is called 'unhealthy' (akallaka). In the Vinaya also, it is said: 'Venerable Sir, I am not healthy (akallaka).' 'Unwieldiness' (akammaññatā) is the mode of unfitness in the task, which is called the sickness of the mind. 'Sluggishness' (olīyanā) is the mode of shrinking. For the mind that produces the postures (iriyāpatha), when it is unable to maintain the posture, it shrinks like a bat [hanging] on a tree or like a jar of molasses hanging on a post. That [state] of the mind...
409:
...referring to that mode, it is called 'sluggishness' (olīyanā). The second term is expanded by means of a prefix (upasagga). 'Līnaṃ' (shrunken) means retracted due to lack of expansion. The other two are explanations of the mode and the state. 'Thinaṃ' (sloth) means remaining in a dense state due to lack of expansion, like a lump of ghee. 'Thiyanā' is an explanation of the mode. 'Thiyitabhāvo' and 'thiyitattaṃ' mean the state of being stiff solely due to lack of expansion.

'Of the body' (kāyassa) refers to the mental body (nāmakāya), which is the collection of the three aggregates: feeling, perception, and formations. 'Unhealthiness' (akallatā) and 'unwieldiness' (akammaññatā) are as explained below. It is called 'shrouding' (onāha) because it shrouds the mental body as a cloud shrouds the sky. It is called 'enveloping' (pariyonāha) because it shrouds from all sides. It is called 'internal obstruction' (antosamorodha) because it obstructs within. Just as when a city is blockaded, people cannot go outside, so too, the states obstructed by torpor (middha) cannot come out by way of expansion. Therefore, it is called 'internal obstruction.' It is called 'torpor' (middha) because it oppresses (medhati); it means it oppresses by way of unwieldiness. It is called 'sleep' (soppa) because beings sleep by means of it. It is called 'drowsiness' (pacalāyikā) because it causes the movement of the eyelids, etc. 'Supanā' and 'supitattaṃ' are explanations of the mode and the state. The reason for repeating the word 'soppa' (sleep) which was before those terms has already been stated. This is called the 'hindrance of sloth and torpor' (thina-middha-nīvaraṇa); sloth and torpor taken together are called the hindrance of sloth and torpor because of their sense of obstructing.

That sloth and torpor which mostly arises in the preceding and following parts of sleep for trainees (sekha) and worldlings (puthujjana) is entirely cut off by the Path of Arahantship. For Arahants, however, there is the sinking into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) due to the weakness of the physical body (karajakāya); when that [bhavaṅga] occurs unmixed [with sleep], they sleep, and that is called their 'sleep' (niddā). Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Aggivessana, I recall that in the last month of summer, having spread out my outer robe (saṅghāṭi) folded in four, I would lie down on my right side and fall asleep, mindful and clearly comprehending.' Such weakness of the physical body is not to be abandoned by the Path; it is found in both the 'clung-to' (upādinnaka) [living] body and the 'not-clung-to' (anupādinnaka) [non-living] matter. In the 'clung-to' body, it occurs when an Arahant has traveled a long distance or is exhausted after performing some task. In 'not-clung-to' matter, it is found in leaves and flowers. The leaves of some trees expand in the sunlight and shrink at night; lotus flowers and others bloom in the sunlight and shrink again at night. But this [defiled] torpor (middha) does not exist in Arahants because it is unwholesome.
410:
In that (exposition of sloth and torpor), there might be the view: 'Torpor (middha) is not unwholesome. Why? Because it is matter (rūpa). Matter is indeterminate (abyākata), and this torpor is matter. Therefore, in this (exposition), the term "body" (kāya) is used in "unwellness of the body, unreadiness of the body for work."' 

If this torpor were matter simply because the word 'of the body' (kāyassa) is used, then states such as tranquility of the body (kāyapassaddhi) and so on would also be matter. The experiences of 'feeling happiness with the body' and 'realizing the ultimate truth with the body' would also occur only through the physical body (rūpakāya). Therefore, it should not be said that 'torpor is matter.' Here, 'body' refers only to the mental body (nāmakāya). 

If it is the mental body, why is it called 'sleeping' and 'drowsiness'? (One might object:) The mental body does not sleep, nor does it drowse. (The response is:) It is said so because these are the fruits of that torpor, just as the signs and so on are the fruits of a faculty. Just as the 'feminine features, feminine signs, feminine behavior, and feminine attire' are mentioned as the fruits of the femininity faculty (itthindriya), so too 'sleeping' and so on are mentioned as the fruits of this torpor, which is known as the sickness of the mental body. When there is torpor, these (sleeping, etc.) occur. By way of metonymy (phalūpacāra), although torpor is mental (arūpa), it is called 'sleeping, drowsiness, slumber, and sleepiness.' 

The meaning is also established by the derivative definition: 'It is called drowsiness (pacalāyikā) because it causes the movement of the eyelids and so on'; thus, torpor is not matter. Its mental nature is also shown by terms like 'enveloping' (onāha) and so on. Matter cannot be the 'enveloping, all-enveloping, or internal-shrouding' of the mental body. 

(If one objects:) 'Is it not for this very reason that it is matter? For a mental state cannot be an enveloping, an all-enveloping, or an internal-shrouding for anything.' If that were so, there would be no 'obstruction' (āvaraṇa) (in mental hindrances). Therefore, just as mental states like sensual desire are called hindrances (nīvaraṇa) in the sense of obstructing, so too should the nature of 'enveloping' and so on be understood in this torpor in the sense of shrouding. 

Furthermore, because of the word: 'Having abandoned the five hindrances, the defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom,' this torpor is mental. Matter is not a defilement of the mind, nor does it weaken wisdom. Why is it not? (One might ask:) 'Was it not said: "Monks, there are some recluses and brahmins who drink liquor and wine, not refraining from drinking liquor and wine; this, monks, is the first defilement (upakkilesa) of recluses and brahmins"?'
411:
Another point was also stated: 'Householder’s son, there are these six dangers in being addicted to liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence: visible loss of wealth, increase in quarrels, susceptibility to disease, producing a bad reputation, shameful exposure of the body, and the sixth is the weakening of wisdom.' (This is stated in the Dīgha Nikāya). This point is also evident through direct perception. Just as when liquor enters the stomach, the mind becomes defiled and wisdom becomes weak, so too torpor should be a defilement of the mind and a weakener of wisdom (so the objector says).

That is not so; it is because of the 'exposition of cause' (paccayaniddesa). If liquor were itself a defilement (saṅkilesa), it would have been included in the 'expositions of defilements' (upakkilesaniddesa) such as: 'Having abandoned these five hindrances, the defilements of the mind...' or 'Monks, there are these five defilements of the mind, defiled by which the mind is neither soft, nor wieldy, nor radiant, but is brittle and not rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints. What five? Sensual desire, monks, is a defilement of the mind...' or 'Monks, what are the defilements of the mind? Covetousness and unrighteous greed are defilements of the mind.'

Since defilements (upakkilesa) that defile the mind and weaken wisdom arise when that liquor is drunk, it is called a defilement by way of the exposition of cause, because it is the cause (paccaya) for those defilements. Torpor, however, is itself a defilement of the mind and a weakener of wisdom; therefore, torpor is purely mental (arūpa).

For what further reason can this be known? Because of the statement on association (sampayoga). For it is said (in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī): 'The hindrance of sloth and torpor is both a hindrance and associated with hindrances through the hindrance of ignorance.' Therefore, because of the statement on association, this is not matter. For matter does not receive the designation 'associated' (sampayutta).

Now, it might be argued: 'This is stated according to what is available (yathālābhavasena). Just as it is said: "(One sees) oysters and shells, gravel and pebbles, and schools of fish, moving or standing," thus grouping them together and speaking according to what is available. For gravel and pebbles only stand and do not move, while the other two both stand and move. Similarly, here too, torpor is only a hindrance and not associated, but since sloth is both a hindrance and associated, they are all grouped together and stated as "both a hindrance and associated with hindrances" according to what is available. Torpor, like gravel and pebbles, only stands and does not move (associate); thus it is only a hindrance and not associated. Therefore, torpor is matter.'

That is not so, because the nature of matter is not established. That gravel and pebbles do not move is established even without the Sutta (by observation). Therefore, in that context, the meaning is taken according to what is available.
412:
Be that as it may. The point that torpor (middha) is matter (rūpa) is not yet established (not evident). Since the materiality of that torpor cannot be proven by this Sutta, and because the materiality of torpor is not established, this statement is not made in a general sense (yathālābhavasena); rather, torpor is only a mental phenomenon (arūpa).

What else is there? It is also because of the words beginning with 'because of being abandoned' (cattattā). For in the Vibhaṅga, it is said: "'One who is free from sloth and torpor' means that because that sloth and torpor have been given up, vomited out, released, abandoned, and relinquished, he is therefore called 'one who is free from sloth and torpor'" (Vibh. 547); and "He cleanses, specially cleanses, thoroughly cleanses, frees, specially frees, and thoroughly frees this mind from this sloth and torpor; therefore it is said, 'He cleanses the mind from sloth and torpor'" (Vibh. 551)—thus it is preached starting with 'because of being abandoned'. Matter (rūpa) is not spoken of in this way. For this reason also, torpor is only a mental phenomenon.

That is not so; it is because it is stated that torpor born of consciousness (cittaja) cannot occur (in Jhana-consciousness). There are three kinds of torpor: that born of consciousness (cittaja), that born of temperature (utuja), and that born of nutriment (āhāraja). Therefore, among those three, the Vibhaṅga states that torpor born of consciousness cannot occur together with Jhana-consciousnesses; it does not establish its immateriality, so torpor is indeed matter.

No, because the materiality of torpor itself is not established. This point could only be gained if the materiality of torpor were evident. In that Vibhaṅga, only the impossibility of torpor born of consciousness is stated. Since the materiality of that torpor itself is not established, torpor is only a mental phenomenon.

What else is there? Because it is preached as something to be abandoned. For the Blessed One said: "Monks, by abandoning six things, one is capable of attaining and dwelling in the first Jhana. Which six? Sensual desire (kāmacchanda), ill-will (byāpāda), sloth and torpor (thina-middha), restlessness (uddhacca), remorse (kukkucca), and doubt (vicikicchā)" (A. Ni. 6.73); and "By abandoning these five hindrances (nīvaraṇa), one will know one's own benefit and the benefit of others through powerful wisdom" (A. Ni. 5.51). In such passages, the abandonment of torpor is also mentioned. Matter, however, is not said to be abandoned. As it is said: "The aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha) should be known with higher knowledge, should be fully understood; it is not to be abandoned, not to be developed, and not to be realized" (Vibh. 1031). Because this torpor is preached as something to be abandoned, torpor is only a mental phenomenon.

No, because it is also preached that matter should be abandoned. "Monks, matter is not yours; abandon that matter" (M. Ni. 1.247, Saṃ. Ni. 3.33). Here, the abandonment of matter is indeed preached. Therefore, this point is not a valid reason.

No, because it is preached in a different way. In that Sutta, it is said: "Monks, whatever removal of desire and lust (chandarāga) there is regarding matter, that is the abandonment thereof" (Saṃ. Ni. 3.25). Thus, the abandonment of matter is preached in terms of abandoning desire and lust; it is not preached as something to be directly abandoned in the same way as "abandoning the six things" or "abandoning the five hindrances." Because it is preached in a different way, matter is not torpor. Therefore, those words such as "He, having abandoned these five hindrances..."
413:
Suttas such as "Defilements of the mind" (cetaso upakkilesa) have been preached. By these Suttas and other Suttas, it should be understood that torpor (middha) is only a mental phenomenon (arūpa). Indeed, it is true: 

"Monks, these five are obstructions, hindrances, which overspread the mind and weaken wisdom. Which five? Monks, sensual desire is an obstruction, a hindrance... Monks, sloth and torpor is an obstruction, a hindrance, which overspreads the mind and weakens wisdom" (Saṃ. Ni. 5.220); and "Monks, the hindrance of sloth and torpor causes blindness, causes lack of vision, causes lack of knowledge, stifles wisdom, is associated with distress, and does not lead to Nibbāna" (Saṃ. Ni. 5.221); and "Brahmin, even so, at the time when one dwells with a mind obsessed by sloth and torpor, overwhelmed by sloth and torpor" (Saṃ. Ni. 5.236); and "Monks, for one who attends unwisely, unarisen sensual desire arises... and unarisen sloth and torpor arises" (Saṃ. Ni. 5.216); and "Monks, this is a total heap of unwholesome states, namely, the five hindrances" (Saṃ. Ni. 5.371)—

These and many other such Suttas clearly illustrate the immaterial (arūpa) nature of this torpor. Because this torpor is a mental phenomenon, it also arises in the formless realm (āruppa). For it is said in the Great Book, the Paṭṭhāna: "Dependent on a hindrance, a hindrance arises, not by way of the pre-existence condition (purejāta-paccaya)." In the analysis (vibhaṅga) of this statement, it is elaborated in detail: "In the formless realm, dependent on the hindrance of sensual desire, sloth and torpor arise... restlessness and the hindrance of ignorance arise" (Paṭṭhāna 3.8.8). Therefore, a conclusion should be reached here that torpor is only a mental phenomenon.

In the exposition of remorse (kukkucca-niddesa), phrases such as "perceiving the unallowable as allowable" are preached to show remorse from its root origin. For when a transgression is committed with such a perception, and when the violation of the object is completed, this remorse arises by way of subsequent regret in one who later regains mindfulness and laments, "I have done poorly." Therefore, to show that remorse from its root, it is said: "perceiving the unallowable as allowable," and so on. Therein, "perceiving the unallowable as allowable" includes: consuming unallowable food perceiving it as allowable; eating unallowable meat perceiving it as allowable meat—such as eating bear meat thinking it is pork, or leopard meat thinking it is venison; perceiving it as the proper time when the time has passed; perceiving that an invitation has not been made when it has been made; eating from a bowl when dust has fallen into it, perceiving it as having been properly received—thus, because of "perceiving the unallowable as allowable," (remorse arises).
414:
It is called committing a transgression (vītikkama). One who eats pork with the perception that it is bear meat, or one who eats during the allowed time with the perception that it is the wrong time, is said to commit a transgression 'due to perceiving the allowable as unallowable.'
