One who performs a blameless act with the perception that it is blameworthy, or a blameworthy act with the perception that it is blameless, is said to commit a transgression 'due to perceiving the blameless as blameworthy and the blameworthy as blameless.'

Because this remorse (kukkucca) arises even when a transgression is committed by perceiving the blameless as blameworthy, such as: "Alas, I have not done what is good, I have not done what is wholesome, I have not done what protects from fear; I have done what is evil, I have done what is cruel, I have done what is wicked." Therefore, wishing to make known other causes of that remorse, [the Teacher] said "yaṃ evarūpaṃ" and so forth.

In that context, the word 'kukkucca' has the meaning already stated. The manner of being remorseful is 'kukkuccāyanā'. The state of one affected by remorse is 'kukkuccāyitatta'. In the phrase "cetaso vippaṭisāro" (remorse of mind), the mind's rushing toward what has been done or not done, or toward what is blameworthy or blameless, is called "vippaṭisāra". Because that remorse cannot make the evil done undone, nor the good not done done, it is called "vippaṭisāra" because it is a distorted or loathsome (kucchita) rushing back (paṭisāra). It is called "remorse of mind" (cetaso vippaṭisāro) to show that it belongs to the mind, not to a being (satta). This is the description of its nature (sabhāva). Arising remorse occurs while scratching the mind, just as a stylus scratches a bronze plate; therefore, it is called "mental scratching" (manovilekha). This is the description of its function (kicca).

In the Vinaya teachings, the remorse that arose for the Venerable Sāriputta—who, after reflecting repeatedly on the lodgings-alms (āvasathapiṇḍa) prohibited by the Blessed One, did not accept them—is not a hindrance (nīvaraṇa). This is because for an Arahant, there is no such regret as "I have done this badly." Although it resembles a hindrance, it is called "Vinaya-remorse" (vinayakukkucca), which consists of investigating "Is it allowable or not?"

In the explanation of the phrase "Which states are both hindrances and associated with hindrances?", because sloth (thina) and torpor (middha) are inseparable and associated with each other, the hindrance of sloth and torpor is mentioned without division along with the hindrance of ignorance as "both a hindrance and associated with hindrances." However, because restlessness (uddhacca) can exist without remorse (kukkucca), and restlessness can arise even in the absence of remorse, they are mentioned separately. It should be understood that when a state does not reach association with another state, it is left unassociated.
415:
These hindrances should be understood according to the sequence of defilements and the sequence of the paths. According to the sequence of defilements: sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and ill-will (byāpāda) are abandoned by the Path of Non-Returning (anāgāmimagga). Sloth, torpor, and restlessness (uddhacca) are abandoned by the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga). Remorse (kukkucca) and doubt (vicikicchā) are abandoned by the Path of Stream-Entry (sotāpattimagga). Ignorance (avijjā) is abandoned by the Path of Arahantship. According to the sequence of the paths: remorse and doubt are abandoned by the Path of Stream-Entry; sensual desire and ill-will by the Path of Non-Returning; and sloth, torpor, restlessness, and ignorance by the Path of Arahantship.

In the Parāmāsagocchaka, the use of the plural in the phrase "excluding those states" is to be consistent with the question "Which states?"

In the description of grasping (upādāna), it is called "grasping at sense-pleasures" (kāmupādāna) because of firmly grasping at the objects of sense-pleasure (vatthukāma). It is also called kāmupādāna because it is both sense-pleasure and grasping. Grasping (upādāna) means firm taking hold. Here, the prefix "upa" denotes "firmness," as in terms like upāyāsa (despair) and upakaṭṭha (nearness). Similarly, it is called "grasping at views" (diṭṭhupādāna) because it is both a view and grasping. It is called diṭṭhupādāna because it firmly grasps a view. For instance, a subsequent view firmly grasps a preceding view, such as "The self and the world are eternal." Likewise, it is called "grasping at rules and observances" (sīlabbatupādāna) because it firmly grasps rules and observances. It is also called sīlabbatupādāna because it is both a rule/observance and grasping. Practices such as the 'cow-virtue' or 'cow-vow' are themselves graspings because of the wrong conviction that "purity comes through this." Similarly, it is called "vāda" (discourse/doctrine) because one speaks by means of it, and "upādāna" because one firmly grasps by means of it. What do they speak of or grasp? The self (attā). It is called "grasping at the doctrine of self" (attavādupādāna) because it is the means of speaking about and grasping the self. Or, it is called attavādupādāna because one firmly grasps the mere expression "self" as "the self" by means of this state.

In the phrase "whatever sensual desire there is for sense-pleasures," here too, "sense-pleasures" (kāma) refers exclusively to the objects of sense-pleasure (vatthukāma). Therefore, having sensual desire for the objects of sense-pleasure is kāmupādāna here. Thus, it is evident that this kāmupādāna still exists for a Non-Returner (anāgāmī). However, for that Non-Returner, there is no longer any sensual lust (kāmarāga) rooted in the five cords of sensual pleasure.

In the description of grasping at views, "there is no merit in giving" means: one knows that giving exists and that it is possible to give something to someone, but one holds the view that there is no fruit or result (vipāka) of giving. "There is no merit in great sacrifice" means: one knows that a great sacrifice (mahāyāga) can be performed, but holds that there is no fruit or result of the sacrifice. "There is no merit in offerings" means: one knows that acts of hospitality, offerings, or auspicious rites can be performed, but that there is no fruit or result of such acts...
416: He holds the view that 'there is nothing.' In the context of 'there is no result of well-done or ill-done deeds,' the ten wholesome courses of action are called 'well-done deeds' (sukata-kamma), and the ten unwholesome courses of action are called 'ill-done deeds' (dukkaṭa-kamma). Although he knows the existence of these deeds, he holds that there is no fruit or result (vipāka). 'There is no this world' means that while existing in the next world, he holds that this world does not exist. 'There is no next world' means that while existing in this world, he holds that the next world does not exist. 'There is no mother, there is no father' means that although he knows the existence of parents, he holds that there is no fruit or result from deeds done towards them. 'There are no spontaneously born beings' means he holds that there are no beings who pass away and are reborn (opapātika). 'Those who have gone well, who have practiced rightly' refers to righteous ascetics and Brahmins who practice the path leading to Nibbāna; he holds that they do not exist in the world. 'Those who, having realized this world and the next world by their own higher knowledge, make it known' means he holds that there is no Omniscient Buddha who is capable of knowing and proclaiming this world and the next world through his own superior knowledge. These clingings (upādāna) should be presented according to the sequence of defilements and the sequence of the paths. According to the sequence of defilements, clinging to sensual pleasures (kāmupādāna) is abandoned by the four paths; the remaining three clingings are abandoned by the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga). According to the sequence of the paths, clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna) and so on are abandoned by the path of stream-entry, while clinging to sensual pleasures is abandoned by the four paths. In the group of defilements (kilesa-gocchaka), only the defilements themselves are the bases of defilements (kilesa-vatthu). Alternatively, they are called 'vatthu' (bases/dwellings) because beings whose taints are not yet exhausted dwell in these defilements, being established in greed and so on. Because they are both defilements and the bases for the beings established in them, they are called 'kilesa-vatthūni.' Furthermore, because the defilements that arise through proximity-condition (anantara-paccaya) and so on also 'dwell' there, they are called 'kilesa-vatthūni' in the sense of being the bases for defilements. Among those defilements, what is greed (lobha)? That which is lust (rāga) or intense lust (sārāga). This greed is explained with more than a hundred terms in these three places: the group of roots (hetu-gocchaka), the group of ties (gantha-gocchaka), and this group of defilements (kilesa-gocchaka). In the groups of taints (āsava), fetters (saṃyojana), floods (ogha), bonds (yoga), hindrances (nīvaraṇa), and clingings (upādāna), it is explained with eight terms each. It should be understood that greed is taken in its entirety (nippadesa) both in the places where it is explained with more than a hundred terms and where it is explained with eight terms each. In those groups of roots, ties, hindrances, clingings, and defilements, the craving (taṇhā) that is to be abandoned by the four paths...
417: ...exists as a single group in the group of roots, the group of ties, the group of hindrances, the group of clingings, and the group of defilements. However, in the taints, fetters, floods, and bonds, the factors to be abandoned by the four paths exist as two groups each. How? In the taints, there are the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava) and the taint of existence (bhavāsava); in the fetters, the fetter of sensual lust (kāmarāga-saṃyojana) and the fetter of lust for existence (bhavarāga-saṃyojana); in the floods, the flood of sensual desire (kāmogha) and the flood of existence (bhavogha); and in the bonds, the bond of sensual desire (kāmayoga) and the bond of existence (bhavayoga). These bases of defilements (kilesa-vatthu) should be presented according to the sequence of defilements and the sequence of the paths. According to the sequence of defilements, greed (lobha) is abandoned by the four paths, hatred (dosa) by the path of non-returning (anāgāmi-magga), delusion (moha) and conceit (māna) by the path of arahantship (arahatta-magga), view (diṭṭhi) and doubt (vicikicchā) by the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), and sloth and torpor (thina-middha) etc., by the path of arahantship. According to the sequence of the paths, view and doubt are abandoned by the path of stream-entry, hatred by the path of non-returning, and the remaining seven defilements by the path of arahantship. In the explanation of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara-niddesa), 'from below' (heṭṭhato) means by the lower part. 'Avīci Hell' (avīci-niraya) is so called because there is no interval (vīci), gap, or break in the flames of fire, in the beings, or in the painful feeling. It is called 'Niraya' because there is no happiness (aya) there. It is also called 'Niraya' in the sense of being devoid of delight or devoid of enjoyment. 'Making it the limit' (pariyantaṃ karitvā) means taking that hell called Avīci as the boundary. 'From above' (uparito) means by the upper part. 'Among the Paranimmitavasavatti gods' refers to the gods who have received this name because they exercise control over the sensual pleasures created by others. 'Including within' (anto karitvā) means putting inside. 'That which is in this interval' refers to the things occurring in this space. By the term 'frequenting this realm' (etthāvacara)—since other things also occasionally occur in some places within this interval—the word 'āvacara' is used to exclude them. By this term, it includes those things that occur by being immersed in this interval, existing everywhere and at all times, and those that occur in the lower part as the occurrence of the primary elements and derived matter below the Avīci Hell. Because they occur by being immersed and occur only in the lower part, they are called 'āvacara.' By the term 'included in this realm' (ettha pariyāpanna)—since these things that frequent this realm also frequent other places but are not included there—it includes those things even when they frequent other places. Now, wishing to show the things included in that realm by way of groups, emptiness, conditions, and individual essence, he said 'aggregates' (khandhā) and so on.
418:
In the Exposition of the Fine-material Sphere (Rūpāvacaraniddesa), 'Brahmaloka' refers to the abode of the Brahmas, known as the plane of the first jhāna. The rest in this Exposition of the Fine-material Sphere should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Exposition of the Sensuous Sphere (Kāmāvacaraniddesa). Among the terms beginning with 'of one who has attained' (samāpannassa vā), it should be understood that the first term refers to wholesome jhāna (kusala-jhāna), the second to resultant jhāna (vipāka-jhāna), and the third to functional jhāna (kiriya-jhāna).

In the Exposition of the Immaterial Sphere (Arūpāvacaraniddesa), 'those who have gone to the sphere of infinite space' (ākāsānañcāyatanūpaga) refers to those who have reached the state of existence known as the sphere of infinite space. The same method applies to the second term as well. The rest should be understood in the same manner as stated below.

In the Exposition of the Dyad of Defilement (Saraṇadukaniddesa), among the three unwholesome roots, there is delusion (moha). When that delusion is associated with greed (lobha), it is called 'with defilement' (saraṇa) as it is accompanied by greed. When it is associated with hatred (dosa), it is called 'with defilement' (saraṇa) as it is accompanied by hatred. Specifically, delusion associated with doubt (vicikicchā) and restlessness (uddhacca) should be understood as 'with defilement' (saraṇa) and 'with dust' (saraja), because it exists in the same individual as the defilement of lust (rāga)—namely, lust for fine-material existence and lust for immaterial existence—which is associated with wrong view, and because it is to be abandoned [together with them].

## Discussion on the Summary of Suttanta Dyads
In the Suttanta dyads, because the meanings are individually distinguished in the Discussion on the Matrix (Mātikākathā), and because their explanatory terms (niddesapada) are easily understood by the method already stated below, they mostly have clear meanings. However, this is the only special point here: First, in the Dyad of the Simile of Lightning (Vijjūpamaduka), a man with eyes travels on a path at night during a dark storm. Because of the darkness, the path is not visible to him. Lightning flashes and destroys the mass of darkness. Then, because the darkness has vanished, the path becomes clear to him. He sets out to travel a second time. A second time, darkness covers him. The path is not visible. Lightning flashes and destroys that mass of darkness. When the darkness has vanished, the path becomes clear. He sets out to travel a third time. Darkness covers him. The path is not visible. Lightning flashes and destroys the mass of darkness.

Among these instances of the man with eyes traveling in the darkness, the undertaking of insight (vipassanā) by a noble disciple for the sake of the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga) should be understood as being like the man with eyes traveling in the darkness. The period when the path is not visible in the darkness should be understood as the intense darkness of delusion that veils the Four Noble Truths. The path of stream-entry arising with its light, like the time when lightning flashes and destroys the mass of darkness...
419:
...is the time when the delusion that veils the Truths is dispelled. The time when the Four Noble Truths become clear to the path of stream-entry is like the time when the path becomes clear when the darkness has vanished. The clarity of the path is indeed clear to the person possessed of the path (maggasamaṅgī).

The undertaking of insight for the sake of the path of once-returning (sakadāgāmimagga) is like setting out to travel for the second time. The delusion that veils the Truths is like the time when the path is not visible in the darkness. The time when the delusion that veils the Truths is dispelled, by the path of once-returning arising with its light, is like the second time lightning flashes and destroys the darkness. The time when the Four Noble Truths become clear to the path of once-returning is like the time when the path becomes clear when the darkness has vanished. The clarity of the path is indeed clear to the person possessed of the path.

The undertaking of insight for the sake of the path of non-returning (anāgāmimagga) is like setting out to travel for the third time. The delusion that veils the Truths is like the time when the path is not visible in the darkness. The time when the delusion that veils the Truths is dispelled, by the path of non-returning arising with its light, is like the third time lightning flashes and destroys the darkness. The time when the Four Noble Truths become clear to the path of non-returning is like the time when the path becomes clear when the darkness has vanished. The clarity of the path is indeed clear to the person possessed of the path.

For the vajira weapon (thunderbolt) of Sakka, there is no such thing as a stone slab or a gem that cannot be broken. Wherever the vajira falls, that place is surely pierced through. When the vajira destroys, it destroys without remainder. The path taken by the vajira can never return to its original state. In the same way, for the path of arahantship (arahattamagga), there is no such thing as a defilement that cannot be slain. Like the vajira, it pierces and destroys all defilements. When the path of arahantship destroys defilements, it destroys them without remainder. Just as the path taken by the vajira does not return to its original state, there is no such thing as the return of defilements that have been abandoned by the path of arahantship.

In the Exposition of the Dyad of Fools (Bāladukaniddesa), among fools, shamelessness (ahirika) and fearlessness of wrongdoing (anottappa) are prominent, and they are the roots of the remaining qualities of a fool. This is because a person who lacks shamelessness and fearlessness of wrongdoing does not refrain from committing any unwholesome act. These two qualities are first taught separately. The same method applies to the Bright Side (sukkapakkha). Likewise, it is the same in the Dark Dyad (kaṇhaduka).

In the Exposition of the Dyad of Remorse (Tapanīyadukaniddesa), remorse (burning) should be understood as arising from what has been done and what has not been done. Remorse is felt because of having committed bodily misconduct (kāyaduccarita) and the like, and because of not having performed bodily good conduct (kāyasucarita) and the like. Thus, a person feels remorse, thinking, 'I have committed bodily misconduct,' and 'I have not performed bodily good conduct.' He feels remorse, thinking, 'I have committed verbal misconduct,' ... (and so on) ... 'I have not performed (verbal good conduct).'
420:
"I have not performed good mental conduct," he burns with remorse. In the Dyad of Non-remorse (Atapanīya-duka), it should be understood in the same way. Indeed, a person who performs good deeds does not burn with remorse, thinking, "I have performed good bodily conduct"; he does not burn with remorse, thinking, "I have not performed bad bodily conduct" ... "I have not performed bad mental conduct."

## Exposition of the Dyad of Designation
In the Exposition of the Dyad of Designation (Adhivacana-duka-niddesa), by the phrase "of those various phenomena" (yā tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ), all phenomena are to be included. It is called saṅkhā (reckoning) because it is reckoned (saṅkhāyati); the meaning is that it is spoken of. How is it spoken of? It is spoken of in various ways such as "I," "mine," "another," "another's," "a being," "nature," "a creature," "a person," "a human," "a youth," "Tissa," "Datta"; or "a couch," "a stool," "a rug," "a pillow," "a monastery," "a precinct," "a door," "a window." Because it is spoken of in such various modes, it is called saṅkhā. It is called samaññā (designation) because it is designated (samaññāyati). How is it known? Because it is known as "I ... window," it is called samaññā. It is called paññatti (concept) because it is conceptualized (paññāpiyati). It is called vohāra (usage) because it is expressed (vohariyati). How is it expressed? Because it is expressed as "I ... window," it is called vohāra.

"Name" (nāma) is of four kinds: conventional name (sāmañña-nāma), attribute name (guṇa-nāma), given name (kittima-nāma), and spontaneous name (opapātika-nāma). Among these four, the name "Mahāsammata" (The Great Elect) given to the king because he was appointed by the multitude at the beginning of the aeon is called a "conventional name." With reference to this name, it was said: "Vāseṭṭha, because he was elected by the multitude (mahājana-sammata), the first syllable 'Mahāsammata' arose." Names that arise from qualities such as Dhamma-preacher (dhammakathika), rag-robe wearer (paṃsukūlika), bearer of the Vinaya (vinayadhara), knower of the Three Pitakas (tepiṭaka), faithful (saddha), and devout (pasanna) are called "attribute names." The hundreds of names of the Blessed One, such as Bhagavā, Arahaṃ, and Sammāsambuddha, are also attribute names. Therefore, it is said:
"Incalculable are the names of the Great Sage according to His qualities;
The names assigned according to His qualities are more than thousands."

The name given to a newborn boy on the naming day, after making offerings to those worthy of gifts, by relatives standing nearby who deliberate and decide, "Let this boy have such-and-such a name," is called a "given name." There are instances where an ancient concept falls into a later concept, or an ancient usage falls into a later usage. For example, in previous aeons, the moon was called "moon," and even now it is called "moon." In the past, the sun, the ocean, the earth, and mountains were called "mountains" ...
421:
Even now, the name "mountain" itself is called a "spontaneous name" (opapātika-nāma). These four kinds of names are simply "name" in this context. Nāmakamma means the act of naming. Nāmadheyya means the assigning of a name. Nirutti means the expression of a name. Byañjana means the syllable of a name (the name that manifests the meaning). Because this name manifests the meaning, it is called byañjana. Abhilāpa is simply the utterance of a name. "All phenomena are paths of designation" means there is no phenomenon that is not a basis for designation. One phenomenon falls within all phenomena, and all phenomena fall within one phenomenon. How? This one phenomenon called "concept of name" (nāma-paññatti) falls within all phenomena of the four planes. There is no being or formation (saṅkhāra) that is free from a name.

In forests, mountains, etc., even a tree is the responsibility of the local people. When those locals are asked, "What is the name of this tree?", they state the name they know, such as "Khadiro" (Cutch tree) or "Palāso" (Flame-of-the-forest). Even if they do not know the name of a tree, they call it "nameless" (anāmaka). That "nameless" itself remains as the assigned name of that tree. The same method applies to fish, turtles, etc., in the ocean. The remaining two dyads have the same meaning as this Dyad of Designation. In the Dyad of Name and Form (Nāmarūpa-duka), it is called "name" (nāma) because of the sense of making a name, the sense of bending towards an object, and the sense of causing [others] to bend towards itself. Among those names, first, the four mental aggregates are called "name" in the sense of making a name. Just as the name "Mahāsammata" arose for King Mahāsammata because he was elected by the multitude, or just as parents give a given name to a son, saying, "Let this boy be named Tissa or Phussa," or just as a name comes from qualities like "Dhamma-preacher" or "bearer of the Vinaya," it is not so with feelings (vedanā) and so on. For feelings and so on arise while making their own names, just like the great earth and so on. When those feelings arise, their names are already arisen. No one says when a feeling arises, "You shall be named feeling." There is no task of naming for that feeling. Just as when the earth arises, there is no task of naming it, "You shall be named earth"; and when the universe (cakkavāḷa), Mount Sineru, the moon, the sun, and the stars arise, there is no task of naming them, "You shall be named universe" or "You shall be named star," for the name is already arisen and falls under spontaneous concept (opapātika-paññatti); likewise, when a feeling arises, there is no task of naming it, "You shall be named feeling."
422:
When that feeling (vedanā) arises, the name 'feeling' is already arisen. It falls under the category of spontaneous designation (upapatti-paññatti). The same applies to perception (saññā) and so on. In the past, feeling was just feeling, perception was just perception, mental formations (saṅkhāra) were just mental formations, and consciousness (viññāṇa) was just consciousness. The same applies to the future and the present. Nibbāna, however, is always just Nibbāna. It is called 'nāma' (name/mentality) in the sense of making a name.

In this context, the four mental aggregates are also called 'nāma' in the sense of bending (namana). They bend towards the object. All 'nāma' (the four aggregates and Nibbāna) is called 'nāma' in the sense of causing to bend (nāmana). The four aggregates cause each other to bend towards the object. Nibbāna, by way of being the object-predominance condition (ārammaṇādhipati-paccaya), causes the faultless states (anavajja-dhamma) to bend towards itself.

Ignorance (avijjā) and craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā) are taken to show the fundamental occurrence of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa).

"The self and the world will be" means taking the five aggregates as the self and the world, and holding the view that "that self and world will exist permanently"; this is the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi). The second view, held in the manner of "it will not be," is the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi).

"Starting from the beginning" (pubbanta) means taking the past portion as the object. By this, the eighteen views concerning the past (pubbantānudiṭṭhi) mentioned in the Brahmajāla Sutta are included. "Starting from the end" (aparanta) means taking the future portion as the object. By this, the forty-four views concerning the future (aparantānudiṭṭhi) mentioned in that same Brahmajāla Sutta are included.

In the explanation of unruliness (dovacassatā), "when spoken to according to the Dhamma" (sahadhammike vuccamāne) means: the training rule (sikkhāpada) prescribed by the Blessed One is called 'sahadhammika'. When, in relation to that training rule, the grounds are shown and an offense is pointed out, saying, "You have fallen into such-and-such an offense; come, confess it, emerge from it, and make amends." In the terms "dovacassāyaṃ" etc., the act of one who is difficult to admonish, which occurs either because of counter-accusation or because of not receiving the advice respectfully when thus exhorted, is called 'dovacassāyaṃ'. That same act is also called 'dovacassa'. The state of being difficult to admonish is 'dovacassiya'. The other term (dovacassatā) is a synonym for that same 'dovacassiya'. "Vippaṭikūlagāhitā" means the state of habitually taking the opposite side. One who takes pleasure in opposition, characterized by taking the contrary view, is "vipaccanīkasāta". This is a designation for one who finds satisfaction in thinking, "By taking a contrary view, I have silenced that person with a single word." The state of such a person is "vipaccanīkasātatā". The state of one who is disrespectful by way of not accepting advice is "anādariya". The other term (anādaratā) is a synonym for that same 'anādariya'. Or, the manner of not accepting advice is 'anādaratā'. The state of disrespect (agāravatā) arises by way of not living under the guidance of those worthy of respect. The state of disobedience (appatissavatā) arises by way of not living under the guidance of those senior to oneself. This is what is said...
423:
Such behavior is called unruliness (dovacassatā). In terms of ultimate reality, it refers to the four mental aggregates, or specifically the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha/cetana), occurring in that disrespectful manner. The same applies to having evil friends (pāpamittatā) and so on. For unruliness, having evil friends, etc., are not separate mental factors (cetasika).

Those who have no faith are called faithless (assaddha); it means they do not believe in the Buddha and so on. 'Dussīla' (immoral) is not a bad name for virtue, but means those who lack virtue. 'Appassuta' (of little learning) means those devoid of knowledge from hearing. Because they possess the five kinds of stinginess, they are called 'macchari' (stingy). 'Duppaññā' (of poor wisdom) means those without wisdom. 'Sevanā' (associating) is by way of associating. 'Nisevanā' is strong (constant) associating. 'Saṃsevanā' is associating in every way. Or, the words are expanded by way of prefixes (upasagga). All three terms refer to associating. 'Bhajanā' means following/resorting to. 'Sambhajanā' means following in every way. Or, the word is expanded by way of prefixes. 'Bhatti' means firm devotion. 'Sambhatti' means devotion in every way. Or, the word is expanded by way of prefixes. Both terms refer to firm devotion. 'Taṃsampavaṅkatā' means the state of being well-bent (inclined) towards those persons by both body and mind. It means leaning towards them, inclining towards them, and tending towards them.

The explanation of the dyad of docility (sovacassatā) should be understood by the method opposite to what has been said.

The five groups of offenses (āpattikkhandha), according to the explanation of the Matrix (mātikā-niddesa), are these five offenses: Pārājika, Saṅghādisesa, Pācittiya, Pāṭidesanīya, and Dukkaṭa. The seven groups of offenses, according to the explanation of the Vinaya (vinaya-niddesa), are these seven offenses: Pārājika, Saṅghādisesa, Thullaccaya, Pācittiya, Pāṭidesanīya, Dukkaṭa, and Dubbhāsita. Among these, the wisdom that knows the classification of those offenses along with their grounds is called skill in offenses (āpatti-kusalatā). The wisdom that knows the classification of emergence from offenses along with the formal act (kammavācā) is called skill in emergence from offenses (āpatti-vuṭṭhāna-kusalatā).

It is called attainment (samāpatti) because it is to be attained. The wisdom that knows the classification of absorption (appanā) along with the preliminary work (parikamma) is called skill in attainments (samāpatti-kusalatā). The state of having the wisdom to emerge exactly at the intended time without fail, thinking, "I will emerge when the moon, the sun, or the stars have reached such-and-such a position," is called skill in emerging from attainments (samāpatti-vuṭṭhāna-kusalatā).
424:
The wisdom that occurs in learning, attending to, hearing, bearing in mind, and discerning the eighteen elements is called skillfulness in elements (dhātukusalatā). The wisdom that knows the learning and attending to those very elements is called skillfulness in attention (manasikārakusalatā).

The wisdom that occurs in learning, attending to, hearing, bearing in mind, and discerning the twelve sense bases is called skillfulness in sense bases (āyatanakusalatā). In all these three types of skillfulness—namely, skillfulness in elements, skillfulness in attention, and skillfulness in sense bases—all aspects such as learning, attending, hearing, investigating, penetrating, and reviewing are appropriate. Among these, hearing, learning, and reviewing are mundane. Penetration (paṭivedha) is supramundane. Investigating and attending are mixed, being both mundane and supramundane. The teachings such as 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise' will become clear in the Vibhaṅga of Dependent Origination. The wisdom that knows 'Because of this cause, this effect arises' is called skillfulness in dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppādakusalatā).

## Exposition of the Dyad on Skillfulness in What is Possible and Impossible

Both 'cause' (hetu) and 'condition' (paccaya) are synonyms for each other. The eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda), having made a visible form its object, is both the cause and the condition for the eye-consciousness that arises. Similarly, the ear-sensitivity and so on are the causes and conditions for ear-consciousness and so on; and mango seeds and so on are the causes and conditions for mango fruits and so on. In the second method, 'whatever states' refers to the indication of dissimilar conditioning states. 'Of whatever states' refers to the indication of states produced by dissimilar conditions. 'Neither cause nor condition' means that the eye-sensitivity, having made a sound its object, is neither the cause nor the condition for the ear-consciousness that arises. Similarly, the ear-sensitivity and so on are not the causes and conditions for the remaining consciousnesses; and mango seeds and so on are not the causes and conditions for the arising of palmyra trees and so on. Thus should the meaning be understood.

## Exposition of Integrity and Mildness

Only the term 'lowliness of mind' (nīcacittatā) has a distinction. Its meaning is: one who has a humble mind due to the absence of conceit is called 'lowly-minded' (nīcacitta). The state of being lowly-minded is 'lowliness of mind' (nīcacittatā). The remaining words have already appeared in the word-analysis (padabhājanīya) of uprightness of mind (cittujukatā) and mildness of mind (cittamudutā).

## Exposition of Patience

It is called 'patience' (khanti) by virtue of enduring. The mode of enduring is 'endurance' (khamanatā). By this patience, they place the wrongs of others upon themselves and let them stay; they do not prohibit them, nor do they stand in opposition; therefore, it is called 'forbearance' (adhivāsanatā). The state of one who is not harsh is 'gentleness' (acaṇḍikka). 'Non-resentment' (anasuropa) means: ill-spoken words are called 'resentment' (asuropa) because they are not well-placed. Because it is the opposite of that resentment, well-spoken words are called 'non-resentment' (anasuropa). Thus, in this context...
425:
The cause is indicated by mentioning the fruit. 'Delight of mind' (attamanatā) means the mind's state of being its own mind through the power of joy (somanassa), being the mind's own nature, and the state of not having a corrupted mind.

In the Exposition of Composure (soracca), 'non-transgression by body' refers to the three types of bodily good conduct. 'Non-transgression by speech' refers to the four types of verbal good conduct. By the phrase 'non-transgression by body and speech,' the virtue of right livelihood as the eighth (ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla) arising in the doors of body and speech is included. 'This is called composure' means this virtue is called composure (soracca) because it is well-withdrawn from evil. 'All restraint of virtue' is said in order to show the inclusion of mental virtue, because one does not only practice base conduct through body and speech, but also through the mind.

In the Exposition of Gentleness (sākhalya), 'excrescences' (aṇḍakā) means that just as lumps and knots grow on a defective tree, so do excrescences arise through words of abuse and contempt due to the presence of faults. 'Harsh' (kakkasā) means that just as a rotten tree is rough with oozing powder, so is [harsh speech] rough. It enters as if scraping the ear. Therefore, it is called 'harsh.' 'Bitter to others' (parakaṭukā) means words that are bitter, unpleasant, and provocative of anger to others. 'Clinging to others' (parābhisajjanī) means words that pierce and cling to others like a crooked thorny branch in the skin, making those who wish to go unable to go. 'Bordering on anger' (kodhasāmantā) means words that occur near anger. 'Not conducive to concentration' (asamādhisamvattanikā) means words that do not lead to either absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi) or access concentration (upacāra-samādhi). Thus, all these are synonyms for speech accompanied by faults. 'Having abandoned such speech' is said to show that for one who remains without abandoning harsh speech, even if gentle speech occurs occasionally, it is still called ungentle speech.

Regarding 'faultless' (neḷā): a fault is called 'eḷa.' Since that speech has no fault (eḷa), it is 'neḷā,' meaning faultless. It is like the 'neḷa' mentioned in 'neḷaṅgo setapacchādo.' 'Pleasant to the ear' (kaṇṇasukhā) means it gives pleasure to the ears because of the sweetness of its phrasing; it does not cause pain in the ear like the piercing of a needle. 'Loving' (pemanīyā) means it does not cause anger in the body but generates love because of the sweetness of its meaning. 'Heart-going' (hadayaṅgamā) means it goes to the heart; it enters the mind easily without being obstructed. 'Urbane' (porī) means it is called 'porī' because it is speech that occurs in a city (pura) due to being full of virtues. It is also called 'porī' because it is delicate like a lady raised in a city. It is also called 'porī' because it belongs to the city; it means the speech of city-dwellers. City-dwellers...
426:
Indeed, city dwellers possess appropriate speech. They address one who is like a father as 'father' and one who is like a brother as 'brother'. Such speech is called 'bahujanakantā' because it is beloved by many people. Because it is pleasing, it delights the hearts of many and causes the mind to flourish; thus it is called 'bahujanamānapā'. 'Yā tattha' refers to the speech present in that person. 'Saṇhavācatā' means having smooth and polished speech. 'Sakhilavācatā' means having gentle speech. 'Apharusavācatā' means having non-harsh speech.

In the Exposition on Hospitality (Paṭisanthāra-niddesa), 'āmisa-paṭisanthāra' (material hospitality) means closing or covering the gap (deficiency) of oneself and others caused by the lack of material things; it refers to reconciling so there is no gap through material gifts. 'Dhamma-paṭisanthāra' (spiritual hospitality) means closing or covering the gap of oneself and others caused by the lack of Dhamma; it refers to reconciling so there is no gap through the Dhamma. 'Paṭisanthārako hoti' means that in truth, there are only two kinds of gaps (deficiencies) among people in the world, and he is one who closes and reconciles those gaps. He is a reconciler through these two kinds of hospitality—material or spiritual; he reconciles so there is no gap and acts continuously (to make it one).

To speak about this hospitality from the beginning—indeed, a monk who practices hospitality, upon seeing a visiting monk arriving, should go out to meet him, take his bowl and robes, offer a seat, fan him with a palmyra fan, wash and anoint his feet, offer medicine if there is ghee or syrup, ask about drinking water, and prepare the lodging. In this way, material hospitality is said to be performed in part.

In the evening, even if the visitor is younger than himself, before the visitor comes to pay respects, he should go to him, sit down, and without asking about unsuitable matters, ask questions about matters suitable for him. Without asking, 'What group of reciters do you belong to?', he should ask, 'What texts do your teachers and preceptors study?' and ask questions in areas where the visitor is capable. If the visitor can answer, it is good. If not, he should explain the answer himself. In this way, spiritual hospitality is said to be performed in part.

If the visitor stays with him, he should take him along regularly for almsround. If the visitor wishes to leave, on the next day, he should accompany him as a companion, go for alms in a village, and then see him off. If monks have been invited to another direction, he should take that monk along if he wishes to go.
427:
'This direction is not suitable for me,' says the visiting monk who is unwilling to go; then other monks should be sent to fetch him and take him for alms. The material gifts (alms) received by oneself should be given to that monk. In this way, 'āmisa-paṭisanthāra' (material hospitality) is said to be performed.

To whom should a monk performing material hospitality give the alms he has received? First, it should be given to the visiting monk. If there is a sick monk or a monk who has not yet spent a vassa (avassika), it should be given to them as well. It should be given to teachers and preceptors (ācariya-upajjhāya). It should be given to the monk who carries one's bowl and robes. A monk who fulfills the 'dhammas of conciliation' (sārāṇīyadhamma), however, gives to all arriving monks, even if they come a hundred or a thousand times, starting from the seat of the elders. A monk practicing hospitality gives to whichever monk has not received material gifts. Going outside the village, if he sees an aged or helpless monk or nun, he should give to them as well.

In this regard, there is this story—it is said that when the village of Guttasāla was plundered by robbers, at that very moment, an Arahant Theri who had just emerged from the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) had a young nun carry her requisites and set out on the road with the people. Reaching the gate of Nakulanagara village at noon, she sat at the foot of a tree. At that time, the Elder Mahānāga, who lived at Kāḷavallimaṇḍapa, came out after wandering for alms in Nakulanagara village, saw the Theri, and invited her with food. She said, 'I have no bowl.' The Elder gave it to her along with his own bowl, saying, 'Please eat from this very bowl.' After finishing her meal, the Theri washed the bowl, gave it back to the Elder, and said, 'Dear brother, today you will be weary from seeking alms; but from this day forward, dear brother, there shall be no such thing as weariness due to seeking alms for you.' From then on, it is said that the Elder never received alms worth less than a deficient kahāpaṇa. This is called 'āmisa-paṭisanthāra'.

Having performed this hospitality, a monk, standing on the side of providing support, should preach the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) to that monk, teach him the Dhamma, dispel his doubts and remorse (kukkucca), perform any major or minor duties that arise, and grant him rehabilitation (abbhāna), emergence (vuṭṭhāna), penance (mānatta), and probation (parivāsa). He should ordain those worthy of novice ordination (pabbajjā) and those worthy of full ordination (upasampadā). For a nun who desires full ordination in his presence, it is also proper to recite the formal act (kammavācā). This is called 'dhamma-paṭisanthāra'.
428:
A monk who practices these two kinds of hospitality produces unarisen gain, makes arisen gain stable, and protects his own life in dangerous places. He is like the Elder who, while holding the bowl by its rim with the same hand that was holding the bowl for the robber king Nāga, poured alms-food into the bowl itself. Regarding the production of unarisen gain, the story of the Great Medicine Donation (Mahābhesajja-dāna) should be told, which was maintained for life at Setambangaṇa by King Mahānāga, who fled from here (Sīhala Island) to the other shore, received hospitality from an Elder, and upon returning, was established in kingship. Regarding the stabilization of arisen gain, the story should be told of how the robbers did not plunder the property of the Saṅgha at Cetiya-pabbata after receiving hospitality from the hand of the Elder Dīghabhāṇaka Abhaya.

In the explanation of 'non-guarding of the sense doors' (indriyesu aguttadvāratā), 'having seen a form with the eye' means having seen a form with eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa), which is capable of seeing forms and is conventionally called 'the eye' by way of its cause. However, the ancient teachers said: 'The eye does not see a form because it lacks consciousness; the mind does not see because it lacks an eye; but one sees with the mind based on the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) through the impingement of the object at the door.' This statement is a 'discourse with its components' (sasam-bhāra-kathā), like saying 'one shoots with a bow.' Therefore, 'having seen a form with eye-consciousness' is the meaning here. 'One who grasps at signs' (nimittaggāhī) means one who, through the power of desire and lust, grasps at a sign that is a basis for defilements, such as the sign of a woman, the sign of a man, or a beautiful sign; he does not stop at merely what is seen. 'One who grasps at details' (anubyañjanaggāhī) means one who grasps at aspects such as the hands, feet, smiles, speech, looking, and gazing, which are called 'details' (anubyañjana) because they make the defilements manifest. In the phrase 'on account of which' (yatvādhikaraṇamenaṃ), it means for whatever reason, due to that lack of restraint of the eye-faculty, these unwholesome states such as covetousness would flow after, follow, and overwhelm that person who dwells with the eye-faculty unrestrained and the eye-door unclosed by the gate of mindfulness. He does not practice for the sake of closing that eye-faculty with the gate of mindfulness. Such a person is said to not guard the eye-faculty and to not achieve restraint over the eye-faculty.

In that regard, there is actually no restraint or non-restraint in the eye-faculty itself, for mindfulness or forgetfulness does not arise depending on the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda). However, when...
429:
When a visible object comes into the range of the eye, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) arises and passes away twice. When it has ceased, the functional mind-element (kiriya-manodhātu), performing the function of adverting (āvajjana), arises and ceases. After that, eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa) performs the function of seeing; then the resultant mind-element (vipaāka-manodhātu) performs the function of receiving (sampaṭicchana); then the resultant rootless mind-consciousness-element (vipaāka-ahetuka-manoviiññāṇadhātu) performs the function of investigating (santīraṇa); then the functional rootless mind-consciousness-element (kiriya-ahetuka-manoviiññāṇadhātu) arises and ceases while performing the function of determining (votthabbana). Immediately after that determining, the impulsion (javana) runs. In that process, there is neither restraint (saṃvara) nor non-restraint (asaṃvara) at the time of the life-continuum, nor at the time of adverting and the others. However, at the moment of impulsion, immorality, forgetfulness, ignorance, impatience, or laziness may arise; then there is non-restraint.

When this occurs, it is called 'non-restraint in the eye-faculty.' Why? Because when that non-restraint exists, the door is also unguarded, the life-continuum is unguarded, and the cognitive processes (vīthi-citta) such as adverting are also unguarded. For example, if the four gates of a city are left open, even if the doors of the houses, gatehouses, and chambers inside are well-secured, all the goods and property within the city are unprotected and unshielded. Indeed, thieves can enter through the city gates and do as they wish. Similarly, when immorality and so forth arise in the impulsion, because of that non-restraint, the door is unguarded, the life-continuum is unguarded, and the cognitive processes such as adverting are also unguarded.

The same method applies to 'having heard a sound with the ear' and so forth. For one who does not achieve restraint in this way, whatever lack of guarding, lack of shielding, lack of protection, and lack of restraint there is in these six faculties, 'athakanaṃ' means not closing (apidahanaṃ).

In the explanation of 'immoderation in eating' (bhojane amattaññutā), 'here someone' (idhekacco) means a certain person in this world of beings. 'Without reflection' (appaṭisaṅkhā) means without knowing or considering with the wisdom of reflection. 'Unwisely' (ayoniso) means by an improper means. 'Food' (āhāraṃ) means that which is to be swallowed, such as what is eaten or drunk. 'Consumes' (āhāreti) means enjoys or swallows. The words 'for fun' (davāya) and so forth are stated to show the improper way. Indeed, one who consumes food in an improper way does so for the sake of play, for intoxication, for decoration, or for beautification, and not for the sake of the maintenance of this body. 'Whatever lack of contentment there is' (yā tattha asantuṭṭhitā) means the lack of satisfaction or the state of being discontented in that unwise consumption of food. 'Immoderation' (amattaññutā) means the state of not knowing the proper amount, the failure to know the measure known as the limit. This state, which proceeds by way of unreflecting consumption, is called 'immoderation in eating.'
430:
In the exposition on guarding the doors of the sense faculties (indriyesu guttadvāratā-niddesa), the words beginning with 'by the eye' (cakkhunā) should be understood in the same way as previously mentioned. 'He is not a grasper of signs' (na nimittaggāhī hoti) means he does not grasp a sign of the kind mentioned by way of desire and lust (chandarāga). Similarly, the remaining terms should also be understood by the opposite method of what was mentioned.

Just as it was said below: 'When immorality (dussīlya) etc. arise in the javana-consciousness, while that lack of restraint (asaṃvara) exists, the door is also unguarded, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is also unguarded, and the process-consciousnesses (vīthi-citta) such as adverting (āvajjana) etc. are also unguarded,' so here, when virtue (sīla) etc. arise in that javana-consciousness, the door is also guarded, the life-continuum is also guarded, and the process-consciousnesses such as adverting etc. are also guarded. How is this? Just as when the city gates are well-secured, even if the interiors of houses etc. are not secured, all the goods inside the city are well-protected and well-guarded (because since the city gates are closed, thieves have no way to enter), even so, when virtue etc. arise in the javana-consciousness, the door is also guarded, the life-continuum is also guarded, and the process-consciousnesses such as adverting etc. are also guarded. Therefore, even though it arises at the moment of javana, it is called 'restraint in the eye-faculty' (cakkhundriye saṃvaro). In cases such as 'having heard a sound with the ear' etc., the method is the same.

In the exposition on moderation in eating (bhojane mattaññutā-niddesa), 'reflecting, he partakes of food with wise cause' means knowing with the wisdom of reflection, he consumes food by means of a proper method. Now, to show that proper method, the words beginning with 'not for amusement' (neva davāya) are said.

In that passage, 'neva davāya' means he does not partake of food for the purpose of amusement. Among those, dancers, acrobats, etc., partake of food for the purpose of amusement. For one who has eaten that food, amusement consisting of dancing, singing, poetry, and praise becomes excessively apparent; they seek that food unrighteously and unfairly and partake of it. But this monk does not partake of it for such amusement.

'Na madāya' (not for intoxication) means he does not partake of food for the purpose of increasing intoxication through conceit (māna-mada) or intoxication through manliness (purisa-mada). Among those, kings and great ministers of kings partake of food for the purpose of intoxication. They eat choice foods such as the cream of milk and butter for the purpose of increasing their conceit-intoxication and manliness-intoxication. But this monk does not partake of it in that way.

'Na maṇḍanāya' (not for adornment) means he does not partake of food for the purpose of adorning the body. Among those, women who live by their beauty and those of the inner palace etc. drink things like ghee and molasses. They partake of smooth, soft, and mild food, thinking, 'By doing this, our limbs...'
431:
"...(the frame of our limbs) will be well-established, and the complexion of the skin on the body will be clear." But this monk does not partake of food in such a manner.

"Na vibhūsanāya" means he does not partake of food for the purpose of embellishing the flesh of the body. Among them, wrestlers, boxers, and so forth nourish the flesh of the body with very smooth fish, meat, and so on, thinking, "In this way, our flesh will become abundant for the purpose of enduring blows." But this monk does not partake of food for the purpose of embellishing the flesh of the body in that way.

"Yāvadeva" is for the purpose of showing the limitation of the benefit of partaking of food. "Imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā" means partaking for the sake of the endurance of this physical body (karajakāya) based on the four great elements. This is the benefit of that monk's partaking of food. "Yāpanāya" means partaking for the sake of maintaining the life-faculty (jīvitindriya). "Vihiṃsūparatiyā" means partaking for the sake of allaying the discomfort called "vihiṃsā," which is the hunger that arises due to not eating. "Brahmacariyānuggahāya" means partaking for the sake of supporting the holy life, which consists of the three trainings (sikkhā) and the entire Dispensation (sāsana).

"Iti" is the indication of the method; it means "by this method." "Puraṇañca vedanaṃ paṭihaṅkhāmi" means partaking with the thought, "I shall destroy the old feeling (hunger) that arises due to not eating." "Navañca vedanaṃ na uppādessāmi" means partaking with the thought, "I shall not produce a new feeling that arises due to overeating." Or, "new feeling" (navavedanā) is the feeling that arises due to eating. He partakes of food only for the purpose of not letting that feeling arise before it has arisen. "Yātrā ca me bhavissati" means "my maintenance will occur." In the phrase "anavajjatā ca," there is blameful partaking and blameless partaking. Therein, unrighteous seeking, unrighteous receiving, and unrighteous partaking are called "blameful" (sāvajja). Seeking righteously, receiving righteously, and partaking after reflection is called "blameless" (anavajja). Some people make even blameless things blameful through their partaking. Thinking "I have received it," they eat beyond moderation. Being unable to digest that food, they suffer through vomiting, diarrhea, and so forth. The monks in the entire monastery must then strive in caring for his body, seeking medicine, and so on. When asked, "What is this?"
432:
“The belly of such-and-such a monk is swollen,” and so forth, they say. “This monk is always of such a greedy and gluttonous nature; he does not know the measure of his own stomach,” thus they criticize him to his face and blame him behind his back. This is called making a fault out of what is faultless requisites. Without doing so, he consumes with the reflection, “There will be faultlessness for me.”

In the phrase “and for living at ease,” there is living at ease and there is not living at ease. Among these, the eating of these five types of Brahmins, namely: Āharahatthaka, Alaṃsāṭaka, Tatthavaṭṭaka, Kākamāsaka, and Bhuttavamitaka, is not called living at ease. Among those five, the one called “Āharahatthaka” (Bring-a-hand) eats so much that he cannot get up by his own effort and must say, “Bring a hand (to pull me up).” The one called “Alaṃsāṭaka” (Enough-cloth) has such a swollen belly that even if he stands up, he cannot wear his lower robe. The one called “Tatthavaṭṭaka” (Roll-right-there) cannot get up and just rolls around right there like a python. The one called “Kākamāsaka” (Crow-peckable) eats until the food reaches the opening of his mouth, such that it could be pecked by crows. The one called “Bhuttavamitaka” (Eat-and-vomit) cannot contain the food in his mouth and vomits right where he ate. Without doing such things, he consumes with the reflection, “There will be living at ease for me.”

Eating four or five mouthfuls less than one's fill is called living at ease. For one who drinks water after eating four or five mouthfuls less, the four postures proceed comfortably. Therefore, the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, said this:

“Having not eaten four or five mouthfuls, one should drink water; this is sufficient for the ease of living of a monk of resolute intent.” (Theragāthā 983)

At this point, the factors should be combined. “Not for fun” is one factor; “not for intoxication” is one; “not for beautification” is one; “not for adornment” is one; “only for the endurance and maintenance of this body” is one; “for ending discomfort and assisting the holy life” is one; “thus I shall terminate old feelings and not produce new feelings” is one; and “there will be maintenance for me” is one factor. Faultlessness and living at ease are the benefits of the meal here.

However, the Elder Mahā Sīva said: The lower four factors are called the rejection. Above that, eight factors should be combined—there, “only for the endurance of this body” is one factor; “for maintenance” is one; “for ending discomfort” is one; “for assisting the holy life” is one; “thus I shall terminate old feelings” is one;
433:
“I shall not produce new feelings” is one; “there will be maintenance for me” is one; and “faultlessness” is one. Living at ease is the benefit of the meal. One who consumes food endowed with these eight factors is called one who is moderate in eating. The phrase “this is said” means that this consumption with reflection, which proceeds by way of knowing the proper measure in seeking, receiving, and consuming, is called moderation in eating (bhojane mattaññutā).

In the description of forgetfulness (muṭṭhassacca), “asati” (non-mindfulness) refers to the four aggregates devoid of mindfulness. “Ananussati” and “appaṭissati” are the expansion of the term by way of prefixes. “Asaraṇatā” is the state of not being able to remember. “Adhāraṇatā” is the inability to retain or bear in mind. A person endowed with that inability to retain does not reach firm memorization and is not capable of storing it in the heart. Because of drifting on the object like a gourd shell on water, it is called “pilāpanatā” (floating/drifting). “Sammusanatā” is the state of having ruined or lost mindfulness. A person endowed with that ruined mindfulness is like a crow with its eyes on food, or like a fox with its eyes on meat.

In the description of the power of development (bhāvanābala), “of wholesome states” (kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ) refers to the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma). “Āsevanā” is the initial cultivation. “Bhāvanā” is the increasing or development. “Bahulīkammaṃ” is the repeated practice.

The description of failure in virtue (sīlavipatti) should be understood as the opposite of the description of success in virtue (sīlasampadā). The description of failure in view (diṭṭhivipatti) is the opposite of the description of success in view (diṭṭhisampadā), and the description of success in view is the opposite of the description of the grasping of views (diṭṭhupādāna). Although the description of purification of virtue (sīlavisuddhi) is similar to the description of success in virtue, in the latter, the Pātimokkha restraint virtue that leads to purification was taught, whereas here, the virtue that has reached purification is taught. By these six pairs—mindfulness and clear comprehension, the power of reflection and the power of development, serenity and insight, the sign of serenity and the sign of exertion, exertion and non-distraction, and success in virtue and success in view—only the mundane and supramundane states pertaining to the four planes are taught.

In the description of purification of view (diṭṭhivisuddhi), “knowledge of ownership of action” (kammassakatañāṇa) is the wisdom that knows, “This action is my own, this is not my own.” In that regard, whether done by oneself or by another, all unwholesome action is not one’s own. Why? Because it destroys welfare and produces harm. Wholesome action, however, is called “one’s own” because it destroys harm and produces welfare. Therein...
434:
For example, just as a man with much wealth and many possessions, while traveling on a long journey, hears the announcement of a festival being held in the villages or towns along the way, he does not think, 'I am a stranger; whom should I rely on to enjoy the festival?' Instead, he enjoys the festival in whatever way he desires with his own resources and crosses the difficult journey happily. In the same way, being established in this knowledge of the ownership of kamma (kammassakatā-ñāṇa), these beings have exerted much wholesome kamma that leads to the round of existence, and experiencing one happiness after another, they reach the fruit of Arahatship and transcend the path of calculation. Knowledge in conformity with the truths (saccānulomika-ñāṇa) is insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) that is in conformity with the Four Truths. The knowledge of one possessed of the path (magga-samangi) and the knowledge of one possessed of the fruit (phala-samangi) are simply the knowledge of the path and the knowledge of the fruit.

## Diṭṭhivisuddhi kho pana
In the explanation of the term [Diṭṭhivisuddhi kho pana], the four knowledges such as the knowledge of the ownership of kamma, which were mentioned below with terms such as 'that wisdom which is understanding,' are analyzed and shown.

## Yathādiṭṭhissa ca padhānaṃ
In the explanation of the term [Yathādiṭṭhissa ca padhānaṃ], the effort (vīriya) shown by terms such as 'that mental exertion of energy' is of the same nature as wisdom. Wisdom is to be understood as mundane in mundane matters and supramundane in supramundane matters.

In the explanation of the dyad of spiritual urgency (saṃvega-duka), 'fear of birth' (jāti-bhaya) is the knowledge established by seeing birth as a danger. The same method applies to the fear of aging (jarā), death (maraṇa), and so on.

By the words 'of unarisen evil states' (anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ) and so on, the right exertion (sammappadhāna) which is the means for one who, seeing birth and so on as a danger, desires to be liberated from birth, aging, sickness, and death, is taught. The meaning of the word-by-word commentary will become clear in the explanation of the factor of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga-pabba) in the Vibhaṅga Commentary (Vibh. A. 367).

## Asantuṭṭhitā ca kusalesu dhammesu
In the explanation of the term [Asantuṭṭhitā ca kusalesu dhammesu], 'desire for more' (bhiyyokamyatā) means the desire for distinction. For in this world, some person at first gives a meal for a fortnight (pakkhika-bhatta), or a meal by tickets (salāka-bhatta), or an uposatha meal (uposathika-bhatta), or a meal on the first day of the fortnight (pāṭipadika-bhatta). Not being content with that, he again gives a regular meal (dhura-bhatta), a meal for the Saṅgha (saṅgha-bhatta), or a meal for the rainy season (vassāvāsika-bhatta); he builds a monastery; he gives the four requisites. Even in giving thus, not being content, he takes the refuges and undertakes the five precepts. Even there, not being content, he ordains. Having ordained, he learns one Nikāya, two Nikāyas, or the word of the Buddha in the three Piṭakas; he develops the eight attainments; having increased insight, [he reaches] the fruit of Arahatship...
435:
...takes [the fruit of Arahatship]. From the time of reaching Arahatship, he is called one with great contentment. Thus, the desire for distinction up until Arahatship is called 'desire for more' (bhiyyokamyatā).

In the explanation of the term 'and unfaltering in effort' (appaṭivānitā ca padhānasmiṃ), because one who is weary in developing the most excellent wholesome states in secluded dwellings is said to cause effort to shrink back, while one who is not weary is said not to cause it to shrink back, therefore, to show that method, the words 'of wholesome states' (kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ) and so on are taught. In that passage, 'acting with care' (sakkaccakiriyatā) means the habit of acting respectfully in performing wholesome deeds. 'Continuous action' (sātaccakiriyatā) means performing them constantly. 'Uninterrupted action' (aṭṭhitakiriyatā) means performing them without stopping or creating gaps. 'Unfaltering livelihood' (anolīnavuttitā) means a way of living that does not shrink back, or an existence that does not shrink back. 'Not abandoning desire' (anikkhittachandatā) means not giving up the desire to do wholesome deeds. 'Not laying down the burden' (anikkhittadhuratā) means not laying down the burden of effort in performing wholesome deeds.

In the phrase 'the knowledge of recollection of past lives is a clear vision' (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇaṃ vijjā), 'past lives' (pubbenivāsa) refers to the aggregates previously lived and things connected to those aggregates. The repeated recollection of those past lives is 'recollection of past lives' (pubbenivāsānussati). The knowledge associated with that mindfulness is 'knowledge of recollection of past lives.' This is called 'clear vision' (vijjā) because it pierces the darkness that covers the aggregates previously lived. It is also called 'clear vision' in the sense of making known, because it pierces that darkness and makes those aggregates known and clear.

'Knowledge of passing away and rebirth' (cutūpapāte ñāṇaṃ) means knowledge regarding the passing away and the rebirth [of beings]. This also is called 'clear vision' because it pierces the darkness that covers the passing away and rebirth of beings. It is also called 'clear vision' in the sense of making known, because it pierces that darkness and makes the passing away and rebirth of beings known and clear. 'Knowledge of the destruction of the taints' (āsavānaṃ khaye ñāṇaṃ) means the knowledge at the time of the destruction of all defilements. This is called 'clear vision' because it pierces the darkness that covers the Four Truths. It is also called 'clear vision' in the sense of making known, because it pierces that darkness and makes the Four Truths known and clear.

In the phrase 'the resolution of the mind and Nibbāna' (cittassa ca adhimutti nibbānañca), the eight attainments are called 'resolution of the mind' (cittassa adhimutti) in the sense of resolving upon the object and in the sense of being well-freed from opposing states. In another way, it is called 'Nibbāna' in the sense that 'there is no craving (vāna) here' or 'it has departed from that craving.' Among those states, the eight attainments are called 'liberation' (vimutti) because they are liberated from defilements suppressed by themselves; Nibbāna, however, is called 'liberation' because it is absolutely liberated from all defilements.
436:
The knowledge of one possessed of the path (magga-samangi) refers to the four path knowledges. The knowledge of one possessed of the fruit (phala-samangi) refers to the four fruit knowledges. Among them, the first path knowledge arises while exhausting, ceasing, calming, and subsiding the five defilements; thus it is known as 'knowledge of destruction' (khaye ñāṇa). The second path knowledge [arises while exhausting, etc.] the four defilements; thus it is likewise known as 'knowledge of destruction.' The third path knowledge is also the same (as it arises while exhausting the four defilements, it is known as 'knowledge of destruction').

The fourth path knowledge, however, arises while exhausting, ceasing, calming, and subsiding the eight defilements; thus it is known as 'knowledge of destruction.' Furthermore, the fruit knowledge of each respective path arises at the end of the exhaustion, the end of the cessation, the end of the calming, the end of the subsiding, the end of the non-arising, and the end of the non-occurrence of those respective defilements; thus it is known as 'knowledge of non-arising' (anuppāde ñāṇa).

## The Explanation of the Summary Section (Nikkhepakaṇḍa-vaṇṇanā)
## in the Commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī named Atthasālinī is finished.
437:
## 4. Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa
## Tikautthāravaṇṇanā

Now, the sequence of the explanation of the Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa (Commentary Section), which is placed immediately after the Nikkhepakaṇḍa (Summary Section), has arrived. Why is this section called the Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa? It is called the Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa because it extracts and sets forth the meaning of the Buddha's words, which are the three Piṭakas. In the three Piṭakas, when a specific Dhamma that appears by way of its individual essence is defined and decided by the Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa alone, it is said to be well-decided. Even a person who cannot grasp the method (nayamagga) in the entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka, or the sequence of questioning and counting in the Mahāpakaraṇa (the Great Treatise, Paṭṭhāna), should bring them together and compare them from the Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa alone.

Where did this Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa originate? It originated from the Elder Sāriputta. The Elder Sāriputta, knowing that one of his co-residents (saddhivihārika) was unable to grasp the extraction of meaning in the Nikkhepakaṇḍa, taught him the Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa. However, the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā rejects this statement and says: Abhidhamma is not the domain of disciples, it is not the range of disciples; it is the domain of the Buddha, it is the range of the Buddha. The General of the Dhamma, the Elder Sāriputta, being asked by his co-resident monk, took him to the presence of the Teacher and reported it to the Fully Enlightened One. The Fully Enlightened One then taught the Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa to that monk. How? The Blessed One asked, "Which states are wholesome?" The meaning is that He reflected, "What kind of states are wholesome states?" Then, to that monk who remained silent, He taught by showing the wholesome and other states by way of extracting the meaning, making them into groups, into pots, and into clusters, in this manner: "Did I not show the wholesome by way of the distinction of planes, in the manner beginning with 'Which states are wholesome? When a wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere has arisen...'? All that is wholesome in the four planes; these states are wholesome."

In that passage, "in the four" means in the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara), and the unincluded (apariyāpanna, i.e., supramundane) planes. "Wholesome" refers to the wholesome states distinguished as contact (phassa) and so on. "These states are wholesome" means all these states such as contact and so on, which are mentioned in those respective planes, are called wholesome.

Since there is no distinction by way of planes for unwholesome states, He said, "the twelve arisings of unwholesome consciousness." In that phrase, "arises" means arising (uppāda). Consciousness itself...
438:
...arising is the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda). This is merely the head of the teaching (the main point of the exposition). For example, just as when it is said "The King has arrived," the arrival of the ministers and others is also said, so too, when "arising of consciousness" is said, the mental factors (cetasika) associated with those consciousnesses are also said. In all places, it should be understood that by the term "arising of consciousness," consciousness together with its associated states is taken. From here on, the meaning of all the terms in the Triads (Tika), Dyads (Duka), and the Analysis (Bhājanīya), such as "resultant in the four planes," and the indeterminable nature (navattabbatā) of pleasure and so on in the Feeling Triad (Vedanātika) and others, should be understood by investigating the meaning of the Pali text according to the method already stated below. I will mention only the specifics.

Among them, first in the Limited Object Triad (Parittārammaṇatika), in the passage "all sense-sphere resultants," the ten-fold sense-consciousness (dvipañcavinnāṇa) depend on the eye-sensitivity and so on and definitely occur by taking as objects the forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles which are distinguished as pleasant (iṭṭha) or unpleasant (aniṭṭha); therefore, they are called "having limited objects." The two mind-elements (manodhātu), which are wholesome resultants and unwholesome resultants, depend on the heart-base and occur immediately after eye-consciousness and so on, definitely taking only forms and so on as objects; therefore, they are called "having limited objects." The rootless wholesome-resultant mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy (somanassa-santīraṇa) occurs by way of investigation (santīraṇa) in the five doors and by way of registration (tadārammaṇa) in the six doors, definitely taking only the six limited objects such as forms and so on; therefore, it is called "having limited objects." The pair of rootless mind-consciousness elements (upekkhā-santīraṇa) which are wholesome and unwholesome resultants, occur by way of investigation in the five doors and by way of registration in the six doors, definitely taking only the six limited objects such as forms and so on. Even when occurring by way of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), it takes a limited kamma, kamma-sign, or destiny-sign as an object. When occurring as life-continuum (bhavaṅga) during the course of existence, or as death (cuti) at the end, it takes that same object; therefore, it is called "having limited objects." The eight arisings of resultant consciousness with roots (sahetuka-vipāka) also occur by way of registration, and by way of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death, taking only limited states as objects, according to the method stated here. The functional mind-element (pañcadvārāvajjana) occurs taking forms and so on as objects in the five doors. The rootless functional mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy (hasituppāda) occurs in the six doors, taking as objects limited states such as forms and so on which are present, or in the mind-door, those which are past or future, producing the state of smiling in Arahants; therefore, it is called "having limited objects." Thus, these twenty-five arisings of consciousness should be known as definitely having limited objects.

The states of the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana) and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana) are called "having lofty objects" (mahaggatārammaṇa) because they occur by taking their respective lower attainments as objects. Similarly, the states of the Path and Fruit are called "having immeasurable objects" (appamāṇārammaṇa) because they take Nibbāna as their object.
439:
The eight consciousness-arisings dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇavippayutta)—four wholesome and four functional—are called those having a limited object (parittārammaṇa) (having a sense-sphere object) when they occur in trainees (sekhas), worldlings (puthujjanas), and Arahants, taking sense-sphere phenomena as objects during casual giving, reflection, listening to the Dhamma, and so on. They are called those having a sublime object (mahaggatārammaṇa) (having a sublime object) when reflecting on the well-practiced first jhāna and so forth. They are called those having an indescribable object (navattabbārammaṇa) (having a concept object) when reflecting on concepts (paññatti) such as the kasiṇa signs.

The four consciousness-arisings associated with wrong view (diṭṭhigatasampayutta) from the unwholesome class are called those having a limited object when they occur while wrongly grasping, enjoying, or delighting in the fifty-five sense-sphere phenomena as "a being, a being." In the same manner, they are called those having a sublime object when they occur taking the twenty-seven sublime phenomena as objects. When they occur taking concepts as objects, they may sometimes be those having an indescribable object.

Regarding consciousness dissociated from wrong view (diṭṭhivippayutta), when they occur taking those same phenomena as objects through mere enjoyment and delight; or in the case of consciousness associated with aversion (paṭighasampayutta) through displeasure (domanassa); or in the case of consciousness-arising associated with doubt (vicikicchā) through indecision; or in the case of consciousness accompanied by restlessness (uddhacca) through distraction and lack of peace—their nature of having limited, sublime, or indescribable objects should be understood. Among these, not even a single state is able to occur taking immeasurable phenomena (appamāṇa) as objects; therefore, they do not have immeasurable objects (nāppamāṇārammaṇā).

The eight consciousness-arisings associated with knowledge (ñāṇasampayutta)—four wholesome and four functional—are those having limited, sublime, or indescribable objects when they occur in trainees, worldlings, and Arahants, taking the aforementioned various phenomena as objects during respectful giving, reflection, listening to the Dhamma, and so on. Their nature of having immeasurable objects (appamāṇārammaṇa) should be understood when they occur as change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) or when reflecting on supramundane phenomena (lokuttara).

There is the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara). That fourth jhāna is of twelve kinds through wholesome and functional aspects: the fourth jhāna as a basis for all (sabbatthapādaka), the fourth jhāna of the space kasiṇa, the fourth jhāna of the light kasiṇa, the fourth jhāna of the divine abidings (brahmavihāra), the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna), the fourth jhāna of supernormal powers (iddhividha), the fourth jhāna of the divine ear (dibbasota), the fourth jhāna of the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa), the fourth jhāna of the knowledge of beings passing away according to their kamma (yathākammupagañāṇa), the fourth jhāna of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu), the fourth jhāna of the recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsañāṇa), and the fourth jhāna of the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsañāṇa).

Among those twelve, the "fourth jhāna as a basis for all" refers to the fourth jhāna occurring in the eight kasiṇas. Because that fourth jhāna serves as a basis (pādaka) for insight (vipassanā), for supernormal knowledge (abhiññā), for the attainment of cessation (nirodha), and even for the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa), it is called "basis for all" (sabbatthapādaka). However, the fourth jhānas of the space kasiṇa and light kasiṇa are bases for insight, supernormal knowledge, and the round of rebirth...
440:
(The fourth jhānas of the space kasiṇa and light kasiṇa) are bases (for insight, etc.), but they are not bases for the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). The "fourth jhāna of the divine abidings and the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing" are bases for insight and the round of rebirth, but they are not bases for supernormal knowledge and the attainment of cessation. Among those fourth jhānas, the ten kinds of kasiṇa jhānas are called "having an indescribable object" (navattabbārammaṇa) (a state having an object that cannot be described) because they occur taking the kasiṇa concept as an object; the fourth jhāna of the divine abidings is so called because it occurs taking the concept of beings (satta-paññatti) as an object; and the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing is so called because it occurs taking the sign (nimitta) as an object, thus having an object that is indescribable as limited and so forth.

The "fourth jhāna of supernormal powers" (iddhividha) has limited and sublime objects. How?
