When one, having made the body dependent on the mind, wishes to go with an invisible body, one directs the body by the power of the mind, merges it into the sublime mind, and fixes it there. At that time, because it is said to be an object obtained through application (upayoga), it has a limited object by way of having the physical body (rūpakāya) as its object. When one, having made the mind dependent on the body, wishes to go with a visible body, one directs the mind by the power of the body, merges the basis-jhāna mind into the physical body, and fixes it there. At that time, because it is said to be an object obtained through application, it has a sublime object by way of having the sublime mind as its object.

The "fourth jhāna of the divine ear" (dibbasota) has exclusively a limited object because it occurs taking sound as its object. The "fourth jhāna of the knowledge of others' minds" (cetopariyañāṇa) has limited, sublime, and immeasurable objects. How? When it knows the sense-sphere minds of others, it has a limited object; when it knows fine-material and immaterial sphere minds, it has a sublime object; and when it knows the paths and fruits (magga-phala), it has an immeasurable object. In this regard, a worldling does not know the mind of a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna); a Stream-enterer does not know the mind of a Once-returner (sakadāgāmī); and so on, this should be extended up to the Arahant. An Arahant, however, knows the minds of all. This distinction should be understood: a higher person other than an Arahant also knows the mind of a lower person. The "fourth jhāna of the knowledge of beings passing away according to their kamma" (yathākammupagañāṇa) has a limited object when knowing sense-sphere kamma, and a sublime object when knowing fine-material and immaterial sphere kamma.

The "fourth jhāna of the divine eye" (dibbacakkhu) has exclusively a limited object because it has a visible form as its object. The "fourth jhāna of the recollection of past lives" (pubbenivāsañāṇa) has limited, sublime, immeasurable, and indescribable objects. How? When recollecting sense-sphere aggregates, it has a limited object. When recollecting fine-material and immaterial sphere aggregates, it has a sublime object. When recollecting the path developed and the fruit realized by oneself or others in the past, it has an immeasurable object. When recollecting that in the past, the Buddhas developed the path, realized the fruit, and through the Nibbāna element...
441:
"Parinibbāyiṃsu" (they attained final Nibbāna) refers to the reflection on the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna by way of recollecting the Buddhas whose cycle of rebirth has been cut off; thus, it is said to have an immeasurable object (appamāṇārammaṇa). When recollecting the name, lineage, place, and signs, such as "In the past, there was a Blessed One named Vipassī; his city was named Bandhumatī, King Bandhumā was his father, and Queen Bandhumatī was his mother," it is a not-to-be-declared object (navattabbārammaṇa).

The same method applies to the fourth jhāna of the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsañāṇa). When this knowledge of the future knows, "This person will be reborn in the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) in the future," it has a limited object (parittārammaṇa). When it knows, "He will be reborn in the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) or the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara)," it has a sublime object (mahaggatārammaṇa). When it knows, "He will develop the Path, realize the Fruition, and attain final Nibbāna through the Nibbāna element," it has an immeasurable object (appamāṇārammaṇa). When knowing the name and lineage in the future, such as "The Blessed One named Metteyya will arise; the brahmin named Subrahmā will be his father, and the brahmin woman named Brahmavatī will be his mother," it has a not-to-be-declared object (navattabbārammaṇa).

As for the fourth immaterial jhāna and the fourth jhāna of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa), I will discuss them where they appear in the Pāḷi text. The functional rootless mind-consciousness element (ahetuka-kiriya-manoviññāṇadhātu) accompanied by equanimity is the precursor to all these wholesome, unwholesome, and functional consciousnesses. The distinction of its objects should be understood in the same way as described for those consciousnesses. However, in the five doors, when it occurs by way of determining (voṭṭhabbana), it has exclusively a limited object (parittārammaṇa). The fine-material sphere triple and quadruple jhānas, etc., have not-to-be-declared objects (navattabbārammaṇa) because they occur by taking as an object those states that cannot be declared as limited, etc. Here, the fine-material sphere jhānas occur in the earth-kasiṇa, etc.; the sphere of infinite space occurs in the space from which the kasiṇa has been removed; and the sphere of nothingness occurs in the absence of consciousness.

In the beginning of the Path-as-object triad (maggārammaṇattika), the eight consciousness-arisings associated with knowledge are Path-as-object (maggārammaṇa) for trainees (sekha) and non-trainees (asekha) when they reflect on the Paths they have personally penetrated. However, they are not Path-rooted (maggahetuka) because they do not arise simultaneously with the Path. When reflecting on the Path they have personally penetrated by making it an object of priority, they are Path-predominant (maggādhipati) by way of object-predominance. When taking other states as objects, they are not to be declared as Path-as-object or Path-predominant. The four noble Paths are exclusively Path-rooted (maggahetuka) because they have roots called the Path or associated with the Path. By making energy (vīriya) or investigation (vīmaṃsā) the chief...
442:
At the time of developing the Path, they may be Path-predominant (maggādhipati) by way of conascent-predominance (sahajātādhipati). When making one of desire (chanda) or consciousness (citta) the chief, they are not to be declared as Path-predominant.

Among the twelve types of fine-material sphere fourth jhānas, the nine jhānas such as the fourth jhāna that serves as a basis for all [supernormal powers] (sabbatthapādaka) are neither Path-as-object, nor Path-rooted, nor Path-predominant. However, the fourth jhānas of the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa), the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsañāṇa), and the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsañāṇa) are Path-as-object (maggārammaṇa) when they know the Path-consciousness of the noble ones (ariyans). But they are not Path-rooted (maggahetuka) because they do not arise simultaneously with the Path. They are not Path-predominant (maggādhipati) because they do not occur by making the Path a priority. Why do these knowledges not make the Path a priority? Because of their own sublime (mahaggata) nature. For example, while the whole world honors a king, his parents do not. They do not rise from their seats upon seeing the king, nor do they perform salutations, etc.; they address him just as they did when he was young. Similarly, these knowledges do not make the Path a priority because of their own sublime nature.

The functional rootless mind-consciousness element (ahetuka-kiriya-manoviññāṇadhātu) is also Path-as-object (maggārammaṇa) when reflecting on the Path of the noble ones, because it is the precursor to reflection. It is not Path-rooted (maggahetuka) because it does not arise simultaneously with the Path. It is not Path-predominant (maggādhipati) because it does not occur by making the Path a priority. Why does it not make it a priority? Because of its own rootless nature, its inferiority, and its dullness. For example, while the whole world honors a king, the servants near him, such as hunchbacks, dwarfs, and menials, do not honor him as greatly as wise men do, because of their own ignorance. In the same way, this consciousness does not make the Path a priority because of its own rootless nature, its inferiority, and its dullness.

Wholesome states dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇavippayutta kusala), etc., do not obtain the status of Path-as-object, etc., both because of the absence of knowledge and because they take only mundane states as objects; they should be understood as being only not-to-be-declared objects (navattabbārammaṇa).

In the Past-Object triad (atītārammaṇattika), the states of the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana) and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana) are exclusively past-objects (atītārammaṇa) because they occur by taking as an object a past attainment [mentioned] below.

Since it is said that there is no "future-object" (anāgatārammaṇa) by way of necessity, there is no specific consciousness that is called "future-object" by rule. Is it not that the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsañāṇa) is exclusively a future-object? And does not the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) also occur by taking the future as an object?
443:
It is not that consciousness with a future object does not occur; it does occur. However, that knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa) and knowledge of others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa) which have future objects do not exist as separate, individual minds. Because they are included within the rūpāvacara fourth jhāna, they are mixed with other mahaggata minds. Therefore, it is said, 'There is no separate mind that is invariably fixed on a future object.'

The ten types of sense-consciousness (dve-pañcavijñāṇa) and the three mind-elements (manodhātu) are called minds with present objects because they occur with respect to present visible forms and so forth. Regarding the 'ten types of consciousness-arising' (dasa cittuppāda), first, the eight sahetuka-vipāka minds that occur at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) for devas and humans, taking kamma or the sign of kamma (kamma-nimitta) as their object, are minds with past objects. The same method applies during the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and at death (cuti). However, when rebirth-linking occurs taking the sign of destiny (gati-nimitta) as the object, and during the subsequent life-continuum, they are minds with present objects. Similarly, they have present objects when occurring by way of registration (tadārammaṇa) in the five doors. In the mind door, however, they are minds with past, future, or present objects because they occur by taking the object of the javanas which have past, future, or present objects. The same method applies to the kusala-vipāka ahetuka upekkhā-sahagata manovijñāṇadhātu (santīraṇa). Specifically, that mind is the rebirth-linking consciousness for those born blind and so forth among humans. The fact that it is a mind with a present object by way of investigation (santīraṇa) in the five doors is the distinction here. The somanassa-sahagata (santīraṇa) mind is a mind with a present object by way of investigation and registration in the five doors. In the mind door, it should be understood as a mind with past, future, or present objects by way of registration, like the sahetuka-vipāka minds.

The akusala-vipāka ahetuka manovijñāṇadhātu is of the same nature as the kusala-vipāka upekkhā-sahagata ahetuka mind. The only distinction here is that it occurs by way of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death for those in the woeful states (apāya). The somanassa-sahagata kiriya ahetuka manovijñāṇadhātu (hasituppāda) is a mind with a present object when it produces the manner of smiling in the five doors for Arahants. In the mind door, when it occurs by way of producing a smile (hasituppāda) with respect to various states such as those of the past, it is a mind with past, future, or present objects.

Among the kāmāvacara-kusala and so forth, in the case of the wholesome (kusala), there are first the four consciousness-arisings associated with knowledge (ñāṇa-sampayutta). When learners (sekhas) and worldlings (puthujjanas) contemplate and review the various aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana) of the past and so forth, these are minds with past, future, or present objects. When reviewing concepts (paññatti) and Nibbāna, they are minds with objects that are 'not to be said' (navattabba, i.e., beyond the three periods of time). In the case of minds dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇa-vippayutta), it is the same...
444:
(In the case of minds dissociated from knowledge), it is the same. However, with those minds dissociated from knowledge, there is no contemplation of the Path, Fruition, or Nibbāna. This is the distinction here.

Among the unwholesome (akusala) minds, the four consciousness-arisings associated with wrong view (diṭṭhi-sampayutta) have past and other objects during the time of enjoying, delighting in, and misapprehending (parāmāsa) the various aggregates, elements, and bases of the past and so forth. For one who enjoys and delights in concepts, or misapprehends them as 'a being, a being,' they have objects that are 'not to be said' (navattabba). In the case of unwholesome minds dissociated from wrong view, it should be understood in the same way. However, with those minds, there is no misapprehension (parāmāsa-ggahaṇa).

The two consciousness-arisings associated with aversion (paṭigha-sampayutta) have past and other objects for those who feel displeasure with respect to various states of the past and so forth. For those who feel displeasure with respect to concepts, they have navattabba objects. The minds associated with doubt (vicikicchā) and restlessness (uddhacca) have past, future, present, and navattabba objects when they occur in the manner of indecision and restlessness regarding those same states.

Among the functional (kiriya) minds, the eight consciousness-arisings with roots (sahetuka) follow the same course as the wholesome consciousness-arisings. The upekkhā-sahagata ahetuka kiriya manovijñāṇadhātu (manodvārāvajjana) is only a mind with a present object when it occurs by way of determining (voṭṭhabbana) in the five doors. In the mind door, during the time preceding javanas that have past, future, or present objects, or those that have concepts or Nibbāna as objects, it has past, future, present, and navattabba objects.

Among the various rūpāvacara jhānas mentioned, these five—the fourth jhāna as a basis for supernormal powers, the fourth jhāna of the space-kasiṇa, the fourth jhāna of the light-kasiṇa, the fourth jhāna of the divine abidings (brahma-vihāra), and the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna)—have only navattabba objects. The 'fourth jhāna of the modes of supernormal power' (iddhividha-catuttha) has a past object for one who inclines the mind by the power of the body, because it occurs with respect to the past basis jhāna consciousness. For those who resolve (adhiṭṭhāna) for the future, like the Elder Mahākassapa and others during the enshrinement of the great relics, it has a future object.

It is said that while the Elder Mahākassapa was performing the enshrinement of the great relics, he resolved: 'For two hundred and eighteen years into the future, let these perfumes not dry up, let these flowers not wither, and let these lamps not go out.' Everything happened exactly as he resolved. The Elder Assagutta, seeing the Saṅgha of monks eating dry food at the Vattaniya monastery, resolved: 'In the pond, every day before the meal, let there be the taste of curd.' The water drawn before the meal had the taste of curd; after the meal, it was just ordinary water. Also, when traveling with an invisible body by making the body dependent on the mind, or when another...
445:
When performing other miracles (pāṭihāriya), because it occurs based on the body, it has a present object.

The 'fourth jhāna of the divine ear' (dibbasota-catuttha-jhāna) has a present object because it occurs based only on an existing sound. The fourth jhāna of the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa-catuttha-jhāna) has past and future objects for one who knows the minds of others within seven days in the past and within seven days in the future. Beyond seven days, however, one is not able to know those minds of others. This is the domain only of the knowledges that know the past and future. It is not the object of this cetopariyañāṇa. Furthermore, when this cetopariyañāṇa knows the present, it has a present object.

This so-called 'present' is of three kinds: the momentary present (khaṇapaccuppanna), the continuity present (santatipaccuppanna), and the duration present (addhāpaccuppanna). Among these three, the dhamma that has reached arising (uppāda), presence (ṭhiti), and dissolution (bhaṅga) is called the 'momentary present.' The dhamma included within one or two continuity-intervals (santativāra) is called the 'continuity present.' In that continuity present, for one who has been sitting in the dark and goes to a bright place, the object is not yet clear; until that object becomes clear, the series of matter or mind occurring in this interval should be known as one or two continuity-intervals. For one who has wandered in a bright place and enters a chamber, the material object is not yet immediately clear; until that object becomes clear, the series of matter or mind occurring in this interval should be known as one or two continuity-intervals. Even when standing at a distance and seeing the hand movements of washermen or the movement of striking a bell or drum, etc., one does not yet hear the sound; until one hears that sound, the series of matter and mind occurring in this interval should also be known as one or two continuity-intervals. Thus first spoke the teachers who recite the Majjhima Nikāya (Majjhimabhāṇaka). The teachers who recite the Saṃyutta Nikāya (Saṃyuttabhāṇaka), however, speak of two kinds of continuity: 'material continuity' (rūpasantati) and 'immaterial continuity' (arūpasantati), saying: "For one who has walked treading on water, as long as the water-marks where he trod on the bank have not yet cleared; for one who has come from a long journey, as long as the heat in the body has not yet subsided; for one who has come from the sunlight and entered a chamber, as long as the state of darkness has not yet disappeared; for one who, having attended to a meditation subject inside a chamber, opens the window during the day and looks out, as long as the flickering of the eyes has not yet subsided—this process is called material continuity (rūpasantati). Two or three impulsion-intervals (javanavāra) are called immaterial continuity (arūpasantati)." Having said this, they say: "Both of these together are called the continuity present."

The period delimited by a single life is called the 'duration present' (addhāpaccuppanna). With reference to that duration present, it was said in the Bhaddekaratta Sutta: "Friends, the mind and the mental objects—both of these are the present. If, in that present, consciousness is bound by desire and lust, because consciousness is bound by desire and lust, one delights in that; one who delights in it is swept away among present dhammas." Here, the continuity present comes in the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā). The duration present comes in the Sutta.
446:
Regarding that cetopariyañāṇa, some teachers say: "A mind that is a momentary present is the object of cetopariyañāṇa." For what reason? They say it is because the mind of the possessor of psychic power and the mind of another arise at the same moment. This is their simile—just as when a handful of flowers is thrown into the sky, one flower inevitably pierces the stalk of another, or stalk hits stalk; so too, when contemplating the minds of many people in a mass with the thought 'I will know the minds of others,' one mind inevitably pierces (knows) another mind at the moment of arising (uppāda), presence (ṭhiti), or dissolution (bhaṅga). However, that statement is rejected in the Commentaries as improper, because even if one contemplates for a hundred or a thousand years, the contemplating mind and the knowing mind do not exist together, and because there is the fault of having various objects in undesirable places for the adverting (āvajjana) and impulsions (javana). It should be understood that only the continuity present and the duration present are the objects.

Among those two types of present, the mind of another occurring within the extent of two or three impulsion-processes (javana-vīthi) by way of past and future from the current impulsion-process is called the continuity present. The statement in the Commentary that the duration present should be shown by way of the impulsion-interval (javanavāra) is well-spoken. This is the explanation—the possessor of psychic power, wishing to know the mind of another, adverts (āvajjana). The adverting mind takes the momentary present (of the other) as an object and ceases along with that very mind. Thereafter, four or five impulsions (javana) occur, the last of which is the psychic mind (iddhi-citta), while the remaining are sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) impulsions. All of them take that very mind of the other, which has already ceased, as an object. And they do not have various objects. They have a single object because they are present objects by way of the duration present. Even though they have a single object, only the psychic mind fully knows the mind of another, not the others; just as at the eye-door, only eye-consciousness sees the form, not the others (such as adverting, etc.). Thus, this cetopariyañāṇa has a present object by way of the continuity present and the duration present. Or, because the continuity present also falls within the duration present, it should be understood as having a present object by way of the duration present.

The 'fourth of the knowledge of recollecting past lives' (pubbenivāsañāṇa-catuttha) is an indeterminable object (navattabbārammaṇa) when recollecting names and clans and when contemplating the sign of Nibbāna. At other times, it is only a past object (atītārammaṇa). The fourth of the knowledge of faring according to deeds (yathākammūpagañāṇa) is also only a past object. In those knowledges, although both pubbenivāsañāṇa and cetopariyañāṇa have past objects, for pubbenivāsañāṇa, there is nothing among past aggregates and things connected to aggregates that is not an object. For that knowledge is similar in power to Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) regarding past aggregates and things connected to aggregates. For cetopariyañāṇa, however, only the past mind within seven days is the object. That knowledge...
447:
(That knowledge of others' minds) does not know other aggregates or things connected with aggregates; however, because it has the mind associated with the Path as its object, it is figuratively said to have 'the Path as its object.' For the knowledge of passing away according to kamma (yathākammūpagañāṇa), only past volition (cetanā) is the object. This distinction should be noted. This is the method of the Commentaries in this matter. However, because it is stated in the Paṭṭhāna: 'Wholesome aggregates are a condition for the knowledge of psychic power, knowledge of others' minds, knowledge of recollection of past lives, knowledge of passing away according to kamma, and knowledge of the future by way of object-condition,' the four aggregates also become objects for the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of passing away according to kamma. Even so, for the knowledge of passing away according to kamma, only wholesome and unwholesome (volitions) are the objects.

The 'fourth divine-eye knowledge' has a present object because its object is a manifest visible form. The 'fourth knowledge of the future' has only a future object. That knowledge of the future, regarding future aggregates and things connected with aggregates, has a scope similar to omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa), like the knowledge of past lives. Among these knowledges, although the knowledge of others' minds also has a future object, that knowledge of others' minds takes as its object only the mind that will arise within seven days. This knowledge of the future, however, takes as its object the mind, the aggregates, and things connected with aggregates that will arise within a hundred thousand future aeons (kappa). The fine-material sphere triads, the four jhānas, etc., should be understood as having only 'indescribable objects' (navattabba-ārammaṇa) (objects that cannot be said to be past, etc.) because they do not arise by taking any single phenomenon among the past, future, or present as an object.

In the Triad of the Internal (ajjhatta-ttika), regarding the statement 'matter not connected with the faculties and Nibbāna are external (bahiddha)'—just as matter connected with the faculties is called 'external' when it occurs in the continuity of another person, yet it is 'personal-internal' (niyakajjhatta) because it is included in that person's own continuity—so this (Nibbāna, etc.) is called 'external' because there is no figurative sense of 'personal-internal,' as it cannot be internal by any figurative means. This is only due to the impossibility of it being personal-internal. Aiming only at the impossibility of it being personal-internal, it is called 'having an external object' (bahiddhārammaṇa) in the Triad of Internal Objects. Because it is merely a departure from internal phenomena, the object of the attainment of the sphere of nothingness is not allowed to be internal, external, or internal-external; thus it is said, 'The attainment of the sphere of nothingness should not be called internal-object,' and so on.

In that matter, not only is that (attainment of the sphere of nothingness) an indescribable object, but its advertings, its access thoughts, the reviewing thoughts that reflect on that object, and the unwholesome thoughts that arise by way of relishing that attainment, etc., are also only those having indescribable objects.
448:
Those (advertings, access, etc.) are not mentioned separately because when that (attainment of the sphere of nothingness) is mentioned, they are considered as mentioned. How are they considered as mentioned? This attainment of the sphere of nothingness, and whatever mind occurs as its precursor by way of adverting, access, etc., would have the same single object as that attainment of the sphere of nothingness. All those minds are called 'indescribable objects' because, in the Triad of Past Objects, regarding the mentioned states—'sense-sphere wholesome, unwholesome, nine types of functional consciousness, and the fine-material sphere fourth jhāna'—their status as indescribable objects is permitted by the method 'they might be indescribable as past objects,' etc.; and because for the attainment of the sphere of nothingness, it is definitely stated as having an indescribable object by the words: 'The sphere of nothingness, the four Paths, and the four fruits of asceticism—these states are indescribable as past objects,' etc. 

Now, although that attainment of the sphere of nothingness is mentioned alone in the Triad of Internal Objects, since the status of sense-sphere wholesome states, etc., as having indescribable objects was mentioned below (in the Triad of Past Objects) by also aiming at the fact of having the same single object as that attainment of the sphere of nothingness, therefore, here too, the status of those sense-sphere wholesome states, etc., as having indescribable objects is shown. Indeed, what obstacle could there be to the status of sense-sphere wholesome states, etc., which have the same single object as that attainment, as having indescribable objects? Thus, when that attainment of the sphere of nothingness is mentioned, those (advertings, etc.) should be understood as 'considered as mentioned.' The remaining words in this Triad of Internal Objects are clear according to the Pali text.

In the classification by way of object, first, regarding the six types of consciousness—the wholesome, resultant, and functional of the sphere of infinite consciousness and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—their status as having internal objects (ajjhattārammaṇa) should be understood because they occur by taking the lower attainment connected with one's own continuity as an object. Among these six types of consciousness, the functional consciousness of the sphere of infinite space is the object only for the functional consciousness of the sphere of infinite consciousness, not for the others. Why? Because for a person possessed of the functional sphere of infinite space, there is no wholesome or resultant consciousness of the sphere of infinite consciousness. However, the wholesome sphere of infinite space is the object for all three: wholesome, resultant, and functional. Why? Because for one who remains after having produced the wholesome sphere of infinite space, the arising of the three types of the sphere of infinite consciousness above that is possible. The resultant sphere of infinite space, however, is not an object for any consciousness. Why? Because it is impossible to direct the mind [to an object] after emerging from a resultant. In making the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception an object, this same method applies. All jhānas, such as the fine-material sphere triads and the four jhānas, should be understood as having external objects (bahiddhārammaṇa) because they occur by taking as objects the earth kasina, etc., which are external since they are outside one's own continuity.

Among all sense-sphere wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states, and the fine-material sphere fourth jhāna, first, from the wholesome, the four types of consciousness associated with knowledge...
449:
For one who contemplates one's own aggregates and so forth, [knowledge-associated consciousnesses] have internal objects (ajjhattārammaṇa). In the contemplation of the aggregates and so forth of others, and in the contemplation of concepts and Nibbāna, they have external objects (bahiddhārammaṇa). By way of both, they have internal and external objects (ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇa). The same method applies to knowledge-dissociated consciousnesses, except that for those consciousnesses, there is no contemplation of Nibbāna. Among unwholesome states, the four types of consciousness-arising associated with wrong view have internal objects at the time of taking pleasure in, delighting in, and misapprehending one's own aggregates and so forth. At the time of occurring similarly regarding the aggregates and so forth of others, and regarding non-sentient matter (anindriyabaddha-rūpa), kasinas, and so forth, they have external objects. By way of both, they have internal and external objects. The same method applies to consciousnesses dissociated from wrong view, except that for those consciousnesses, there is no misapprehension (parāmāsa). The two types of consciousness associated with aversion have internal objects for one who is displeased with one's own aggregates and so forth. They have external objects regarding the aggregates and so forth of others, and regarding non-sentient matter and concepts. By way of both, they have internal and external objects. Regarding consciousnesses associated with doubt and restlessness, their state of having internal objects and so forth should be understood by way of the occurrence of doubting and agitation concerning the aforementioned states.

These thirteen types of consciousness-arising—the ten sense-consciousnesses and the three mind-elements—have internal objects when occurring with reference to one's own matter and so forth. If they occur regarding the matter and so forth of others, they have external objects. By way of both, they have internal and external objects. The joy-accompanied rootless resultant mind-consciousness element, when occurring at the five doors by way of investigation (santīraṇa) and registration (tadārammaṇa) with reference to one's own five states such as matter and so forth, and at the mind door by way of registration only with reference to other sense-sphere states occurring within one's own continuity, has internal objects. If occurring regarding the states of others, it has external objects. By way of both, it has internal and external objects. The same method applies to the two equanimity-accompanied resultant rootless mind-consciousness elements. However, specifically, these occur in the happy and unhappy destinations by way of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and death (cuti), regarding kamma and so forth, which are distinguished as internal and so forth.

The eight great resultant consciousnesses also have the same destination as those two [equanimity-accompanied resultant rootless mind-consciousness elements]. However, specifically, these do not occur by way of investigation. These consciousnesses occur only in the happy destinations by way of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death. The joy-accompanied rootless functional consciousness, when occurring at the five doors by way of performing an act of joy with reference to one's own matter and so forth, has internal objects. If occurring regarding the matter and so forth of others, it has external objects. At the mind door, for the Blessed One, when contemplating the functional acts performed by Himself during the times of the youth Jotipāla, King Maghadevarāja, the ascetic Kaṇha, and so forth, it occurs by way of producing a smile...
450:
...it has internal objects (ajjhattārammaṇa). At the time of occurring with reference to the performance of functional acts by such persons as Queen Mallikā, the great minister Santati, and the florist Sumana, it has external objects (bahiddhārammaṇa). By way of both, it has internal and external objects (ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇa). The equanimity-accompanied functional rootless mind-consciousness element [mind-door adverting], when occurring at the five doors by way of determining (votthabbana) and at the mind door by way of adverting (āvajjana), has internal objects and so forth. The eight great functional consciousnesses follow the same course as wholesome consciousnesses. However, specifically, those great functional consciousnesses arise for Arahants (khīṇāsava), while great wholesome consciousnesses arise for learners (sekha) and worldlings (puthujjana); this is the only difference here.

In the aforementioned manner, in the fine-material sphere fourth jhana, the five jhanas such as the universal-basis fourth jhana (sabbatthapādaka-catuttha) and so forth, find an opportunity in this triad. Indeed, these have external objects because they have the sign of a kasina concept as their object.

The 'fourth jhana of supernormal powers' (iddhividha-abhiññā) has internal objects when, by the power of the body, one directs the mind, or by the power of the mind, one directs the body, and when creating the form of a youth and so forth for oneself, because it makes one's own body and mind the object. When displaying elephants, horses, and so forth externally, it has external objects. Because of occurring sometimes internally and sometimes externally, it has internal and external objects.

The 'fourth jhana of the divine ear' (dibbasota-abhiññā) has internal objects when hearing sounds within one's own belly. When hearing the sounds of others, it has external objects. By way of both, it has internal and external objects. The 'fourth jhana of the knowledge of others' minds' (cetopariyañāṇa-abhiññā) has only external objects because it takes the minds of others as its object. There is no purpose for that knowledge in knowing one's own mind. The 'fourth jhana of the recollection of past lives' (pubbenivāsa-abhiññā) has internal objects when recollecting one's own aggregates. It has external objects because of recollecting the aggregates of others, non-sentient matter (anindriyabaddha-rūpa), and the three types of concepts. By way of both, it has internal and external objects.

The 'fourth jhana of the divine eye' (dibbacakkhu-abhiññā) has internal objects when seeing matter and so forth within one's own belly. When seeing other matter, it has external objects. By way of both, it has internal and external objects. The 'fourth jhana of the knowledge of the future' (anāgataṃsañāṇa-abhiññā) has internal objects when recollecting one's own future aggregates. When recollecting the future aggregates of others or non-sentient matter, it has external objects. By way of both, it has internal and external objects. The reason for the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) having an object that is 'not to be described' [as internal or external] has already been mentioned below.
451:
## Commentary on the Summary of the Dyads

In the Exposition of the Cluster of Roots (Hetugocchaka-niddesa), after showing the roots by way of the "three wholesome roots" etc., it is said, "they arise in the wholesome states belonging to the four planes," in order to show those same roots again by way of their place of arising. In this way, the method of teaching in the remaining clusters (gocchakas) should be understood.

In the phrase, "in which mind two or three taints (āsavas) arise together," the arising together of taints should be understood in three ways. Among those taints, the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava) arises together in two ways: with the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava) in the four minds dissociated from views (diṭṭhivippayutta), and with the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava) and the taint of ignorance in the minds associated with views (diṭṭhisampayutta). The taint of existence (bhavāsava) arises together in only one way: with the taint of ignorance in the four minds dissociated from views. Just as it is with these taints, so also in the phrase, "in which mind two or three fetters (saṃyojanas) arise together," the arising together of fetters occurs in ten ways. Among those fetters, sensual lust (kāmarāga) arises together in four ways, aversion (paṭigha) in three ways, and conceit (māna) in one way. Likewise, doubt (vicikicchā) and lust for existence (bhavarāga) each arise together in one way.

How does this occur? Firstly, sensual lust arises together in four ways: with the fetters of conceit and ignorance; with the fetters of views and ignorance; with the fetters of adherence to rites and rituals (sīlabbataparāmāsa) and ignorance; and with the fetter of ignorance alone. Aversion, however, arises together in three ways: with the fetters of envy (issā) and ignorance; with the fetters of stinginess (macchariya) and ignorance; and with the fetter of ignorance alone. Conceit arises together in only one way: with the fetters of lust for existence and ignorance. Doubt is the same; it arises in one way with the fetter of ignorance. The same method applies to lust for existence. Thus, in these fetters, two or three fetters arise together.

In the Cluster of Hindrances (Nīvaraṇagocchaka), there is the statement: "in which mind two or three hindrances arise together." There too, the arising together of hindrances should be understood in eight ways. Among those hindrances, sensual desire (kāmacchanda) arises together in two ways, ill will (byāpāda) in four ways, and restlessness (uddhacca) in one way. Doubt is the same. How does this occur? Firstly, sensual desire arises together in two ways: with the hindrances of restlessness and ignorance in unprompted (asaṅkhārika) minds; and with the hindrances of sloth and torpor (thina-middha), restlessness, and ignorance in prompted (sasaṅkhārika) minds. The statement "two or three" is said by way of the lower limit. Therefore, even four [arise] together...
452:
The word "arises" is indeed appropriate. The hindrance of ill-will (byāpāda-nīvaraṇa) arises simultaneously in four ways: in unprompted consciousness with the hindrances of restlessness (uddhacca) and ignorance (avijjā); in prompted consciousness with sloth-and-torpor (thina-middha), restlessness, and ignorance; in unprompted consciousness with restlessness, remorse (kukkucca), and ignorance; and in prompted consciousness with sloth-and-torpor, restlessness, remorse, and ignorance. The hindrance of restlessness (uddhacca-nīvaraṇa) arises simultaneously in only one way, together with the hindrance of ignorance. The hindrance of doubt (vicikicchā-nīvaraṇa) arises simultaneously in only one way, together with restlessness and ignorance.

In the Kilesagocchaka (Cluster of Defilements), where it is said, "In whatever place two or three defilements arise together," the meaning should be understood as: "Two defilements arise together with other defilements, or three defilements arise together with other defilements." Why? Because it is impossible for only two or three defilements to arise alone.

Among those defilements, the simultaneous arising of defilements (in a single thought-moment) occurs in ten ways. Among these defilements, greed (lobha) arises simultaneously in six ways. Aversion (patigha) arises in two ways. Similarly, delusion (moha) should be understood to arise in two ways. How should it be understood? Firstly, greed arises simultaneously in six ways: in unprompted consciousness dissociated from views with delusion, restlessness, shamelessness (ahirika), and fearlessness of wrongdoing (anottappa); in prompted consciousness with delusion, sloth (thina), restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing; in unprompted consciousness with delusion, conceit (māna), restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing; in prompted consciousness with delusion, conceit, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing; in unprompted consciousness associated with views with delusion, restlessness, views (diṭṭhi), shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing; and in prompted consciousness with delusion, views, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing.

Aversion (patigha) arises simultaneously in two ways: in unprompted consciousness with delusion, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing; and in prompted consciousness with delusion, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing. Delusion (moha) arises simultaneously in two ways: in consciousness associated with doubt with doubt, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing; and in consciousness associated with restlessness with restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing. The rest of the text has a clear meaning in all respects.

## In the Commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī named Atthasālinī,
## The Explanation of the Commentary Section (Aṭṭhakathā-kaṇḍa-vaṇṇanā) is finished.
## Concluding Remarks (Nigamanakathā)
453:
By this arrangement of words—

The Lord Buddha, the refuge of the three worlds, taught the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, dividing it into the delightful Cittuppāda-kaṇḍa, Rūpa-kaṇḍa, Nikkhepa-kaṇḍa, and Atthuddhāra-kaṇḍa.

I have undertaken this explanation of the meaning of that Dhammasaṅgaṇī, which encompasses all the dhammas of the Abhidhamma Piṭaka without remainder.

Because it is the source of meanings free from confusion, this explanation of the meaning has reached completion under the name Atthasālinī.

By me, completing this for the sake of the long endurance of the Dhamma, with thirty-nine bhāṇavāras of the Pali text—

Whatever merit has been attained, by the power of that merit, may all beings, having known the happiness-bringing Dhamma of the King of the True Dhamma,

Reach the supreme bliss of Nibbāna, which is free from sorrow and despair, through the pure and happy practice.

May the True Dhamma endure long; may all beings have respect for the Dhamma; may the rain-god rain properly in due season.

Just as the good and noble kings of old protected the multitude of beings, so may the King protect the multitude of beings, like his own children, in accordance with the Dhamma.

By the one adorned with supreme and pure faith, wisdom, and energy; endowed with the collection of virtues such as morality, conduct, integrity, and gentleness; capable of diving into the thickets of his own and other doctrines; possessed of the sharpness and clarity of wisdom; with unhindered power of knowledge in the Buddha's dispensation consisting of the three Piṭakas and their commentaries; a great grammarian; possessed of the charm of sweet and noble speech arising from the perfection of the vocal organs; a speaker of appropriate and liberated words; the best of speakers; a great poet; an ornament to the lineage of the Mahāvihāra monks who are lamps of the lineage of Elders (Theravaṃsa), whose wisdom is well-established in the supramundane states (uttarimanussadhamma) adorned with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) and the six higher knowledges (abhiññā); of vast and pure wisdom—Buddhaghosa,
454:
This commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaha named Atthasālinī, composed by the Elder whose name was given by his teachers.

May it remain in the world, showing the way to the purification of wisdom for sons of good family seeking deliverance from the world,

As long as even the name 'Buddha' of the Great Sage, the Chief of the World, who has a pure mind and is unshakable (tādi), continues in the world.

## The Dhammasaṅgaha-Atthakathā
## named Atthasālinī is finished.
